en: The Mānava Śrauta Sūtra: The sacrificial ground (vihāra) is prepared with the ritual movements toward the north. 1. The intermediate sacrificial acts belong to the performer. 2. Perceiving four acts at a time, one should perform them up to the fourth act. 3. One should join the beginning of an act with the end of the mantra. 4. One should know the end of the preceding [act] by means of the beginning of the subsequent one. 5. Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), acting with the right hand foremost (dakṣiṇācāraḥ), and facing east, one should perform the prescribed rites according to the Yajurveda. 6. The rules for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapaurṇamāsa) are common. 7. They are established according to specific instructions. 8. Four...

The officiating priests (ṛtvij) are the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the Agnīdhra. (9) In the absence of a specific injunction, the Adhvaryu should perform the rites. (10) When he has eaten his meal while intending to fast, he leads forward the blazing Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya fire.
(11) "O gods who know the way, find the way for the sacrifice!
By the divine Lord of the Mind, let the sacrifice be set in motion from the wind."

Having recited this, he approaches a branch for one who has undertaken the vow—either a *parṇa* branch or a *śamī* branch—that is facing east or north, belonging to trees used for vehicles, possessing many branches and many leaves, with unwithered tips and free from hollows. (12) With the words "For food, thee! (iṣe tvā), he cuts it. (13) With the words "For wool, thee! (ūrṇe tvā), he strokes it. (14) With the words "For well-being! (subhūtāya), he bends it. (15) With the words "Ye are winds! (vāyavaḥ stha), he drives away the calves with the branch—three times with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*) and three times silently. (16) Of those that have been driven away, he touches one silently with the branch. (17) Together with the branch and blades of *darbha* grass, [he says] "The god... (devo).

"May Savitṛ drive you forth," with these words he drives the cows forward. (18) "Swell up, O inviolable ones, for the gods as their portion, for Indra"—with these words [he addresses] those who sacrifice to Indra; "for Mahendra"—with these words [he addresses] those who sacrifice to Mahendra. (19) "Drinking pure waters at a good watering-place, yielding milk for Indra for a hundred autumns—may the missile of Rudra pass you by! With this verse he consecrates them as they walk away. (20) "May you remain many and firm under this lord of cattle," with this he turns back toward the house of the sacrificer.

Looking at the sacrificer, he mutters: "O Agni, protect the cattle of the sacrificer! (21) He pulls a branch with its tip pointing westward [into the fire] while standing either by the post fixed to the cart or in the fire-hall. (22) To the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, he takes up the flint-stone with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... (23) With the formula: "Thou art the seat of the cows," he pays homage to the *gārhapatya* fire. (24) With the formula: "Go through the wide atmosphere," he steps forward. (25) With the formula: "The Rakṣas is burnt away," he heats it over the *āhavanīya* fire. (26) He mutters: "This one has gone forth. (27) Having stepped forward toward the northeast, or eastward, or northward...

He approaches the sacrificial grass with the formula, "Thou art the portion of the gods, gathered around" (barhir achaiti devānām pariṣūtam asi), and he gathers the darbha blades for the prastara-bunch (darbhān prastarāya pariṣuvati). He touches a clump of darbha grass with the formula, "The tuft of Viṣṇu" (viṣṇoḥ stupa iti). He releases [the rest] to one side with the formula, "The portion of the cattle has been released" (atisṛṣṭo gavām bhāga iti). He leaves the remainder for the prastara. He mutters, "May I not be below, may I not be above; may the prastara prosper" (mādho mopari parusta ṛdhyāsam iti). With the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ" (devasya tvā savituḥ prasave iti), he cuts the forked branches into a fistful together with the fingernails. Having placed a blade of grass between [the prastara and the ground] with the formula, "Protect me from contact with the earth" (pṛthivyāḥ saṃpṛcaḥ pāhi iti), he [places] the prastara...

He places [the grains] down (35). He cuts plenty of unblemished *darbha* grass without shaking it (36). He mutters: "May I, as the cutter, not harm thee" (37). He touches the trimmed [grass] with: "From this, O sacrificial grass (*barhis*), may you grow with a hundred shoots" (38). He touches himself with: "With a thousand shoots may we grow forth" (39). With the formula, "The womb is unfallen," he applies the cord, winding it three times to the right with uneven strands (40). He strokes the cord three times in the direction of the hair with: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi" (41). [The grass should be] as cut from there, or well-prepared.

42. With the formula, "I gather thee," he gathers the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) three times into the cord. 43. With the formula, "An uninjured womb," [he gathers] the *prastara* bundle. 44. Having joined the two ends together with the formula, "O Indra, [I grasp] thy binding," he winds it around from left to right with the formula, "May Pūṣan tie thy knot. 45. With the formula, "May it not slip from thee," he draws it toward the east from behind. "O Waters, you; O Aśvins, you; the seven seers have straightened you. I take hold of the sacrificial grass, the banner of the dawns, with the rays of the sun."

Thus he begins. 46. "I lift you up with the arms of Indra," with these words he lifts it up. 47. "I carry you on the head of Bṛhaspati," with these words he places it upon his head. 48. "Go through the wide atmosphere," with these words he goes forth. 49. "I set you down on the back of Aditi," with these words he sets it down behind the western [post], or below the axle. 50. "Thou art sacrificial grass (barhis), going to the gods," with these words he places it on top. 51. With Darbha grass having roots, he binds together a fuel-stick of Palāśa, Khadira, or Rohītaka wood consisting of eighteen pieces.

The sacrificial wood for the three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) is of a tree suitable for sacrifice; of these, the middle one is the thickest, the southern one is longer, and the northern one is thinner and shortest. (52) He places the fuel (*idhma*) on top. (53)

On the new moon day when the moon is not visible, having bound together the fuel and the sacrificial grass, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña in the afternoon, moving toward the south-east. Wearing the sacred cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), having spread the sacrificial grass to the north-west of the southern fire, he sets out the vessels: the strainer, the black antelope skin, the mortar and pestle, the winnowing basket, the *udaṅkī* ladle, the *āyavanī* winnowing fan, the wooden spoon, and the wooden sword (*sphya*), placing each one to the south of the preceding one. Having ascended the southernmost post to the south, and having placed a single-strand strainer upon the *udaṅkī* ladle and filled it, he wipes the rim.

The wife husks [the grain] upon a black antelope skin, separating the husks from the grain and threshing it once. Having placed the *udakī* (water-vessel) on the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire with its opening facing north, having poured water into it over a strainer, and having added the rice grains, she cooks it until the grains remain whole, stirring it clockwise with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*). Having sprinkled the cooked rice with either unstrained clarified butter or strained fresh butter, she removes it from the fire toward the south. To the south-east of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, at a distance of three steps or in an unlimited space, [he marks the ground] with the wooden sword (*sphya*).

Having sprinkled [the water] once from above, he pours it out: "May the Asuras who have the form of Pitṛs, who wander about having assumed various forms, may Agni drive them away from this world—those who carry off *parāpuras* and *nipuras*."

Thus he leads forward the fire. Having dug up the ground in front and sprinkled it with water, he places [the fire] there. Having gathered the other [plants] together with their roots and having thrice strewn grass around the trench and the fire from left to right (apradakṣiṇa), he spreads [grass] over the dug-up earth in the trench. Having walked around [the fire], he brings each item one after another on his left side: a seat, a ladle, boiled rice, collyrium, ointment, a tuft of wool, and a water-pot. "Come, O Fathers, swift as thought; come, O Fathers, swift as thought," with these words he invokes them. He should enclose [the place] if the sun is shining.

13. With the verse, "Come hither, O Soma-loving fathers," he goes around the fire three times from right to left, sprinkling water from a water-pot. 14. With the verse, "With this station," having set down [the water] each time, he goes around three times in the opposite direction without sprinkling. 15. With the formula, "May the fathers be purified; may the grandfathers be purified; may the great-grandfathers be purified," he pours three handfuls of water at the root-end of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). 16. Having scooped up [ghee] with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), he offers it with the formula, "To Soma accompanied by the fathers, *svadhā*! Adoration! 17. To Agni... [he offers].

Having offered the second oblation in the eastern part of the southern half with the formula, "To Kavyavāhana, svadhā! Adoration! he places the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa) upon the fire along with the sacrificial grass (pavitra) and the garment-fringes (kañcuka). Having lifted the offering-ladle (darvī) from the embers, he places the rice-balls (piṇḍas) upon the fresh earth.

With the formula, "This is for you, [Name], by the name of your father; and for those who follow you here; to them, *svadhā*! he first wipes the smear on the northernmost ball with the name of the grandfather; the middle one, which is larger, with the name of the great-grandfather; and the southernmost, which is largest, with the name of the second ancestor. While pronouncing the names of two ancestors, he wipes the smear at the base of the balls. The offering of the balls is omitted for one whose father is living, or for one whose grandfather is living.

One should not give [the remainder] while a living person is present; if one should give it, one should give it to those very ones to whom the father gave it. (21) If the name of the kinsman is unknown, he should place the first *piṇḍa* with the formula: "Svadhā to the Fathers dwelling on earth"; the second with: "Svadhā to the Fathers dwelling in the intermediate space"; and the third with: "Svadhā to the Fathers dwelling in heaven. (22) Looking toward the southern direction, he mutters: "O Fathers, rejoice here with that which is the *svadhā*. (23) O Fathers who are here...

Having said, "May we live long, enjoying this [offering]," he turns back. (24) He remains seated until the sun sets, gazing at the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire. (25) When the stars have appeared and the rice balls have been consumed, he turns around, saying, "The fathers have rejoiced. (26) Having sprinkled a tuft of wool from a garment or a fringe of it, he places it on the spot where the rice balls were offered. (27) Having cut off hair from an old person, or a fringe from a garment, he should place it there with the words, "O fathers, do not deprive us of anything other than this. (28) For each rice ball, he applies a smear of collyrium, saying, "Anoint yourself, O so-and-so!"

"Rub him! Anoint him!"—with these words, he performs the anointing. (29) "May the fathers purify themselves; may the grandfathers purify themselves; may the great-grandfathers purify themselves"—saying this, he pours three handfuls of water upon each rice-ball. (30) "O fathers, bestow a fetus, a boy adorned with a lotus-wreath; O drinkers of heat, act so that there may be a male here."

Thus, the wife should eat the middle ball; the other two he should place on the fire, or a Brāhmaṇa may eat them, or he should cast them into the water. Having thrown the scrapings into the fire, he should smell the Udakumbha with the words, "O Fathers, give us a hero. Having touched water, he pays homage with the words, "Homage to you, O Fathers. Pointing to one direction with the words, "This is for you, O Fathers," he points to the other directions with the words, "These are for us. He mutters, "May you live; may we, being alive, remain here. [He concludes] with the verse, "Depart, O Soma-loving Fathers..."

He causes [the water] to flow; with the verse "O Prajāpati, there is none other than you," he stands up. With the verse "They have eaten, they have rejoiced," he returns. Muttering the *manasvatī* verses, he worships the Gārhapatya fire with the verse "O Agni, today. Having sprinkled the vessels, he carries them around two by two. This rite should be performed even by one who has not established the sacred fires.

He makes the *veda* grass-bundle with knees as high as a calf’s; having wound it to the left with tufts of grass, with the southern [end] uppermost, he places a cord upon the tufts, winds it three times, and binds it, each subsequent turn being to the right. (1) Having cut off a span’s length from the cord, he causes the roots to go to the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) and deposits those roots. (2) Having made the *veda*, he prepares the altar (*vedi*) on the previous day, prior to the northern boundary-marking of the new moon sacrifice. (3) Having stripped the leaves from the branches within the altar and having cut away the roots from the bottom, he [places] that [grass] within the altar.

He should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) four times and prepare the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick); with it, he places the potsherds upon the fire. He should cast a *darbha*-grass filter and a triple-strand rope onto the branch, letting them hang down with the fibers pointing in the direction of growth, without tying a knot. "Moving hitherward, yielding honey, bringing forth offspring, of every form for the sake of glory—becoming many as they are born, may Indra cause these cows to delight here."

7. Here, with the words "May Mahendra delight you, O cows," he consecrates the cows as they approach. 8. On that night, the sacrificer performs the Agnihotra with barley-gruel; he should set aside a lump of that [gruel]. 9. He strews sacrificial grass around the fire, first the eastern one and then the other two. 10. To the north of the Gārhapatya fire, upon the strewn grass, he places two pairs of items: two pots, a branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*), two supports (*nidāna*), a milking vessel, and a sprinkling-water ladle (*prokṣaṇī*). 11. He prepares two strainers from *barhis* grass, a span long, equal in size, with uncut edges. 12. [He prepares them] for the herb belonging to Viṣṇu.

With the words, "Ye are established," he cuts [the grass-blades]. With the words, "Ye are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu," he wipes them three times with water. Having poured water into the *sruva* ladle and having placed his hands palm-upward, taking [the blades] with the thumb and the ring finger, he purifies the waters with the verse, "May the god Savitṛ purify you," part by part. With the words, "Be cleansed," he sprinkles the vessels. Having given the two supports (*nidāna*) to the milker, he says, "Tell me when she has been let loose for milking; do not walk between the sacrificial ground and the cow once she is let loose. When [the milker] says, "I am letting her loose," [he responds]: 12. With the words, "Ye are established," he cuts [the grass-blades]. 13. With the words, "Ye are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu," he wipes them three times with water. 14. Having poured water into the *sruva* ladle and having placed his hands palm-upward, taking [the blades] with the thumb and the ring finger, he purifies the waters with the verse, "May the god Savitṛ purify you," part by part. 15. With the words, "Be cleansed," he sprinkles the vessels. 16. Having given the two supports (*nidāna*) to the milker, he says, "Tell me when she has been let loose for milking; do not walk between the sacrificial ground and the cow once she is let loose. When [the milker] says, "I am letting her loose," [he responds]:

He addresses the calf being released for nourishment with the mantra: "May I unite you with health through progeny, and with abundance of wealth, becoming manifold. He addresses the cow as she is being joined [with the calf] with: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi. When [the husband] says, "I sit down near thee," he mutters: "Swell with strength, milk, and ghee; living and causing life, may we sit near you. He takes the branch-strainer with the formula: "Thou art the purifier of the Vasus."

"You are the sky; you are the earth," [with these words] he places the fire-pan (ukhā) on the hearth. "The heat (gharma) of Mātariśvan," [with this] he sets it over the fire. He places the strainer (pavitra). Having taken hold [of the pan], he restrains his speech. In the evening he places the strainer from east to west; in the morning, crosswise. They milk the well, the four-holed jar, the cow of plenty (iḍā), the honey-sweet one, for well-being. May Indra and Agni cause that to swell, full of pleasant truth; may that establish the sacrificer in immortality.

While the *dhārāghoṣa* mantra is being recited thus, [he says] "23. Having milked, he pours it into the pot. 24. 'May Heaven and Earth together milk this sacrifice; may Dhātṛ together with Soma and Vāyu grant wealth to the sacrificer'—this he recites while the milk is being poured in. 25. 'Have you milked? he asks. 'This one,' says the other. 26. 'May she be the life of all, O so-and-so!'—thus he utters the name of the cow. 'May she be the all-encompassing' at the second milking; 'may she be the all-maker' at the third. 27. The milking is the same for all. 28. When the three have been milked, much..."

Having recited three times, "O Indra, those who [offer] the oblation to the gods," he releases his speech; or [he says], "O Mahendra, those who... Having released his speech, without touching [the cows], he silently milks the next three [cows]. When all have been milked, he mutters: "Be united, O you who possess nectar, with your wave, most full of sweetness; mingling your milk with milk, you who are delightful, for the winning of wealth."

Thus, having poured the milk from the milking vessel into the cooking pot and rinsed the vessel, he pours it back. With the formula, "I have strengthened the cows, I have strengthened the lord of the cows; may the master of the sacrifice not come to harm," he causes it to settle while making a path [for the ladle] toward the north. Once it has cooled, he mixes it with the remnant of the *agnihotra* curd, saying, "I anoint you with Soma for your portion, O Indra. He thus anoints it.

With the words "Or [they belong] to Mahendra" (34), he places a lump of barley-gruel with the formula "This for Viṣṇu" (35). With the words "O Viṣṇu, guard the oblation," he covers it from above (36). With the words "O Waters, be watchful," he seals it with a sweetmeat using either a wooden vessel or an iron vessel.

If it should be made of clay, one should place grass or wood between [the fire and the vessel]. (37) He drives away the calves for the morning milking. (38) From the secondary items onwards, the procedure is the same until the removal of the fires. (39) He cooks the sacrificial offerings on the Gārhapatya fire and offers them in the Āhavanīya fire. (40) One should not turn away from the fires; one should perform the rites without bypassing them. (41) For the purpose of a cord, the cord is wound to the right; for the purpose of a rope, the rope is twisted to the right. (42) Sprinkling, purifying, and sweeping—these are performed three times each. (43) One should perform the rites pertaining to the sacrificial ground with *darbha* grass; these are the rites pertaining to the sacrificial ground. (44) Thus ends the first chapter in the Mānava Sūtra, concerning the Soma sacrifice.

On the following day, having swept up the ground to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, he spreads [grass] over it. He spreads a continuous row of *ulapa* grass to the south of the sacrificial area (*vihāra*). A second [row] he spreads from the eastern half of the *āhavanīya* fire to the north of the sacrificial area; from the front of the *āhavanīya*, he spreads the northern [rows] with the southern [ends] facing forward. To the south of the altar, he spreads for the *brahmán*; further back, for the sacrificer; and at the western end, for the wife. From the north, he spreads toward the south.

Having washed the sacrificial strainer, the *camasa* cups, the wooden sword (*sphya*), the potsherds, the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, the winnowing basket, the black antelope skin, the *śamyā* peg, the mortar and pestle, the large and small grinding stones, the *vedā* grass-bundle, the *kuṭaru* fan, the *sruva* and *juhū* ladles, the *upabhṛt* and *dhruvā* ladles, the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel, the *iḍā* vessel, the *ājyasthālī* butter-pot, and the *saṃvapana-pātrī* mixing-vessel, he places them in pairs upon the strewn grass.

The other [spoons] are made of *kuṭaru* wood (4). The *sphya* and the *sruva* are made of *khadira* wood; the *juhū* is of *pālāśa* wood; the *upabhṛt* is of *aśvattha* wood; and the *dhruvā* is of *vikaṅkata* wood (5). Their handles are one *aratni* long from the base, their bowls are the size of a palm, they are hollowed out, have no internal ridges, are two finger-breadths deep, and four finger-breadths high. Their pouring-spouts are one span (*prādeśa*) long (6). The *sphya* is shaped like a sickle. The *śamyā* is made of *varaṇa* wood (7). Having washed his hands with the formula "For the service of you two," he brings forward the water with the *camasa* ladle.

For one desiring spiritual luster, he takes a *kāṃsya* vessel; for one desiring cattle, a *godohana* vessel; and for one desiring prosperity or stability, an earthen (*mārttika*) vessel. With the words, "Thou art made of wood," he takes the *camasa*; with "Thou art Bārhaspatya," the *kāṃsya* vessel; and with "Thou art earthly," the earthen vessel. With the words, "Be purified for the gods," he washes the *camasa*; with "Be cleansed for the gods," the *kāṃsya* vessel and the earthen vessel. To the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, upon the *pavitra*.

"Whatever of yours is wealthy, O wealthy ones; whatever of yours is fit for oblation, O you who are fit for oblation; whatever vigor and whatever manly strength you possess—of that I take a wave, rich in sweetness, acceptable for the sacrifice to the gods," with these words he fills the cup up to its brim. (11) "O divine waters," with this he consecrates the waters. (12) Having said, "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters; O sacrificer, restrain your speech," he restrains his speech. (13) "Who leads you forward? Let him lead you forward. For whom does he lead you forward? For him he leads you forward. Bṛhaspati [leads] you."

"Let him lead forward," [saying this] he leads them forward mentally. 14 Having made the wooden sword (*sphya*) the base (*upayāma*), holding it level with his breaths, he joins [the ladles] with the formula: "Who joins you? Let him join you. For whom does he join you? For him let him join you. May Bṛhaspati join you. 15 He places them to the north of the eastern one with the formula: "For all desires, for the sacrifice to the gods, you are sprinkled. 16 He spreads a layer of *ulapa* grass. 17 Having taken up the two strainers with the formula, "I place the out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer," he places them in their proper place.

Having placed the wooden sword (sphyá) and the strainers (pavitrá), he sets down the vessels with the formula: "May the divine subjects sit together. 18 He spreads a continuous line of *ulapa* grass from the western part toward the eastern part with the formula: "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; for the continuity of the sacrifice, I spread thee. 19 He takes up the wooden ladle (sruk) with the formula: "Thou art made of wood (vānaspatyā)."

With the formula, "Thou art increased by the rains," [he takes] the winnowing basket (20). With the formula, "Go through the wide atmosphere," he goes forward (21). With the formula, "The Rakṣas is burnt away," he heats [the grains] over the Āhavanīya fire (22). He pours out [the grains] to the south, behind the western Agniṣṭha post.

Having drawn the wooden sword (sphya) across the vessel, he should mutter the formulas beginning with "anoma. 23. With the formula "Thou art the yoke-pole" (dhūr asi), he touches the yoke-pole and the northern one. 24. Having stepped northward, he takes hold of the northern pole of the cart and mutters: "Thou art the best bearer of the gods. 25. With the formula "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he places his foot upon the right wheel. 26. With the formula "Thou art the unshakable oblation-holder," he mounts [the cart]. 27. With the formula "Wide space for the wind," he lowers [the cart]. 28. With the formula "With the eye of Mitra, I gaze," he looks at the sacrificial grains—either rice or barley—[placed] in the winnowing basket. 29. [He looks] at the winnowing basket.

Having placed the *sruva*-ladle on the altar and having said, "I shall pour out the sacrificial oblation into the *sruc* upon the two strainers," he pours out the oblation. For one who is away from home, he says, "O Agni... (VS 1.16). With the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... (VS 1.17), he thrice pours grains fit for the oblation into the *agnihotra-havaṇī* with his fist; the fourth time he pours silently. (30–31) In the same manner, he performs the second [pouring] for the offering to Agni and Soma at the full moon, and for the offering to Indra-Agni at the new moon for one who does not practice the *saṃnayana* rite. (32) For one who practices the *saṃnayana*, [the offerings are] to Indra-Vāyu or to Indra. According to some, [the offering is] to Mahendra. One who desires prosperity should sacrifice to Indra. (33)

For those who have performed the Soma sacrifice, Mahendra is the deity. Those who have performed the Soma sacrifice—having lost their prosperity, being of the Auruva, Gautama, or Bhāradvāja gotras—should sacrifice to Mahendra. (34) Then the others, having sacrificed to Indra for a year, and having offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati, should sacrifice to Mahendra. (35) He touches the poured-out portions with the mantra, "This belongs to the gods," and pours out the remainder from that [same vessel] with the mantra, "And this is ours together. (36) With the mantra, "May the dwellings be firm," he descends. (37) With the mantra, "Svāhā to Heaven and Earth," he mutters. (38)

"Out from the noose of Varuṇa," with these words he creeps out (39). "May I see the light of heaven," with these words he gazes at either the fire or the sun (40). "Go through the wide atmosphere," with these words he goes forward (41). "I place you in the lap of Aditi," with these words he places it behind the western [fire] (42).

Having poured [the water] into the vessel that has not been wiped clean, the purification (*utpavana*) is explained by the formulas beginning with "Purified are you by the mind of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇormanasā pūte sthaḥ*). Having purified [the water], he sprinkles the sacrificial materials (*haviṣya*) according to their respective deities, saying, "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni," while not sprinkling the rear [portion]. He places the sacrificial materials in front of the rear [fire] with the formula, "O Agni, protect the oblation" (*agne havyam rakṣasva*). He sprinkles the vessels with the formula, "Whatever of yours is impure" (*yad vo 'śuddham*). Having turned them over so they are face up, having sprinkled them, and having turned the former ones back again, he places the *sruk* ladle in a place where there is no passage, with the formula, "The skin of Aditi art thou" (*ādityās tvag asi*).

He takes a black antelope skin by the neck with the formula, "The Rakṣas is shaken off. He shakes it three times toward the north on the rubbish-heap (utkara) with the formula, "The Rakṣas is shaken off. With the formula, "Thou art the skin of Aditi," he spreads it behind the rubbish-heap, with the neck to the west and the hair upwards. He throws the tail-end toward the west. He does not let it go empty. With the formula, "Thou art the wide-hammered stone," he places the mortar. With the formula, "Thou art the tongue of Agni," he pours three handfuls of sacrificial grains into it, and a fourth time silently. With the formula, "Thou art the great-hammered stone," he takes up the pestle. [He strikes] with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).

Striking [the pestle] three times, he calls out; both the sacrificer and [the Adhvaryu] release their speech. He says, "O preparer of the oblation, come! for a Brāhmaṇa; "O preparer of the oblation, approach! for a Rājanya; and "O preparer of the oblation, come hither! for a Vaiśya. The wife pounds and grinds. The Āgnīdhra strikes together the lower and upper millstones. With the formula, "Thou art a cutter," he takes up the stone.

"Bring us nourishment," [he says] over the eastern half; "bring us strength," over the western half; "bring us increase of wealth," over the upper millstone. In this manner he pours together [the flour] nine times. (17) With the formula, "Thou art increased by rain," he pushes the winnowing basket toward the west over the husks that have been produced. (18) With the formula, "May the one increased by rain recognize thee," he pours [the grain] out. (19) With the formula, "The Rakṣas is blown away," he winnows [the grain] onto the rubbish heap. (20) With the formula, "The portion of the Rakṣases is cast forth," he throws away the husks. (21) Having thrown the husks onto the potsherds for the sacrificial cake, [he says]: "Here I strike down the Rakṣas; here I..."

Thinking, "I lead the lowest of Rākṣasas into darkness," he scatters [the husks] beneath the black antelope skin. 22. With the formula, "May Vāyu separate you for food and strength," he separates them. 23. With the formula, "Be purified for the gods," he thrice cleanses the grains. 24. From the time of taking [the mortar] onwards, the procedure for the black antelope skin is the same up to its spreading; he does not throw the buttocks [of the skin] upon it. 25. He does not let it go empty. With the formula, "Thou art the mountain-born bowl," he places the grinding stone upon the black antelope skin.

"You are the bowl; may the bowl recognize you," [with these words] he places the upper millstone upon the lower one. "You are the pillar of Aditi," [with these words] he draws the yoke-pin westward behind it, with its head pointing north. "You are grain; satisfy the gods," [with these words] he pours [the grain] over [the mortar] three times. "For out-breathing, you," [with these words] he pushes the upper stone eastward; "for in-breathing, you," [with these words] he pulls it back westward.

With the words, "For the diffusive breath (vyāna) thee," he separates [the dough] in the middle. 29. With the words, "Along the long extension," he grinds it continuously, longwise, toward the east. 30. With the words, "I look upon you with the eye of Mitra," he looks at the ground flour. 31. With the words, "May the god Savitṛ, golden-handed, receive you," he consecrates the flour as it is being poured out. 32. He gives the command, "Make it fine. 33. With the words, "Thou art bold," he takes up the fire-stirring stick (upaveṣa). 34.

1. With the words, "The Rakṣas is burnt," he places a glowing coal. 2. With the words, "Thou art firm; thou art the earth; make firm," having placed a potsherd upon that [coal] and touched it, he throws the coal and the ashes outside with the words, "O Agni, slay the fire-eating demon. 3. With the words, "O Agni, carry the place of sacrifice for the gods," he sets aside another [coal] by means of [the formula] directed toward it. 4. With the words, "Thou art the support; make firm the atmosphere," [he places a potsherd] in front; with the words, "Thou art the upholder; make firm the sky," [he places one] on the eastern half; with the words, "Thou art the law; make firm all things," [he places one] to the south of the middle; and with the words, "Thou art consciousness... [he places one].

From the rear half, he places one and a half bricks toward the north with the formula, "Thou art the surrounding one"; from the front half, one toward the south with, "Sit in all directions"; from the rear half, one toward the south with, "Surround the kinsmen for this sacrificer"; and from the front half, one and a half toward the north. (4) Thus, the laying down of the three [bricks] on the eleven-brick cake is the same. (5) On a single measure to the south of the middle one, and likewise to the north. (6) With the fourth mantra, he lays down the first of the two southern ones; with the fifth, the second of the two northern ones; and with the sixth, [the third].

The western [space] of the two southern [hearths] with the seventh [verse], the eastern [space] of the two northern [hearths] with the last [verse], and the remaining [spaces] in the *kuṣṭha* [spaces] moving clockwise; with the verse, "Of the Vasus, of the Rudras," he scatters the embers.

"May you two heat [the milk]"—this he says twice; "Heat [the flour]"—this he says once. (8) Having heated them and having placed the morning milk upon them, he causes it to be milked. (9) Having heated the vessel while it is being filled and having placed the flour into it, he pours the flour in three times with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," and silently a fourth time. (10) He restrains his speech until the covering of the dough. (11) Having set aside the flour-dust and having purified [the flour], he purifies the flour with the formula, "With the two strainers of the two tawny ones, I purify thee. (12) With the Veda as the base, he brings water from the *praṇītā* waters with the *sruva* spoon until it reaches the end.

With the words, "By means of herbs," he pours [water] over them while they are still hot. With the words, "You are born from the waters; be united with the waters," he moves them around while they are hot. With the words, "May the subjects sit down," he brings together the ground flour. With the words, "Thou art the head of Makha," he touches the dough-ball. With the words, "May Pūṣan, the all-knowing, divide you two," he divides them into two equal parts. With the words, "For Agni thee," he touches the southern sacrificial cake; the northern one according to its respective deity. With the words, "Here do I strike away the face of the attacking army," [he strikes].

With the *veda*, he removes the ashes from the potsherds (19). With the formula, "Thou art heat, for the life of all," he places [the cake] upon them; in this same manner, he performs the subsequent [actions] (20). He should perform each ritual act for both [the cakes] (21). With the formula, "Spread out widely," he spreads the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on each potsherd so that it takes the shape of a tortoise (22). With the formula, "May thy bodies be united with thy body," he wipes it around three times with a smear of flour, ensuring no part remains dry (23). Having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*) over the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire and having placed it over the *gārhapatya* fire, he purifies it.

With the formula, "The Vedas are the approach; Aditi is the girdle; O you whose wings are unbroken," he takes up the butter-pot (24). To the south of the Gārhapatya fire, over the strainers, he pours out [the flour] into the butter-pot which contains the strainers, with the formula: "You are the milk of Pṛśni; you are the swift-moving; of you, who are undecaying and swelling, I pour out that which is swelling" (25). With the formula, "The lord of booty," he carries fire around the oblations three times (26). With the formula, "May the god Savitṛ cook you," he heats it with a fire-brand, as well as the flour-smear (27). "May Agni not [injure] your body..."

With the formula "Without burning," he causes the skin to be seized with *darbha* grass. (28) He does not drive away the flames. (29) With the formula "O Agni, accept the *brahman*," he covers the embers with ash using the *veda* grass-bundle. (30) He issues the command: "Cook without burning! (31) Both the [Adhvaryu] and the sacrificer release their speech. (32)

Thereafter, he mentally measures out for the sacrificer an altar (vedi) as large as himself behind the Āhavanīya fire, so that the oblations may find room; it is narrower toward the east. 1. At the eastern half of the altar, at a distance of one-third its length, he draws three lines with the wooden sword (sphya), directed toward the northeast. 2. With the formulas, "To Ekatā svāhā! To Dvitā svāhā! To Tritā svāhā!"—pouring the flour-mixture without letting it flow together—he pours it onto the lines. 3. "This Veda has found the earth, which was hidden, placed in secret, and concealed in deep caverns."

"May he find a world for me who sacrifices; may he of abundant seed make the sacrifice flawless. With these words, he takes up the *veda* grass-bundle. "With the *veda*, they found the earth as the altar; that earth spread out for all that is earthly. She bears the germ within the worlds; from there, the sacrifice is extended at all times."

Thus, with the Veda, he wipes the altar three times toward the east. To the north of the Gārhapatya fire, [he takes up] the wooden sword (sphya) with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... He strokes it along with a plant, saying: "Thou art the arm of Indra."

He does not touch the tip [of the *sphya*]. 7. To the north of the lines, the Āgnīdhra sits down at the *utkara*, having made a hollow for his hands at a distance of one step. 8. With the formula, "Thou art the armor of the earth," he places a blade of grass crosswise at the edge of the line. 9. With the formula, "O Earth, place of sacrifice to the gods," he cuts it crosswise with the *sphya*. 10. With the formula, "Go to the fold, the cow-pen," he throws the blades of grass together with the earth into the *pām̐sūnāṃ pada* (the footprint of the dust). 11. With the formula, "May Parjanya rain for thee," he looks at the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) and the sacrificer. 12. With the formula, "Bind [it], O God Savitṛ," [he places it] in the hollow for his hands.

He scatters [the grains]: (13) the second with "May the auspicious plants not [harm] you," the third with "The drop... The rest is the same; the fourth is done silently. (14) With the wooden sword (*sphya*), he encloses the altar (*vedi*): on the south with "May the Vasus enclose you," on the west with "May the Rudras [enclose] you," and on the north with "May the Ādityas [enclose] you. (15) With "Unbarred from the earth," he digs two or four finger-breadths deep. (16) From the excavated spot, the Āgnīdhra carries away [the earth] three times. (17) "Under the impulse of the god Savitṛ, men performing the work..."

"Do not harm these auspicious plants. With this, he cuts the roots with the wooden sword (*sphya*). He carries them away together with the grass. "O men, prepare this altar; let it be dear to the gods in the lap of Aditi.
All the gods have delighted in this; may they enter the sacrificer for the increase of wealth."
Thus he prepares the middle [part of the altar], making it slightly depressed, sloping toward the northeast, smooth, well-constructed, and even; thereon he places the Āhavanīya fire.

He takes hold of the Gārhapatya fire-pit with his two hips for one who desires cattle, filling it with loose soil from the outside. He washes the wooden sword (sphyá), not touching its tip. Having sprinkled the altar (vedí) and addressed the Brahman priest, he performs the second tracing around (parigrahá): with "Thou art the seat of truth" on the south, with "Thou art the seat of the cosmic order" on the west, and with "Thou art the seat of the heat" on the north. With the formula "Before the cruel [deed]," he rubs the altar westward with the wooden sword, creating a furrow. On the western half of the altar, at a distance of one-third, he places the wooden sword crosswise.

Having steadied [the wooden sword], he gives the instructions: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; wipe the offering-spoons; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter. (23) He pours out the sprinkling waters with his right hand, pours some over the tip [of the grass], and lifts up the wooden sword. (24) He places it on the path and fills the sprinkling waters. (25) Saying, "Thou art the slayer of the hater," he, facing westward, strikes the mound of earth with the wooden sword from the front. (26) Having sprinkled it, he sets it down again. (27) To the north.

He should place the fuel and the sacrificial grass for the Āhavanīya fire; the fuel to the south and the sacrificial grass to the north. He cleanses the *sruva* ladle, the *sruk* ladles, and the vessel for the *prāśitra* portion.

"Scorched is the Rakṣas," he says, as he heats the vessels over the Āhavanīya fire. Having divided or not divided the clippings of the Veda, he wipes the spoons crosswise: the tips with the tips and the handles with the roots; having sprinkled them with water, he heats them in the fire. "Thou art the ladle, unassailable, overcoming rivals"—with these words he takes up the *sruva* spoon. "Do not wipe away my life and breath"—with these words he wipes it, just as he does the *juhū* and the *prāśitraharaṇa*. "Thou art the *juhū*, unassailable, overcoming rivals"—with these words he takes up the *juhū* spoon.

"May the eye and the ear not wipe me off"—saying this, he cleanses [the *darvī*] inwardly from the east and outwardly from the west. "Thou art the *upabhṛt*, unassailable, overcoming rivals"—saying this, he takes up the *upabhṛt*. "May speech and the cattle not wipe me off"—saying this, he cleanses it inwardly from the west and outwardly from the east. "Thou art the *dhruvā*, unassailable, overcoming rivals"—saying this, he takes up the *dhruvā*.

"Lest they wipe away the sacrifice and the progeny," [he says]; thus he wipes it all around toward the east. "The Prāśitra-vessel, unassailable, overcoming rivals"—with these words he takes up the Prāśitra-vessel. "Lest I should erase the color from its form; O vigorous one, I cleanse thee, the overcomer of rivals"—with these words he cleanses it. "The craft of heaven is spread abroad, resting upon the peaks of the earth. With that which has a thousand joints, we cause our enemy to burn. May those who hate us suffer much torment."

Having thus discarded the brooms and rinsed them, he places them on the fire. He sets down the cleansed ladles, turned upward, in their respective places. He gives the command: "O wife, perform the worship of the wife’s place. [The Adhvaryu says: "O wife, this is your place; homage be unto you; do not harm me," and from the south, behind the western [post], he causes her to stand in the wife’s place. [The Adhvaryu says: "O Agni, lord of the house, call upon me; O wives of the gods, call upon me."

"Like Aditi with her sons, may this secret doctrine (upanishad) be for you, O Indra-like woman, as is a non-widowed wife. With these words she sits down, stretching out her knees. "Desiring goodwill, offspring, prosperity, and fortune, being devoted to the service of Agni, I gird myself for the sake of good deeds."

Having thus bound the wife with the girdle beneath her garment, and having touched water, she gazes at the clarified butter while the Veda and the supporting vessel are present, saying: "With an unerring eye, I gaze upon thee. (12) Saying, "Thou art splendor," she places the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire. (13) Saying, "Thou art splendor; follow after splendor; may Vāyu protect thee from the atmosphere, and Sūrya from heaven," she carries it toward the Āhavanīya fire. (14) Saying, "May Agni not take away thy splendor," she places it over the Āhavanīya fire. (15) With the verse, "Over this Viṣṇu strode," [she sprinkles] to the north of the *prokṣaṇī* waters.

He places the Veda [down]. With the formula, "Thou art splendor," the sacrificer gazes at the clarified butter, whether it has been purified or not. With the verse, "May the god Savitṛ purify thee," he purifies the clarified butter step by step (verse by verse).

With the formula, "May Savitṛ the god [purify] you," he sprinkles the *prokṣaṇī* waters (18). With the formula, "Thou art the abode," he takes the clarified butter with the *sruva*-ladle: four times into the *juhū*, eight times into the *upabhṛt*, less than that into the *dhruvā*, and most of it into the *dhruvā* (19). He places the *ājyasthālī*, the *sruva*-ladle, and the *veda* at the edge of the *gārhapatya* fire (20). Taking a handful of *darbha* grass, having thrown half of it to the south of the altar, he causes the *prokṣaṇī* waters to flow forth with the formula, "O divine waters" (21). Having taken up the *prokṣaṇī* waters, they mark the footprints on the altar (22). These markings are for the *utkara*.

Having sprinkled water around [the fire] and touched it, having placed fuel on [the fire], having taken up the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and having addressed the Brahman priest, he sprinkles the fuel with [the formula]: "Thou art black, dwelling in the mountain"; the altar (*vedi*) with [the formula]: "Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), thee!"; and the sacrificial grass with [the formula]: "Thou art the sacrificial grass; for the altar, thee! (23). Having sprinkled them, he places the sacrificial grass at the rear part of the altar, at a distance of one-third [of its length]. (24). He places the knot toward the east. (25). He causes the tips [of the grass] to drink from the sprinkling waters. (26). With [the formula]: "Svāhā to the fathers who drink the Gharma," he [places the grass] to the right around the base of the sacrificial grass.

He pours out the sprinkling waters (27). Having lifted up the offering-ladle and taken it, and having gone around to the south with the two strainers, he unties the knot of the sacrificial grass (barhis) with the formula: "May Pūṣan untie your knot" (28).

With the formula, "Thou art the tuft of Viṣṇu," he takes up the *prastara* (grass-bundle). With the formula, "I place the out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer," he releases the two *pavitra* strainers upon the *prastara*. Having carried the *prastara* around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he hands it over either to the Brahman priest or to the sacrificer. With the formula, "Thou art prosperity; for prosperity I take thee; I seize thee, full of wealth and full of prosperity," he seizes the *prastara* by its front end. He should not wipe it upward, nor wipe it downward, nor shake it; if it should touch [anything], he should grasp it [there]. Let the cord be loosened.

Having gathered the *darbha* grass together, he spreads it upon the southern half of the altar. With the formula, "Spread yourself wide," he covers the altar, spreading it from the back toward the front, thickly and without gaps. Having walked around the back of the altar while holding the *prastara* bundle, he lays the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) around it: with the formula, "Thou art the Gandharva," he places the middle one; with "Thou art the arm of Indra," the southern one; and with "Thee, O Mitra and Varuṇa," the northern one. Without changing their positions, he joins them together, making the southern junction of the enclosing sticks the most firmly joined. Then, taking fuel-sticks and wood...

With the verse, "The eternal Hotṛ, thee... he places the Āghāra fuel-stick; with "In the highest heaven... he places the second one. With "Sūrya, with his rays... he encloses the fire-altar from the east for the sake of the Āditya. With "Ye two are the separators of all people," he lays down two blades of grass crosswise, at a distance of four finger-breadths from each other. With "Of the Vasus, of the Rudras... he places the *prastara* (handful of grass) upon the two separating blades. With "Thou art the sky by birth," he places the *juhū* ladle on the *prastara*. He does not let it go empty.

He makes the staff equal in height to the roots [of the ladles]. With the formula, "Thou art the atmosphere by birth," he places the *upabhṛt* below the two *vidhṛtis*; with the formula, "Thou art the earth by birth," he places the *dhruvā* above the two *vidhṛtis*. He sets down the ladles so that they do not touch one another, arranged in order, with the *juhū* placed closest [to him]. With the formula, "Here I drive away the face of the attacking army," he sweeps away the ashes from the two *puroḍāśas* with the *veda*. The *veda* is the support; with the *sruva* from the *ājya-sthālī*, [he recites]: "May Agni, whose womb is ghee, swell; may he accept our oblations."

"Be patient; touch [the skin]; may you be well-formed, the finder of wealth. With the splendor of cattle, I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni"—with these words he sprinkles the cake for Agni; the subsequent one he sprinkles according to its respective deity. (18) "I prepare a pleasant seat for you; with a stream of clarified butter I fashion it as a comfortable resting place"—with these words he spreads a base in the pan. (19) "Moist, broad-nosed, the guardian of the world, the cooked one, the progenitor of thoughts—may he emerge."

Thus he carries [the rice] upward. With the Veda-grass, he removes the ashes from it, without striking it with his hand or with the top of the Veda-grass. He places it upon the fine layer [of grass], saying: "Sit down in this nectar; be established, being well-disposed, as the essence of the rice grains."

"Of barley, the essence"—thus [he says] regarding the barley. "May the nourishment, the prosperity, the sap of the earth not depart"—with these words he pours clarified butter over the first potsherd that has been placed down. "Thou art satisfaction; the Gāyatrī metre—satisfy me with splendor and Vedic luster. Thou art satisfaction; the Triṣṭubh metre—satisfy me with sensory power and vigor. Thou art satisfaction; the Jagatī metre—satisfy me with offspring and cattle. Thus he adorns it, having anointed it well, without removing the scrapings, without letting drops fall, and without turning it over, and he anoints it from below as well.

That Self of yours which has entered into the cattle, or which surveys from above the heights of heaven—O Soma, come hither, endowed with the self and with clarity; go to heaven, find the light for me, the sacrificer.

Thus he adorns the *dohā* (25). He offers the oblations (26). With the formula, "Thou art the bull, belonging to the Śakvarī verses," he places the full *sruva* ladle to the south of the *juhū*; in front of the *dhruvā*, the *veda*; to the north of the *dhruvā*, the butter-pot; behind the handles of the *sruk*s, the *pātrī*; the evening milking on the southern corner of the altar, and the morning milking on the northern corner (27). He strews grass upon the altar without covering the edges (28). Behind the *hotṛ*, he spreads a three-layered mat with its tufts pointing southward, in the middle (29). Having touched water, he touches the clarified butters with the formula, "The *dhruvās* have sat down" (30). He touches them again.

Thus ends the second chapter in the Mānava Sūtra concerning the rites prior to the Soma sacrifice. When the Hotṛ priest has taken his place, [the Adhvaryu], having said, "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled," places a fuel-stick upon the fire at each *praṇava* (syllable *om*). Having set aside that stick intended for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), he does not allow it to remain in excess of the faggot (*idhma*). He unties the binding-cord of the faggot, loosens its single knot, and uses it to sweep the fire. Once the deities have been invoked, he touches water and thrice fans the fire with the Veda-grass-bundle, sweeping from the front of the altar. Having poured the full *sruva*-ladle into the *dhruvā* vessel and having dipped the Veda-grass-bundle into it, he uses it as a support to place the *upayāma* beneath the northern junction of the enclosing sticks.

Having touched the northern half of the fire that has been kindled, he makes an offering into the flame with his mind, saying: "To Prajāpati, svāhā! (5). Having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle with the residue, he places the *sruva* and the *veda* in their respective places. (6). He gives the command: "O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire three times each. (7). The Āgnīdhra, having taken up the cleansing brush and the wooden sword (*sphya*), cleanses them three times each, following the direction of the grain along the enclosing sticks. (8). [He recites: "O Agni, for thee who art about to run the race, who art about to win the prize, for the gods..."

"I cleanse you, the vigorous one, who are about to carry the oblation, for the winning of the prize; O Agni, win the prize!"—saying this, while throwing the fire [into the pan] with the wooden sword (*sphya*), he wipes it thoroughly three times. (9) He removes it. (10) Having placed his two hands palm-upward, he mutters over the tips of the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles: "May they be well-yoked for me today. (11) "O *juhū*, come! Agni calls you; we shall sacrifice to the gods for the sake of the divine worship"—saying this, he takes up the *juhū* ladle.

"Come, O Upabhṛt; the god Savitṛ calls you; we two shall sacrifice to the gods for the sake of the sacrifice to the gods"—having thus taken hold of the Upabhṛt ladle, he steps across to the south with both ladles, saying, "O Agni and Viṣṇu, make way. He places his left foot so as to touch [the ground] within the altar, and his right foot [within the altar].

He mutters, "Thou art the station of Viṣṇu. (14) Having touched the southern junction of the enclosing sticks, he pours the Āghāra libation—continuous, directed eastward, long, straight, upward, and unbroken—over the southern half of the fire that has been kindled, with the mantra, "Upright is the sacrifice. (15) He offers the majority of the butter-oblations, leaving a remainder for the Prayāja offerings. (16) Having poured the Āghāra, he breathes out over it. (17) "O Agni, protect me from evil conduct; lead me to good conduct."

Thus, without touching [the *dhruvā*], he steps across with the *sruva*. (18) With the mantra, "The light with the light," he anoints the *dhruvā* three times with the *juhū*. He causes the *dhruvā* to swell by means of the *juhū*. (19) He places the two ladles in their respective positions. (20) With the mantra, "Brought up for wealth," he draws [ghee] from the *dhruvā* using the *sruva*.

21. With the formula, "To Suvīra, svāhā! he causes the *juhū* ladle to swell. 22. With the formula, "The breath is connected with the breath," he places the *sruva* spoon upon the *dhruvā* ladle. 23. Taking a fuel-stick and a splinter, he stands [ready]. 24. Having drawn his right foot forward and having lifted a blade of sacrificial grass so as to be continuous [with the other blades], and having said, "O Brahman, I shall cause the announcement for the *pravara* selection," he causes the announcement to be made with the words, "O Śrauṣaṭ! 25. The *āgnīdhra*, holding the *sphya* and the means of cleansing in his hands, standing behind the *utkara* mound and facing upward, responds with the words, "Let there be *śrauṣaṭ*. When the response has been given...

"Agni, the god, the divine Hotṛ, shall sacrifice to the gods—he who is wise and discerning—as did Manu, as did Bharata, as did so-and-so, as did so-and-so. Thus he chooses the ancestral ṛṣis of the sacrificer, one, two, three, or five. He mutters: "May he bring [the gods] accompanied by the Brahman; may the Brāhmaṇas be the protectors of this sacrifice."

If he is separated from his *hotṛ*, having uttered the name of that [priest] with the formula "O Upāṃśu," he should call out "O human" loudly. (26) He throws a splinter of wood into the fire. (27) If one who is not a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, he should choose the *pravara* (ancestral lineage) of his domestic priest (*purohita*). (28) He should place the *juhū* spoon in front of the *upabhṛt* and lift it up. (29) With his right hand he steps across to the south, and with his left hand to the north. (30) Sitting between the joints of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he offers on the northern side with the *svāhā* formula; standing upright on the southern side facing northeast, he offers with the *vaṣaṭ* formula. (31)

Having caused [the announcement] to be heard, he should not move until the *āhuti* is offered (32). At each *vaṣaṭ*-call, or when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers equally (33). He proceeds with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings in a low tone, with a medium tone for the *anuyāja*s, and with the highest tone for the *śaṃyor* formula (34).

When the verse "ghṛtavatī adhvaryo" is being recited, he takes up the two offering-ladles (srucau) and steps across to the south. Stepping forward while calling for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he performs five *prayāja* offerings. He says, "Sacrifice to the *samidhs*" for the first, and "Sacrifice, sacrifice! for the subsequent ones. Having performed with three [verses], he pours from the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *juhū* and offers them together in one place. Having stepped across, he sprinkles the *dhruvā* ladle, the southern *puroḍāśa*, the *dhruvā* again, the northern *puroḍāśa* following the *upāṃśuyāja*, the evening milk, the morning milk, and finally the *upabhṛt*.

He cuts the portions with the *sruva* spoon four times for others, but five times for a descendant of Jamadagni; having addressed him as a descendant of Jamadagni, he should perform the five-fold cutting. He offers the two *ājyabhāga* oblations: the one for Agni in the northern half and the one for Soma in the southern half, making them equal and not across the diagonal. Having taken a portion from the *dhruva* ladle, [he recites]: "May the *dhruva* be replenished with ghee for every sacrifice for those seeking the gods. Be a well from the udder of Sūryā, from the lap of Aditi; be a milch-cow for the sacrificer."

Having thus cut off [the portions] repeatedly from the *ājya-sthālī*, he causes the *dhruvā* ladle to swell. (7) He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) with the words, "Recite for Agni" (*agnaye 'nubrūhi*). (8) Having joined the end of the *anuvākyā* with the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), he causes [the Āgnīdhra] to call for the *śrauṣaṭ*. (9) When the response has been given, he issues the direction, "Sacrifice to Agni" (*agnim yaja*). (10) In this same manner, he proceeds with the offering to Soma. (11) Having spread a base of clarified butter (*upastīrya*) and touched water, [he takes a portion] from the middle of the southern [cake], saying: "Do not fear; do not tremble; may I not harm you. We take you up as an offering. You are the portions being cut out; I shall cut you out in return. Homage be to you; do not harm me."

Holding it with his two hands, he cuts off portions the size of a thumb-joint with his fingers and thumbs: the first from the middle and the front half, the second from the rear half, and the third if it is a five-fold portion. Having sprinkled the cut-off portions with clarified butter, [he recites]: "Whatever I have done contrary to the proper order while cutting your portions for myself, I counteract that with clarified butter; may it swell again."

Thus he pours clarified butter over the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). (13) He causes the invitatory verse to be recited with the words, "Recite for Agni. (14) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he gives the direction, "Sacrifice to Agni. (15) Between the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, he causes the oblations to flow out toward the north-east. (16) Having taken a portion from the *dhruva* ladle, he offers the *upām̐śuyāja*; at the full moon sacrifice, it is dedicated to Agni-Soma, and at the new moon sacrifice, it is dedicated to Viṣṇu; thus he designates the deities for the *upām̐śu* offering. (17) Having similarly taken a portion from the northern [ladle], he proceeds according to the respective deity. (18) For one who performs the *saṃnayana* rite, having spread an under-layer of butter, he takes the portions together according to the prescribed manner.

He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse for Indra with the words, "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra," or for Mahendra with the words, "Recite the invitatory verse for Mahendra. He should offer the *puroḍāśa* and the two milk-offerings (*dohas*) by the side; the liquid offerings he offers by pouring them out. The procedure for the performance has been explained. "O Full Moon, we invoke the bull, the vigorous one; may he yield us abundance of wealth, thousandfold, accompanied by heroic sons. With the formula, "To the Full Moon, the bountiful, Svāhā! he makes an offering with the *sruva*-ladle on the day of the full moon.

The new moon is fortunate and very gracious; like a cow, it swells again and again. May she milk for us abundance of heroes and thousandfold increase of wealth. "To the new moon, the bounteous one, Svāhā!"—thus he says at the new moon. For the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he cuts twice as much from the northern half as was previously cut.

Or twice, if [the portion] of the five-fold cutting has not been cut; having sprinkled it twice with clarified butter, he does not sprinkle the oblations (havīṃṣi) beyond this point. He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) with the words, "Recite for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he issues the command, "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. He offers [the oblation] without letting [the ladle] touch [the previous one], in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire]. Having stepped across, he places the two ladles in their respective positions.

Having arranged the *prāśitraharaṇa* behind the junction of the two northern enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he places it upon the sprinkled ground after spreading the sacrificial herbs. Into that vessel he cuts the *prāśitra* portion from the middle of the southern cake, taking a thumb-sized piece with his thumb and ring finger, and then pours clarified butter over it. Having heated the *iḍā*-vessel, he spreads a base of butter in it and cuts portions for the *iḍā* twice each time, making the portions for the deities larger. He cuts the portions for the *bhakṣas* from the southern cake. Having cut from the southern half of the southern cake, he cuts the sacrificer’s portion from the eastern half, making it small.

Having spread the long smear of clarified butter upon the *vedī*, he places it down. Having cut the second portion of the *iḍā* from the middle and other parts without breaking it, and having taken portions from the *dhruvā* vessel, he takes portions from the others in successive order. Having sprinkled the *iḍā* with clarified butter, sitting facing west, he hands it to the *hotṛ*. The *adhvaryu* passes between the *hotṛ* and the *iḍā*, moving toward the south. The *hotṛ* takes hold of it without letting go; he anoints the two finger-joints of the *hotṛ*—first the inner one, then the outer one. He spreads a double-layered smear upon the hand of the *hotṛ*. The *hotṛ* [takes] the portion.

He cooks it. Having spread a layer of ointment [on the sacrificial grass], he takes another portion from that same [substance] and pours a double-layered stream of ointment over it. When the [portion] is being invited, the officiating priests and the sacrificer touch it from behind. Once invited, he cuts off portions separately into his two hands and offers them to the Āgnīdhra. He then issues the command.

He should say, "Those that are on the north, bring them around to the south," or "Those that are on the south, bring them around to the north. (14) The officiating priests and the sacrificer eat the portion that has been invoked. (15) The Hotṛ eats first, saying: "I eat thee by the gift of the earth; I eat thee by the gift of the atmosphere; I eat thee by the gift of the sky; I eat thee by the gift of the quarters. (16) Having placed the branch-strainer, which is spread out, into the Agnihotra-ladle, the Hotṛ [places it] within the altar.

He places it down. 17. There, reciting the *apohiṣṭhīya* verses, they sprinkle themselves for purification (*mārjana*). 18. Having cut off the largest portion from the sacrificer’s share as the *brahmabhāga*, and having poured the remnants of the clarified butter over it, he places it on the *vedī*. 19. Having made the southern end four-cornered, he sets it down upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). 20. Having touched it, he places it in a vessel. 21. Having carried the *prāśitra-haraṇa* around the front of the *āhavanīya* fire, he hands it to the *brahman*. 22. Having carried the two portions around with the *veda*-broom, he hands them to the *brahman* and to the sacrificer. 23.

Having carried it around, he places the Veda in its proper place. 24. Having poured clarified butter over the large boiled rice cooked in a vessel with a southern handle, he causes it to be removed towards the north behind the handles of the offering-spoons; likewise the two milk-pails and the mixing-bowl. 25.

Having taken the *anuyājika* fuel-stick, he gives the command: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Āgnīdh, having placed the fuel-stick, cleanse the enclosing-sticks and the fire once each. The Āgnīdhra, having grasped the cleansing-broom and the wooden sword (*sphya*), cleanses them once each in the direction of the grain following the order of the enclosing-sticks, saying: "I cleanse thee, O Agni, who hast run the race, who hast won the prize, who hast offered the oblation to the gods, the vigorous one, the winner of booty—O Agni, I cleanse thee for the sake of winning booty. [He cleanses] the fire with the verse: "Thou who art of the gods..."

"O Śreṣṭha, Ugra, Tanticara, Vṛṣan! Be gracious to us, O Rudra; let that which has been offered to you be yours. Svāhā! Having thus sprinkled the *saṃmārga* grass with water, he throws it into the fire. Then, having brought the butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he performs three *anuyāja* offerings.

"Offer to the gods!"—with this he offers the first oblation; "Sacrifice, sacrifice!"—with these words he offers the two subsequent ones. He offers the *samidh* oblations toward the west. With the last formula, from the rear half [of the altar], he joins the two spoons together while facing eastward. Having stepped across, he places the two spoons in their respective positions. The sacrificer, with the formula "By the impulse of strength," takes up the *juhū* spoon along with the *prastara* grass-bundle with his right hand, palm upward; then, with the formula "Indra [drives] my rivals away," he holds down the *upabhṛt* spoon with his left hand, palm downward. With the formula "The lifting and the pressing down," he separates them. Then, with the formula "Indra and Agni [drive] my rivals away..."

With the word "ma," he moves the *juhū* ladle eastward from the *prastara* bundle and the *upabhṛt* ladle westward; he throws them outside the altar. Having sprinkled them with water, he sets them down again, but not the *juhū* upon the *prastara*. He anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the *juhū*: with "Thou art Vasu," the middle one; with "Thou art Upavasu," the southern one; with "Thou art Viśvāvasu," the northern one. Having joined the tip of the *sruk* ladle to the middle stick and having placed the tips of the *prastara* against the handles of the ladles, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*. When the response has been heard, [he says] "The divine Hotṛ-priests have been impelled; may auspicious speech be uttered."

The human [priest] is sent forth for the *sūktavāka* with the command, "Recite the *sūkta*s. (12) He takes up the *prastara* [grass-bundle]. (13) Saying, "I place the out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer," he places the two *vidhṛti*s upon the *barhis* grass; saying, "For support (*āyuṣ*), thee," he mixes a blade of grass [with them]. (14) With the formula, "Licking with the waters, may they go forth with vigor," he anoints the *prastara* in the offering-ladles: the tips in the *juhū*, the middles in the *upabhṛt*, and the roots in the *dhruvā*. (15) Having silently anointed the tips in the *juhū*, [he anoints] the [middle and root parts] in the *vaśā*.

Saying, "Having become *pṛśni*," he sets fire to the tips of the *prastara* without moving them aside. 16. While [the Adhvaryu] says, "This sacrificer prays for...", he throws the *prastara* along with the branch into the fire. 17. He gives the command, "O Āgnīdhra, cause it to go! 18. The Āgnīdhra causes the *prastara* to go three times by means of his hand. 19. He says, "Throw it after [the other offerings]; speak together! 20. Then, saying, "Protect us with rain," he throws a blade of grass into the fire. 21. Saying, "Thou art the foundation," he touches the earth. 22. "Yama has given sight back again; Agni has given it back; Bhaga has given it back."

"O Aśvins, restore sight once more to my two eyes. With these words, he touches his eyes. (23) Having touched water and taken hold of the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), he says, "O Āgnīdhra, come forward! The Āgnīdhra replies, "I have come. The Adhvaryu says, "Make the announcement! The Āgnīdhra replies, "Śrauṣaṭ! (24) He gives the command: "Go happily to the divine Hotṛs; may there be well-being for the human ones; recite the *śamyor* [formula]! (25) While the verse "We choose that *śamyor*" is being recited, he takes both the middle and the southern [enclosing-sticks].

"O divine Agni, that enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) which you placed around yourself while being chosen by the *paṇis*, that very one I bring back to you according to your pleasure, so that it may not be alienated from you. Having said, "Come together for the path of the sacrifice," he draws [the stick] out obliquely from beneath the *prastara* bundle. (26) Having placed the tip of the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *juhū*, he makes an offering over the enclosing-sticks with the formula, "Those who have a share in the remnants of the pouring. (27) With the formula, "You two are the butter-smeared ones; you are the two leaders of the sacrificer; protect [us]," he releases the two ladles upon the two ends of the altar.

Either in the *kastamba* region or wherever he has joined [the ladles], from there he releases them, saying, "I release. (28) He does not set them down until the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been released. (29) Taking the *sruva* and the *juhū* ladles, the Adhvaryu steps back; the Hotṛ takes a blade of grass from the sacrificial grass and the *veda*; the Āgnīdhra takes the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) and places it behind the Gārhapatya fire on a blade of grass with its tip pointing eastward. (30) The Adhvaryu steps back between the Hotṛ and the fire. (31) The Hotṛ, seated in the middle, performs the *saṃyāga* sacrifice for the wives with a low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśu*). (32)

He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words, "The approach for the Soma; recite the offering prayer for Soma. He performs the sacrifice to Soma in the northern half [of the altar] and to Tvaṣṭṛ in the southern half. Having enclosed [the space], he sacrifices to the wives of the gods starting from the Āhavanīya fire. Before the wives of the gods, one who desires cattle should sacrifice to Sinīvālī; after them, one who desires heroes should sacrifice to Rākā; and one who desires stability should sacrifice to Kuhū. With the mantra, "May the wife go with her husband to their good deeds," he makes the wife take hold [of the ladle] and offers an oblation with the *sruva* spoon. Then, having removed the enclosure, [he addresses] the fire.

He offers to the Gṛhapati in the place of the Sviṣṭakṛt. Having cut off portions ten times, while not releasing the Hotṛ, he anoints the two finger-joints of the Hotṛ—the outer one first, then the inner one. He spreads a base of butter twice upon the Hotṛ’s hand. The Hotṛ causes the portion to be offered.

Having spread a layer of the flour-leavings from that [grain] and another from the other [grain], he sprinkles them twice with clarified butter. (9) While the [Sarasvatī offering] is being invoked, the wife and the Āgnīdhra touch it from behind. (10) Once it has been invoked, the Hotṛ and the Āgnīdhra eat it. (11) Having placed the wood-shavings from the faggot onto the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, having poured the *phalīkaraṇa* grains into four-drawn clarified butter, he offers with the verse: "O Sarasvatī, who brings people together... (12) Having drawn [butter] into that same ladle again, having taken a double portion of the flour-leavings and sprinkled it with butter, [he offers it] over the mortar, the pestle, the potsherds, the millstone, and the grinding stone.

He shall hold it [with the formula]: "I join together the drops and the sprays; may all the gods enjoy this oblation, svāhā! (13) Having wiped with the *veda* and having taken a portion of the clarified butter, he offers for one who desires a village [with the formula]: "O Indra, make the dwellings of our kinsmen free from distress and full of joy; make our kinsmen well-disposed, svāhā! (14) He hands the *veda* to the wife.

"Thou art the Veda; bring me the Veda," he mutters. 15. "I am satisfied, thou art satisfied," with these words he accepts [the gift]. One desiring a son should place it in her lap. 16. "I loosen this noose of Varuṇa, which Savitṛ, whose laws are true, and Dhātṛ have fastened; may he establish me, unharmed, together with my husband, in the womb of the Creator and in the world of good deeds. Having thus loosened the noose of the cord, she forms a hollowed cup (añjali) with the cord still attached. 17. "Be united with long life, be united with offspring, and again, O Agni, be united with splendor!"

"May I go together with my husband as a wife; may my self be united with my body. Having thus poured out a handful of water and wiped his face, (18) the Hotṛ spreads the Veda-grass continuously from the Gārhapatya fire up to the Āhavanīya fire. (19) With the formula "And thou art the unswerving one, O Agni," he offers once a portion from the Dhruvā ladle. (20) Having replenished the Dhruvā once and taken a handful of Darbha grass from the sacrificial grass while standing upright within the altar, he offers the Samiṣṭayajus continuously with the Dhruvā, reciting the mantra until its conclusion: "O gods, you who know the way..."

Before the completion [of the rite] and before the utterance of *svāhā*, he throws the handful of *darbha* grass after [the vessel]. (21) With the verse, "The potsherds which were on the cauldron," he releases the potsherds. (22) Having counted them, he carries them away toward the north; with the two verses, "Those which were on the cauldron" and "What was on the cauldron. (23) With the verse, "Who shall release you?", he mentally releases the *praṇītā* water, carries it around the front of the *āhavanīya* fire, and places it within the altar with the formula, "For prosperity, thee! (24) With the verse, "In heaven the craft is spread out," he throws the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) after [the other materials]. (25) "Spread the sacrificial grass, enclose the altar, [avoid] kinship..."

"Let them not sit nor lie down; strew the altar with green, well-feathered *darbha* grass, for these are the golden ornaments of the sacrificer. With this, he covers the altar with the seats of the *hotṛ*. (26) He issues the command: "Satisfy the Brahmins! (27) Having concluded the Full Moon sacrifice, one who has rivals should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vaimṛdha; in that case, he should give as he pleases. (28) There is an option regarding the commencement [of the rite], but once begun, one should not desist. (29) One who desires cattle, having performed the New Moon sacrifice, should offer a pap of rice in ghee to Aditi. (30) One who desires cattle, one who desires cattle.

Thus ends the third chapter in the Mānava Sūtra, concerning the rites prior to the Soma sacrifice. When the moon is full, one should fast on the full-moon day; when it is not seen, one should fast on the new-moon day. Or else, on the preceding day, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved: he has the hair shaved starting from the right side and the nails trimmed starting from the left, beginning with the little fingers of the hands, but not the armpits. The wife also has her nails trimmed. [He recites: "The plants are full of sap; the sap of the creepers is full of sap. With that sap which is the sap of waters, O Indra, unite me."

Having thus washed their hands, they should eat their meal, provided it contains clarified butter, but not beans or meat. Having eaten on the full moon day, they should not eat to satiety on the new moon day. Standing facing east and looking westward, he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra "O Agni, [grant] me splendor," and silently places two more on the other two fires. Having washed his hands, he enters upon the vow from the south, approaching the Āhavanīya fire with the words: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall undertake the vow."

He should look at the sun [with the formulas]: "Thou art the sovereign; thou art the protector of vows; thou art the lord of vows. If the sun has already set, they two should eat forest-food in the *āhavanīya* shed. He for whom there is a sacrifice on the morrow should not eat in the evening. One who observes the vow should sleep on the ground in the *āhavanīya* shed; the wife sleeps in the *gārhapatya* shed. While the *praṇītā* waters are being drawn, he should meditate upon them mentally with the formula: "This is your vessel; by this I take you. When the oblation is being poured out, [he recites]: "I invoke Agni, the Hotṛ, him..."

He should touch the *sruk* ladle and the winnowing basket as each is being prepared. (13) He mutters, "Thee for the forward-measure of the sacrifice, for the backward-measure," while the altar (*vedi*) is being enclosed. (14) He mutters, "I take thee for the support of the five winds," from the time the clarified butter (*ājya*) is being taken until the end of the section. (15) He mutters, "I yoke thee with the divine prayer (*brahman*)," while the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are being placed around the fire. (16) With the *Caturhotṛ* formula and the *Vihavya* hymn, he should touch the oblations that have been set down. (17) To the east of the *sruk* ladles, within the altar, [he places] the southern [enclosing-stick].

Having taken up the Veda in his joined palms with the *jāntrācya* formula, he mutters: "Thou art the Veda; bring me the Veda. (18) He accepts it [with the words]: "I am satisfied; thou art satisfied. (19) He should mutter the *daśahotṛ* formula before the *sāmidhenī* verses. (20) "May Agni, kindled, invoked, and consecrated with *svāhā*, fulfill our desires."

21. When [the fire] has been thus kindled, [he recites]: "Thou art mind, belonging to Prajāpati; enter me with mind and being," while the *sruva* ladle is being poured over it. 22.
