"Thou art speech, belonging to Indra, the destroyer of rivals; enter me with speech and power," while the *sruc* ladle is being poured over it. 24. From the beginning up to the word "iti" during the *pravara* (invocation of ancestors), [he recites]: "O gods, O fathers. 25. He should mutter the *Caturhotṛ* formula before the *prayāja* offerings. 26. When the *āśrāvaṇa* has been made, he should say: "The gods for me"; when the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* has been made, [he says]: "Sacrifice to the god for me"; and when [the *samidh*] has been offered, [he says]: "They have established the deities for me according to their respective portions."

When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered: "In the heavenly world. (26) Regarding the *prayāja* offerings: "I gratify the spring among the seasons; may it, being gratified, gratify me. Through the sacrifice to the deity Spring, may I become full of splendor and full of milk. I gratify the summer among the seasons; may it, being gratified, gratify me. Through the sacrifice to the deity Summer, may I become full of vigor and full of strength. I gratify the rains among the seasons; may they, being gratified, gratify me. Through the sacrifice to the deity the Rains, may I become full of nourishment and full of cattle."

"I gratify Śarad among the seasons; may she, being gratified, gratify me. Through the sacrifice to the gods, may I become possessed of food and luster. "I gratify Hemanta and Śiśira among the seasons; may they, being gratified, gratify me. Through the sacrifice to the gods in Hemanta and Śiśira, may I become possessed of strength and ascetic fervor. With each individual sequence, he consecrates the *prayāja* offerings separately. (27) In the case of an increase in the number of *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, he should repeat all of them; or alternatively, he should repeat the penultimate one and the final one at the end. (28)

"By Agni the sacrifice becomes possessed of sight; through the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become possessed of sight with my eye"—with these words he consecrates the *ājyabhāga* offering. "By Soma the sacrifice becomes possessed of sight; through the sacrifice to the god Soma, may I become possessed of sight with my eye"—with these words he consecrates the second [offering]. (1) He should mutter the *pañcahotṛ* formula before the principal oblations. (2) "Agni is the eater of food; through the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become an eater of food"—with these words [he consecrates] the oblation of the *havis*. (3) "Dabdhi by name art thou; unharmed may I smite my rival"—with these words [he consecrates] the two *upāṃśuyāja* offerings. (4)

"O Agni and Soma, slayers of Vṛtra! Through the sacrifice to Agni and Soma, may I become a slayer of Vṛtra"—this is for the offering to Agni and Soma (5). "Through the sacrifice to Indra and Agni, may I become possessed of power and possessed of heroism. Through the sacrifice to Indra, may I become possessed of power. Through the sacrifice to Mahendra, may I attain victory and greatness. Through the sacrifice to Indra Vaimṛdha, may I become free from rivals. Through the sacrifice to Savitṛ, may I become impelled by Savitṛ."

Through the sacrifice to the goddess Sarasvatī, may I nourish speech and the eating of food. Through the sacrifice to the god Pūṣan, may I become possessed of nourishment and cattle. Through the sacrifice to Agni and Indra, may I become heroic and endowed with sensory power. Through the sacrifice to the Viśve Devas, may I attain progeny and abundance.

"Through the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, may I be procreated with offspring and cattle. Through the sacrifice to Vanaspati, may I reach the conclusion of this sacrifice’s performance; may I reach the conclusion of this sacrifice’s performance. This is for those [formulas] not explicitly prescribed. "For Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the foundation of the sacrifice. Through the sacrifice to him, may I attain a firm foundation by means of the sacrifice"—this is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. "May Agni protect me from ill-sacrificed offerings; may Savitṛ protect me from the malevolent. Whoever curses us from nearby, may I overcome him with this [formula]."

He recites the mantra over the *prāśitra* as it is being cut off: "8. At the silent invitation (*upahava*) of Iḍā, he mutters: 'Come to what is better; come to what is more excellent. 9. He says aloud: 'Thou art consciousness, thou art mind, thou art intelligence,' ending with 'May Indra bestow power upon us through ghee,' and also [the verse] 'Bradhna, protect! 10. He touches [the *prāśitra*] at its four ends. 11. [He says: 'Thou art the portion of Prajāpati, full of vigor, full of milk; protect my out-breath and in-breath; protect my common breath and diffused breath; protect the forms of my upward breath; thou art vigor, place vigor in me.'"

"Grant [this] to me, O Imperishable One, for the sake of imperishability; may it not perish for me there in yonder world and here in this one. May I, as Prajāpati, prosper visibly through you"—with these words he consecrates the Anvāhārya rice that has been placed near.

He should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (12). When the *idhma-saṃnahana* offering has been made with the mantra, "May my auspicious convergences converge" (13), he should mutter the *saptahotṛ* formula prior to the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s) (14). For the final [after-offering], he should say: "Through the sacrifice to the god Barhis, may I become possessed of progeny; through the sacrifice to the god Narāśaṃsa, may I become possessed of power; Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the foundation of the sacrifice; through the sacrifice to that god, may I attain a firm foundation by means of the sacrifice" (15). "May I follow the victory of Agni with victory."

"May I win after the winning of Soma," with these words he recites the consecratory formulas from the *ājyabhāga* offerings up to the *sviṣṭakṛt*. 16. Regarding the other [formulas], they are recited at the two *upāṃśuyāja* offerings and in the *sūktavāka*. 17. "May this my true blessing reach the gods," he says when the *prastara* is being thrown into the fire. 18. Therein, he chooses whatever boon he may desire. 19. "Viṣṇu is the peaceful one, the foundation of the sacrifice; through the sacrifice of that deity, may I attain the foundation," he says during the *śamyorvāka*. 20. "I loosen thy cord, I loosen thy reins," he says over the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

When the [sacrificial vessels] are being struck, [he says], "The sacrifice was desired by the Bhṛgus," at the portions of the *saṃsrāva*. At the end, he chooses boons [with the words], "May this not come to me; may this not happen to me."

Through the sacrifice to the god Soma, may I deposit all seed. Through the sacrifice to the god Tvaṣṭṛ, may I nourish all forms of cattle. Through the sacrifice to the wives of the gods, may I procreate with offspring and cattle. Through the sacrifice to Rākā, may I find heroic sons. Through the sacrifice to Sinīvālī, may I find cattle. Through the sacrifice to the Juhū-ladle, may I attain a firm foundation; for Agni, the lord of the house, is the foundation of the sacrifice—through his sacrifice to the gods, through the sacrifice, and through my home, may I attain that foundation.

"May I attain a firm foundation," [he says] to Agni Gṛhapati. May Iḍā favor us with clarified butter—she at whose footstep those seeking the gods purify themselves. May the Vaiśvānarī Śakvarī, increasing in power, come to our sacrifice; may she who belongs to all the gods (Vaiśvadevī) likewise approach.

With the verse, "Iḍā... Sarasvatī, who brings wealth to the household," he wipes his mouth. With the verse, "Burn away the hater, burn away the enemy," he consecrates the sacrificial grass as it is being strewn. With the formula, "The lord of the sacrifice has attained his desire," the sacrificer eats his portion. If he should be away on a journey, he should offer it together with the *samiṣṭayajus* oblation. Sitting behind the altar, facing eastward, while the *praṇītā* water is being poured in an unbroken stream into the *sadas*, he consecrates it with the formula, "May there be for me that which is in the assembly. "By the eastern direction, the gods, the officiating priests..."

"May they cleanse [me]," he says, as prescribed for each direction. (8) "Like unto the ocean I send you forth; go back to your own source. May our heroes be unharmed; let not my strength flow away. With this verse, he consecrates the water that has been poured out. (9) "What wealth of yours is in the waters, O Sarasvatī, what is in the cows and in the horses—with that, O Sarasvatī, rich in prizes, cleanse my mouth with splendor. With this verse, he wipes his mouth. (10) To the east of the southern *vedī*, he strides the steps of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇukrama*) with his right foot.

"Viṣṇu strode out upon the earth"—this is the first; "Viṣṇu strode out in the intermediate space"—this is the second; "Viṣṇu strode out in heaven"—this is the third. "May I be ever higher and higher. (VS 11) "I here bind the breath of so-and-so," saying this, he winds [the cord] around it clockwise with his heel. (12) He should utter the name of one whom he hates; if he does not intend to practice sorcery, he should do so silently. (13) Having turned toward the left, he worships the Āhavanīya fire with "Thou art splendor"; he worships the Gārhapatya fire with "O Agni, lord of the house. (14)

"May these [fires] extend along my body," he says, pronouncing the name of his son; "may those [fires] extend along my body," if there are two; "may these [fires] extend along my body," if there are many. He worships the fires with the *atīmokṣa* formulas.

"Those gods who, as destroyers of the sacrifice, dwell upon the earth"—with these words he offers to the Gārhapatya fire; "those gods who, as destroyers of the sacrifice, dwell in the intermediate space"—with these words to the Dakṣiṇāgni; "those gods who, as destroyers of the sacrifice, dwell in heaven"—with these words to the Āhavanīya. (16) "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I have declared it to you; I was able to perform it; through that I was able; through that I succeeded; may that [vow] protect me. Thus, while placing fuel-sticks into the fires, he releases the vow. (17) The sacrifice has come into being; indeed, it has come into being; it has been born; indeed, it has grown.

"May he again become the lord of the gods; may he make us lords; may we be masters of riches. Thus he mutters the *punarālambha* formula. (18) "O Agni, [be] rich in cattle, rich in sheep, rich in horses, [be] the sacrifice," thus he mutters while stepping forward toward the east. (19) The sacrificer, being a Brāhmaṇa, eats the *sāṃnāyya* either after the *sam-iṣṭayajus* offering or before it. (20) Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Mānava Sūtra*, concerning the *Prāksoma* [rite].

A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn; for all classes, the cool season (śiśira) is also permitted. For one intending to sacrifice with Soma, there is no restriction regarding the season or the lunar mansion. On the full moon day of Phālguna, he should establish the fires one day or two days prior. A Brāhmaṇa who has a son born to him may establish the fires under the Kṛttikās. Rohiṇī, the two Phalgunīs, and Citrā are also prescribed. He may establish the fires under Mṛgaśiras. Under the two Punarvasūs, one becomes more wretched; under Viśākhā, one who desires offspring [should establish them].

One who desires prosperity [should perform it] under the *anurādhā* asterism; one who desires firm standing, under the *proṣṭhapadā* asterisms. He should establish the fires on the full moon day or the new moon day. "The *aśvattha* tree which has grown from the womb of the *śamī*, having ascended together with thee—that I take for thee with the sacred word (*brahman*), along with the sacrificial signs."

Thus he brings the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) made of *aśvattha* wood from a tree that has grown upon a sacrificial peg (*śamyā*). He mutters: "Bestow life upon me; bestow life upon the sacrificer. The shaving [of the hair] is as at the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Having bathed and put on two unwashed linen garments, they both eat food fit for a fast. On ground sloping toward the east, in a shed facing north, he makes a mark in the afternoon to the west of the central beam. Having dug up and sprinkled that spot, he establishes there either the domestic fire (*aupāsanīya*), the fire for the *brāhmaudana* rite, or the hall-fire produced by friction.

Before the invocation, he chooses the officiating priests: "To the wise, the seer, the pure, the bull, the vigorous one, let there be this word of adoration. May that from which fear arises become for us free from fear. I appease the wrath of the gods; Svāhā!"

Thus he offers the oblation. (16) Having poured out four handfuls of rice on the hide of a red bull, with the neck toward the east and the hair side up, they thresh the grain while it is still moist. (17) At night, they surround it. (18) He cooks the *brahmaudana* rice, using grains that remain alive. (19) Having sprinkled the cooked rice with either unstrained clarified butter or strained fresh butter, he removes it from the fire to the north. (20) Having transferred it to another vessel and poured out the dregs, he pours abundant ghee over it; then the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), who are of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) and have been chosen, sit down around the *brahmaudana*.

Brahman stands to the south, the Hotṛ behind, the Udgātṛ to the north, and the Adhvaryu to the east. (21) Having taken the rice-balls, having poured them into clarified butter, and having stepped forward, they consume them. (22) To them he gives a cow. (23) From a holy fig tree (*aśvattha*) growing on a sacred mound (*caitya*), he takes three fuel-sticks that are thick, together with their leaves, a span in length, and smeared with clarified butter; he places them on the boiled rice with these three *gāyatrī* verses ending in *svāhā*: "Forward your strengths, O ye who go to heaven," and "Be mindful, O Agni. (24) For a Brāhmaṇa, [he uses] the verse beginning with "Awake, O Agni. (25) He offers the oblation with the verse beginning with "O Agni, come hither" (*agne ā yāhi*). (26) He causes the sacrificer to recite the verse beginning with "O Agni, do thou protect us from tribulation" (*agne tvaṃ pāraya*). (27) He causes him to recite the verse beginning with "May we be in thy keeping, O Agni" (*tava agne pāyubhiḥ*). (28) He causes him to recite the verse beginning with "May we be in thy protection, O Agni" (*tava agne rakṣitāraḥ*). (71) He causes him to recite the verse beginning with "O Agni, do thou guard us from tribulation" (*

For a Rājanya, [he should kindle] with *triṣṭubh* verses; for a Vaiśya, with *jagatī* verses, beginning with "The guardian of the people" (*janasya gopā*). 24. Without offering oblations, he should kindle the fire continuously for a year, or for twelve nights, or three nights, or one night. 25. They shall not carry his fire away from the house, nor shall they bring it from elsewhere. 26. He shall not go on a journey. 27. He shall not speak untruth. 28. He shall not eat meat. 29. He shall not approach a woman. 30. One who is about to establish the fires on the morrow should fast during the preceding full moon or the succeeding new moon.

On the [appropriate] lunar mansion (nakṣatra), the officiating priests (ṛtvij) who observe the vow dwell together. With the mantra, "O Agni, cause the subjects to dwell together," he binds a spotted goat to the dwelling in the north-eastern direction.

"Kindling the fire with wood-shavings, I win both worlds; I prosper in both worlds; I cross over death. With these words, he kindles the fire with wood-shavings. (1) He hands the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) to the sacrificer. (2) "O great ones, mistresses of the people, in the seat of Order, come hither, you who are the support of riches. Being pregnant, bring forth the kinsman, Jātavedas, the leader of the sacrifices. With these words, he receives them. (3) "You two are possessed of the proper season; you are the seed of Agni. Bestow seed for prosperity and procreation."

"That is the truth: that which has borne a hero will bear a hero; you two shall procreate for me in the morning; having procreated, they shall procreate for me through offspring and cattle. From untruth I go to truth; from the human I go to the divine; I restrain my speech. Having said this, he restrains his speech. (4) The wife takes the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) in her hand from the southern fire. (5) With speech restrained and holding the kindling-sticks in their hands, the two remain awake. (6) At the break of dawn, she heats the two kindling-sticks over the *brāhmaudana* fire. (7) [He places them] upon the two kindling-sticks with the verse: "This is your seasonal womb..."

Having followed it [the fire] and drawn it out, he makes a mark for the *gārhapatya* fire; having dug up the ground and sprinkled it with water, he places the materials in the order of the marks: to the south-east of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, at a distance of one-third [of the space], closer to the mark of the *gārhapatya*, and level with it toward the east for the *āhavanīya*. He pours down the materials following the sequence of the marks: "From the ocean has come a honeyed wave, bestowing further sovereignty. May we, those wealthy patrons and we ourselves, gather together food, strength, and sweetness."

Thus he pours out water that does not diminish. "In this much [space] it was at first; from there the goddess, expanding, was scattered apart by the gods through her greatness. Having thus poured out the earth dug up by a boar, he silently pours down the mound of an anthill. "That which is yonder in heaven, and that which is here on earth, which has come together toward a common womb—upon its back let Jātavedas sit; may he be auspicious for our offspring, and may wealth be ours here."

While scattering the saline earth, he should meditate in his mind upon this verse: "That which is black in the moon, let him bring that here. "The gods have established here the Moon—Agni with a shining chariot, surrounded by bay horses, Vaiśvānara who dwells in the waters, the finder of heaven; the one who plunges in, the swift, covered with powers, the impetuous, the highly glorious one."

Thus he scatters the fine sand with the verse: "Thou hast made firm the earth with pebbles of triple-edged stones; thou hast conquered the worlds and the four quarters. (14) He scatters brown pebbles with the verse: "He whom he hates, him he should contemplate in his mind. (15-16) "Go forth, O Agni, from the mother earth; enter the people from the great dwelling-place. The god-seeking ones have established thee as the swift one in battle, the bearer of oblations, the guardian of the world. (17)

With these words he scatters the *akhukirī* seeds (17). Silently [he places] a lotus leaf, one made of *udumbara* wood, one of *vikaṅkata*, one of *śamī*, one of *aśvattha*, one of *palāśa*, and a seventh made from a tree struck by lightning (18): "I unite your hearts; may your minds be united; may your breath be united; may your bodies be united."

Thus he prepares the ritual materials (saṃbhāra). With the verse, "The spotted bull has stepped forth," he touches the materials at the mark of the Gārhapatya fire; with the words, "he moves within," [he touches] those of the Dakṣiṇāgni; with the words, "thirtyfold support," [he touches] those of the Āhavanīya. He stations a noble horse in front, facing westward.

To the west of the Gārhapatya fire-mark, having placed either a bundle of muñja grass or another [fire-drill] upon a swift fire, he says, "You two are the testicles. There, he places two darbha blades with uncut ends pointing eastward, saying, "Thou art Urvaśī. Upon them, he places the lower fire-drill (adharāraṇi) with its tufts facing north and its rear part turned toward the front (the fire), and the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi) at its base, saying, "The ten Hotṛs. Having established them, he causes the sacrificer to recite the Caturhotṛ formulas. He gives the command: "Sing the Sāman on the verse, 'The men [kindle] Agni with their thoughts from the two fire-drills'. Once they have been brought together, he churns the fire while reciting, "From here was he born."

"Thy brilliant smoke rises up"—this [he says] when the smoke has arisen. (4) "The best finder of the path has been seen"—this [he says] when [the fire] has been born. (5) "O Prajāpati, I breathe upon thee with my breath for the nourishment of Pūṣan, for my long life of a hundred autumns"—with these words he breathes upon the one that has been born. (6) "The Agni who is ours, O Fathers"—beginning from the region of the heart, the sacrificer mutters this while lifting [the fire]; then, raising it up, he fans it three times with his mouth full [of air]. (7) "That immortal essence of the earth which came into being together with thee..."

"May Agni give that to Agni; let this be placed upon him"—thus the Brahman, seated to the south, should gaze at the golden fragment as it is being placed among the ritual materials. (8) The sacrificer should hand over silver to his enemy; if none is available, he should cast it away. (9) With the formula "That which [is] of the intermediate space," he addresses the Dakṣiṇāgni; with "Of heaven," the Āhavanīya. (10) He mutters: "And thou art the milker and the bearer of milk. (11) He causes the sacrificer to recite: "The Gharma is the head. (12) With the words "I take [it] into myself," he forms a mental resolve regarding his heart.

The Adhvaryu and the sacrificer [recite]: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ! By the vow of the Aṅgirases, the gods, I place thee. He should place [the fire] for one of the Aṅgirases with this; for others, with "By the vow of Agni"; for a Rājanya, with "By the vow of Indra"; for a Vaiśya, with "By the vow of Manu. In all cases, he appends "for the sake of protection" (*achadi*). Having placed his hands in his lap, he places the blazing [fire] with the word "Bhūḥ. He releases [the fire] while it is being sung around with the Vāravantīya [Sāman]. With the verses, "O Agni, thou purifiest our lives," "Agni is the seer," and "O Agni, purify," he places three fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood.

He prepares three sticks of *śamī* wood and one of *udumbara* wood. 17. He places them one by one on the fire with the formula, "To Agni, svāhā! for each of the anointed sticks. 18. Having placed the implements for carrying the fire upon the *gārhapatya*, 19. he consecrates the horse with the verse, "O steed, [the drops] of Agni... 1. The sacrificer mutters the verse, "When you neighed... into the right ear of the horse. 2. Having made the remaining materials into supporting blocks (*upayamanī*), he lifts up the fire with the formula, "For vigor, for strength, thee! 3. Having handed it to the *āgnīdhra*, he churns the *dakṣiṇa-agni* while facing north.

He should lead [the fire] forward from either the *bhraṣṭra* or the *gārhapatya*. With the word "Bhuvaḥ," he places [the fuel] while keeping his knees raised. He releases [the horse] after it has been sung around with the *Vāmadevya* chant. Having taken up the implements for the leading of the fire, they proceed eastward with the horse at their head, reciting: "O wise one, go forth toward the eastern quarter. As the fire is being led forward, the sacrificer walks to its north. To the south, the *brahmán* turns the chariot or the chariot wheel, reciting: "Thou art the vault, thou art the sun, thou art the most excellent support and means of crossing," at the midpoint.

Having placed and established gold, the sacrificer gives a choice gift. Having circumambulated by the north of the mark, he makes the horse step upon the side of the ritual materials with his right foot, reciting "I have overcome all hostile armies," causing it to turn around without making it look back. Having made the horse step down and having taken hold of it, he should lift the fire-carrying vessels to the height of the ankle, then to the height of the knee, then to the height of the navel, then to the height of the mouth, and finally to the height of the ear; he should not lift them higher than that, reciting "Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ."

He establishes the fires according to the Ṛṣi’s tradition: "O bright one, with that which is your bright light, your bright, eternal abode—with that I establish you; we [establish you] in the place of Iḍā. Standing facing north, looking westward, and remaining upright at sunrise, he places [the fire] from the side of the footprint with the words, "Svaḥ! He releases [the chant] following the Yajñāyajñīya when it has been fully sung. One who has rivals or enemies should turn a chariot wheel three times around the sacrificial ground. The sacrificer worships the fires with the mantra, "The sovereign and the self-ruler..."

With the verse "The Virāṭ and the Prabhū," he places fuel on the Gārhapatya fire; with "The Vibhū and the Paribhū," on the Dakṣiṇāgni; and with [the same], on the Āhavanīya. (17) Having swept around the fires, sprinkled water around them, and strewn grass around them, having melted clarified butter over the Dakṣiṇāgni and placed it on the Gārhapatya, and having purified it, they perform the necessary rites for such [an occasion]. (18) He places three fuel sticks made of Śamī wood, anointed with ghee, upon the fire with these three verses ending in "svāhā": "From the ocean, the wave... and so forth.

With the verse, "The fires that are of one mind," they anoint the Audumbarī post (19). With the verse, "Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni," he offers the full oblation. With the verse, "The fires that are from heaven, those that are from earth," he offers the Agniviparaṇayanīyā oblation (20). "I give the horse to the Adhvaryu"—with these words the sacrificer releases his speech and bestows a choice gift (vara) (21).

The procedure for the *iṣṭis* is that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. We shall now enumerate their modifications. One should slowly observe the deities according to the traditional recitation. All the rites beginning with the *āgnyādheya*, the *sadyaskrā*, and those involving the *upāṃśu* deity follow this sequence. Having offered the cake on eight potsherds for Agni and set it down, one should release the sacrificial animal before the sprinkling of water, saying "I think of Agni. Then, having dug up the earth in front of the *āhavanīya* fire and sprinkled it, one establishes the *sabhyāgni* from the *āhavanīya*, and the *āvasathyāgni* from the *sabhyāgni*. Having sprinkled the ground to the north, [one prepares] for the gambling board.

First, he spreads [the cloth] for the invitation. Having spread an unwashed garment with its fringes pointing north upon the gaming board (*adhidevana*), he pours four hundred dice onto it. The noble gamblers sit around him. Having gathered the dice in the middle of the gaming board and placed gold down, he offers an oblation over them with the verse, "He has sat down, firm in his vows. Having scattered the dice, he offers an oblation on the assembly fire (*sabhya*) with the verse, "And for us, O Ahibudhnya, O King. The sacrificer releases a cow; he gives him one hundred dice.

He should select them (12). Having defeated those gamblers, he issues the command: "Let the sacrificer win the cow; do so! (13). They should release her limb by limb, so that no injury may come to her joints (14). Having caused her to be won, he should present her to the members of the assembly (15). Whatever he may receive from her, he should give that to the officiating priests at the time of the sacrificial fees; they should consecrate it right here with the formula *ramaṇīyam* (16). He offers the oblation on the *āvasathya* fire with the verse: *enā rājan*.

"Now indeed, Brahmaṇaspati... with these words of address (17), the sacrificer stands near the fires: facing east behind the Gārhapatya fire with the formula "The Gharma is the head"; facing west in front of the Āhavanīya fire with "The Sun is light"; facing north to the south of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with "The wind is the breath"; and standing in the middle facing north with "May Heaven and Earth be prepared; may the fires that are of one mind... (18). Having proceeded with the sprinkling of water, the sacrifice is completed as a successful rite (19).

When [the Soma] has been concluded, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna; the sacrificial fee is gold weighing thirty mānas. When it has been concluded, two cakes on eight potsherds for Agni Pāvaka and Agni Śuci; the sacrificial fee is gold weighing seventy mānas. When it has been concluded, [one should offer] a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu, and a pap cooked in clarified butter in three layers for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. For one desiring cattle, a pap cooked in clarified butter for Aditi, and a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma, O Brāhmaṇa.

He brings the *caru* for Aditi to the Brahman priest together with the *brahmabhāga* and the *yajamānabhāga*, along with the dipping-spoon (*mekṣa� goat*) used for pouring and boiling. At the time of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives a goat and a pillow to the *Āgnīdhra*; to the *Adhvaryu*, an ox that has not yet borne a load and a cow; and to the *Hotṛ*, a milch-cow. At the conclusion of the sacrifice, he gives to the *Adhvaryu* two young bulls—one being a castrated one two years old—along with a chariot yoked [with them] and a *śatamāna* gold coin, as well as two garments. When the *samiṣṭayajus* oblation has been offered, the four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) eat the *caru* for Aditi.

To them he gives a castrated young bull. (9) One who, having established the sacred fires, intends not to sacrifice with Soma, should feed the officiating priests with boiled rice made from living grains in four bowls. (10) He should offer oblations of clarified butter to the deities of the sacrifice. (11) At the end of the year, he offers the sacrificial oblations. (12) No Brahmin shall dwell in his house without eating. (13) He shall not eat food cooked in a pit. (14) He shall not sip water from waters that flow within a river. (15) He shall not place wet wood on the fire. (16) He shall not reside in a natural salt-flat. (17) [The section on] Invitation.

One should not go uninvited; one should go to an invitation during the afternoon. (18) One who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices performs the *ārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice: an offering on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, an offering on eight potsherds for Bhaga-Agni, a pap for Sarasvatī, and an offering on twelve potsherds for Sarasvant. (19) Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having taken twelve portions into the *juhū* ladle, he offers the *jaya* oblations with the twelve formulas beginning with "To Ākūti, svāhā! To Kṛti, svāhā!", while holding the ladles apart.

"Prajāpati gave [it]," with this [verse] he offers the thirteenth portion if he should desire, "May I be preeminent and endowed with spiritual luster. "O Agni, come with strength," with this he offers the fourteenth portion if he should desire, "May I be distinguished among this assembly. He becomes distinguished among that assembly, but a variegated [nature] arises within himself. (20) With the stirring-spoon, he cuts portions from the sacrificial porridges for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering and for the Iḍā. (21) A pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee. (22) At the Sūktavāka, he places the stirring-spoon upon the fire. (23) Having performed the establishment of the fires on the full moon day...

Having performed the *upavasatha* and the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering], one should sacrifice with the *paurṇamāsī* [Full Moon sacrifice] of the same-day performance (*sadyaskāla*). 24. Having established the fires on the new moon day or under a [favorable] lunar mansion, one should fast on the preceding full moon day and perform the *ārambhaṇīyā*; then, having fasted on the subsequent [full moon day], one should sacrifice with the *paurṇamāsī*. One should sacrifice. 25.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Mānava-Śrautasūtra concerning the Soma sacrifice preceded by the establishment of the fires.

Having said, "Lift up the Āhavanīya," he leads forth the flaming Āhavanīya from the Gārhapatya in the afternoon, or at dawn when the night has faded. He lifts it up with the formula: "With speech as the Hotṛ, with breath as the Udgātṛ, with the eye as the Adhvaryu, with the mind as the Brahman, and with the ear as the Agnīdh—by means of these five divine officiating priests, I lift thee up. While it is being lifted up, [he recites]: "Lift me up from evil, whatever I have done unknowingly or knowingly."

"Whatever sin or evil has been committed by day, release me from all of that!"—with these words he carries [the fire] away. "Whatever sin [has been committed] by night"—with these words in the morning. (3) "I offer the oblation of immortality into immortality; I place Agni upon the earth for the conquest of immortality. Through you, O Agni, I conquer my desire—the very one which Prajāpati first conquered in Agni within Agni. Svāhā!"—with these words he deposits [the fire] in the evening.

"In the fire [is] the sun," [with these words] he takes [the milk] in the morning; or he may take it at night. One who has attained prosperity, a learned Brāhmaṇa, a village headman who is a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya who possesses much livestock—these are those for whom [the Agnihotra] is to be maintained perpetually. He places a large log on the Āhavanīya fire. The Agnihotra is to be offered at the onset of night, and at dawn in the morning. With "O Agni, be purified," he wipes around the Āhavanīya; with "O Agni, lord of the house," the Gārhapatya; and with "O Agni, bearer," the Dakṣiṇāgni. In the evening, he sprinkles water around [the fires] with the formula: "I sprinkle thee with Ṛta and Satya."

With the formula, "By truth and by cosmic order," he strews around the fires in the morning. He strews darbha grass with its tips pointing north behind the Āhavanīya fire. To the north of the Gārhapatya fire, upon the strewn grass, he places a fuel-stick, a sruva-spoon, and an Agnihotra-offering ladle made by an Ārya. To the north, he lets the calf loose.

He approaches her while she faces east and causes her to milk for the sake of the noble ones; or he causes a Śūdra woman to milk her while facing north. Having pushed out embers from the Gārhapatya fire toward the north with the words, "Driven away is the danger from strangers, driven away are the attacking armies," he says: "O Jātavedas, enjoy this oblation, the station of Iḍā, rich in ghee, moving and unmoving. May there be nourishment here for those seven domestic animals that possess all forms."

With this [formula], he places [the vessel] on the fire. (15) "You are origins," he says, looking at it. (16) "May I increase with offspring and cattle," he says, heating it with a firebrand. (17) "May I not lose your heat," he says, pouring back the water-drops that have spilled over. (18) "You are the all-light," he says, lighting it again. (19) "The *rakṣas* has been excluded; the enemies have been excluded," he says, carrying fire around it three times with a blade of grass. (20) "Rise up! Increase our altar with offspring; drive away hatred; may there be safety for us."

"May the curse not harm us, nor sorcery; in a gracious field, free from enemies, may we shine. With these words, he carries [the coals] out toward the north, making a path. (21) "The fear of the enemy has been driven away; the attacking armies have been driven away"—with these words, he pushes back the embers and fills in the path. (22) He offers an oblation with milk, or with curd, or with barley-gruel, or with clarified butter. (23) There should be no placing of the curd and the clarified butter over the fire, nor heating them. (24) "Burnt is the Rakṣas, burnt are the enemies"—with these words, he heats the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles over the Gārhapatya fire.

He heats [the spoon] twenty-five times. Having placed a fuel-stick upon the *sruva* spoon, he says, "I shall draw out," and [the other replies], "I am drawing out. In the morning, he draws out [the ghee] with each verse: "The *iḍā* of the earth; the *iḍā* of the intermediate space; the *iḍā* of heaven; the *iḍā* of people"—drawing out more and more each time, the last being full, or all of them equal. He touches what has been drawn out with the formula, "This for the gods," and the remainder with, "And this for us together. He places it on the *darbha* grass with the formula, "Grant me cattle," or toward the east. He touches the *agnihotra* oblation that has been drawn out with the *daśahotr* formula. [He places it] above on the handle of the ladle.

30. He approaches the fuel with the formula, "O Agni, enter the atmosphere! and carries it across the fire. 31. With the formula, "Svāhā to Agni Vaiśvānara! he places it halfway across. 32. With the formula, "To Vāyu thee! he lifts it up. 33. With the formula, "Grant me life," he sets it down upon the *darbha* grass. 34. He places the fuel-stick with the formula, "This is thy fuel, O Agni; through it mayest thou increase and swell; may we also increase and swell, svāhā! 35. He should meditate on the out-breath and in-breath while blinking his eyes at a distance of two finger-breadths.

He makes an offering over the fuel-stick that is either white or flaming. 36. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Agnihotra! Agni is light, light is Agni! Svāhā!"—with this he offers in the evening. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Agnihotra! Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya! Svāhā!"—with this he offers in the morning. 37. "Grant me luster," saying this, he places [the remainder] upon the *darbha* grass. 38. "O Prajāpati, grant me cattle," saying this, he gazes at the *gārhapatya* fire. 39. "To Prajāpati, svāhā!"—with this, he mentally offers the second [oblation], which is more abundant. 40. Having left the greatest portion remaining, O Anābhī, be gracious.

Saying "O rogue," he points three times toward the north at the *samaya*-fire (41). With the words "For sap, thee," he wipes downward in the evening; with "For strength, thee," he wipes upward toward the sky (42). Saying "Grant me offspring," he places [the vessel] with its handle pointing north (43). Saying "Quicken the plants," he wipes the smear onto the *darbha* grasses (44). Saying "To the ancestors, svadhā," he places his hand with the palm facing upward to the south (45). Saying "Thou art Pūṣan," he eats twice with his finger, not letting his teeth touch it (46). Saying "To other people, svāhā," he licks the remainder off.

47. "To the Gandharvas and other beings, svāhā!"—thus in the morning. 48. Having poured [water] into the vessel that has not been wiped clean, he pours out water three times toward the north-east, saying: "I gratify the serpents and ants; to the serpents and ants, svāhā! 49. Having washed it with *darbha* grass and poured [water] into it, he pours it out silently three times. 50. Taking up the full vessel, he pours it out to the north of the Āhavanīya fire toward the west, saying: "In the immortal I offer the breath, svāhā!"

"In the immortal [I offer] the breath; I offer the breath, svāhā!"—thus at dawn. (50) Having heated the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, he places his hand into it; or, having heated his hand, he places it into the *agnihotra-havaṇī*, lifts it up, and sets it down toward the north. (51) With the *sruva* spoon, he offers into the two western fires: into the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse "O Agni, lord of the house," and half a *sruva*-measure with "svāhā"; into the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire with the verse "O Lord of food, give us food," and half a *sruva*-measure with "svāhā. Or, he may not offer into the two western fires. (52) That cow which one milks for the first *agnihotra* sacrifice—[that is the one...]

The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for a Kṣatriya who maintains the *agnihotra* is either milk or a bow; this is the constant rule for him, while for another it is on the festival days (*parvan*). He should also always give food to a Brāhmaṇa.

Restraining his speech while the oblation is being placed on the fire or while it is being ladled out, he washes his hands and mutters the four verses of the *vihavya* hymn. Standing to the south, facing northeast and looking upward, when told "I shall ladle out," he gives permission by saying, "Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ, ladle out! Having sat down, he touches the oblation that has been brought forward with the *daśahotṛ* formula and the *vyāhṛtis*. Every year, after the previous offering has been made, he stands up and recites the two verses beginning with "upaprayanto adhvaram."

With the verse, "You two [have performed] these... (RV 1.93.5), he worships with the Agniṣomīyā [verse] during the moonlit night; with the Aindrāgnī [verse], "This one here has been first established by the establishers... (RV 8.39.1), during the dark night. 4. Before the Agniṣomīyā [verse], he mutters four verses of the Vihavya hymn. 5. Beginning with "O Agni and Soma, this [oblation] well... (RV 1.93.1), he places three fuel-sticks using those verses characterized by the word *samit* (fuel-stick). 6. He repeats three times the formula common [to all]: "O you of variegated wealth, may I reach your end in safety. 7. With the words, "You are water; may I partake of your water," he touches the calf. 8. "Near you, O Agni, day after day... (RV 8.44.16).

With the verse beginning "diva" (heaven), he worships the householder’s fire eight times. With the words "ūrjā vaḥ paśyāmi" (I look upon you with vigor), he touches the cow. With the words "mahi trīṇām avo astu" (May the great protection of the three be ours), he worships the Āhavanīya fire. With the words "nimrado 'si" (You are the one who sinks down), he acts as prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa. With the words "pūṣā mā pathipāḥ pātu" (May Pūṣan, the protector of paths, protect me), he worships each of the following: the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky. He worships each direction in turn according to the traditional text: "The eastern direction, Agni is its deity," and so forth.

"May Dharma protect me from unrighteousness," as it is handed down in the tradition (14). Having sat down between the two fires, he mutters: "For light, for the thread" (15). In the evening, the wife sits beside him, but not in the morning (16). On the following day, [he recites]: "The divine Dawns, the wives of Sūrya, approaching—may those mothers of the sacrifice sprinkle me with splendor! May the goddesses sprinkle me with splendor and with wealth. May those who hate me be overcome; may I not be overcome by those who hate me."

"I am the seer, the sole hero; I am the radiant one, the subduer of men. I am the leaper forward, the leaper back; I am the thunderbolt, the slayer of rivals. I have slain my rivals, the enemies; the adversaries are struck down, the enemies are struck down. May we move about unharmed. Having recited "arvāgvasu" three times, he mutters the four verses of the *vihavya* hymn. (17) The sacrificer who is not superior [to his rival] should worship with the *vihavya* hymn. (18)

Having stayed for at least ten nights and intending to depart with his wealth, he should place the fires on the *āneya* bricks; he does not remove those that are not to be removed, but removes those that are to be removed. After the morning oblation has been offered and all the fires have been yoked, he recites these two verses, "O Lord of the Dwelling, O Lord of the Dwelling," and offers an oblation with the verse: "To thee, O best of Angirases, all the well-settled people have separately bowed down, O Agni, out of desire. This is the second [verse]. When about to go abroad, he consigns the fires into the two kindling woods with the verse: "This is thy seasonal womb."

"If one's fortune has departed, [he should sacrifice] to all [the gods]. O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice—come, ascend it by yourself, having bestowed upon yourself many noble riches. Having become the sacrifice, sit upon the sacrifice, your own womb; being born from the earth, come to your own abode. With these words, he either consigns [the fire] into himself or, having extinguished and burned [the fire], he departs for another place of worship and proceeds as a *yāyāvara*. "Descend again, O Jātavedas! Knowing [the way], carry the oblations to the gods. Bestow upon us long life, progeny, and wealth, O Eternal One!"

"Shine for us in our home"—thus he mutters when about to churn the fire. In this very same way, every day, when about to set out on a journey, he consigns the fires [into the kindling wood], and [when returning] he descends them with the words, "Descend! Having said, "Make the fires radiant," he, when about to depart on a journey, stands worshipping the burning fires.

"O Hirbhuṣya, protect my mantra; guard it for me until our return"—with these words he worships the *āvasathya* fire. "O broad one, protect my assembly hall; guard it for me until our return"—with these words [he worships] the *sabhya* fire. "Be auspicious to my cattle and protect them"—[this is for] the *āhavanīya*. "O manly one, protect my offspring"—[this is for] the *gārhapatya*. "O wakeful one, protect my food"—[this is for] the *dakṣiṇāgni*. (7) Standing between the two fires, he mutters: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two guard these houses of mine. (8) "My name is first... [and so on].

"O Jātavedas, father and mother bestowed [thee] upon us in the beginning; do thou bear that true essence back to me again. O Agni, I shall bear thy name. With these words, he worships the Āhavanīya fire. (9) "May we not stray from the path, nor from the sacrifice, O Indra, we who possess Soma. May no enemies stand against us. Having set out on his journey, he restrains his speech in the presence of the fires and releases it when out of their sight. (10) While traveling, at the time of the oblation, he worships the fires in each direction: "Bringing [offerings] at all times with an unafflicted mind... (11)

"O Agni, may we, your neighbors, not come to harm. Having returned thus, he brings two pieces of fuel; he restrains his speech when away from the fire, and releases it when near the fire. (12) Having said, "Kindle the fire," he worships the ashes. (13) He worships the *āvasathya* fire with: "The serpent has protected my mantra; give that back to me. He worships the *sabhya* fire with: "The wide-extending one has protected my assembly hall; give that back to me. He worships the *āhavanīya* fire with: "He has protected my cattle for my well-being," and "He has protected my offspring for my manly strength."

"May he protect my food at the *gārhapatya* fire with his wisdom," [he says] regarding the *dakṣiṇāgni*. "O Mitra and Varuṇa, may you two protect these houses of mine," [he] mutters while standing between the two fires. "Thy name and mine, O Jātavedas, we move about wearing like two garments; for you indeed sustain us both for greatness and for life—grant that to us both accordingly, O Jātavedas."

Thus, he silently places fuel-sticks into the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires. (16) Having worshipped the other fires with verses containing words indicative of fuel-sticks (*samit*), if he does not depart on a journey, he should worship them again upon his return. (17) If he should go abroad without having worshipped the fires, he worships them [upon returning] with: "Right here you are established; being there, O Agni, I sustain you with heart, speech, and mind. May the sacrifice not leave my life; I worship you with the eye of Vaiśvānara. (18) Thus he worships.

One should perform the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice on the full-moon day: of barley in the spring, and of rice in the autumn. Having sacrificed the first-fruits, one may eat of the new grain. [The procedure] is established up to the pouring out of the oblation-materials. He pours out [the material] for Agni and Indra, for the Viśve Devas, and for Heaven and Earth. In the autumn, he offers *śyāmāka* millet to Soma in another vessel. We shall prescribe the rule for various seeds, as well as for those offerings presented with the *vaṣaṭ*-call and for cakes on a single potsherd. There is a separate touching of the various seeds. He calls the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*) at the principal offerings.

From the pouring [of the grain] until the end of the winnowing, this is for each [deity]; for the barley, it is up to the end of the threshing. 9. It is established from the placing of the potsherds. 10. He places twelve potsherds for Agni-Indra and one for Dyāvā-Pṛthivī. 11. It is established up to the placing on the fire. 12. Having placed the offering for Agni-Indra on the fire, he places the *caru* (mixture) for the Viśvedevas on the fire. 13. Having poured milk over the strainer and added the rice grains, he places the portion for Dyāvā-Pṛthivī on the fire—[the size being] about the thickness of a thumb-joint or the width of a *kūṭī* leaf—and then the Soma portion.

He places the *caru* on the fire (14). Having poured water over it while the two strainers are placed between, and having added the rice grains, he cooks the *caru* with a stirring-spoon, moving from left to right (15). Once it is cooked, he removes it from the fire (16). He fills a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) with [the sacrificial substance], decorating it in another vessel (17). At the time of the ritual performance, having placed it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he spreads an underlayer of ghee and cuts off the entire portion from the single potsherd at once (18). Having poured ghee over the remnant of the vessel and having sprinkled ghee twice over it, he proceeds with the single potsherd; when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers it straight with his hand into the middle [of the fire].

He offers with a firm intention. (19) If [the fire] should turn back, it has been explained by the Brāhmaṇa. (20) Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers six oblations of clarified butter: "To him who possesses a hundred weapons, a hundred powers, a hundred aids, the overcomer of enemies—he who may lead us for a hundred autumns to the further shore of all misfortune. "These four paths, which traverse the atmosphere between heaven and earth, let them go forth. Whichever of these leads us without failure, to that one, O All-Gods, deliver us. (RV 10.57.4–5)

May spring, summer, the honey-sweet rains, autumn, and winter bestow upon you a state of well-being. May we remain in their protection for a hundred autumns, free from fear within these seasons. Offer great homage to the Samvatsara, the Parivatsara, the Idavatsara, the Anuvatsara, and the Udvatsara. May we, living long and unslain, abide in the good favor of these worshipful ones.
May this well-being—pertaining to the Samvatsara, the Parivatsara, the Idāvatsara, the Anuvatsara, and the Udāvatsara—carry us across; may we, free from debt, attain this day, this very day.

"May Prajāpati produce offspring for us"—this is the sixth [verse]. (21) He cuts portions together from the cake on one potsherd for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and for the *iḍā*. (22) The sacrificer eats of the *iḍā*. (23) "That very barley, mixed with honey, which they ploughed upon the banks of the Sarasvatī—Indra, the lord of the hundred powers, was the master of the plough, and the Maruts, the bounteous givers, were the ploughmen."

Thus for the barley (24): "O gods, you have brought us prosperity; through you as our protection, may we attain well-being. As one who brings joy, you have entered into us like a father; be auspicious to our offspring and to our bodies. Thus for the rice (25): "May Agni eat first, for he knows how the oblation is; may he, who dwells among all people, make the plants auspicious for us."

Thus [is the sacrifice] of śyāmāka grains in the spring; for bamboo-yavas, [the same applies]. (26) A first-born calf is the sacrificial fee. (27) Having sacrificed with śyāmāka while desiring food, one should give a brownish-pink young bull and a garment. (28)

If one’s sacrificial fires become unsuccessful after they have been established, he should fast on the preceding full-moon day and offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. On the full-moon day, he should release the fires while they are blazing. The re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) has been explained by means of the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya). We shall now enumerate the modifications. According to the traditional teaching, [the establishment of the fires] takes place during the rainy season or in autumn under the asterisms of Punarvasu or Anurādhā. Among the ritual materials, he should include *upolapa* grass instead of ordinary *darbha* grass. This has been fully prescribed; this has been fully prescribed.

With the three verses beginning, "That which you, being angry, scattered with fury," he kindles [the fire] three times. With the verse, "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again," he offers six continuous oblations before the *pūrṇāhuti*. There is an offering on five potsherds for Agni; the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings contain the *vibhakti* formulas, and the two *ājyabhāga* portions are dedicated to Agni. Before the *prayāja* offerings, he offers an oblation with the verse, "Return with strength. At the time of giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), a garment that has been mended and a chariot that has been renewed are to be given.

Furthermore, a bull that has been set free, a golden ornament weighing one hundred *mānas*, and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) pertaining to the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) [are given]. 11. After the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), he offers four oblations with the formula: "Return together with wealth. 12. In the case of an unintentional interruption, he should not perform the kindling verses (*samindhanī*). 13. The introductory offering (*ārambhaṇīyā*) is required everywhere; the introductory offering is required everywhere. 14.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Mānava Sūtra concerning the rites prior to the *Soma* sacrifice.

One who is about to begin the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, having fasted on the preceding full-moon day, offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara and a pap of cooked rice to Pārjanya. When he is about to carry forward the waters, he offers an oblation after mentally reciting the Pañcahotṛ formula. A milch cow and a draft ox are the sacrificial fees. The sacrifice concludes when it is completed. One should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice on ground sloping toward the east, on the full moon of Phālguna or Caitra, or in the spring. During the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the sacrificer does not have his hair and beard shaved on the day of fasting.

Having fetched a branch from one who has undertaken the vow, he drives away the calves with [the formula]: "Swell up, O inviolable ones, as a portion for all the gods. He sends forth the cows. The *prastara* is provided with blossoms.

The fuel and the sacrificial grass are tied in three parts; he ties two parts silently, and the third remains untied. When he ties [the grass] in one part with a mantra, he ties the fuel silently. (9) The milking is the same. (10) When the three [cows] have been milked, having said three times, "Milk much! An oblation for all the gods!", he releases his speech. (11) "I anoint you, a portion for all the gods, with Soma," [with these words] he anoints it. (12) The procedure is established up to the employment of the vessels. (13) He employs the potsherds for the *caru* offering.

He places a second vessel for clarified butter and a spoon for the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) immediately after the upabhṛt ladle. 14. [The procedure] is established up to the pouring out of the grains. 15. He pours out five offerings, beginning with "To Agni, an eight-potherd cake," [then] "To the Maruts, those possessing their own strength, a seven-potherd cake," and "To Heaven and Earth, a one-potherd cake. 16. [The procedure] is established up to the placing of the grains upon the potsherds. 17. Prior to the placing of the grains, he causes the rice-grains for the cooked offering (caru) to be brought forward. 18. Having poured the grains onto the potsherds, he places the potsherds down. 19. He causes the morning milk to be milked. 20. From the purified flour, he causes the portion for Pūṣan to be brought forward. 21.

Pūṣan is the recipient of the flour-portion in the *caru* offerings everywhere (22). He places the sacrificial oblations (*haviṣ*) on the fire in successive order (23). Having placed the *māruta* [oblation] on the fire, he brings the evening milk into the heated morning milk and prepares the *āmikṣā* (clotted curd) (24). By this, the preparation of the *āmikṣā* is explained for all cases (25). Having set aside the clarified butter (*ājya*), he pours out the curds for the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter), which shares the same ritual characteristics as the *ājya* (26). The procedure is established up to the wiping of the ladles (*sruc*) (27). The wiping of the *upabhṛt* and the *pṛṣadājyadhānī* (the vessel for holding the spotted butter) is the same (28). The procedure is established up to the taking of the portions of *ājya* (29).

Having spread a double layer [of ghee] in the *pṛṣadājya* vessel, having brought the curds, and pouring [ghee] over it once, he makes it speckled (*pṛṣat*). (30) In the rainy season, he should spread [the ghee] once and pour [ghee] over it twice. (31) The procedure for the *ājya*s is established up to their placement. (32) The placing of the *upabhṛt* and the *pṛṣadājya* vessel is the same. (33) The procedure is established up to the removal from the fire. (34) Prior to the pouring of ghee, having made the *āmikṣā* without whey (*avājina*), he places the whey (*vājina*) on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). (35) Having adorned them, he lifts the sacrificial offerings (*haviṣ*) one after another in succession. (36)

Success comes from the touching [of the fire-drills]. (37) Before the touching, he proceeds with the *nirmanthya* fire. (38) Behind the western junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he places a piece of wood for churning (*adhimanthana-śakala*) with the formula, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni. (39) With the formula, "Ye two are the testicles," he places two blades of *darbha* grass there, pointing eastward, with their ends uncut; then, with the formula, "Thou art Urvaśī," he places the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*) upon them with its tufts facing north and its procreative part toward the west, and the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) at the base with its tufts facing north, saying, "Thou art Āyu"; he then moistens the cavity of the clarified butter vessel three times with the formula, "Thou art a woman. (40) Purūravas...

He joins [the kindling wood] eighty times (41). He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words, "Recite for the fire being churned" (42). He churns [the fire] three times clockwise with the formulas, "Thou art the Gāyatrī; thou art the Triṣṭubh; thou art the Jagatī" (43). When [the fire] has been produced, he recites, "For Agni, the born one" (44). While it is being cast forward, he recites, "For Agni, being cast forward" (45). Having brought [the fire] along the front of the northern enclosing stick while the sacrificer maintains contact [with him], and causing the sacrificer to recite, "May you two be of one mind for us," he casts it forward with the formula ending in *svāhā* and throws a wooden chip into the fire (46) with the verse, "Agni moves within Agni."
He makes an offering with the *sruva* ladle (47). Having set down the full *sruva*, he touches the *Cāturmāsya* offerings with the *Pañcahotṛ* formula (48).

The rite is established up to the *prayāja* offerings. (1) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he performs nine *prayāja* offerings. (2) Having offered three, he pours the butter together; having offered three, he pours it together again; having offered two, he pours all the butter together; having offered one, he steps across and pours clarified butter over the oblations in regular order, ending with the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), but not from the *upabhṛt* ladle. (3) The rite is established up to the performance of the main offering. (4) He proceeds with the *upāṃśu* [offering] and the cake on one potsherd for Savitṛ. (5) The rite is established up to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. (6) Prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt*, [he offers] with the names of the months beginning with "To Madhu, svāhā! and so forth.

He offers oblations: four at the Vaiśvadeva, four at the Varuṇapraghāsas, four at the Sākamedhas, and one at the Śunāsīrya. At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the first-born calf is the fee. The procedure is established up to the after-offerings (*anuyāja*). Having poured speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) into the *juhū* ladle, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* and performs nine after-offerings. Together with the *upabhṛt* ladle containing the *vājavatī* formula, he holds the *pṛṣadājya-dhānī* vessel; he separates it, lifts it up, and casts it out. [He addresses] the two ends of the altar-bench (*vedi*) with the words: "You two are the butter-smeared ones; protect the two shoulders of the sacrificer."

He releases the two *sruva*-ladles. 12. Standing within the altar (*antarvedi*) with the *sruc* or the cup (*camasa*) held upwards, he pours water along the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and draws the *vājina* (the whey). 13. He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the call, "Recite for the *vājins*! 14. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he gives the direction, "Sacrifice to the *vājins*! 15. Having offered at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* calls, he sacrifices to the quarters with the remnants, saying "To the quarters, svāhā! beginning from the eastern part of the quarters and proceeding clockwise; with the fifth [offering] in the middle, and with the sixth in the eastern part. 16. Having divided the remainder into equal portions...

Having said, "Invite the many," [the priests respond] either with "We have been invited" or "Invite [us]. Then the officiating priests and the sacrificer consume [the remains], reciting: "May the drops enter me; may the juices of the vessels enter my veins. With my own essence, fill my essence. May the vigorous ones carry my sacrifice."

The *hotṛ* eats first. (18) This is established up to the *samiṣṭayajus*. (19) Having twice replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, he offers two *samiṣṭayajus* oblations with the formulas: "This is your sacrifice" and "O gods, you who know the way. (20) The sacrificer says, "May I attain well-being for the coming year. (21) The sacrifice is completed as established. (22) Having immediately concluded the Full Moon sacrifice: "Truth indeed is the Supreme Lord; truth nothing whatsoever transgresses. Upon truth the ocean is set; by truth the earth is made firm."

With a sharp flame, O Agni, heat the head that has been seized by the *uṣṇih* and placed within the fervor of Vaiśvānara’s splendor. By means of the *ṛta*, turn it back; by means of the *satya*, turn it around; by means of austerity, follow it along; by means of what is auspicious, bring it near; by means of what is efficacious, turn it toward [the goal].

With this verse, "Thus with the three-spotted porcupine quill and the iron razor," he turns [the hair] back; he shaves the hair and the beard. Then the sacrificer mutters: "That is Ṛta, that is Satya; may I be able through it, may I be capable through it, may I succeed through it, may it be successful for me. For four months he does not eat meat, he does not approach a woman, and he does not sit on high ground. He should avoid untruth and sleep facing the east. He eats honey and approaches his wife during her season.

The Varuṇapraghāsa offerings take place during four months. 1. The procedure is like that of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. 2. There are five [portions] of the *saṃcaras*. 3. The Pratiprasthātṛ drives away the calves for the offering to Marut, and the Adhvaryu does so for the offering to Varuṇa. 4. They separately bind together the fuel and the sacrificial grass.

The Pratiprasthātṛ, having once donned his sacrificial girdle, causes the two milkings to be performed separately at the appropriate times. The procedure is established up to the employment of the vessels. The Pratiprasthātṛ employs separate vessels: five *sruk* ladles, with the *sruva* spoon as the fifth; two *caru*-pots; the wooden sword (*sphya*); and the *veda* grass-bundle. The procedure is established up to the pouring out of the oblation materials. Having poured out the five common offerings, the Adhvaryu pours out the cake for Indra and Agni on twelve potsherds and the cake for Ka on one potsherd. At the appropriate times, they each prepare their respective portions of *āmikṣā* curd-mixture separately.

Success! From the preparation [of the site] onwards: having placed a coating of flour in front of the Āhavanīya fire, at a distance of three steps or in an unlimited space, he fixes the *pṛṣṭhya* peg; then, beginning with the taking up of the *veda*, he prepares the altar—six *śaya*s long from east to west, four *śaya*s broad behind, and three *śaya*s broad in front. In the eastern half of the altar, at a distance of one-third [from the front], he prepares the *uttaravedi*, one *aratni* high and marked on four sides. Having dug up a space of one step in front of the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) and sprinkled it, he marks out the *cātvāla* with a yoke-pin.

He measures it out: "Thou art the path for me to heat," on the south; "Thou art the path for me to find wealth," on the west; "Protect what is distressed for me," on the north; "Protect what is afflicted," on the east. With the formula, "O Agni Aṅgiras," facing westward, he strikes the *cātvāla* pit with the wooden sword (*sphyá*) from the east. With the formula, "Come hither by the name of Āyu," he takes the *pām̐sūn* (earth) in his hand. Facing eastward, he pours it down upon the *uttaravedī* with the formulas beginning, "May the Vasus carry thee."

"That which is on the second [line]"—this is the second; "that which is on the third"—this is the third. The rest is the same, and the fourth is performed silently. (18) Having dug straight down to the depth of the knee and making it square, he pours [earth] onto the high altar (*uttaravedi*) with the formula: "O Agni, find the name 'Sky' which is yours. (19) He prepares the high altar with the formula: "Thou art the boundary-mark; thou art the sovereign queen. (20) In its center, he makes a square navel (*nābhi*) measuring one span (*prādeśa*). (21) He sprinkles it with water with the formula: "Be purified for the gods! (22) [He sprinkles it] with sand with the formula: "Be beautified for the gods! (23)

He encourages [the sacrificer] with the words, "O waters, carry away the impurity. From above the navel, he causes the water to flow out toward the northeast. The Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the southern altar at a distance of one cubit from the northern boundary-line. Both [altars] are level and oriented toward the east.

He should arrange it so that the oblations may fit together; thus there are twenty-six [bricks]. (26) There is one rubbish-heap. (27) To the west of the northern [post], he carries away the *stambayajus* (the sacrificial grass from the stump). (28) Having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters, facing eastward, he sprinkles the high altar (*uttaravedi*) with the formulas beginning, "May Indra’s roar protect thee in front with the Vasus," while moving clockwise around it with the subsequent [formulas]. (29) Having completed the circuit, he pours out the remainder of the water to the south of the high altar with the formula, "Thou art the portion of the Pitṛs. (30) Having placed gold in between...

With the fivefold-seized butter, he sprinkles the navel with the formulas beginning, "Thou art the lion, the subduer of rivals, svāhā!"—[namely] on the right shoulder, the left hip, the right hip, the left shoulder, and the fifth time in the middle. (31) With the formula, "For the beings, thee," he holds the ladle upwards. (32) They two place back the fire-bringing implements into the Āhavanīya fire. (33) He encloses the navel with pieces of *pūtudāru* wood.

With the formula, "Thou art the life of all," he places the middle one; with "Thou art firmly established," the southern one; and with "Thou art of unshakable foundation," the northern one. (34) He pours down the ritual materials with the formulas, "Thou art the ash of Agni" and "Thou art the soil of Agni": namely, purified wood, guggulu resin, erka-wood, and fragrant *tejana* grass; and a tuft of wool from between the horns of a bull that has not previously been castrated. (35) With the verse, "The radiant, great [Soma] shall drink," he touches the ritual materials. (36) From the *cātvāla* pit, the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the supporting hearths (*upayamanī*) from the earth of the altar mound (*vedipurīṣa*). (37) For Agni...

"Recite for [the fire] being led forward," he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite. When it has been recited three times, they lift up the implements for the leading forward of the fires. The Adhvaryu, having handed them to the Āgnīdhra, [recites]: "Whatever sin we have committed against you, O Purifier, whether as one who was previously present but now becomes absent, may you increase your body with clarified butter; do not harm me when I have approached you from the front. Svāhā!"

Thus he offers the remaining oblations. 40. Taking up the implements for carrying forward the fire, they carry it forth with the verse: "Go forward along the eastern direction, O wise one. 41. While the verse "The woolly one" is being recited, [he recites]: "The sacrifice has stood up in the favor of thoughts; where the sages bring many [offerings], find long life for the sacrificer; sit down for great good fortune."

Having sprinkled water, the Pratiprasthātṛ places the fire in the middle of the eastern half of the southern altar-pile with the materials, [saying]: "Like Manu, we set thee down; like Manu, we kindle thee. O Agni Aṅgiras, like Manu, offer the oblation with *svāhā* to the gods for the god-seeking sacrificer."

Thus they two place the two fuel-sticks. 43. With the formula, "O Agni, thou art the nest," he scatters the supporting earth (upayamanī) to the south of the Āhavanīya fire. 44. Having strewn around the two Āhavanīya fires with two rows of grass-bunches (ulaparāji), they both offer the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti) with the verse, "Seven are thy fuel-sticks, O Agni. 45. The Pratiprasthātṛ, from above the northern buttock of the southern altar, cuts once with the wooden sword (sphya); [the Adhvaryu] cuts from the southern shoulder of the northern altar. 46. They perform their respective duties separately. 47. The Adhvaryu gives the directions (praiṣas). 48. [The formulas for] the flour-smears (piṣṭalepa).

Having led [the fire] forward, they perform the two subsequent enclosures (parigraha). 49. The procedure up to the taking of the clarified butter (ājya) is established. 50. He takes four portions of clarified butter, each mixed with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya). 51. The procedure up to the placing of the clarified butter is established. 52.

To the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, the *pratiprasthātṛ* prepares the *karambha* vessels from barley flour mixed with curds; they are made in a single row, each about the size of a thumb-joint, as many as there are members of the sacrificer’s household plus one. Having filled them with *śamī* leaves, he places them in a winnowing basket. Having made a ram, he makes a ewe; the *pratiprasthātṛ* makes as many female forms as there are male ones that can be accommodated. They wash the wool and attach it [to the figures]. There are more than a hundred and more than a thousand [of these] in front.

5. They scatter *śamī* leaves. 6. Having caused [the fires] to be announced, they place portions of the two curd-masses (*āmikṣā*) into two vessels. 7. Having set aside the scrapings for Varuṇa, they pour the flour of *karīra* fruits into the two milk-preparations (*payasyā*). 8. He places a ram into the vessel for the Maruts and a ewe into that for Varuṇa. 9. While setting them down, they transpose them: those with Indra-Agni as the sixth are on the northern side; the one for the Maruts is on the southern side; the one for Varuṇa is on the northern side; in both cases, there is a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) prepared from fire-drifted wood. 10. The procedure is established up to the wiping. 11. It has been wiped.
To the north, at the edge of the Gārhapatya fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ asks: "O wife, how many husbands do you have? If you speak falsely, your most beloved husband shall perish."

Whatever [portion] he points out, he should say, "May Varuṇa seize that! (11). The wife says, "We invoke the Praghāsya [deities]" (12). Taking the vessels of *karambha* porridge, she passes behind the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) to the south, and together with him, they stand facing west in front of the southern fire, having placed the winnowing basket upon their heads. (13). Standing to the north, the sacrificer mutters, "O Indra, do not [forsake] us" (14). With the winnowing basket, they offer the *karambha* vessels while reciting, "What in the village, what in the forest... (15). [The Hotṛ recites: "The performers of the rite have performed the rite... (16).

16. They step across. 17. The offering for the *dakṣiṇāgni* is completed up to the choosing of the *pravara*. 18. The *adhvaryu* chooses the *pravara*. 19. [The ritual] is completed up to the performance of the offerings. 20. Having performed the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, the *pratiprasthātṛ* waits upon [the fire]. 21. The *adhvaryu* proceeds with the offerings for Indra-Agni and the six [deities]. 22. The *pratiprasthātṛ*, giving the command, proceeds with the offering for the Maruts. 23. With the first cutting-off portion of that [offering], the *adhvaryu* cuts off the female sheep; with the second, he cuts off the male sheep for Varuṇa. Having performed the offering with the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*), [he recites] the names of the months.

He offers the oblation (juhoti) at both [sacrifices]. (24) At both, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *iḍā* are common. (25) A pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (26) [The ritual] is established up to the *vājina* offering. (27) Both proceed with the *vājina* offerings. (28) Having brought together the remnants, they consume them. (29) [The ritual] is established up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. (30) The *adhvaryu* performs the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with modification; he causes the wife to recite with modification; the sacrificer consecrates with the formula with modification. (31) [The ritual] is established up to the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings. (32) Having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle three times, [he says]: "O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; this is your sacrifice."

With the verse, "O gods, you who know the way," he offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations; the Pratiprasthātṛ [offers] in the southern [fire]. (33) Having poured together the remnants of the clarified butter, the Adhvaryu takes the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles and the butter-pot; the Pratiprasthātṛ [takes] the husk-remains; the Āgnīdhra [takes] the *sruc*; the Adhvaryu [takes] the [other] *sruc*. (34) As they proceed from the *cātvāla* pit, they mutter the verse, "For King Varuṇa has made wide space. (35) Having looked at the waters with the verse, "A hundred [are yours], O King," they proceed to the *avabhṛtha* bath while standing. (36) Having thrown grass into still waters, he offers the oblation into the water. (37)

With the verse, "The face of Agni," he pours the *sruva*-ladle's *āghāra* libation from the fourfold-drawn butter (38). He performs the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings excluding the *barhis* grass (39). Having proceeded with the two *ājyabhāga* portions, he takes a cutting from the husks and the scrapings and sacrifices to Varuṇa; with the remainder, he sacrifices to Agnīvaruṇa in the place of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering (40). That concludes the rite (41). At the untying, they pour out water with the words, "The noose of Varuṇa is untied"; they cast it away with the words, "The noose of Varuṇa is thrown back."

"Obeisance to the noose of Varuṇa"—with these words they pay homage (42). With the three verses beginning "From every station," they cleanse themselves outside the cow-pen (43). Without looking back, they return (44). From that very place, they bring two pieces of fuel (45). He places a piece of fuel with the formula, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper through thee"; the second he places with, "Thou art kindling; may we thrive through thee" (46). They worship the Gārhapatya fire with the verse, "Today I have walked along the waters," while the wife does so silently (47). They throw the two blades of sacrificial grass into the fire (48). "I invoke the prosperity of the full year," he says.

The sacrificer [performs the rite]. (49) The *siddheṣṭi* is concluded. (50) "Immediately from the full moon," [the sacrificer] says, "I invoke the prosperity (*svasti*) for the year. (49) The *siddheṣṭi* is concluded. (50) Having immediately completed the full-moon sacrifice, [he recites]: "That which Dharma turned around from the end of the earth, by that sacred formula (*brahman*) I turn [it] back for life. (51) "Agni with his sharp flame... and so forth; the rest is the same. (52)

The Sākamedha sacrifices take place after four months. Having fasted on the preceding full moon day, he offers an eight-potherd cake to Agni Anīkavant in the morning. When the sacrifice is completed, it concludes; he does not throw the sacrificial grass (barhis) into the fire. At the Gṛhamedhīya rite, the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) are offered silently.

With a branch of the *palāśa* tree, he drives away all the calves. 5. At midday, there is a *caru* offering for the Maruts Sāṃtapanas. 6. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used for that belongs to the Ānīkavata sacrifice. 7. The sacrifice concludes once it is completed. 8. He throws the sacrificial grass into the fire. 9. For the Gṛhamedhīya rite, he binds together the fuel and the sacrificial grass, excluding the *prastara* and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). 10. When the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, he cooks rice porridge with the milk of all the cows for the Maruts Gṛhamedhas. 11. He causes the cows to be milked without strainers. 12. He pours out the clarified butter (*ājya*). 13.

He places the fuel and the sacrificial grass (idhmābarhis) down; he cleans the offering-spoon and the dipping-spoon (sruk-sruva); he causes the wife to stand near with a mantra; having sprinkled the fuel and the sacrificial grass, having strewn around the Āhavanīya fire, he encloses it with pieces of wood for the fuel; he sets down the scrapings of the frying-pan (śaraṇiṣkāṣa); having spread an underlayer of ghee, he draws out three portions of boiled rice; he decorates them with purified butter; he places the clarified butter to the west of the Āhavanīya fire, facing north; having added fuel to the fire and performed the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga), he takes a portion from all [the offerings], pours ghee over it, and...

"Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhas," he says, causing [the Hotṛ] to recite. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he gives the direction: "Sacrifice to the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhas. The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is unexpressed (*anirukta*).
