Having taken portions together in the southern [ladle] and having invited [the gods] to the *iḍā*, they shall consume it. Having anointed them with clarified butter, they become well-satisfied by the Gṛhamedhīya [oblation]. There may also be another rice-mess as a neighbor's portion.

The ministers of that [king] become well-satisfied (27). Cows with their calves dwell there, except for the barren cow (abhivānyā) (28). Before the morning Agnihotra, one should offer a full ladle on the Gārhapatya fire with these two verses, "Give me a full ladle" and "O Śarā," having summoned a bellowing bull while offering from a vessel filled with the scrapings of the rice-gruel (śara-niṣkāṣa) (29). If the bull does not bellow, one should offer after addressing the Brahman priest (30). After the morning Agnihotra has been offered, [one should offer] a cake on seven potsherds to the sporting Maruts, together with the rays.

When the rays have risen, he proceeds with the eight offerings beginning with "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni" and ending with "for Viśvakarman," which he carries forward across the northern altar as was done during the Varuṇapraghāsa rites. He pours the *āghāra* libation from the *sruc* ladle using the fourfold-drawn butter with the mantra, "O Agni, [know] the office of the Hotṛ. Prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers the oblations named after the months. A bull is the sacrificial fee.

Following the ancient southern practice, they perform the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña). They cut the sacrificial grass (barhis) near its base, except for the prastara bundle. Having bound together a greater quantity of fuel and grass and having strewn the two [mounds] around, he sets out the vessels one by one, with the exception of the prāśitra-vessel. He places the praṇītā waters to the south-east of the southern fire. He heats [the grains] over the southern fire. To the south of the fire, he pours out the oblation-grains from the agniṣṭha vessel.

[He prepares] a cake on six potsherds for Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs; barley-grains for the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad); barley-grains for the Pitṛs consumed by Agni (agniṣvātta); and a stirred drink (mantha) for the Pitṛs. 6. [The preparation] up to the placing on the fire is established [as already described]. 7. While the grains are being roasted, he carries fire around them. 8. He grinds half of the roasted grains for the stirred drink. 9. [The preparation] up to the covering with grass is established [as already described]. 10. Having set aside the flour-dust, he makes an altar in front of the southern fire, at a distance of three steps or in an unlimited space, measuring one man's height, square, and leveled toward the cardinal directions. 11.

He encloses [the altar] from the northern enclosing-stick (parigrāha). He makes the door toward the northern buttock (śroṇi). Having sprinkled a single firebrand from the Dakṣiṇāgni, having placed it in the middle of the altar, having added fuel to it, having swept around it, having sprinkled water around it, and having poured out the flour-residue, he encloses the northern enclosing-stick. The procedure up to the taking of the clarified butter (ājya) is established. He takes four portions of clarified butter at the edge of the Gārhapatya fire. The procedure up to the spreading of the grass is established. Having shaken the sacrificial grass (barhis), he spreads it. He sweeps around it counter-clockwise (prasavya).

Having strewn [the grass] three times around [the fire], he silently takes up the *prastara* from the north. 19. With a stalk of sugarcane, he stirs a mash of curdled milk from the milk of a cow that has recently calved into a half-vessel, [stirring] counter-clockwise; he does not remove the stalk. 20. Having adorned each one, he brings forward the water-jar, the clarified butters, the oblations, and likewise the other sacrificial implements. 21. [The ritual proceeds] successfully until the kindling of the fire. 22. There is a single *sāmidhenī* verse.

At its third *praṇava*, he places the fuel-stick once. (23) [The rite] is established up to the *pravara* invocation. (24) He does not perform the *pravara*. (25) He performs the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings excluding the *barhis* grass. (26) Having proceeded with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, they turn the sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) inside out so that they become *prācīnāvīta*. (27) The officiating priests move about according to their respective positions.

Having circumambulated from the front of the Hotṛ, who has been highly honored, he sits down to the north; the Adhvaryu sits behind the Hotṛ, to the west of him. 28. The Āgnīdhra carries the oblations around. 29. Each is placed in its proper place: the *juhū* in the middle, the *upabhṛt* and the *dhruvā* to the south. 30. Each is placed in its proper place: the *puroḍāśa* in the middle, the parched grains (*dhānā*) and the stirred drink (*mantha*) to the south. He cuts off [the portions] five times.

Six times for the son of Jamadagni (31). Having stepped past the handles of the offering-spoons toward the north, he causes [the Adhvaryu] to recite, "Recite the invitatory verse for Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā! He causes [the Āgnīdhra] to respond, "Om, svadhā! and [the Āgnīdhra] responds, "Let there be svadhā! (32). When the response has been given, he issues the direction, "Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā! (33). When "svadhā namaḥ" has been uttered, standing to the south, he makes the offering in the middle. (34) He proceeds in this same manner with the parched grains; likewise with the stirred drink. (35) He takes portions together for Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt.

If [the offering] of the five-fold portion is performed twice or thrice, he offers it in the southern and eastern halves of the fire-altar while it is still unattached. Having circumambulated, they loosen their *prācīnāvīta* garments and put them on as *yajñopavīta* garments. The officiating priests circumambulate back.

He distributes the oblations. (39) Having taken a portion of the remnants of the *mantha* offering, they invoke the *iḍā* but do not consume it. (40) Having proceeded with the *samidh* offerings, he performs two after-offerings (*anuyāja*): for the first he says, “Sacrifice to the gods,” and for the last, “Sacrifice! (41) He holds up all the offering-spoons (*sruk*). (42) Having offered the two oblations belonging to the *Dakṣiṇāgni*, he releases the potsherds. (43) From the water-offering with joined palms onwards, the rite is established as in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, except for the oblations. (44) They perform the water-rites using the water from the water-pitcher. (45) Having brought together the *iḍā*.

He places the rice-balls on the corners [of the altar], naming three ancestors beyond the great-grandfather, from that one downward. (46) On the northern hip of the altar, he wipes off the smearings. (47) Saying, "O Fathers, rejoice here," they go out from the enclosed space. (48) With the verse, "Thee, who art fair to behold, we [approach]," they pay homage to the Āhavanīya fire; at the end of each mantra, they conclude with the syllable *praṇava*.

With the verse, "That which is the intermediate space," he addresses the Gārhapatya fire (49). With the verse, "The fathers have rejoiced," they enter the enclosed space (50). From the wool-fiber onwards, the procedure is established as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña (51). With the verse, "Go forth, O Soma-loving fathers," he goes around the fire three times from right to left, sprinkling water from a water-pot (52). Having set down the water each time, he goes back around three times without sprinkling (53). Having thrown the rice-balls into the fire, he sweeps around the altar (54). From the verse, "They have eaten, they have rejoiced," onwards, the procedure is the same (55).

To the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, he bakes the cakes on single potsherds (*ekakapāla*), as many as there are vessels of porridge (*karambha-pātra*). Having silently sprinkled them with clarified butter, he removes them toward the north. From the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire, they carry away a smoking brand toward the east-northeast, without looking back. There, in that direction, they place the single-potsherd cakes in a sack. With the formula, "O Rudra, I make the rat your animal," he throws a single [cake] into a rat-hole. Having placed the brand at a crossroads, having kindled a fire upon it, swept around it, sprinkled water around it, and strewn grass around it, [he places the cake] in the middle leaf.

Having taken portions from all [the offerings] together and having sprinkled them with clarified butter, he offers [the oblation] with the formula: "This, O Rudra, is thy portion. (5) Having taken [the portions] separately, they walk around three times with the three verses beginning, "O Mother Rudrā, we have appeased thee," and so too a woman desiring a husband. (6) They mutter: "As a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, not from immortality."

"May I be released from death, not from my husband," says one who desires a husband. Having thrown them up repeatedly, [the priests] say, "Thou art Bhaga; may we obtain Bhaga," and they take hold of them. They pour them together for the sacrificer and for the woman desiring a husband. Having placed them in a cloth, he hangs them on a tree with the formula, "O Rudra, this is thy portion. The verse beginning with "From every abode" has already been explained. He should offer a pap of rice cooked in ghee to Āditya. Having returned home, the sacrificer says, "I invoke the prosperity that returns year by year. The sacrifice is completed.

It concludes. 14. Having concluded the full-moon sacrifice immediately, [he says]: "He who, from above this earth's surface, causes the plants to turn back—by that sacred formula (*brahman*) of his, I cause [the disease] to turn back for the sake of life. 15. "Agni with his sharp flame," etc.; the rest is the same. 16.

The Śunāsīrīya sacrifice is performed after four months, either immediately, after four days, or at the end of the month; this has been explained by the rules for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. There are eight offerings beginning with "A cake on eight potsherds for Agni" and ending with "A cake on one potsherd for Sūrya. Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers oblations with the names of the months. The sacrificial fee is a plough with twelve yokes, or a bull that has pulled the plough. The sacrificer says, "May I obtain well-being for the coming year and the past year. The sacrifice concludes once it is completed. Having immediately concluded the Full Moon sacrifice, [the procedure] by which the months [are established]...

The half-months, the seasons, and the years—by that [formula] with which they turn back for Prajāpati when he has sacrificed, by that sacred word (*brahman*) do I turn him back so that he may live. (8) "May Agni with his sharp flame... and so forth; the rest is the same as up to the *vrata* [observances]. (9) The sacrificer has all his hair and beard shaved off. (10) On the following full-moon day, he should sacrifice with Soma or with an animal victim. (11) Now follow the five-year [cycle]. (12) The *vaiśvānarapārjanya* [offering] is the common framework (*tantra*). (13) The first year is well-known [as the *saṃvatsara*]. (14)

On the full moon that precedes its end, he observes the fast for the Śunāsīrya sacrifice; on the one that follows, the fast for the Vaiśvadeva. (14) The second year is established in the same manner. (15) Likewise the third. Having omitted one month, he should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva. (16) The fourth year is established in the same manner. (17) Likewise the fifth. For that [fifth year], the Śunāsīrya takes place every five months, following upon the Sākamedhas.
(18) Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Mānava-Śrautasūtra concerning the rites prior to the Soma sacrifice.

One who is about to sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Indra and Agni recites the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula mentally and offers it, saying: "Vāc is the Hotṛ, Dīkṣā is the wife, the Waters are the Adhvaryu, Vāta is the Abhigara, Prāṇa is the oblation, Manas is the Brahman; I offer this into austerity, svāhā! He then prepares an offering on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, or he offers a full-oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Having offered it into the Āhavanīya fire while reciting, "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely," he approaches the sacrificial post, which is made of Palāśa, Khadira, or Rohītaka wood.

[He chooses] a tree made of *bailva* wood for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Having passed by those trees that are not suitable for sacrificial posts, he chooses a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with the formula: "I have gone beyond others; I have not approached others. [The post should be] many-branched, many-leaved, with an unwithered top, without hollows, without side-branches growing upward, straight, with vertical bark-shavings, and sloping downward at the top toward the northeast. Its casting [into the ground] may be toward the east, north, east, or west. With the formula, "For Viṣṇu, thee," he anoints it all around with clarified butter, either where the bark is joined or where the bark-shavings meet. With the formula, "O herb, protect him," he places a blade of *darbha* grass between [the post and the ground] at the southern end of the post.

"O Svadhiti, do not harm him," with these words he strikes with the axe. (7) He catches the first chip as it flies up. (8) The carpenter cuts [the wood] so as not to strike his own body; he fells the stump. (9) "Thee whom this [axe]," with these words, he causes it to fall toward the east. (10) "Do not harm the sky with its tip," with these words, he consecrates it as it falls. (11) "O Vanaspati, grow with a hundred shoots," with these words, he offers an oblation on the stump. (12) "May we grow with a thousand shoots," with these words, he touches himself. (13) [He prepares] an eight-edged [post].

He makes the top-knot (gopuccha) neither too thick nor too thin, with its base smoothed. 14. Its measurement is prescribed as starting from five *aratnis*. 15. He should make for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) a *svaru* and a *caṣāla*; the *caṣāla* should be of the width of a span, eight-cornered, and attached in the middle. 16. The corners [of the post] are to be joined by the corners [of the *caṣāla*]; one should make the *svaru* of the post one finger-breadth higher than the *caṣāla*. 17. For one who has undertaken the vow, he binds together the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); the *prastara* is made of *aśvavāla* grass, the two *vidhṛtis* likewise, and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are made of *kārṣmarya* wood.

He prepares the altar with fuel-sticks of *śamī* wood, measuring eighteen [prādeśas], according to the dimensions of the northern altar used for the Vāruṇapraghāsa sacrifice. Having performed the rites up to the removal [of the fires], they dwell there. On the following day, having washed his hands and strewn around the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), he sets out the vessels belonging to the animal sacrifice: first the spade, then a branch of the *plakṣa* tree that has grown upward, the two omentum-roasting spits, the two ropes, the spit, the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, the vessel for cooking the cut-off portions (*avadāna*), the *svaru*, and the axe. From the sprinkling of the high altar (*uttaravedi*) onwards, the procedure is established up to the full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*).

He sets out the vessels containing *pṛṣadājya* (clotted butter). Having strewn the sacrificial grass with its tips pointing toward the north, he sprinkles the vessels with water purified by the *yajus*-formula, pours out the curd and clarified butter, and carries fire around them. He performs the second tracing of the altar. The procedure up to the taking of the portions of clarified butter is established. He takes four portions of clarified butter mixed with *pṛṣadājya*. The procedure up to the setting down of the clarified butter is established.

To the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, [the priest] takes up the spade with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... (TS 1.3.1.a). He consecrates it with: "Thou art a spade; thou art a woman" (TS 1.3.1.b). With the formula: "Here I cut off the neck of the Rākṣasa," he draws a line around the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭa*) in front of the *āhavanīya* fire. A second time with: "Here I [cut off] him who is my equal," and a third time with: "He who is not my equal. The rest is the same, and the fourth time is done silently. He digs half of it within the altar and half outside the altar, digging as deep as the upper part [of the post]. Having washed the sacrificial post...

Having carried it along the sacrificial path, he places it facing eastward upon the ground strewn in front of the post-hole; first, the root [of the tree], then the *svaru* in the middle, the girdle, and finally the top-ring at the tip. Having thrown barley-grains into the water, he sprinkles the sacrificial post with water.

With the words, "For the earth, thee," he [places] the base; with "For the intermediate space, thee," the middle; with "For heaven, thee," the top. 6. With the words, "May the worlds, the seats of the fathers, be purified," he sprinkles the hole for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭa*). 7. With the words, "Thou art barley," he scatters barley grains. 8. With the words, "I strew thee, the seat of the fathers, the world," he strews *darbha* grass. 9. With the words, "Thou art easy of access," he places the first splinter that has fallen out. 10. With the words, "Fill heaven and earth with clarified butter," he makes an oblation over it. 11. Having taken up the vessel of clarified butter and the dipping-spoon (*sruva*).

He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite: "Recite for the sacrificial post being anointed! (12) The sacrificer anoints the anointed [post] with honey, from the top down to the base, saying: "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey! and [he anoints] the *caṣāla* [wooden ring] saying: "Thou art Indra’s *caṣāla*. (13) He fixes it on, saying: "Make the plants bear good fruit! (14) He should not let go of the anointed [post] until the encircling with the cord. (15) He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite: "Recite for the sacrificial post being raised up! (16) He raises it up, saying: "Supporting the sky with its top! (17) He settles it, saying: "These are thy stations! (18) [And he recites: "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu! (19)

Thereafter, he places the fire-stand level behind [the altar], facing the fire, with its rear post (agniṣṭhā) toward the fire. 19. With the formula, "I pile thee around, winner of Brahman, winner of Kṣatra," he piles it around with clods of earth. 20. With the formula, "May the Brahman be firm, may the Kṣatra be firm," the sacrificer strokes it clockwise with the staff of Maitrāvaruṇa. 21. He sprinkles water around it. 22. There are two cords of darbha grass: one is double-stranded and two cubits long; the other is triple-stranded and three cubits long. 23. With the verse, "That highest step of Viṣṇu... and with the *svaru* chip, [he performs the rite] using the threefold cord.

He wipes the top of the sacrificial post three times upward. (24) He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the call, "Recite for the post being girt. (25) With the formula, "Thou art girt," he girds it three times at the height of the navel with a triple-stranded cord, each time moving further to the right. (26) At the height of a span, he draws the thinner end toward the thicker end. (27) Having pulled the cord upward, he draws the *svaru* over the uppermost loop on the side facing the fire, with the formula, "Upon the summit of heaven. (28) He issues the command, "Bring the bathed [animal]. (29) A goat is used unless otherwise prohibited.
Having led up by the ford a red bull, two-colored, with black marks, fat, symmetrical in limb, and with teeth fully grown, he makes it stand in front, facing west.

"O Prajāpati, these creatures that are being born and those that have already been born—make them known to him; may the wise one grant his approval. O Lord of Cattle, today I bind this animal for you, O Agni, in the midst of good deeds. Grant your approval; sacrifice with a well-performed sacrifice. May this offering be acceptable to the gods. With these words, he offers the two *aupākaraṇa* oblations. With "For food, thee," he takes two blades of darbha grass.

With the words, "Thou art the assistant," he touches a yellow Plakṣa branch provided with Palāśa leaves; then, with the words, "Approach the gods, O divine subjects," having touched [the victim] with two Darbha blades and the branch, and having brought it forward, he offers five oblations: "May the ancestors, knowing [him], receive him as he issues forth from the limbs as life-breath. Being offered, go by the paths traveled by the gods; take thy stand among the plants with thy bodies. [He offers for] those who were bound: "Those wild animals of many forms, though diverse in appearance, yet being manifold, are of one form."

"May the god Vāyu release you first, Prajāpati, bestowing you along with offspring. Of those animals over whom Paśupati is lord—both those that are four-footed and those that are two-footed—may they, being ransomed, go to their sacrificial portion; may the increase of wealth attend the sacrificer. Releasing the seed of the world, O gods, grant a path for the sacrificer. Having been brought forward from its place and having performed its service, may it, living, enter the domain of the gods. Having offered thus, he proceeds with the *nirmanthya* fire.

This has been explained. 3. With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the cord. 4. Having passed it around the right arm and wiped it upwards, with the words, "Thee, the divine oblation of Ṛta, with a noose," he fastens it across the head according to the respective deity. 5. With the words, "Be bold, O man," he binds it downwards to the north of the sacrificial post with the cord. 6. With the words, "For the waters, for the plants," he sprinkles it. 7. With the words, "May thy mother give her consent," he leads it [towards the water]. 8. With the words, "Thou art the drinker of the waters," he makes it drink water. 9. [With the words,] "Well-savored..."

Sprinkling with faith as his chest, he sprinkles [the victim] on all sides. (10) Having set down the full *sruva* ladle, the procedure is established up to the *āghāra* libation. (11) Having performed the *śrauca-āghāra* libation, he anoints the victim with the *juhū* ladle: with "United be thy breath, O Vāyu," at the place of the nostrils; with "United be the limbs of the worshipful one," at the shoulder-region; with "United be the lord of the sacrifice and his blessings," at the rump. (12) The procedure is established up to the *pravara*. (13) When the *pravara* has been invoked, he hands over to the Maitrāvaruṇa a staff made of *udumbara* wood reaching to his mouth, saying: "I give thee by the arms of Mitra and Varuṇa. (14)

Success! Up to the *prayāja* offerings [is the procedure]. (15) He issues the call for the announcement (*āśrāvaṇa*) and performs eleven *prayāja* offerings. (16) He gives the first command with "Prompt for the *samidh*s! and the subsequent ones with "Prompt, prompt! (17) Having brought together [the portions] at every fourth [offering], and having set aside one for the eleventh, he steps across, takes hold of the *svaru* and the axe, anoints them in the *juhū* ladle, and says, "Anointed with ghee, may you two protect the victim. Without touching it with the axe, he anoints the victim between its horns using the *svaru*. (18) From what has been cooked, he cuts off portions with the anointed [axe]; he dissects it with the unanointed one. (19) To the north of the *cātvāla* pit...

He makes a mark for the *śāmitra* fire (20). Having dug up [the ground] and sprinkled it with water, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite: "Recite for the fire being carried around" (21). Having placed the animal, the *āhavanīya* fire, the sacrificial post, and the clarified butter one by one from the *āhavanīya* onto the *utseka* (the fire-brand), and having placed them upon the mark for the *śāmitra*, he carries the fire around them three times (22). Having handed the fire-brand to the *āgnīdhra*, he offers three oblations with the verses: "Those who [are bound] while being bound," "Those who are wild," and "While being released" (23). Having released the animal from the sacrificial post and taken hold of it, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* (24). The response is given (*pratyāśruta*).

"O Hotṛ, having sent forth, offer the oblations to the gods," he thus gives the command. 25 The two omentum-roasting spits are made of *kārṣmarya* wood—one with a single prong and one with two prongs. With these two, the sacrificer, while reciting "O wealthy one, go forward," touches the animal from behind. 26 Reciting "The breast, the intermediate space," he causes it to step northward. 27 The Āgnīdhra, having carried a fire-brand in front, places it at the mark for the *śāmitra* (the place where the animal is slaughtered). 28 To the south-west of the *śāmitra*, he lays down a blade of *darbha* grass used for the preliminary rite (*aupākaraṇa*), reciting "May you be united with your body. Upon that, the slaughterer—

With its head toward the west and its feet toward the north, he causes it to be quieted within the heat: "May the life-breath of the sacrificer be distinct from that of the animal; may the sacrifice go with the gods along the path of the gods; bestow full vitality upon the lord of the sacrifice."

Thus he turns around. 31. While the animal is being slaughtered, the sacrificer mutters, "Thou art the knower of the tone. 32. Looking on, they pray for the speckled butter, saying, "May offspring of every form rejoice here," until the slaughter of the animal is complete. 33. "If the animal has uttered a cry, or if it strikes with its feet, may Agni deliver us from that sin; may the All-seeing One release us from all evil."

Thus he offers the *saṃjñaptahoma* oblation (34). He mutters, "O slaughterers, come hither" (35). With the words, "Aditi [releases] the bonds," he unlooses the rope from the animal (36). One who performs malevolent magic should place a clump of grass or a piece of wood [on the ground] with the words, "May he who hates us fall low" (37). For one not performing malevolent magic, he silently casts the rope into the *cātvāla* pit using a single-pronged fork (38).

"Salutation to you, O spreader," with these words he causes the wife to stand facing the Āditya. "Go, unhindered," with these words he leads her forward. "O divine waters," with these words the wife consecrates the water at the *cātvāla* pit. "Do not harm his speech; do not harm his breath"—with these words, according to their respective characteristics, she washes his limbs and pours water over them.

With the verse, "Whatever in thee is cruel," he touches the throat; with "Do not harm its limbs, do not harm its movements," he touches the various parts according to their respective characteristics. With "Peace to the waters," he consecrates the drops of water that have fallen upon the ground. With "O herb, protect this one," he places the blade of *darbha* grass used for the introductory rite near the side of the navel at the front. With "O axe, do not harm this one," he cuts it across with the axe. Having brought the skin and the tip together, and having smeared the root on the cutting-board, [he recites] "For the earth, thee."

With the words, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣasas," he throws [the earth] toward the south-western intermediate direction. With the words, "Here I strike down the Rakṣas; here I lead the Rakṣas into the lowest darkness," he stands upon it with his heel. With the words, "For food thee," he extracts the omentum (vapā). With the words, "For strength thee," he pierces its thinnest part with the single-pronged fork. With the words, "Be pure for the gods," he sprinkles it with water. With the words, "Be beautiful for the gods," he pushes back the omentum with the knife. With the words, "May Heaven and Earth be covered with ghee."

He covers the two-horned [offering]. (15) He cuts off the omentum according to the respective deity with the formula, "For such-and-such one thee. (16) The slaughterer, having grasped the vessel for removing the omentum with his fist, remains seated until the offering of the omentum. (17) With the formula, "Homage to the sight of Sūrya," he worships the sun. (18) With the formula, "Go through the wide atmosphere," he carries the omentum across the middle of the animal. (19) With the formula, "The Rakṣas is burnt up," he heats it over the *śāmitra* fire. (20) The Āgnīdhra, having carried a firebrand in front, discards it into the *āhavanīya* fire. (21) Between the fire and the sacrificial post.

22. The Pratiprasthātṛ, sitting to the south, cooks the omentum. 23. With the words, "Of Vāyu, of the drops," he throws a tip of darbha grass [into the fire]. 24. "Thee, O Agni, the seekers of the gods have established as the bearer of oblations, the preparer of the cooked offering, and the one worthy of sacrifice; having become one of great skill and beautiful form, O Jātavedas, carry the offerings to the gods."

Thus he makes an offering over the omentum (vapā). (25) He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words, "Recite for the drops" (stokebhyaḥ). (26) With the formula, "Make the falcon-like [omentum] cooked; make the plants well-fruited," he places it on the sacrificial grass (barhis) to the south. (27) With the formula, "Drive away our enemies," he pushes aside the two omentum-spits (vapāśrapaṇī). (28) Having performed the final fore-offering (prayāja) with the call, "Prompt for the Svāhā-utterances" (svāhākṛtibhyaḥ), he steps across and pours butter over the *dhruvā* spoon, the clotted butter (pṛṣadājya), and the omentum, but not over the *upabhṛt* spoon. (29) The two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) may be either performed or omitted. (30) Having performed the rite with the offering to Agni, [he proceeds] behind...

Having crossed over the southern side of the handle of the *sruk*, he proceeds by way of the north. 31. Standing right there, having spread an underlayer of ghee, he takes a portion [of the omentum], a piece of gold, the omentum, and another piece of gold; then he pours clarified butter over it. 32. He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words: "Recite for Indra and Agni the fat of the omentum of the goat. 33. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he proceeds with the offering, saying: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for Indra and Agni regarding the fat of the omentum of the goat. 34. He should offer before the omentum with the words, "Svāhā to the gods," and after it with the words, "To the Viśve Devas, Svāhā. 35.
O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum; for you were the first Hotṛ. O Agni, become united with your body through the clarified butter; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.

Having recited "Svāhā! and at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the omentum (36). Having stepped across, he bastes the animal on the cutting-board according to the respective deity (37). With the formula "Svāhā to the upward-moving atmosphere," he throws the two omentum-spits away: the single-pronged one toward the east and the double-pronged one toward the west (38). He makes an offering with the remnants of the basting-ghee (39): "O Waters, carry away this whatever evil is in me—whether it be that I have committed violence or that I have uttered falsehood."

Having thus performed the purification at the *cātvāla* pit, he will say, "Satisfy the Brāhmaṇas. (40) He throws the *ūvadhyam* (the contents of the stomach) into the pit. (41) Without turning the rectum over, he cooks the portions for the sacrificial offerings; they are clearly distinguished as being on the left and the right. The heart is placed on a spit. (42) Taking the *sruk* ladle and the winnowing basket, the Adhvaryu priest steps forward. (1) He subsequently offers the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of rice grains, dedicated to the same deity as the animal, on eleven or twelve potsherds. (2) He does not sprinkle water upon the vessels.

He does not pour out clarified butter. Having scattered plants behind the high altar (uttaravedi), he pours out the flour-residue. Having adorned the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles and having taken portions [of the cake], he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words, "Recite for Indra and Agni the cake. Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he proceeds with the direction, "Prompt for Indra and Agni the cake. Having brought the portion from the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with "For Agni, the cake," and proceeds with the direction, "Prompt for Agni, the cake. He causes the portion belonging to the Āgnīdhra to be carried away and sprinkles clarified butter over the *iḍā* portion of the cake.

Having offered the two oblations pertaining to the *dākṣiṇāgni*, he releases the potsherds. When the portions have been cooked, the *pratiprasthātṛ*, having dipped the *sruva* spoon into the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), asks with the formula: "O *vedopayāma*, is the oblation cooked by the *śamitṛ*? He replies, "It is cooked."

Having reached the second [portion] at the half-measure, he consecrates the third [portion] with the formula, "Svāhā! May I not be harmed by the heat" (VS 6.19), thereby consecrating the heat. Having placed the heart among the portions, he sets down the spit without touching those things that are forbidden to touch. Having walked around to the north, he bastes the animal according to the respective deity with the formula, "Acceptable to the gods" (VS 6.20). Having removed the fat-tissues, he carries [the portions] between the fire and the sacrificial post. To the south, the Pratiprasthātṛ places them on the sacrificial grass with the Pañcahotṛ formula. He spreads an underlayer [of ghee].

[He places portions] in the *juhū*, the *upabhṛt*, the *iḍā* vessel, and the *vasāhomahavanī*. (16) Having placed a piece of gold in the *juhū*, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite: "Recite for the Manotā as the oblation is being cut. (17) From the joints of the limbs, he cuts twice each with the axe upon a branch of the *plakṣa* tree: from the heart, the tongue, the breast, the left shoulder-blade, the forehead, the two sides, the liver, the two kidneys, the right hip, and having divided the rectum into three parts, from its smallest portion. (18) In the *upabhṛt* [he places] the three parts.

He cuts portions for the Sviṣṭakṛt from the front half of the right shoulder-blade, from the middle of the rectum, and from the rear half of the left hip. (19) Having cut the *iḍā* from the boneless sacrificial portions, he sprinkles it with broth. (20) With the formula, "The essence of waters and plants," he stirs the broth with the knife. (21) He spreads fat over it. (22) He cuts it three times: into the *juhū*, the *upabhṛt*, and the *iḍā*-vessel. (23) Having taken the fat-oblation into the *vasāhomahavanī* with the formula, "O *reḍasī*," he covers it with a rib. (24) Into the *juhū*...

Having placed a fragment of gold [on the ladle], he pours clarified butter over it twice from the *upabhṛt* ladle. He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) with the words: "Recite for Indra and Agni the oblation of the goat. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for Indra and Agni for the oblation of the goat," and then he proceeds with the offering. At the half-verse of the *yājyā*, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the *vasāhoma* (fat-oblation) with the verse: "O drinkers of fat, drink the fat. Having performed the offerings to the deities, he sacrifices toward the quarters with the remainder of the *vasāhoma*, just as he did with the *vājina*.

Having once cut off a portion of the speckled butter for Vanaspati, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words, "Recite for Vanaspati" (30). Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he proceeds with the offering, saying, "Prompt for Vanaspati" (31). Having poured the butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū* ladle, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words, "Recite for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" (32). Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he proceeds with the offering, saying, "Prompt for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" (33). With the formula, "The breath belongs to Indra," he touches the remnants of the portions and the *iḍā* (34). While the *iḍā* is being invoked, they bring the *adhyūdhnī* milk to the Hotṛ and the *vaniṣṭhu* (rectum) to the Āgnīdhra (35). Having consumed [the portions], they perform the ritual purification (36). A choice gift is the sacrificial fee (37).

Having taken the *anuyājika* fuel-stick, he issues the command: "O Āgnīdhra, bring the embers for the *upayaj* offerings; O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down; O Brahman, we shall proceed; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdhra, wipe the enclosing sticks and the fire once each. The Āgnīdhra then pours embers from the *śāmitra* fire onto the ground within the altar (*antarvedi*) in front of the Hotṛ.

He cleanses [the ladle] as directed; it is prepared for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s). Having taken the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) into the *juhū* ladle, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* and performs eleven after-offerings. He gives the first direction with "Prompt for the gods! and the subsequent ones with "Prompt! Prompt! The Pratiprasthātṛ, without breaking the connection, takes a portion from the thickest part of the rectum and offers it at each *vaṣaṭ*-call with the formulas beginning with "Go to the ocean, svāhā! Beginning from the region of the heart, he mutters, "Bestow mind and heart," over the darbha grass with the formula, "For the plants, thee."

He wipes off the smear. 8 Having stepped across and grasped it, he anoints the *svaru* three times below and three times above with the *juhū* ladle. 9 Having placed the *svaru* into the *juhū*, he offers it with the formula: "May your smoke go to heaven. 10 Before the offering of the *svaru* and before the subsequent assignment (*anudeśa*), the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) must not be touched. 11 [The rite] is established up to the *sūktavāka*. 12 "Recite the *sūkta* and give the command!"—this is the formal direction. 13 [The rite] is established up to the offerings to the wives of the gods (*patnīsaṃyāja*). 14 He causes the wives to sacrifice with the tail of the victim (*jāghanī*). 15 From the tail held face upwards, he cuts portions for the wives of the gods and for Agni.

For the householder, [he offers] the *iḍā* from the low-lying [portion] turned face upwards. 16. This is established up to the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings. 17. He performs three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations. 18. They go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the spit, either eastward or southward. 19. With the mantra, "Thou art heat; burn him who hates us and whom we hate," he buries the wet [spit] in waterless ground. 20. Regarding the verse, "From every station... that has already been explained. 21. "May he stand for me, the sacrificer, having performed the *svagā* call, bestowing goodwill, progeny, prosperity, and fortune."

"O Vāyu, this salutation is for you; for the great Maruts who are the sacrificial posts (svaru), may we not fall away from what has been established; having offered, may I become possessed of food"—with these words the sacrificer assigns the sacrificial post. He circumambulates the altar. One should sacrifice with an animal victim every six months, or every year. No year should pass while he has not sacrificed. If it should pass, he should not eat meat until the performance of an animal sacrifice. The water brought forward (praṇītā) should not be brought forward when the fires have already been carried forward, except where there is a specific injunction. From the Viṣṇu-strides onwards, the ritual duties of the sacrificer are the same as previously described.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the section prior to the Soma sacrifice in the Mānava-sūtra;
thus the first five-part division of the Mānava-sūtra, known as the Prāksoma, is completed.

One should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma in the spring. (1) The sacrificial grounds for the gods have been prescribed. (2) A site sloping toward the east is for the sake of the obligatory rites. (3) He chooses the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*): from among those who are great and young, and who belong to a lineage of seers (*ārṣeya*), he chooses Āditya as the *adhvaryu*, saying: "Āditya is my *adhvaryu*; O *adhvaryu*, you are my *adhvaryu*. [He chooses] Candra as the *brahman*, saying: "Candra is my *brahman*; O *brahman*, you are my *brahman*. [He chooses] Agni as the *hotṛ*, saying: "Agni is my *hotṛ*; O *hotṛ*, you are my *hotṛ*. (4)

"Parjanya is the Udgātṛ; may he be my Udgātṛ; O Udgātṛ, you are my Udgātṛ"—thus [he addresses] the Udgātṛ. "The quarters are the Hotṛ-śaṃsinas; may they be my Hotṛ-śaṃsinas; O Hotṛ-śaṃsinas, may you be my Hotṛ-śaṃsinas"—thus [he addresses] the twelve Hotṛkāḥ. "Great [bliss] have you spoken for me"—thus they mutter when chosen. "We have come to this place of sacrifice on earth, where all the gods took delight; crossing over by means of the Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus, may we rejoice in the increase of wealth and in nourishment."

Thus he settles upon the sacrificial ground together with its foundation. There they construct the shed with its ridge-pole facing east, elevated in front and sloping down behind. They enclose it with a thin mixture [of earth and water]. While enclosing it, they leave openings for light. They make doors in the cardinal directions, double-layered and well-proportioned. Having entered by the eastern door and performed the formal assignment of the ritual, he distributes the fires therein. "I shall give this" is the formal assignment. They partake of the initiation-food, consisting of curds mixed with honey.

The sacrificer and his wife should undergo initiation on the new moon day, or on such a day as the Soma-pressing may fall. Having mentally recited the *saptahotṛ* formula, he offers with the cup [of water] while saying, "May we be provided with food. He prepares the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, or a pap cooked in ghee. When about to lead forward the waters, he offers twelve *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas beginning with "Agni with the *yajus*-verses"; having pronounced four of them at a time, he makes the offerings. The *dīkṣaṇīyā* concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

18. In that [chanting], the voice is softer than that used for the New and Full Moon sacrifices; it is softer at the Prāyaṇīyā, softer at the Ātithyā, and the Upasads are performed with a low drone (*dhvāna*). All the deities are recited in a low tone (*upāṃśu*). 19. Having closed the doors, he proceeds with the ritual. 20. To the north of the site of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, having enclosed the area, he sprinkles water with the formula, "O divine waters... 21. With the formula, "O herb, protect him," he places a blade of *darbha* grass between [the hair] on the right side of the parting of the hair. 22. With the formula, "O razor, do not harm him," he applies the razor. 23.

"O God-hearing one, shave me," with these words he has his hair shaved (24). "May I attain well-being hereafter," the sacrificer mutters (25). The sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved (26). He cleanses his teeth (27). Having had his body hair removed, he has his nails trimmed.

He should not have his armpits or nails trimmed by his wife (28–29). Having plunged into a ford with water present, he bathes in still waters while reciting, "Golden-hued, pure... (RV X.9.1–2); having rubbed himself dry and sipped water, he steps out [of the water] while reciting, "From the purifying waters, pure and purified, I come forth" (RV IX.1.6) (30). He covers himself with a linen garment while reciting, "Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu" (VS IV.1) (31). He makes a knot at the waist while reciting, "For strength, thee" (VS IV.1) (32). The wife does so silently for the sake of the initiation-thread (33). Having bathed, he causes the wife to put on a linen garment with its fringes pointing eastward (34). [He touches her] with two blades of Darbha grass while reciting, "Thou art the milk of the great ones" (VS IV.1).

He applies fresh butter with the formula, "Thou art the bestower of luster" (VS 1.22), anointing three times in the natural direction; he anoints the face first, then the head, until he is well-anointed down to his feet. With what remains, the wife anoints herself. With four stalks of *darbha* grass or *śara* reeds, including their *uñja* fibers and tufts—one by one—he scrapes up Traikakuba ointment and anoints his right eye three times with the formula, "Thou art the eye of Vṛtra," using a different stalk for each application, and likewise the left eye. With what remains, the wife anoints herself.

Having divided the bunches of *darbha* grass into three parts, he purifies [the sacrificer] three times with twenty-one [stalks]: with the formula "O Lord of Thought (*citpati*), thee... he purifies him upwards; with "O Lord of Speech (*vācaspati*), thee... downwards; and with "O God Savitṛ, thee... upwards. To each of these, he everywhere appends the phrase "with the flawless strainer (*pavitreṇa*). (40) With the formula "Of that thine, O Lord of the Strainer (*pavitrapati*), by the strainer... the sacrificer mutters [the remainder]. (41) He should not purify [the sacrificer] beyond his vital breaths. (42) If he should hate someone, he should purify him crosswise. (43) Having caused the sacrificer to enter by the eastern door and having circumambulated the *āhavanīya* fire to the north...

Thereafter, he causes [the sacrificer] to sit down behind the Āhavanīya fire. The Pratiprasthātṛ, having silently purified the wife and having led her in through the western door, establishes her in the wife’s place to the south-west of the western [fire] and causes her to sit down.

With the *sruva* ladle, he offers the oblations accompanied by the recited *yajus*-formulas, beginning with "For intention, for impulse. With the *sruc* ladle, he offers the fifth oblation with "O divine waters. For the sixth, the full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*) consisting of twelve scoops, he offers while reciting "Viśva of the god, the leader... 1. To the west of the *āhavanīya* fire, he spreads out the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), having smoothed it together with its neck toward the east and its hairy side upward. 2. If there is only one skin, he should sew together the southern foot of the black antelope skin, having smoothed it together with its neck toward the east. 3. With the formula "You two are the artistic forms of the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*," he places the black and white [wools].

The wife touches [the earth] four times. She ascends the ashes with the formula: "Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu. With palms joined, she mutters: "Sūrya and Agni, Heaven and Earth. Having fastened a net with loops on both sides upon the head of the wife, he says: "I bind thee with the milk of the earth; I bind thee with the waters and the plants; I bind thee with offspring and wealth. Thus consecrated, do not release thy speech from this point."

Thus the Pratiprasthātṛ girdles the wife with the yoktra. 7. The initiated one ties on a girdle made of muñja grass, broad, triple-stranded, and with the loop facing north, with the formula: "Thou art prosperity. 8. He makes a loose knot. 9. Having taken up a black antelope horn with an odd number of ridges, he consecrates the horn with the formula: "Thou art the womb of Indra. 10. With the formula: "Plow well for a good harvest," he digs toward the east outside the altar with the horn. 11. With the formula: "O horn, do thou scratch," he ties it with a cord. 12. He scratches himself with it [for the sake of] plowing.

With the verse, "Make the limbs well-ploughed in the fertile field," he addresses the body; with "Make the plants bear good fruit," he addresses the head. (13) The wife should scratch herself with a wooden peg (*śaṅku*) made of *vānaspatya* wood. (14) Having carried around the front of the Āhavanīya fire a staff of *audumbara* wood reaching up to the mouth, he hands it to the sacrificer with the formula, "Great art thou, O *vānaspatya*. (15) He receives it with the formula, "Thou art well-established, O *vānaspatya*; protect me for strength until the end. (16) He covers himself with it from the northern edge [of the fire] with the words, "From the sight of the stars. (17) He mutters the verse, "O gods, we entreat you... (18)

He should not cover [the skin] until the purchase [of the Soma]. With the formulas beginning with "Svāhā to the sacrifice from the mind," he closes his fingers two by two and forms two fists. He restrains his speech. The wife, having silently formed her fists, restrains her speech. He should cover himself with the black antelope skin, hair-side out; if there are two skins, he should fasten them crosswise. Having announced that the initiated sacrificer has been touched by the front of the sacrificial post while facing eastward, he makes the announcement.

He pronounces his name, saying, "This one is initiated"; he pronounces his lineage, saying, "the son of so-and-so"; he pronounces his father's name, saying, "the son of so-and-so"; he pronounces his grandfather's name, saying, "the grandson of so-and-so"; and he pronounces his great-grandfather's name, saying, "the great-grandson of so-and-so."

He announces the consecration (dīkṣā) to Indra and Agni; he announces the consecration to Mitra and Varuṇa; he announces the consecration to the Viśve Devas, to the Brāhmaṇas, to those worthy of Soma, and to the Soma-drinkers—thus he announces it loudly three times. "O you who desire [the sacrifice]," with these words he releases three fingers of one hand and three of the other. The wife does so silently. Having seen a star, he releases his speech with the formula: "From the presence of the stars."

When [the Adhvaryu] has uttered, "Perform the vow for those who are the cattle," (27) the wife, having spoken an auspicious word, releases her speech. (28) She should not address anyone by their actual name. When conversing with one worthy of honor, she should say, "O Canasita"; with others, she should say, "O Vicakṣaṇa. (29) This is the movement of the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*).

Having passed to the south between the Āhavanīya fire and the altar, he sits to the south of the Āhavanīya facing north; this is the path of movement (saṃcara). (30) His bed, seat, and covering consist of the hairy side of the black antelope skin. (31) Spitting, laughing, urinating, showing the teeth, looking at impure things, splashing water, performing oblations, and speaking untruth are forbidden. (32) From a distance to the east of the sacrificial grass, there should be neither the rising nor the setting [of the sun], nor the calling for the *śrauṣaṭ* response. (33) One should void urine and feces at night, if [it must be done] during the day.

34. If he laughs while in the shade, 35. having covered his mouth, he should murmur when it rains: "Wetting [us], bestow vigor; bestow strength; do not destroy my consecration (*dīkṣā*), nor my ascetic heat (*tapas*). 36. Having seen something impure, he should murmur: "Unassailable is the eye, uninjured is the mind; Sūrya is the best of lights; may the consecration not abandon me, O good one. 37. If he should speak the speech of one unconsecrated, he should murmur: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows (*vratapā*). 38. Having released his speech at an improper time, he should recite these [verses]: one addressed to Viṣṇu, one to Agni and Viṣṇu, one to Sarasvatī, and one to Bṛhaspati.

Having spoken these words, he restrains his speech (38). Before releasing his speech, he causes the *vrata* milk to be milked once (39). Milk is the *vrata* for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel for a Rājanya, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for a Vaiśya; however, during the *upasads*, milk is prescribed for all (40). He silently cooks the *vrata* on the Gārhapatya fire according to the procedure for the Agnihotra, and [cooks] for the wife on the Dakṣiṇāgni. Once cooked, he places it behind the Āhavanīya fire (41).

Whatever expiation there is for spilled *agnihotra* milk, that is the expiation for the vow (*vrata*). 1. Having passed over the evening meal, he consumes the vow-food; or, having passed over the morning meal until sunrise, or until sunset. 2. One who has not been initiated must not look at one consuming the vow-food. 3. Having said, "Make the fires radiant; enter the vow, O observer of the vow," and having carried [the food] across by the path used by the initiated, he hands the vow-food to him from the south of the *āhavanīya* fire in a bronze vessel or a wooden cup. 4. With the words, "We meditate upon divine thought," he washes his hands. 5. Those...

He causes [the sacrificer] to consume the fast-food with the mantra, "The gods, born of Manu, are joined by the mind" (RV 10.128.6). He mutters over the region of the navel, beginning from there, with the words, "May they, having been drunk, be auspicious" (RV 7.49.3). In the western half, the wife consumes the fast-food. From sunrise until the sun sets, the giver of the fast-food restrains his speech, saying, "O initiated one, restrain your speech; O wife, restrain your speech. And likewise at sunset. To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, facing north, not turning around, he should sleep with his head toward the east. [He recites: "Desire is most exhilarated by the oblations; you, O Agni, are the guardian of vows" (RV 10.121.1).

One who is about to sleep should mutter: "O Agni, you are the mind; you are the guardian of vows. Upon waking, he should do the same. 11. One initiated for sacrifice should seek sustenance with the mantra: "Pūṣan is the winner of gains. 12. He addresses those wandering as beggars with: "Pūṣā sanīnām. 13. He addresses those who have returned with: "The god Savitṛ... When about to depart on a journey, he consigns the fire into the two kindling woods with: "This is your seasonal womb. If he has already attained worldly prosperity, he consigns all the fires. 14. [He departs with: "May auspicious fortune come to you; go toward what is better. Let Bṛhaspati be your leader. Now, in the wide space of the earth, make your enemies far away, you who are possessed of all heroes."

Thus he departs together with the two kindling-sticks and the chariot-wheel. (15) When plunging into the waters, reciting "O divine waters, O son of the waters," he should press a clod of earth up to his navel. (16) If he crosses by boat or by some other means, he should press a clod of earth up to his navel while reciting, "May I follow the unbroken thread of the earth. (17) The rising and setting [of the sun] should take place at the end of the sacrificial enclosure. (18) The consecrations are unlimited; of these, one remains awake during the first.

There are three *upasads*, or they may be unlimited; there are three repetitions of them. He remains awake during the first one, thinking, "The Soma-pressing is tomorrow. 19. After the consecrations (*dīkṣā*), he offers the *prāyaṇīya* oblation: a pap of rice cooked in the milk of a cow for Aditi. 20. [The ritual proceeds] successfully until the formal instruction. 21. He does not gird the wife of the consecrated sacrificer. 22. He causes the wife to stand near with the mantra. 23. He does not offer the two *ājyabhāga* portions. 24. Having taken a portion from the *dhruva* ladle, he sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti in the eastern half, to Agni in the southern half, and to Soma in the western half.

He offers to Savitṛ in the northern half [of the altar]; to Aditi in the middle of the *caru* (25). He proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: having taken a portion from the *dhruva* ladle, he takes a portion from the *caru* and pours clarified butter over it twice (26). It concludes with the formula "May they be peaceful" (27). He sets aside the scrapings of the *caru* and the stirring-spoon for the concluding oblation (28). He takes four spoonfuls of clarified butter as a residue from the *dhruvā* ladle (29). The *rājakrayaṇī* cow, with her ears intact, is prescribed for the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice (30). Having enclosed the space in front of the *vamśa* pole, he stations her facing west in front [of the altar] (31).

Having tied gold with a blade of *darbha* grass, he offers it while reciting, "This is thy bright body, O pure one," and places it into the fourfold-drawn butter (32). Looking at the cow for purchasing the King [Soma], he makes an offering with the mantra, "Thou art swift" (33). Having taken up butter again into that same vessel, he removes the gold with the mantra, "Thou art bright, thou art shining" (34). He praises the cow for purchasing the King with the mantra, "Thou art consciousness, thou art mind, thou art intellect" (35). He causes her to follow him with the mantra, "May thy mother permit thee" (36). He turns her clockwise with the mantra, "O Rudra, turn her back" (37).

He causes [the sacrificer] to step forward toward the east with the verses beginning "Thou art a Vasvi" (VS 5.26), and he follows along for six steps from the eastern part of the right foot. Having silently grasped the seventh step, he touches it with the formula, "May Bṛhaspati make thee rest in happiness. Having placed gold upon it, he makes an offering over it with the formula, "I sprinkle thee on the head of the earth. Having outlined the footprint with the wooden sword (sphya), he outlines it again with the horn. Having lifted up as much earth as is covered by the footprint, he says, "Rejoice in us."

He scatters earth from the *carusthālī* (the pot for the cooked rice) onto the footprint. (42) He pours water into the pit with the mantra, "Unfold [the earth]. (43) He hands the footprint [of the cow] to the sacrificer with the mantra, "Thine is wealth," without letting it slip from his hand; the sacrificer, likewise without letting it slip, returns it to the *adhvaryu* with the mantra, "Thine is wealth. (44) Beginning with the mantra, "May [I not be separated] from the abundance of wealth," the sacrificer mutters [this prayer]. (45) He places the footprint inside the house. (46) Having circumambulated to the north of the mark (*lakṣaṇa*), he causes the wife to look at the cow used for purchasing the Soma with the mantra, "O Tvaṣṭṛ-like one, thee... (47) [This is done] with a cart that has a roof-cover.

They honor the King (Soma) with the verse, "I have mounted the eye of the Sun" (VS 4.8). The Adhvaryu and the sacrificer follow him as he departs. They lead the cow for the purchase of the King (rājakrayaṇī) along. At the edge of the Uttaravedi, within the enclosure, either the Soma-seller, a Kutsa, or a Śūdra pours out the King upon a red bull's hide that has its neck toward the east and the hair side up. To the south, he unyokes the cart facing eastward. He gives the command to the Soma-seller: "Cleanse the Soma; throw out the impurity. The selection and inspection of the Soma are forbidden by the rule: "The Adhvaryu shall not select the Soma."

Having tied gold to the middle finger, they enter the enclosure with the formula, "Thou art ours. With the formula, "The *śukra* is thy cup," he touches [the Soma] with his hand holding the gold. On a piece of linen cloth with its fringe pointing eastward, he measures out the King (Soma), joining it straight with the fingers and the thumb; starting from the little finger, he measures five times with each finger beginning with the little one, and five times silently with the formula, "To that god Savitṛ... and so on.

That by which he [binds] the first, by that same [cord] he binds the fifth and the last. With the formula, "For the offspring, may you be abundant," he adds [the cord]. With the formula, "May the offspring breathe after you," he fastens it with a linen turban as a halter for the plough. "This is your Gāyatra portion; announce this to Soma for me. "This is your Triṣṭubh portion; announce this to Soma for me. "This is your Jagatī portion; announce this to Soma for me. "This is your Anuṣṭubh portion; announce this to Soma for me. "This is your Paṅkti portion; announce this to Soma for me."

"Speak for Soma: 'May he attain the sovereignty of the Chandomas!'"—thus the sacrificer addresses the King (Soma). "Speak for me, O Soma!"—with these words, the sacrificer stands near the King. (6) The seller of Soma places the King (Soma) into a water-pitcher. (7) He addresses him: "O seller of Soma, I shall buy your Soma. "Buy it," he replies. (8) "I shall buy it from you for a sixteenth part"—thus he bargains with each item according to the prescribed ritual formula.

"Or rather, King Soma deserves more than this," he replies. "This is the cow; with her I shall purchase [you]. Her form, her color, her self, her offspring, and her milk [are yours]. "Purchased," he replies. He then drives away the Soma-purchasing cows according to the traditional injunctions.

With the formula, "Thy bright [seed], O bright one, with the bright," he seizes the gold; with "The essence of heat art thou," he seizes the goat; having snatched it from the Soma-purchaser, he points it out with "Good speech, the cloudless. He should give something to the Soma-seller. With the formula, "Light for us," he hands over the white tuft of wool from between the black and white [wools] to the sacrificer.

He should make that the navel of the strainer. Having tied a knot in the black wool with the formula, "Here I bind the necks of the biting serpents," he should place it upon the Soma-seller with the word, "That one. With the formula, "Thou art self-born," he takes up the King (Soma). While it is being brought, the sacrificer turns away and sits down. He mutters, "Come to us like Mitra. Drawing back the end of his garment, he places [the Soma] on his right thigh with the formula, "Enter the lap of Indra. Taking it up with the formula, "Up with life," he stands up. [With the formula,] "The wide atmosphere..."

Having mounted the cart with the formula, "Go forth, O cart," he spreads a black antelope skin on the front half of the seat with the formula, "Thou art the skin of Aditi" (20). With the formula, "Sit upon the seat of Aditi," he places the King [Soma] upon it (21). He worships the cart with the formula, "He has propped up the sky" (22). He covers the cart with a cloth with the formula, "In the woods, the atmosphere" (23). He touches the pole and the northern yoke-end with the formula, "Thou art the pole" (24). Having stepped northward, he takes hold of the northern pole with the formula, "Thou belongest to Varuṇa," and mutters [the same] (25). He props it up with the formula, "May Varuṇa prop thee up" (26).

"O two draft-oxen, come hither; be yoked, tearless and not slayers of men, impellers of the *brahman*, prolonging the life of the sacrifice; go in safety to the house of the sacrificer"—with these words he yokes the two lead oxen. (27) "Thou art the pillar of Varuṇa"—with this he yokes the one on the north. (28) Grasping the edge of the southern roof-covering, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite: "Recite for Soma, who has been purchased and is being carried forward! (29) When the verse has been recited three times, he gives the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, summon the Subrahmaṇyā! (30) "Depart, O Lord of the World!"

Having thus proceeded toward the east, he turns to the right. 31. Having gone around to the front, he places a large fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire. 32. In front of the *praṇītā*-water, they station the goat dedicated to Agni and Soma—its ears held forward, its tail tied with black thread, and it being fat. 33. He raises up a throne made of Udumbara wood, knee-high in height, a cubit in width, and woven with *muñja* grass. 34. While it is being carried, the sacrificer mutters the mantra, "Obeisance to Mitra... 35. In front of the *praṇītā*-water, he stations the cart facing north with the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa. 36.

37. With the words, "May Varuṇa prop you up," he props it up. 38. With the words, "Thou art the support of Varuṇa's pillar," he draws out the southern pin. 39. With the words, "The noose of Varuṇa is loosened," he unties the noose of the yoke-thong. 40. With the words, "The noose of Varuṇa is cast off," he casts it away. 41. With the words, "Homage to the noose of Varuṇa," he pays homage.

He binds the fuel and the sacrificial grass for the guest-offering (*ātithyā*) just as in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). The procedure is established up to the pouring out of the oblation (*nirvapaṇa*). The wife should hold that from which he pours out. He pours out five times with the formulas beginning with those dedicated to Savitṛ and ending with "Thou art the body of Agni. [He offers] a cake on nine potsherds for Viṣṇu. The procedure is established up to the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation, he unyokes the northern ox.

He gives it to the Adhvaryu. Having carried it across by the path used for the consecrated, he places a stool to the south of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa. He brings down the King (Soma) with the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa, firm in thy vow," over the left pole and together with the black antelope skin. Having carried him across by the path used for the consecrated, he seats the King on the stool to the south of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Sit upon the seat of Varuṇa’s truth. He covers him with a cloth with the formula, "For Varuṇa, thee."

The procedure from the taking of the winnowing basket up to the drawing of the clarified butter is established [as in the model sacrifice]. (11) The clarified butter is drawn four times. (12) The procedure up to the touching [of the oblation] is established. (13) Prior to the touching, he proceeds with the fire-drilling. (14) He touches [the oblation] with the *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas. (15) The procedure up to the *pravara* invocation is established. (16) Once the *pravara* has been invoked, in sacrifices that do not have after-offerings (*anuyāja*), he cleanses the implements, sprinkles them with water, and throws them away in a cow-pen or in another enclosure. (17) At the time of the pouring together [of the butter], having poured all the butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he does not pour butter back over the *aupabhṛta*. (18)

Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and released the two ladles, he throws them outside the altar. (19) He does not cut off the *prāśitra* portion, nor the sacrificer’s share. (20) It concludes with the *iḍā*; it concludes with the *iḍā*. (21) Thus ends the first chapter on the Agniṣṭoma in the Mānava Sūtra.

He takes the *tānūnaptra* (the anointing of the body) either in a wooden cup (*camasa*) or in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsya*). With the formulas, "I take thee for the lord of the house; I take thee for the protector; I take thee for the grandson of the body; I take thee for power, for the mighty one, for the most powerful through power," he pours four portions from the *dhruva* ladle [into the vessel]. 2. Behind the *āhavanīya* fire, the officiating priests and the sacrificer approach the *tānūnaptra*. 3. Having touched it all at once, they mutter, "Thou art unassailable," and also, "O grandson of the body, who... 4. "I offer thee into Prajāpati, into the mind, svāhā!"

The sacrificer smells [the offering] three times; he enters the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). He places a fuel-stick on the fire with the formula: "O Agni, lord of vows, that body of mine which is this, let it be in you. He mutters: "O Agni, lord of vows, that body of yours which is this, let it be in me. Having fastened the girdle with the formula, "May our vows be together, O lord of vows," he bends his fingers more tightly inward.

The wife, having silently fastened the cord, bends down more deeply. Having placed the boiling waters (*madantī*) on the *gārhapatya* fire, they prepare them for the purpose of heating the water. At the place where they would attend to the King Soma from the clarified butter, they should wash their hands or [wash] the clarified butter for the King. The Adhvaryu announces: "O Agnis, the boiling waters! The Āgnīdhra responds: "The divine, immortal waters that increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*)."

With the words "Come with them," the Adhvaryu [takes the King Soma]. The Brahman places gold upon the King Soma for the sake of its nourishment. Having begun with the words "O divine Soma, be strong, be pure for us," the officiating priests and the sacrificer mutter [the following]. Placing their hands on the *prastara* grass-bundle, they perform the *nihnuvana* (concealment of the hands): the left hands low and the right hands turned upward; then the right hands low and the left hands turned upward. In the afternoon, they mutter: "May we seek wealth; may we seek desirable things. Having performed the *pravargya* rite, they proceed with the *upasad* rites, provided that they perform the *pravargya*.

The sacrificial grass (barhis) is strewn once for both the *ātithyā* and the *upasads*, except for the prastara-bunch. (15) He binds ten pieces of wood from the *dāru* tree as fuel. (16) He sets out the vessels: two offering-spoons (*sruc*) with the *sruva*-ladle as the third, a vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the wooden sword (*sphya*), and the *veda*-broom. (17) The procedure is established up to the point of the formal setting down (*sādana*). (18) Having sprinkled the vessels with water purified by the *yajus*-formula and having poured out the clarified butter, he carries fire around them (*paryagni-karoti*). (19) The sacrificial grass has been strewn; the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are laid down. (20) From above the sacrificial grass, he removes the clump of earth for the *stambayajus*. (21) "Set down the *prokṣaṇī* waters; place the fuel (*idhma*) nearby."

"Clean the two *sruva*-ladles and pour out the clarified butter," he instructs. To the south, over the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he disposes of the *praṇītā* waters that were not used for the final sprinkling. The procedure from the taking of the portions of clarified butter is established. He takes eight times with the *juhū* ladle and four times with the *upabhṛt*. Having sprinkled the fuel (*idhma*), he pours out the *prokṣaṇī* waters clockwise around the base of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Taking the fuel-wood, he places the *prastara* bundle upon the two separating blades (*vidhṛtī*). He sets down the portions of clarified butter, the *sruva*-ladle as the third, the two *sruk*-ladles, the butter-pot, and the wooden sword (*sphya*).

The Veda [is recited] up to the kindling (siddham ā samindhanāt). He places the fuel-wood on three times (trir idhmam ādadhāti). [It continues] up to the formal command (saṃpraiṣa). He issues the command: "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fire thrice; sit down, O Hotṛ! The *srauva* oblation and the *pravara* invocation are omitted. When the formula "O Adhvaryu, [the ladles] full of ghee" is being recited, he takes up the two ladles, steps across to the south, and causes [the sacrificer] to recite the invitatory verse according to the respective deity. He offers to Agni in the eastern part, to Soma in the middle, having poured the entire contents of the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *juhū*, and to Viṣṇu in the western part. Having released the two ladles—

He throws [the grass] outside the altar. Having caused the King (Soma) to swell, they perform the *nihnuvanam* (concealment). The Brahman priest ties up the King (Soma). Taking the *prastara* and the two *vidhṛtis*, he offers the *upasads* with the *sruva*-ladle: "O Agni, that which is thy seat in iron" on the first day; "O Agni, that which is thy seat in silver" on the middle day; "O Agni, that which is thy seat in gold" on the last day.

He joins the verse "tanūrvarṣiṣṭhā" to every [verse]. 39. While carrying the *prastara* towards the *āhavanīya* fire, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; O Āgnīdhra, announce the wives of the gods. 40. At the end of the *gārhapatya*, the Āgnīdhra announces the wives of the gods.

He appends [the formulas] "Vāc is the wife of Vāyu" and "Pathyā is the wife of Pūṣan" everywhere. 41. He performs the Pravargya and Upasad rites in the forenoon and in the afternoon. 42. Between the two Upasads, he observes the vow at the proper time, namely in the evening. 43. In this manner they proceed with the Upasads for three days. 44. He hands over the *tānūnaptra* (the shared portion of clarified butter) during the vow. 45. He observes the vow with the formula, "O Agni, that body of yours which is Rudra-like. 46. They both become observers of the heated vow (*taptavrata*). 47. At the proper time, [he says]: "O observer of the vow, restrain your speech; O wife, restrain your speech."

The one who bestows the vow restrains his speech. (48) On the first day [the milk] is from four teats; on the middle day, from three teats and two teats; on the last day, from one teat. (49) In the case of an increase in the *upasad* days, one should increase both the arrangement of the teats and the *upasad* oblations. (50) Having performed the morning rite on the middle *upasad* day, he goes toward the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). (51) Having fixed the *pṛṣṭhya*-peg in front of the *vamśa* at a distance of three steps or in an unlimited space, he prepares the altar (*vedi*) starting from the taking of the earth for the altar.

The prescribed measurement is thirty-six steps toward the east (52). He carries away the *stambayajus* from the location of the *uparava* holes (53). One should make the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) ten paces long, ending at the edge of the *niḥsaraṇa* (54). Having performed the morning rite on the final *upasad* day, he goes for the sacrificial branch (55).

Having given [the offering] for the half-vow immediately, he should perform the afternoon rites. Having wiped the vessels for the *gharma*, he binds the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice according to the ritual procedure beginning with the cord (*śulba*). He binds the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) together with the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). From the sprinkling of the high altar (*uttaravedi*) onwards, the rite is established up to the *pūrṇāhuti* offering. On the altar, they mark out the footprints; as many as there are on the south side, so many are there on the north side. Without crossing over one another, they move away along the *pṛṣṭhyā* line. The markings are made on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).

They throw [the clods] away; they do not step upon what has not been sprinkled. Having performed the second tracing of the altar and having wiped [the wooden sword], he fixes the wooden sword (sphya) crosswise in front of the *pṛṣṭhyā*-peg. He issues the directions: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the offering-spoons; bring the clarified butter. Having set down the sprinkling waters to the south, he places the fuel and the sacrificial grass to the north. From the raising [of the wooden sword] onwards, the procedure is established up to the sprinkling of the sacrificial grass. Having laid down the fuel and the sacrificial grass, [he prepares] a continuous row of *ulapa* grass.

He spreads [the grass] over the *pṛṣṭhyā-śaṅku* from the *uttaravedi*. Having untied the knots first tied on the two *havirdhāna* carts, having washed them, anointed them, and re-tied them, they place them on both sides of the *pṛṣṭhyā* at the distance of one *aratni*; the wheels are outside the altar and the supporting posts are inside the altar. He offers an oblation in the *śālāmukhīya* fire with the verse: "They harness the mind and they harness the thoughts. On the southern axle-pole of the two *havirdhāna* carts, at a distance of half a footstep of the *rājakrayaṇī* cow, he addresses the two supports with: "O you who are heard by the gods, announce it among the gods!"

The wife anoints one [of the two poles] three times and the other three times, without turning her toward the east. He causes [the Adhvaryu] to recite the invitatory verse: "Recite for the two *havirdhāna* carts as they are being set in motion. When the verse has been recited three times, they set them in motion while covered with a canopy, reciting: "Drive away the fear of the enemy host. Holding them up, having established them one after another within the altar, they anoint the two poles; then, having placed gold upon the tracks at the junction of the altar, he makes an offering over it with the verse, "This Viṣṇu strode out," on the southern [track], [and] "The waters are flowing" on the northern.

With the verse "Rich in cows" (RV 1.82.2), they follow [the cart] while holding it up. If the axle creaks, he should mutter: "O divine speech, speak well for our dwellings. Behind the *uttaravedi*, at a distance of three steps, he establishes [the cart] on the navel-mark with the words "Rejoice here, upon the height of the earth," and then secures it. With the formula "Thou art Vaiṣṇava," he touches the northern pole while muttering. He supports it with the formula "May Viṣṇu support thee"; in the same way, he does so for the northern [cart]. He drives two stakes into the southern poles of the two *havirdhāna* carts with the formula "From heaven..."

With "O Viṣṇu," he fixes the southern [peg], and with "Now for Viṣṇu's... the northern one. 24. He ties the two door-posts with a cord, without making a knot. 25. With "May your lap be wide," he erects the Havirdhāna cart-shed facing eastward. 26. With "Thou art the back of Viṣṇu," he places the roof-covering in the middle.

27. Behind [the front part], which is wider, having fixed four pillars reaching to the height of the mouth at the ends of the roof-beams of the eastern half, he places a beam facing north; likewise behind, on the shorter [beams]. 28. In the middle of the *tejanī* (cross-beam), he makes a bundle of *darbha* grass. 29. Having wound a rope around it so as to draw the *darbhas* toward it and having joined the two ends of the *tejanī*, he places it on the front part of the beam with the formula, "Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu. 30. Having enclosed [the space] and when the southern beam has been settled, having placed *darbhas* upon the *tejanī*.

With the mantra, "O two lips of Viṣṇu, you are," he unties the ends [of the cord]. (31) With the mantra, "Thou art the needle of Viṣṇu," he sews it through. (32) With the mantra, "Thou art the fixed point of Viṣṇu," he makes the first knot. (33) He should sew up to the end. (34) Having sewn the other side, he sews the two door-posts. (35) Having pulled up the upright pins, he ties them together. (36) Having consecrated the completed structure with the mantra, "Thou belongest to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu thee," the sacrificer, having stepped three steps eastward from the Āhavanīya fire, mutters the verse, "Pra tad viṣṇuḥ. (37)
To the west of the support-post of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, having constructed a square measuring two *prādeśas* on each side... 38.

To the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, [the sacrificer] takes up the spade with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... (VS 1.28).
