With this, he makes the second offering. (26) "O *praśāstṛ*, give the command!"—thus he issues the direction. (27) Having been commanded, they proceed; they proceed.
(28) Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Mānava Sūtra* regarding the *agniṣṭoma*.

They proceed to the third pressing. He draws the Āditya cup; having covered the two *havirdhāna* carts, he pours the third portion from the *āditya-sthālī* into the *āditya-pātra* with the verse: "Never indeed art thou barren..."

"Yajño devānām" (The sacrifice of the gods)—with this [verse], he pours warm curds (*taptātaṅkya*) into it. "Kadā cana prayuchasi" (Never indeed do you neglect)—with this, he fills it from the *ādityasthālī* (the vessel for the Ādityas). "Yā divyā vṛṣṭis tayā tvā śrīṇāmi" (With that which is divine rain, with that I mix thee)—with these words, he mixes it with cold curds (*śītātaṅkya*). "Vivasvan, Āditya, eṣa te somapīthaḥ" (O Vivasvat, Āditya, this is thy draught of Soma)—with this, he stirs the rim with the *upām̐śusavana* stone. Having covered it, he steps out with *darbha* grass and his hand. "Ahaṃ parastāt" (I am beyond)—with this, the sacrificer takes hold of it. [It is] for the dear Ādityas.

"Recite the invitatory verse for those who have dear abodes, who follow dear vows, who are the lords of the great dwelling-place, the overseers of the wide mid-air," thus he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite. (8) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he proceeds with the offering, saying, "Prompt the offering for the Ādityas, who have dear abodes, who follow dear vows, who are the lords of the great dwelling-place, the overseers of the wide mid-air. (9) Having cast away the darbha-blades and looking elsewhere, he pronounces the response, "Make them swell! and at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he does not offer the entire oblation. (10)

"O pressers, press! O Āgnīdhra, prepare the milk-mixture (āśira)! O Pratiprasthātṛ, pour the stalk into the Upāṃśu-vessel; having poured it into the residue, mix it thoroughly, and having carried it northward after pressing, let it flow into the Ādhavanīya vessel"—thus he gives the command. 11. They press with the Vasatīvarī waters. 12. Behind the Āgnīdhrīya shed, he churns the milk-mixture. 13. Having spread the filter over the Pūtabhṛt vessel, he collects the stream of pure juice. 14. He places the Āgrayaṇa bowl, the Āditya bowl, and the Āditya cup upside down [on the mound]. 15.

From the *ādhavanīya* vessel, using the *udañcana* ladle, he draws the *āgrayaṇa* from four streams with the formula, "O gods who are eleven in heaven... He utters the *hiṅkāra* more loudly. (16) In the *agniṣṭoma*, he does not draw the *ukthya* at the third pressing. (17) If there is a *ṣoḍaśin*, having drawn the *ukthya*, he draws the *ṣoḍaśin* from the *āgrayaṇa* with the verse, "Indra, the two bays carry him... (18) In a sacrifice without a *ṣoḍaśin*, having drawn the *ukthya*, having purified the King Soma, and having pressed it through the filter, the procedure is established up until the *sarpaṇa*. (19) They proceed with the *ṛjudehīyā* verses for the *ārbhava* [stotra].

The *saṃpāvana* [chant] by which the midday *pavamāna* was explained has been described; likewise, the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) of the *pavamāna*. Prior to the *ārbhava-pavamāna*, the sacrificer mutters the *saptahotṛ* formula and says, "Utter the *hiṅkāra* for the sake of long life."

"You are a friend, you are the meter of the world; I take hold of you. Carry me safely across," he says. 22. When [the Śastra] has been recited, he issues the direction: "O Āgnīdh, distribute the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the *puroḍāśa*; O Pratiprasthātṛ, give the signal for the animal sacrifice. 23. The procedure for distributing the fires and the *ulaparājī* (grass-bundle) has been explained. 24. Having touched the vessels with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, the Pratiprasthātṛ and the wife, having spread a filter over the *pūtabhṛt* vessel, pour the *āśir* (milk-mixture) while reciting, "The blessing, the strength... 25. He proceeds with the animal sacrifice. Together...

From the *vāda* up to the *iḍā*, [the procedure for] the *savanīya* offerings is established; from the removal [of the cakes] up to the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*), it is established. (26–27) For the third pressing, the modified formal command is: "O Indra, [accept] the sacrificial cakes. (28) Having performed the rites with the *savanīya* offerings, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite: "Recite the invitatory verse for those being drawn out. (29) He draws out the cups belonging to the *achāvāka*. (30) It is established up to the formal command. (31) For the third pressing, [he offers] to the Ṛbhumat, the Vibhumat, the Vājavat, the Bṛhaspativat, the Viśvadevyavat, the Tīvrasut, the Āśīrvat, and to Indra. (28–31)

"Recite the *praisha* for the Soma cups set forth," and it is established as at the midday pressing. 32. "O God Soma, belonging to the troop of Adityas, you who know the mind, of the third pressing, of the Jagatī meter, offered into the fire, drunk by Indra"—thus the *bhakṣa-mantra* is modified. 33. It is established up to the placing [of the cups]. 34. At the Mārjālīya site, those wearing the sacred cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*) cast three small balls of sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa-piṇḍa*), mixed with fine grains, behind each cup, saying: "O Fathers, rejoice here; eat according to your respective portions. Thus they cast them out.

Each [priest] fills his own cup; the *hotṛ* fills the *hotṛ*-cup. (35) Having loosened their *prācīnāvīta* knots, they set down the cups in their respective places. (36) In the *āgnīdhra* shed, they consume the *savanīya* oblations.

That has been explained. (37) From the *āgrayaṇa* vessel, he draws the *sāvitra* cup into the *antaryāma* vessel with the formula, "With thy undeceivable [eyes], O Savitṛ... (38) It is offered while still remaining in the vessel. (39) He causes the recitation to be made with the words, "Recite the invitatory verse for the god Savitṛ. (40) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he proceeds with the call, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the god Savitṛ! (41) When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he does not offer the entire portion. (42) After the residue of the *sāvitra* cup has been poured into the *pūtabhṛt*, he draws the *vaiśvadeva* cup. (43) He draws it with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; thou art a good refuge, a firm foundation. This is thy womb: for the Viśve Devas, thee!"

Thus he sets it down (44). He responds to the *vaiśvadeva* cup (45). While the verse "With one and with ten" (*ekayā ca daśabhiśca*) is being recited, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having washed the cups for the dual deities, places them on the mound (*khara*) (46). [He responds] to the *dyāvāpṛthivīya* cup with the verse "May Heaven and Earth increase through the sacrifices according to the cosmic order" (*pra dyāvā yajñaiḥ pṛthivī ṛtāvṛdhā*).

In that [rite], the response (*pratigara*) is "madā modaiva modā modaiva," containing the word *mad* (intoxicating joy). 47. The response begins with "surūpakṛtnumūtaye" and continues until the end. 48. When the recitation (*śastra*) is completed, the procedure from the taking up of the cup (*grahādāna*) onwards is the same up to the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) of the portion for Indra and Agni. 49. The formula for the consumption is modified as follows: "O divine Soma, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, you who possess wisdom, of the third pressing, of the Jagatī metre, drunk by the ancestors... 50. It is established up to the placing [of the cups]. 51.

He recites [the offering formula] for the Soma-oblation: having taken a portion of clarified butter, having stepped across to the west of the handles of the offering-spoons toward the south, and having stood facing the junction of the southern enclosing-stick, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* and issues the direction: "Recite the offering-verse for the ghee (*ghṛtasya yaja*). He makes the oblation in the southern half. Standing from that very spot and wearing the sacred cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*), having taken a portion of the Soma-oblation, having stepped across toward the north, and having stood facing the junction of the northern enclosing-stick, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* and issues the direction: "Recite the offering-verse for the Soma-oblation (*saumyasya yaja*)."

Standing in the south, he offers in the middle. Having circumambulated, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he takes a portion of clarified butter, steps northward, stands facing the northern junction of the enclosing sticks, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and gives the direction: "Sacrifice the clarified butter! He offers in the northern half. Having pushed aside the Soma-vessel, he fills it with clarified butter. The sacrificer looks at it, saying: "Truly yours is this, that which is here. If he does not see it, he should mutter: "My mind that has gone to Yama... Having looked at it, he hands it to the Udgātṛ priests.

8. Having made eight handfuls of *darbha* grass into eight firmly bound bundles, he, sitting facing west while the eight portions taken with the *pracaraṇī* ladle are held over the flaming hearths (*dhiṣṇya*), sprinkles them with the offerings while reciting the *upasthāna* formulas. 9. He takes the *pātnīvata* cup from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel into the *upāṃśu* cup with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; of thee, pressed by Bṛhaspati... 10. It is offered when [the fire] has been moved away. 11. He mixes it with the remnants of the hearth-sprinkling, saying: "O Agni, accompanied by the wives... 12. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he gives the direction: "O Āgnīdh, sacrifice for the *pātnīvata*. 13. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered...

He does not offer the entire portion; he hands a portion to the Āgnīdhra. Having mounted the lap of the Neṣṭṛ and moved northward, he consumes [the Soma] from behind the Neṣṭṛ’s seat with the formula: "May Vāc, the goddess, drink of the Soma. In the Agniṣṭoma, he pours the entire contents of the Hotṛ’s cup and the other Agniṣṭoma cups. In the Ukthya sacrifice, there should be an excess. Having made room in the Hotṛ’s cup for the Dhruva vessel, he inaugurates the Agniṣṭoma stotra.

In front of him, the sacrificer mutters the *saptahotṛ* formula (ĀpŚS 19.19). While the *stotra* is being chanted, the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*) should remain with their ears covered (19). Once the *prastāva* has been chanted, the wife, holding the *pānnejana* jar between her thighs with her right leg, causes it to flow northward, saying, "To the ocean, whose lord is the Gandharva" (20). The *neṣṭṛ* makes the wife look at the *udgātṛ* three times while the latter performs the *udgītha* on the first three *stotriya* verses, before the *pratihāra*, saying, "O beautiful one, thy appearance is lovely" (21). He responds to the *āgnimāruta* hymn as soon as it is near completion (22).

The *viyāt* [verse] is the *āpohiṣṭhīya*. At that point, they take hold of the *hotṛ*. 23. Beginning with "Truly, this [Soma] is sweet" (*svāduṣkila ayam*), there is the *svāduṣkilīya*. At that point, he responds with a verse containing the word "intoxicating" (*madvat*). 24. The response begins with "By whose might the two worlds were propped apart" (*yayorojasā skabhitā rajāṃsi*) and continues until the end. 25. "Thus indeed is Indra, the bountiful, the exuberant" (*evā na indro maghavā virapśī*) is the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*).

When the half-verse has been repeated, the Pratiprasthātṛ, standing facing west and holding on [to the Hotṛ], while the sacrificer holds on as well, pours the *dhruva* [soma] into the Hotṛ’s cup, making him recite from "The *dhruva* with the *dhruva*" up to the end of "May I become visible to all" (*aham viśvadarśato bhūyāsam*). Having responded to the final *śastra*, he should say, "The *uktha* is in speech; O Indra... The Adhvaryu takes the Hotṛ’s cup, and the Camasādhvaryus take their cups. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, [the Adhvaryu says] "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice! (26–28).

He gives the command, "Of the Soma-juices... (29). At the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*, both [the Adhvaryu] and the cup-bearers (*camasādhvaryu*) offer their libations (30). From this point onward, the procedure for the commands and the offering of the Soma-juices remains the same (31). They consume the portions of all [the cups] with the formula, "May the goddess Speech drink of the Soma" (32). Having washed them at the *mārjālīya* shed, they set them down at the edge of the *cātvāla* pit in an *agniṣṭoma*; if it is an *ukthya* sacrifice, they set them down at the edge of the *pūtabhṛt* vessel (33).

If the Ukthya is separated [from the Agniṣṭoma], he draws the first cup with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; for Indra and Varuṇa, thee! the second with "Thou art taken with a support; for Indra and Bṛhaspati, thee! and the third with "Thou art taken with a support; for Indra and Viṣṇu, thee! The rest is the same. He draws the entire [Soma] into the Ukthya vessel. There should be an excess in the Ṣoḍaśin. He draws the entire [Soma] into the Ṣoḍaśin cups. There should be an excess in the Atirātra. When the sun has half-set, he [offers] to Indra with two blades of darbha grass and with gold.

"O Maruts, turn back; come hither; approach, O sacrificer!"—with these words he introduces the Stotra in the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice. (7) A dark-grey horse, snorting, stands nearby. (8) At the conclusion of the Stotra, he gives a female mule to the Udgātṛ. (9) The response (pratigara) at the third pressing is "śikṣyaḥ. (10) From this point forward, the formula for the consumption (bhakṣamantra) is modified in the Ṣoḍaśin as follows: "Of that which was offered into the fire, O Indra, accompanied by the Haris, and drunk, [of that] which has the Anuṣṭubh metre... (11) If the Atirātra is not a Ṣoḍaśin, having performed the rites with the Ukthyas, he proceeds with the night-round (rātriparyāya) after sunset.

12. There are four groups of *camasa* cups accompanied by *stotra* and *śastra* hymns. Of these, the first belongs to the *hotṛ*, then that of the *maitrāvaruṇa*, the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, and the *acchāvāka*. 13. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, who art acceptable to Indra for the sake of the night," with these words he draws each principal cup. 14. "O Agni, thou art offered in the *anuṣṭubh* metre; O Indra, [thou art] drunk by him for the sake of the night"—thus the *bhakṣa-mantra* (consumption formula) is modified. 15. In this manner there is a second turn; the third takes place at night, during the deep of the night (*mahārātra*). 16.

The *saṃdhi-camasas* have the *hotṛ-camasa* as their chief; into these he pours all [the soma] at the *atirātra*. 17. At the *aptoryāman*, there should be an additional draught. 18. When the *stotra* has been introduced, the *pratiprasthātṛ* prepares the *aśvin* cake on two potsherds, which has been processed silently. 19. He utters the *pratihāra* for the great *āśvina-śastra*.

After the recitation of the *paramasahasra* and the stepping forward, when the sun has risen, he recites the verses dedicated to Sūrya (20). When the *śastra* is completed, the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts off the entire portion for the Aśvins at once (21). The Adhvaryu takes up the Hotṛ’s cup, and the Camasādhvaryus take up their respective cups (22). He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words: "Recite the invitatory verse for the Somas of the day-after-tomorrow belonging to the Aśvins" (23). Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he proceeds with the action, saying: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the Somas of the day-after-tomorrow belonging to the Aśvins which have been set forth" (24). At the first *vaṣaṭ*-call, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the entire portion for the Aśvins as a complete oblation (25).

"The *paṅkti* metre, offered into Agni, drunk by the Aśvins"—thus is the modified mantra for the consumption [of the soma]. (26) In the *aptoryāma*, there is one night-round (*rātriparyāya*). (27) He draws the principal cups silently. (28) "The *aticchandas* metre, offered into Agni, drunk by Prajāpati"—thus is the modified mantra for the consumption [of the soma]. (29) They set down the *saṃsthā-camasas* at the edge of the *catvāla*. (30)

The rites from the *ānuyāja* offerings onwards are established up to the releasing of the offering-ladles (1). The *unnetṛ* priest takes the entire *hāriyojana* draught from the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, starting from the *āgrayaṇa*, with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the bay horse, belonging to the yoker of bays" (2). He mixes it with parched grains (*dhānā*) with the formula: "The parched grains for the two bays, accompanied by the bays" (3). The *unnetṛ* places the *droṇakalaśa* on his head and causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse: "O Indra, for the sake of the bays, for the parched grains and the Soma-draughts, recite the invitatory verse" (4). Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "O Adhvaryu, for Indra, for the sake of the bays, for the parched grains and the Soma-draughts set forth, give the command," and then he steps apart.

It proceeds; he offers at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ*. They consume the *māhāriyajana* [portion] by wiping it out, making a sucking sound as they all chew the parched grains (*dhānāḥ*), and having tasted them with the words, "For prosperity, for nourishment, thee! they scatter them upon the high altar (*uttaravedī*). "You are the expiation for sin committed against the gods; you are the expiation for sin committed against the ancestors; you are the expiation for sin committed against men; you are the expiation for sin committed against oneself; you are the expiation for sin committed against others; you are the expiation for every sin."

Saying "Svāhā! they place six pieces of wood from each sacrificial post into the Āhavanīya fire. "O Gods, whatever heavy offense against the gods we have committed with our tongue or through the negligence of our mind—O Vasus, lay that sin upon him who is hostile to us and seeks to bring us misfortune."

Thus they worship the Āhavanīya fire. 9. They pour *dūrvā* grass into the cups, immersing them repeatedly in water, and consume [the Soma] with their noses, saying: "O divine Soma, of thee who art washed... 10. Saying, "Svadhā to the father, svadhā to the grandfather, svadhā to the great-grandfather," they pour out the contents of each cup upon the sacrificial grass toward the *cātvāla* pit. 11. "I send you forth to the ocean; O Maruts, may this song of praise reach you; may it reach Viṣṇu, the protector of the poured [Soma], with his aids."

"And may you bestow vigor upon the progeny of the one who praises you; do you ever protect us with your blessings. With these words, having led [the bride] away, he recites the consecratory formula. "O great sages, young ones, upholders of truth from the foundation of Dharma—by the law of Truth, let us dissolve our bonds of friendship."

13. Thus, to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, they release their bonds of friendship. 14. With the verse, "I have praised Dadhikrāvan," they consume the curd at the Āgnīdhra fire. 15. The ritual from the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings onwards is established up to the Samiṣṭayajus oblations. 16. Having replenished the Dhruvā ladle nine times, he offers the nine Samiṣṭayajus oblations continuously with the formula beginning, "Dhātā is the giver. 17. "This is the third pressing of the seers; those Saudhanvanas who, by means of the Truth, set the cup in motion, attaining immortality—may that well-offered sacrifice lead us to greater prosperity."

"Let them lead [him] away. With these words, he offers the oblation that effects the pressing (*savanakaraṇī*). He offers the second oblation with the verse, "The drop has fallen" (*drapsaś caskanda*). 17. He offers a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) to Varuṇa. 18. [The ritual] is established as usual up to the removal from the fire (*udvāsanāt*). 19. He makes an additional offering (*abhijuhoti*) with the verse: "O God, giver of life, choosing old age... 20. "Releasing the supporter for his mother, the supporter suckling his mother—may he bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor."

Thus the Udgātṛ unbinds the Audumbarī post. 21. They proceed together to the Cātvāla pit for the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). 22. He places the Audumbarī post upon the two pressing-boards and the throne-seat; likewise, he places those items smeared with Soma, other than the Soma-vessels. 23. "The god Savitṛ has become worthy of praise for us now; he is to be invoked by men at this time of day—he who distributes treasures to human beings, so that he may grant us the most excellent wealth here. He has bestowed his body with milk; one form of his becomes another.

We have been invited to that [sacrifice]; therefore, O Soma, as you are being born, bring us a hero. O King Soma, that limb of yours which the pressing-stone has severed, that dear part of your body—unite it again and let it grow whole; with all my limbs, I become one with you. O Soma, do not lead us astray through crookedness; do not take away our supreme wealth, nor our very life-force, nor cast us into blind darkness; may Rudra not strike us down with his heavy weapon.

"May Soma be keen of sight and keen of hearing; may his skin be pure and full again. May he bestow wealth upon us here in our cups; may we rejoice, joined with vigor and refreshment. With these verses, he pours curds over the *ṛjīṣa* in the pressing-vessel. (24) He gives the command: "O Udgātṛ, sing the Sāman! or "O Prastotṛ! (25) All [the priests] join in the *nidhana* of that [Sāman].

Having reached the second half of the day, the third [rite] follows. (26) The purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) belongs to the Vāruṇapraghāsa sacrifice. (27) He sacrifices to Varuṇa with a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*), and to Agnīvaruṇa with a mixture of curd and parched grain (*āśayena*). (28) Having placed the residue of the Soma (*ṛjīṣa*) in the offering-spoon (*sruk*), he strikes it together with the spoon while reciting: "In the ocean is thy heart, within the waters. (29) With the verse, "O purificatory bath, Nicuṅkuṇa," he scatters the throne-seat (*āsandī*) and the items smeared with Soma. (30) They consume the floating residue of the Soma in the water with the filter (*avadhra*), reciting: "Of thee, O divine Soma, who art washed... (31) He holds it in the region of his mouth. (32)

He gives a black antelope skin to his beloved wife; upon it they perform the grinding. With the formula, "The bond of Varuṇa is untied," he unfastens the girdle and the garment. The wife silently [unfastens] her waist-band and the net. Having bathed at the purificatory rite (avabhṛtha), they wash each other's backs. The sacrificer puts on the Soma-robe, and the wife puts on the saddle-cloth.

At the time of giving the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *udavasānīyā* offering, [the fee] is given to the *adhvaryu*. (36) The sacrificer says to the *unnetṛ*, "O *unnetṛ*, may you be more prosperous. (37) With the verse, "Upward for thee the most honeyed songs," the *unnetṛ* causes [the sacrificer] to step forward. (38) The throwing back [of the grass-bundle] and the sprinkling (*mārjana*) have been explained. (39) "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal; we have reached the light, we have found the gods. What can hostility now do to us? What, O Immortal One, can the malice of a mortal do? (RV 8.48.3)
Thus they mutter. Having placed the Unnetṛ in front, they return without looking back; that has been explained.

The *udayanīya* [concluding offering] is explained by the *prāyaṇīya* [opening offering]. (1) He offers the *udayanīya* after the scrapings (*niṣkāṣa*) of the *prāyaṇīya*. (2) He proceeds with the rites at the *Śālāmukhīya* fire. (3) Before sunrise, he sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti in the eastern part [of the altar]. (4) He places the *veda*-grass-bundle for the *anūbandhyā* cow. (5) He binds together the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice. (6) He immolates the *anūbandhyā*, a barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. (7) "At the time of the goat, for the cow"—this is the formal summons (*saṃpraiṣa*). (8) The procedure is established up to the offering of the omentum (*vapā*). (9) When the omentum has been offered, [he proceeds] at the *cātvāla* pit.

Having cleansed himself, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved within an enclosure on the southern hip of the altar. Following the animal cake-offering, he offers the Devikā oblations: a *caru* for Anumati, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Rākā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, and Dhātṛ.

He cooks [the oblations] in Soma-pots (11). It is completed up to the point of the *pracaraṇa* (12). Having performed the rite with the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), he proceeds with the *devikā* offerings (13). This is the ritual procedure for the *anvaya* (14). Taking portions from both the animal-cake and the *devikā* offerings together, he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with an undefined verse (15). The animal sacrifice is thus completed.

Or [they perform] the *payasyā* offering. They loosen the first knots made on the two *havirdhāna* carts and move them northward; one with the front half and the other with the rear half of the *āhavanīya*. "Whatever debt was not repaid by me here, by which we have lived under Yama’s treasury—by this, O Agni, I become free from debt; while still living, I give it back and I repay it."

With these words, the sacrificer circumambulates the altar starting from the Āhavanīya fire. (18) "O Viśloka, I offer you into the all-consuming forest fire, svāhā!"—with this, the sacrificer offers a handful of parched barley-grains into the forest fire. (19) "One has been sacrificed, one has not been sacrificed; one is offered, one is unoffered; one is performed, one is unperformed; one is done, one is undone; one is ancient, one is both ancient and non-ancient; may they provide us with healing, a dwelling, strength, and what is desirable"—with this, the sacrificer worships the forest fire. (20) "This treasure which you have brought hither, I entrust it to you, O place of assembly."

"Jātavedas shall follow after you, O lords of the sacrifice, here; recognize him in the highest heaven! O gods who dwell together, recognize him in the highest heaven; know his form—he who has come by the paths traveled by the gods—make manifest for him the merit of his sacrifices and charitable works. Thus the sacrificer entrusts [him]. "Debt-free in this world, debt-free in the next, and debt-free in the third world may we be. In all the worlds—the worlds of the gods and the worlds of the ancestors—may we move about free from debt."

Thus the sacrificer mutters. 22. He consigns the two fires into the kindling woods; if he has attained prosperity, he consigns the Śālāmukhīya fire as well. 23. Having moved northward and churned out the fire from the two kindling woods, he performs the Udavasānīyā offering. 24. It consists of a cake on five potsherds for Agni alone; there are separate portions for the fore-offerings and after-offerings, and the two butter-portions (ājyabhāgas) are dedicated to Agni. 25. An ox is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 26. Or alternatively, having offered a full-oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to Viṣṇu, [the fire is consigned]. 27. "May Agni, the first of those worthy of sacrifice, go forth unextinguished; may the Lord of Rest find rest for me."
"Having shone forth, may we follow after you. With these words, the sacrificer, placing the sacrificial ground (vihāra) before him, goes to his home; he goes.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Mānava-Śulba-Sūtra* regarding the Agniṣṭoma;
thus ends the Agniṣṭoma in the *Mānava-Śulba-Sūtra*.

Brahmā offers expiations with the *sruva* ladle: if there is a failure regarding the *ṛc*, he says "bhūḥ svāhā" over the Gārhapatya fire; if regarding the *yajus*, "bhuvaḥ svāhā" over the Dakṣiṇāgni; if regarding the *sāman*, "svaḥ svāhā" over the Āhavanīya; and if it is a failure in all respects, "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā" over the Āhavanīya itself. (1) One should throw spoiled items into the water, then wipe the vessels clean: one should scrape metal, heat wood, wash earthenware with water, and polish gold and silver. (2) In the event of the loss of a substance, one should substitute another that is generally fit for sacrifice. (3)

If an action is interrupted, one should perform the expiation at the next consecration; if there is a change of materials, one should repeat the mantra along with it, or perform it silently. In the event of a transposition of deities, portions of the offering, *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, the *havis*, mantras, or ritual actions—and for those cases where no specific expiation has been prescribed—one should, in times of distress, offer oblations with the verses "Thou, O Agni, art ours," "So thou, O Agni, art ours," and "O Agni, thou art *ayās*," as well as with the *vyāhṛtis*; or alternatively, with the *vyāhṛtis* alone.

6. Even at the time of the *homa*, in all cases where no specific expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been prescribed, one should offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* alone. 7. If one releases speech at an improper time, one should recite a verse addressed to Viṣṇu and restrain it again. 8. If the *āhavanīya* fire should go out while one is engaged in a vow, having mentally undertaken the vow once the fire has been led forward (*praṇīta*), one should worship it with the syllable *bhūḥ*. 9. If the calves, having been separated from their mothers, should suckle [at another cow], one should perform an offering of barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) to Vāyu and then proceed with the morning milk-offering; if the morning milk-offering itself is spoiled, there is another offering to Vāyu. 10. If one should steal the evening milk-offering, or if it should become spoiled.

Having caused the morning milk to be milked in two portions and having curdled one half, he should proceed with the ritual. (10) If the evening milk should meet with misfortune, he should offer grains for Indra; on the following day, he should perform a supplementary offering upon those grains. (11) If the morning milk should meet with misfortune, [he should offer] a cake for Indra; if both [milks] should meet with misfortune, he should cook five-śarāva-measures of rice for Indra and first sacrifice to Agni with clarified butter. (12) When [the offerings] have been omitted or when misfortune has occurred, having driven away the calves, he should sacrifice again. (13) For him whose *sāṃnāyya* offering is overtaken by the moon, he should drive back the calves. (14)

The evening milking is the curdling agent for the oblation; observing that vow, he should sacrifice at the proper time. (15) For one who is unable to maintain the vow, there is the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice; and once the grains have been poured out, having driven away the calves, he should sacrifice again. (16) If they should carry off the oblations or if they should be spoiled, he should conclude with clarified butter and sacrifice again. (17) If the oblations should become confused, he should divide them equally among the vessels and proceed with them in their proper order. (18) In the case of everything being spilled, lost, or spoiled, there is a re-preparation as before. (19)

If [the oblation] spills, one should consecrate it with the mantra, "The gods have accepted the sacrifice," and pour water over it. (20) If the clarified butter spills before it has been purified, he gives [a gift]; if it spills while being purified, [he gives] something bright; if it spills after it has been purified, [he gives] a boon. (21) In the case of two [portions] that are poorly cooked, if only the portions are offered, there is no expiation if they become well-cooked.

Likewise, for two [offerings] requiring expiation (kṣāma): 22. Having sacrificed with the left [hand], he should give away a fertile field as a gift (dakṣiṇā). 23. If the potsherd should break, he should join it together with pure substances that serve for joining, saying: "With the Gāyatrī of a hundred syllables, I join thee. Then, having joined that potsherd, he should cast it into the water, saying: "The supporter, the father of the Father, the unbroken heat (gharma), the life of all—whence it was born, thither it has gone; svāhā! Then, having brought another potsherd and performed the placing, touching, sprinkling, and so forth, he should insert it among the previously prepared potsherds.

If, however, that which has been placed [on the fire] is broken, one should perform its rejoining and so forth as before; having prepared another [potsherd], one should place it at the time of laying down the potsherds in its place with the very same mantra with which the original was placed. (24) If a potsherd should be lost, [the procedure] explained in the Brāhmaṇa applies: "The Ordainer, the Ordainer of the father, the father of the father; the lost Law... Having thrown the lost [sherd] into the water, one should consecrate the newly found one with the mantra: "Homage to you, O Rudra, as you go; homage be to you as you go away; homage where you sit down. (25) If [the sherd is lost] prior to the Prayājas...

If a coal should fall outside the enclosing stones, he should address it with the mantra: "Do not harm the Adhvaryu! Do not harm the sacrifice!"—to the east; "Do not harm the Brahman! Do not harm the progeny!"—to the south; "Do not harm the Hotṛ! Do not harm the wife!"—to the west; "Do not harm the Āgnīdhra! Do not harm the cattle!"—to the north.

"May you not harm the sacrificer"—with these words he appends [the formula] everywhere. (26) Having smeared [the wood] with the bottom of the *sruva* ladle, he says: "I establish the sacrifice in the lap of Nirṛti; I entrust it to myself among the gods, being wise. May we enjoy good offspring for a hundred winters; O gods, bestow protection upon me here. With this, he takes [the wood]. (27) "The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas, offered with clarified butter, whose back is the *stoma*, the possessor of good heroes—may he not abandon me; I do not forsake you, though I am in need. Bestow upon us prosperity in cattle and prosperity in heroes."

"Do not harm our great, nor our small; do not harm our growing, nor our grown. Do not slay our father, nor our mother; do not injure our dear bodies, O Rudra. With this, he makes the final offering. "O Agni, you are ours; O Agni, you are ours—Soma, the sun-rayed, the bull of the people, the omniform, the invincible, Bṛhaspati, the most excellent. "Loosen the highest bond from us, O Varuṇa; loosen the highest, release the middle bond from me."

"Driving away [the enemies] so that we may live"—with these six verses he performs the *abhijuhoti* offerings. (29) If he should invoke a deity for whom no portion has been set aside, he should sacrifice with clarified butter (*ājya*) according to the manner in which it was invoked. If he has not invoked the *bhāginī* (the "share-holding" deity), he should rise up and invoke her. (30) If an oblation should spill outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he should say to the *Āgnīdhra*, "Having gathered this together, offer it. Having prepared it as an offering-portion, he offers it with his hand in the center at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.

He should give a full vessel to him [the Adhvaryu] with the formula: "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā! He should consecrate what has spilled outside the enclosing sticks [with this same formula]. (31–32) If there is a lapse of time, and the Pathikṛt offering has not yet arrived—(33) if, prior to the pouring out [of the oblation], he should touch upon the commencement of the time for either the Full Moon or the New Moon sacrifice, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt. (34) If, when the Brāhmaudana has been set aside, the fire should go out and he should follow it, or if he should let the time pass, he should cook the Brāhmaudana again, anoint the kindling woods, and place them on the fire. (35)

If the cow let down her knee for the Agnihotra, he addresses her with: "From whatever you are afraid that you sit down, from that grant us fearlessness; do not harm our cattle! Homage to Rudra, the bountiful one! Then he says: "The goddess Aditi has arisen; she has bestowed long life upon the lord of the sacrifice, providing a portion for Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa."

Having raised her up in this manner, one should cause her to hold a water-pot at her breast and at her mouth; one should give that [milk] to him whose food one would not otherwise eat. If the *agnihotra* milk should spill before it has been placed on the fire, one should pour water over it with the mantra, "I send you away to the ocean," and then recite: "That milk which today has entered the earth, which has flowed into the plants, and which is in the waters—that milk may be in the earth, in the plants, in the cows, in the calves, in our houses; may that be ours."

Thus he consecrates [the milk]. (2) If the cow being milked should break [the vessel], he should wash another vessel prepared by an Ārya and milk again. (3) If the milk placed on the fire should spill, this has been explained [in the previous section].

Having recited the *vāruṇī* verse, he should offer clarified butter with the *vāruṇī* formula. (4) If [the ghee] being carried forward should spill, he should touch it with the formula, "Thou art offered in the all-sustaining body of Prajāpati, svāhā! and he should pour it out as if it had been licked by a dog. (5) If that which has been placed on the fire should overflow, he should say, "May it burn up so-and-so," naming the one whom he hates. (6) If it has been spilled, he should pour it back within the enclosing sticks using the middle leaf with the verse addressed to Heaven and Earth; if it has been defiled by insects, he should pour it into an ant-hill with the verse addressed to Prajāpati and worship it with the syllable *bhūḥ*.

Or [if it is] decomposed, or fallen into an anthill, or infested by insects, [he should place it] within the enclosing sticks. When it has rained down: "Mitra, speaking, impels the people; Mitra has supported the earth and the sky; Mitra gazes upon the tribes with unblinking eyes; for Mitra, offer the oblation rich in ghee."

Thus he should offer the first oblation; having then milked another [cow], he should perform the *agnihotra* again. (8) If the *āhavanīya* fire should go out after the first oblation has been offered, he should place gold down, saying, "Fire is in the wood; the wood is in the fire," and then offer the subsequent oblation; having then milked another [cow], he should perform the *agnihotra* again. (9) If [the oblation] should spill after the first has been offered, [he recites]: "O Lord of the Forest, wherever you know the secret names of the gods, there cause the offerings to go."

Having thus placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he should offer the subsequent oblation; then, having milked another cow, he should perform the *agnihotra* again. (10) If Rudra should take ill-will toward the cattle, he should have two cows milked into a vessel and a milk-pail, pour them together, and offer the first oblation with the verse, "In harmony, O Jātavedas"; then, having milked another cow, he should perform the *agnihotra* again. (11) If [the fire] should go out for seven days, he should offer an oblation beforehand with the verse, "O Agni, you who are difficult to soothe"; then, having milked another cow, he should perform the *agnihotra* again, if...

If he should suffer from that affliction, he should offer clarified butter every evening for twelve nights. (12) If Rudra should afflict his offspring, he should walk about muttering the Śatarudriya in the north-eastern direction. (13) If the sun should set while the fire has not yet been taken out, once the Agnihotra has been drawn out, a learned Brāhmaṇa should carry it forth; having tied gold with Darbha grass, he should carry it in front, and follow behind with the Agnihotra; a boon is the sacrificial fee. (14) If the sun should rise while [the fire] has not been taken out, the procedure for carrying it forth has already been explained.

One should carry four portions of clarified butter forward and offer it from the east while facing west, saying: "May the Dawns with their banner enjoy [it], Svāhā! He should remain seated until the fire goes out, until the oblation is completed. The rule regarding whose two fires have both gone out has already been explained.

If, before the Agnihotra has been offered, the eastern fire should go out, one should carry it forth together with the fire for the Agnihotra itself, while consecrating the fire that has been drawn out with the verse: "From there indeed was he first born. With the words, "For food and wealth, rejoice," he establishes the fire when it is about to be established; with the words, "Thou art the sovereign ruler," he establishes it once it has been placed. With the words, "May the two springs of Sarasvatī protect thee," he addresses the fire once it has been established.

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat and a porridge of barley to Varuṇa. If, when the Agnihotra has not yet been offered, another fire should follow [the first], one should follow the former fire and, having churned a fire from the latter, carry it forward. If one is in haste, then having taken out fire from that very spot and having brought the Dakṣiṇāgni, one should perform the evening and morning oblations. On the following day, having consigned the fire and churned it again, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pākkavat. And in all cases where the fire is followed, [one should offer] to him who is Agni...

"For the feast of the gods, the one possessing the oblation desires to invite [you]; O Purifier, be gracious to him. With this verse, he should immediately offer the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-offering). If they should carry fire into the fire, he should recite over it, "May you two be of one mind for us," and offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Agnimat. If the time for the evening *agnihotra* should be passed, he should append [the formula] at the end of the first offering: "To the Night, to the Dawn, obeisance, svāhā! [The same applies to] the morning *agnihotra*.
If the fire should rise up after the dawns, he consecrates the drawn-out portion with the mantra: "It has eaten the tip of the dawns; O Āhavanīya, be secure right here, do not abandon me!"

He pronounces the name [of the sacrificer] as "me" or "so-and-so," and the lineage as "the descendant of so-and-so. At the first oblation, he should append at the end: "Homage to Vastor, Svāhā! (8). When the offering has been made, he should offer a *caru* for Mitra and a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya (9). Alternatively, the husband and wife, restrained in speech and fasting, should remain in attendance throughout the entire day by the two kindling woods (10). In the evening, he should perform the *agnihotra* with the milk of two cows (11). On the following day, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati (12).

If the fire should go out before the throwing of the yoke-pin, he gathers everything together and brings it back with the verse: "This is one [fire] for you, and that beyond is another; unite with the third light! Then he says: "Be pleasant for the body at the time of entering; be dear to the gods in the highest birthplace."

Thus he scatters [the grains]. 1. If he should bring the other two fires further away and offer the oblations in the evening and morning, then on the following day he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the path-maker); the sacrificial grass should be from near the path, and the fee is an ox. 2. He who should sacrifice in other fires, or in whose fires others should sacrifice, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. 3. If his fires should become mixed with one another, or if there is a collision of *iṣṭis*, the *vaiśvī* [offering] comes first. 4. "To Agni Śuci..."—this has been explained. 5.

The rule regarding "the one whose *āhitāgni* [is extinguished]" has been explained (6). The rule regarding "whose fire should go out" has been explained (7). If one’s [fire] should be constantly interrupted, having offered the omitted oblations, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat; or alternatively, having offered a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he need not concern himself with the omitted oblations, but should proceed with the evening oblation (8). If, while the *agnihotra* has been set down, or when the sacrificial food has been poured out, or while the *soma* sacrifice is in progress, a chariot, a horse, a man, a dog, a black bird, or any other living being should pass between [the fires], [he should perform] three times thirty...

Having offered [the oblation] with the verse "O you who possess a hundred ends" into the Āhavanīya fire, he turns back toward the cow and makes her turn around. With the verse "Viṣṇu strode through this," he steps upon the footprint and sprinkles water over it. Alternatively, having taken ashes from the Gārhapatya fire and scattering them along the footprint from the Āhavanīya with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he should run forward. Having caused the cow to follow, he should lead her out from the western side. He places the fire with the verse: "O Agni, that former footprint which was laid down for thee, there thou didst stretch out after the rays of the sun; may they carry wealth there; unite us with a benevolent mind full of vigor. Thus he establishes the fire. 9–10.

If the speckled butter should spill, one should place gold in between, pour more out, have a horse sniff it, and offer two oblations with these two verses: "May the mind, the light, increase; may prosperity [increase]" (Taitt. Br. 2.4.6.5). If the animal dedicated for sacrifice should run away, or if it should meet with some other mishap, one should set aside barley-gruel for Vāyu and then dedicate another animal of the same form, the same color, and the same age.

Having proceeded with the barley-gruel (yavāgū) for Vāyu, he should proceed with the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) of the animal sacrifice, together with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *iḍā*. This same procedure applies in the event of the [animal] dying. If it should be brought back, he should offer two oblations with the verses "Thou, O Agni, for us... and "So thou, O Agni, for us..."; he should then cut portions from that sacrificed animal; he should remain standing for as long as it takes for the other [animal] to become the remainder. If it should fly up after [the immolation], he should offer two oblations with the verses "O you who stand upright in the sacrifice... and "Upward, indeed, for us...".

He should offer four oblations with [the verse], "May the Marut Nitāna strike you down," if he should pull up or move the sacrificial post (yūpa). He should perform the sprinkling around it as it stands. If the cord should break, snap, or bite through, he should join the knot with the verse, "Thirty-three threads," and offer an oblation with that same verse. If the wooden chip (svaru) or the axe should be lost, he should smear another piece of wood from the post onto the offering-spoon and make it the svaru; likewise, he should anoint the top-ring (caṣāla) in the same manner.

"Those who protect our sacrifice from what is well-offered and from what is ill-offered—may they not harm our cattle; may they protect the sacrifice. With this, one should offer an oblation. (7) If [the animal] should void dung or urine, one should make it drink again, sprinkle it, and offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* alone. (8) If it leaps up while trembling out of fear, one should offer [an oblation] with: "From whom you tremble, O leaper! (9) If it shakes while trembling out of fear, [one should offer] with: "From whom you shake, O shaker! (10) If it whines while trembling out of fear, [one should offer] with: "From whom you whine, O wailer! (11) "If you sit down out of fear of someone, grant us freedom from fear because of that. (12)

"Do not harm our cattle; salutations to Rudra, the bountiful one"—this he should recite when [the fire] has settled. (12) "Agni, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Prajāpati, Varuṇa, and he who is for me—may they take pleasure in this. Seize the body of him who hates us, but spare the heroes of the sinless sacrificer"—this he should offer as oblation while [the fire] is resting. (13) If the cauldron (*ukhā*) should leak, [he should recite]: "The flowing cauldron, the unshaken, the work of Agni the Hotṛ, the earth, the atmosphere—wherever it hisses, let that not reach Agni, but let Nirṛti be beyond."

Thus he consecrates [the offering]. 14 If a hawk should carry off the omentum, or some other creature, or some other portion of the offering, he should sacrifice with the verse: "Whatever the bird has torn away with its beak, O Nirṛti, that Agni shall protect—the bearer of oblations, the purifier with ghee. 15 If he should not find the portion of the offering, he should take a portion of clarified butter; in the event of the loss of the heart, he should immolate another animal.

One should cut portions from the gold for the double-sacrifice (dvirājya). (16) If he should desire, "May they crush their cattle; may they meet with misfortune," he should offer an oblation on the Āgnīdhrīya fire with the verse containing the word *namas* and the words "kuvidaṅga yavamanto yavaṃ cit" (RV 8.91.2). (17) If there should be an eight-footed [creature], having placed the fetus of that eight-footed one upon a spit, having smeared it with clay, he should bury it in the Śāmitra fire-pit. Having drawn an iron vessel beneath it, he should cook it. With its juice, before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he should sacrifice with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ" (RV 10.121), verse by verse.

He should offer oblations; gold with eight ridges is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). When the rite is completed, he pours the embryo into the animal-cooking fire with the verse, "May the great heaven and earth... He worships [the fire] with the five verses beginning, "Homage to the Greatness... 18.

If a sacrificial post should grow crooked toward the west before the completion of the Soma sacrifice, one should offer a multi-colored animal to Tvaṣṭṛ. With the formulas beginning, "Prajāpati in the mind; Sarasvant when speech is released; Dhātṛ at the consecration; Brahman at the vow," one should unite the body of the sacrifice with these and offer oblations if there should be distress regarding the former part, merging it into the latter: "To Prajāpati in the mind, svāhā! To Sarasvant when speech is released, svāhā!"

If [the Soma] is stolen in the north, when speech has been released, he should offer with the formula "To Dhātṛ, for consecration, svāhā!"—thus, having combined whichever part is damaged with the following [verse], he should sacrifice; or alternatively, he should sacrifice three fourfold-drawn portions with the three Anuvākas. If they should carry off the King (Soma), he should press that Soma which is nearest; he should give something to the non-Soma-seller. If he cannot find Soma, he should press Pūtīka plants; if not Pūtīkas, then Arjuna plants or the down of red Rohita deer.

In place of [the shoots] from the Himalaya, he uses brown cotton-wool; in place of those from the Mūjavat, he uses either Arjuna shoots or whatever wild herbs are available. At the morning pressing they mix the Soma with curds that have been freshly milked; at the midday pressing, with boiled milk; at the third pressing, with curds. He gives five sacrificial gifts. Having completed the sacrifice, he may perform it again using whichever [method] he desires.

In that case, he should give whatever he desires. Whatever he intends to give as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he should give a choice boon (*vara*) from that to the *adhvaryu*. If the *prastotṛ* should falter while the snakes are moving, having given a choice boon to the *brahman*, he chooses him again. If the *udgātṛ* should falter, having sacrificed with the non-southern fee, he should sacrifice again with that same [fee].

If the Pratihartṛ should give away all his possessions; if at the morning pressing a pressing-stone should break, they should chant with the *sāman* of Dyutāna Māruta; if at the midday pressing, with the *bṛhat*; if at the third pressing, with the *anuṣṭubh*. If at the morning pressing the jar should break, one should perform the *brahmasāman* with the *ṣaṭkārānidhana*; if at the midday pressing, one should perform the *śrāyantīya* as the *brahmasāman*; if at the third pressing, one should perform the *vāravantīya* as the *agniṣṭomasāman*. If the *nārāśamsa*...

If the draughts should spill, one should pour out a drop for each of those [spilled] draughts to which one has offered reverence. If the two Soma portions, whether already offered or not yet offered, or whether already drunk or not yet drunk, should become mixed together, one should push a coal inside the enclosing sticks toward the south and offer it with: "O Indra and Agni, drink the pressed Soma, whether offered or unoffered, whether drunk or undrunk; Svāhā!"

Thus he should offer oblations. With the formula, "To Prajāpati, svāhā," he should pour that which is not to be consumed into the eastern of the two northern pits. With the formula, "Indu has approached Indu; of thee, O Indu, who art drunk by Indra, who art possessed of power, who art full of sweetness, who art accompanied by all thy hosts, being invited as one invited by all thy hosts, I partake," he should consume what has been sprinkled down. If he should not find a tortoise, he should place a lizard there; if he should not find that either, he should cook a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) in the shape of a tortoise.

One should place a piece of gold [on the vessel]; some say there should be gold on both sides. (16) If the Āgrayaṇa cup should spill or be lost, one should draw it from the other cups; if the other cups should spill or be lost, one should draw them from the Āgrayaṇa. (17) If one cannot find gold in the Droṇakalaśa, or in the Pūtabhṛt, one should press [the Soma] even upon the *ṛjīṣa*; one should bring up the gold and offer it together with the gold. (18) If one should overturn the cup in the *sadas*, [one should recite] "Hiraṇyagarbha... [etc.].

Thus he should offer the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) in the Āgnīdhrīya fire. (19) If the *dhruva* vessel should spill, he should set it in motion again, consecrate it with the mantra "Thou art the bestower of life," and after giving a boon, set it down. If it should run dry, he should replenish the Soma three times by turns with the formulas "Svāhā! Be replenished from heaven! (20) If the Soma should spill, [the procedure] has been explained regarding the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).

If gold should be lost, one should press [the Soma] even upon the *ṛjīṣa*; one should recover the gold and offer it together with the gold. (21) If the King [Soma] should be consumed by fire, the Adhvaryu should touch the cups, the Udgātṛ the chants (*stotra*), and the Hotṛ the recitations (*śastra*); then, having gathered the sacrificial materials, they should proceed in due order. (22) He gives five sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). (23) Having completed the rite, he may sacrifice again by whatever means he desires.

In that case, he should give whatever he desires. (24) Whatever he would have given as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he should give the best of it to the *adhvaryu*. (25) Before the twelfth day, they should undergo initiation; by means of those very [days], the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should cause him to sacrifice. (26)

If they should praise before [the sun has risen], they should praise with as many verses as they did not use; or they should praise with more verses, or they should perform the *traiḍa* as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*. If the dawn should break while the chant has not been completed with all the *paryāyas*, they should praise the *hotṛ* with fifteen verses, and the others with five verses each. If it breaks with two [verses remaining], they should praise the *hotṛ* and the *maitrāvaruṇa* with one [set], and the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* and the *acchāvāka* with the other.

If they should chant for the Hotṛ with one [verse] and for the others with three each, then, should the sun not rise while the *Aśvin* hymn is being recited, he should station a white horse adorned with gold ornaments facing westward in front [of the altar] and offer a multicolored animal to Āditya; a white goat dedicated to Sūrya is to be offered as well. The *Upāṃśu* deities are [associated] with the sacrifice performed according to the *Samṛt* [ritual]; the *Sambhāra-yajus* formulas have been explained.

The opening verse (*pratipad*) contains the word *vṛṣan*, and the *ājya* hymns contain both [the word *vṛṣan* and *vṛṣaṇvant*]. Or they may contain [only] *vṛṣaṇvant*. He should offer before the morning pressing with the formula: "To *saṃveśa*, to *upaveśa*, to the *gāyatrī* metre, to the overpowering one, svāhā! He should offer before the midday pressing with the formula: "To *saṃveśa*, to *upaveśa*, to the *triṣṭubh* metre, to the overpowering one, svāhā! He should offer before the *ārbhava-pavamāna* with the formula: "To *saṃveśa*, to *upaveśa*, to the *jagatī* metre, to the overpowering one, svāhā! This applies if the *rathantara-sāman* is used.

Soma should be used during the *pavamāna* of the morning pressing; if the *bṛhat* is the *sāman*, one should perform the *bṛhat* at the midday *pavamāna*, and the *rathaṃtara* if it is the *sāman*. If two rival parties hold a joint Soma-pressing in the same region, if the other’s sacrifice is an *agniṣṭoma*, one should perform an *ukthya*; if it is an *ukthya*, a *ṣoḍaśin*; and if it is a *ṣoḍaśin*, an *atirātra*.

If one should perform an Atirātra sacrifice consisting of the Viśvajit or the Abhijit with all the Stomas (sarvastoma), if the Soma should remain over, having drawn the portions beginning with the Hotṛ’s cup, he introduces the Stotra; the Hotṛ recites the invitatory verse for Indra-Viṣṇu. If there is Soma remaining at the morning pressing, they should chant with the Gāyatra melody on verses addressed to the Maruts, beginning with "This pressed [Soma]"; if at the midday pressing, they should chant with the Gaurīvita melody on verses addressed to Āditya, beginning with "Thou art great, O Sūrya"; if at the third pressing, they should chant with the Gaurīvita melody on verses addressed to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.

They should chant with the Ukthya-stotras; or, if there is an excess at the Ukthya, they should chant with the Ṣoḍaśin; if there is an excess at the Ṣoḍaśin, they should chant with the Atirātra; and if there is an excess at the Atirātra, they should chant with the Bṛhat-sāman on the verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa* of Viṣṇu.

If the *ukhya* fire should go out, one should lead it forth again and rekindle it, having placed the regular fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with these three verses: “O Agni, those moist wombs of thine which thou, desiring, didst enter into the woods, and when thou didst go to thy mothers, the waters—O Agni, thy returning from there is not to be forgotten, since thou, though far away, hast become present here. For together with the pure [fire], the pure *praśāstṛ* has been born through his mental power (*kratu*); he knows its firm ordinances; he grows like the branches of a tree. [One should proceed] with these three verses.

A black garment or a black cow should be given as a gift. (1) If the *ukhā* should break, or if the *mahāvīra* or its potsherds should be shattered, one should grind them to powder, mix them with other clay, and fashion a new *ukhā* with the verse, "He who, even without joining... and likewise a new *mahāvīra*. (2) If the consecrated (*dīkṣita*) should suffer from heat-fever, one should pour water into a vessel, place twenty-one barley grains and twenty-one blades of *darbha*-grass into it, and sprinkle the water around the consecrated person by turns while pronouncing his name, saying: "You are named 'Living' (*jīvā*); revive him! (3) *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 3.2.2.18–24.

He should touch his own limbs with the formula, "May Prāṇa and Apāna drink you, O Upāṃśu and Antaryāma; may so-and-so [drink] you. Having addressed the consecrated one with this mantra, he should offer a full-oblation (pūrṇāhuti) on the Āgnīdhrīya fire with the verse, "O Lord of Nourishment," followed by the section beginning, "The plants that were born first. Four Brāhmaṇas of different lineages (gotras), carrying water in a hawk-shaped vessel, should sprinkle the consecrated one. He should not perform [the sprinkling] again. If the consecrated one should die, they should carry the two kindling woods (araṇis) by way of the sacred ford (tīrtha) and the body by way other than the ford; having cremated him with fire produced by friction (nirmanthya) to the south of the sacrificial enclosure (vihāra), [the ritual concludes].

Having bound the bones in a black antelope skin and having initiated either a son or a brother with the fires of the deceased, they should sacrifice. Having placed the bones on the southern buttock of the altar, they should remain with their faces turned away while the *Sārparājñī* verses are being recited by the *Yāma* priest. While muttering those [verses], the initiated priests, led by the *Hotṛ*, should walk three times around the *Mārjālīya* fire-altar to the left, striking their left thighs, with the verse "O Agni, purify our lives" as the introductory formula (*pratipad*). The *Rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant. If it is a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), the cremation of the bones takes place once the ritual is concluded.

They may carry [the bones] away. (5) If the sacrificial session (*sattra*) has concluded, the sacrificers, maintaining the sacred fires, should kindle the fire and offer oblations for a full year. (6) When the year-long period is completed, there is the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice for the sake of sacrificing for the bones. The cups (*graha*) are preceded by those for Indra and Vāyu, or preceded by those for Mitra and Varuṇa. They should place the bones within the *stotra* chants. The *pavamāna* lauds are in the *trivṛt* pattern; the remainder is in the *saptadaśa* pattern.

The rest is the same. (7) If the Āhavanīya fire should go out, one should carry it forward from the Āgnīdhrīya; if the Āgnīdhrīya, from the Śālāmukhīya; if the Śālāmukhīya, from the Gārhapatya; if the Gārhapatya, it must be produced by friction right there. (8) If one should be consecrated for a *sattra* sacrifice and then depart from it, he should perform the *Viśvajit* *atirātra* sacrifice, distributing even the *soma*, with all the *stomas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, and giving away his entire property as the sacrificial fee—he should perform it, he should perform it.
(9) Thus ends the chapter on expiations (*prāyaścitta*) in the Mānava Sūtra.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the *pravargya*. One who is about to prepare the *pravargya* [should do so] on the new moon day, the full moon day, or during the waxing fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). This [rite] has its own specific rules as its archetype (1). The connection with the substances follows the sequence of the mantras as they have been taught (2). It is not performed at the first sacrifice, nor in the *jyotiṣṭoma* or *ukthya* sacrifices, [except] by one desiring offspring or desiring cattle.

The Bṛhaspatisava is prescribed for those desiring offspring. It is known from scripture: "The sacrifice of one for whom they do not perform the *pravargya* is indeed headless. The instruction is that one should not perform more than twelve *pravargyas*. Having taken curds into a vessel or a cup behind the Gārhapatya fire, and having entered with the words, "The Gāyatrī metre," he eats the curds three times with the verse, "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan. For one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), he places a fuel-stick on the fire with the verse, "They yoke. For one who is not initiated, he should offer an oblation. This is to the north of the Gārhapatya fire.

When the altar has been strewn, he sets down four pressing-boards—made of *khadira*, *vaiṇava*, *vaikaṅkata*, and *audumbara* wood—and takes up a *sruva*-ladle made of *audumbara*. With the verse addressed to Savitṛ, "At the impulse of the god... (*devasya tvā*), he takes each one, repeating the mantra for each. Having risen with the words, "Arise," and having stepped forward with, "May Brahmanaspati go forth," he spreads a black antelope skin in front of the Āhavanīya fire. Upon it, he pours out the ritual materials: earth from the western half [of the altar], a clod of earth from an anthill, soil dug up by a boar, *pūtīka* herbs, flour, and goat's milk from the eastern half.

With the verse, "O divine Heaven and Earth," he strikes earth from a *khadira* tree. Having taken it up with the formula, "For Makha thee," he pours it out on the northern edge of the black antelope skin with the formula, "For Makha's [strength] thee. With the verse, "The divine ants," he covers it with a mound of earth from an anthill using a bamboo tool; and with the verse, "Wherein the tip was," he covers it with earth dug up by a boar using a *vikaṅkata* tool.

With the verse, "The goddesses Ūrjā and Āhutī," [he takes] pūtīka shoots from an udumbara branch; with the formula, "O Indra, you are vigor," he pours goat’s milk into the *sruva* ladle (11). With the formula, "You are the body of Agni," he pours [the mixture] into all the receptacles until they are filled (12). Having mixed the remainder with the materials for the fire-pan (*ukhā*), he brings it together with the formula, "Honey indeed" (13). Having formed a lump and caused the horse to smell it with the formula, "Bestow long life," he divides it into three parts and wipes the smearings onto the Gharma potsherds (14). He touches it with the formula, "You are the head of Makha" (15). "You two are the feet of the sacrifice."

Thus, with his two thumbs, he forms the opening [of the vessel] until it is capable of receiving the oblations of fat (medas). 16. At the time of the battle, he prepares the great cauldrons (mahāvīra) in the manner of the Vāyavya [vessels]: "Thou art Gāyatra" for the first, "Thou art Traiṣṭubha" for the second, "Thou art Jāgata" for the third; or he may prepare all of them with all [the formulas]. 17. With the formula, "Thou art the girdle of Makha," he makes the girdle (rāsnā) two finger-breadths below the door [of the cauldron]. 18. With the formula, "With the heat of the Sun," he establishes it upon the sand. 19. From the remaining clay, he fashions the milch-cow cauldrons (dogdhrī ukhā).

In a space shaped like a cart, he places the smaller *āyasthālī* in one part and the larger *gharmeṣṭakā* in another; there are four *rauhiṇa* potsherds and two marked ones. At the time of marking, he marks them; at the time of cleansing, he cleanses them. When they have become thoroughly dry, he then pushes the embers toward the north and fumigates the site of the *khara* with horse-dung, saying, "O bull! Or else, the previously described pit may be used.

The cooking [of the rice] takes place to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, or to the northeast of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). Having piled the *śalaparicāyya* altar with clods of earth, he should cook [the rice] by means of fire produced by friction; or, as for the kindling, he may take the flame from the *gārhapatya*. He attends to the fire with these two verses: "Him with his greatness [he has made] heaven... and "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people... (RV 3.59.6–7).

Wherever one may perform service, one should perform it with these two [formulas]. (23) When they have become proficient in cooking, he then sweeps away the ashes toward the north, saying, "I deprive him," if performing malevolent magic; "I prosper him," if not performing malevolent magic. (24) "O God, thee!"—this is the formula for lifting [the pot] out. (25) "Of the Sun, thee!"—this is the formula for looking at [the vessel]. (26) "For the Upright, thee!"—this is the formula for raising [the vessel]. (27) With each successive verse beginning with "Here do I [seize] so-and-so, the son of such-and-such," he wipes each *mahāvīra* vessel three times with *darbha* blades. (28) "May it heat thee!"...

With the formulas beginning with "Speech," he moistens each one with goat's milk (29). Having spread a black antelope skin on the throne-seat (*āsandi*) with the formula "O God, go before [the sacrifice]," he places the *mahāvīra* vessels upon it—either the rear ones first and the front ones last, or the front ones first and the rear ones last—and likewise the *parigharmya* vessels upon it (30). Having covered them with *darbha* grass and a black antelope skin, and having carried them across using the equipment of the initiated, he draws the throne-seat south of the *āhavanīya* fire; then, with the formula "Homage to Speech," he purifies himself while holding herbs in his hand (31). The application of the mantras is restricted to the *mahāvīra* vessels alone (32). One who desires offspring must not look at them; one who desires offspring must not look at them (33).

The preliminary performance of the Upasad rites: He prepares two gold and silver plates (rukmas) weighing a śatamāna each, as prescribed; seven fuel-sticks made of Udumbara wood; thirteen of Vikaṅkata wood; three fans with handles a cubit long, the tips of which are made of bamboo; and having split them, he attaches to them pouches made of black antelope skin measuring a span (prādeśa). He also prepares two unperforated offering-spoons (sruvas).

The taking hold (*parigrāha*) and the formal acceptance (*upayāma*) are as prescribed for the Soma sacrifice; the Soma-bench (*saumikī āsandī*), the girdle of muñja grass (*mauñjo vedaḥ*), and the carrying away of the Soma (*saumikaṃ haraṇam*) have been explained. 2. To the north of the Gārhapatya fire, he prepares a mound (*khara*) of sand; to the north of that, another for the Āhavanīya; and to the north-east, outside, a place for washing the feet (*adhinirṇejanīya*). 3. Having opened the doors, he proceeds according to the ritual procedure for the enclosure (*pariśrayaṇāvṛt*). 4. Having strewn grass around the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), he spreads a three-layered layer of grass to the south for the Brahman and the Sacrificer, for the wife and the Udgātṛ, and behind them for the Hotṛ. 5. In front...

Having strewn grass around the Gārhapatya fire outside the altar for the sake of the vessels, he sets out the vessels: the *sruva* spoon as the largest, the Mahāvīra pot, the two enclosures (*parigrāha*), the base (*upayāma*), the fans (*dhavitra*), the two supports (*nidāna*), the two milch-cows (*dogdhrī*), the sacrificial post (*methī*), the tethering rope (*abhidhānī*), the butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*), and other implements belonging to the *gharma* rite; the *sruk* ladle and the *kapāla* potsherds (not yet scattered), the two gold plates (*rukma*), the cuttings from the *veda* grass-bundle, the *veda* broom, and the fuel-sticks (*samidh*). He prepares two strainers (*pavitra*) from the *veda*-cuttings, using Darbha grass-blades as the strainers. In front of the Gārhapatya fire, within the altar, he prepares the sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇī*) according to the ritual procedure for the *prokṣaṇī*.

Having performed the consecration (*saṃskṛtya*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) enter [the sacrificial ground] behind the *gārhapatya* fire, saying, "The *gāyatrī* metre. (8) Having risen, they proceed with the *pravargya* rite in a loud voice. (9) He issues the command: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Hotṛ, recite for the *gharma*; O Udgātṛ, chant the Sāmans! (10) Being authorized by the Brahman with the words, "It is joined with the Yajus," he sprinkles the Mahāvīra vessel three times with the formula, "O God, go before us," and then sprinkles the vessels, the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and the two mounds (*khara*). (11) Having placed the Veda-grass mat between [himself and the vessels], he [proceeds] with the Sāvitra formula.

He silently takes up the Mahāvīra vessel, the sruva ladle, and the butter-pot (ājyasthālī). Behind the Gārhapatya fire, having silently prepared the clarified butter, he offers oblations into the Gārhapatya with the sruva ladle, beginning with the formula "To Life, Svāhā! and so forth. He wipes the Mahāvīra three times with the Veda-grass-bundle.

With the formula, "For Yama thee," he places the base; with "For Makha thee," the middle; and with "For the heat of Sūrya thee," the top. 14. With the formula, "May the god Savitṛ [impel] thee," he pours clarified butter into the Mahāvīra. 15. With the formula, "Of the earth," he draws a silver disk (*rukmá*) beneath the mound (*khara*). 16. With the formulas beginning with "For the flame thee," having kindled the Veda-shavings with their tips pointing in all directions, he sets fire to the Mahāvīra with them using the formula, "Thou art the flame. 17. With the formula, "Heat the heat of Sūrya," he places them on the mound. 18. Having recited the verse, "They anoint [thee]," he says, "Sit down together" over them.
He establishes the Mahāvīra [vessel] with the verses beginning "anādhṛṣṭe" (O invincible one), and with a span-measure, he marks out the Mahāvīra on all sides, moving clockwise from each direction.

With "Manoḥ" (VS 15.61), he spreads [the earth] from the south toward the east upon the ground. With "Cidasi" (VS 15.62), he pushes the embers together from the Gārhapatya fire. With "Svāhā marudbhyaḥ" (VS 15.63), he encloses it on all sides. Having surrounded the *śalaparicāyya* with twelve Vaikaṅkata sticks starting with "Mā asi" (VS 15.64–75), two by two, and having fastened a gold plate (*rukma*) on the thirteenth day, and having filled the Mahāvīra vessel with clarified butter, he covers the Mahāvīra with that [plate] while reciting "Antarikṣasyāntardhirasi" (VS 15.76). They stand in worship with the verse "Arhan bibharṣi" (VS 15.77).

The officiating priests and the sacrificer take up the fans with the formulas beginning "Thou art the Gāyatra" (TS 1.4.34.1). With these, he fans the Mahāvīra pot three times downward with the formula "O Honey! (madhu), and three times upward with the formula "Quicken! (jinvā); or alternatively, three times downward with "Quicken! and three times upward with "O Honey! (TS 1.4.34.2). He hands over two of them, those belonging to the Triṣṭubh and Jagatī meters, to the Pratiprasthātṛ; the Pratiprasthātṛ gives the one belonging to the Jagatī meter to the Āgnīdhra. Having heard the verse "Around thee, O lover of songs, [flow] the songs" (RV 8.99.1), they, led by the Adhvaryu, shake the fans while moving clockwise with the formula "Thou art the breath" (prāṇo 'si).

They circumambulate the Mahāvīra vessel three times; the fourth [circumambulation] is optional. Having heard [the verse] "āyuṣṭe," the sacrificer [recites] "śukraṃ te"; having thrown a fuel-stick into the fire, he places the gold plate (rukma) in the vessel. From this point forward, at each *praṇava*, the Adhvaryu causes the Gharma to shine with clarified butter. Having heard [the verse] "samyak samyañcaḥ," they all shake [the ladles] until the verse containing the word "pavitra. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the two Rauhiṇa cakes made of flour.

Having silently prepared and consecrated the two *puroḍāśas*, and having heard the call "O press-stones!", he places them upon the two [grains] that have not been scattered. 32. Having heard the call "I praise Heaven and Earth," he goes by the north of the *mahāvīra* and, by way of the oblation-path, sets down the southern joint of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and the other (the northern one) on the north. 33. Having heard the call "With those [verses] which [they praised] Kṛśānu," the [priests], led by the *Āgnīdhra*, wave [the fans] and circumambulate the *mahāvīra* three times to the left. 34. Having heard the call "The active one," he gives the direction: "The *dharma* has shone. 34. "Ten eastward... [he says].
The officiating priests and the sacrificer stand around on all sides. 36. With the mantra "tvaṣṭrimantas tvā," the sacrificer gazes together with his wife. 37.

With the *sāvitra* formula, he takes up the tethering-post for the milch-cow silently; having taken the rope, he calls out "O *iḍā*, come! three times day after day. Having gone out by the eastern door, he calls out loudly three times with the verse, "That breast of thine... He drives in the post to the north of the place for the *pṛṣṭhyā*-line and ties [the cow] to it. While placing [the head-cover] upon it with the formula, "Thou art the turban of Aditi," [he addresses] the water-vessel with "Thou art Pūṣan. As they approach, [he says] "Thou art Vāyu. For the one who is about to pour out [the milk], [he says] "For the Gharma, thee. [He addresses] Aditi...

When [the cow] is being led forward with the formula, "Thou art rāsnā," [the Adhvaryu] approaches her with, "May Bṛhaspati sit near thee. With, "Ye are givers, ye are flowing," he touches her udders. With, "For the Aśvins," [he addresses] the milking vessel. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently causes a milch goat to swell. Having heard, "Arise! they both approach with, "Come hither! Having heard, "Pour into the Gharma," he pours from the milch cow into the Mahāvīra vessel with, "Thou art honey, thou art oblation. By means of this Gharma, the Adhvaryu performs three times in one order and three times in the reverse order.

The Pratiprasthātṛ silently pours everything from the Adhvaryu’s cup into his own, leaving the remainder, and takes up the two supporting vessels with the formulas, "Thou art Gāyatra" for the *parigrāha* and "Thou art Jāgata" for the *upayāma*. Having grasped them with the formula, "I grasp thee for Heaven and Earth," he places [the *parigrāha*] upon the *upayāma* with the formula, "I support thee with the intermediate space. While holding them, he mutters, "Of the gods... He places them according to their respective positions with the formula, "Touching the sky. With the formula, "Thou art splendor," he shakes them seventeen times. Having risen with the formula, "Place him in heaven," he [addresses] the god...

Having stepped forward with the words "To Savitṛ," and having heard [the response] "The eagle on the vault of heaven," he crosses over to the south with the words "All the quarters. (22) He causes the sacrificer to recite, "He has sacrificed here to all the gods. (23) Having gone to his place, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*. (24) When the response is given, he issues the command, "Recite the offering-verse for the Gharma! (25) Having pronounced, "O Aśvins, the Gharma!", he does not offer the entire portion when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

"O Indra, svāhā! Vaṣaṭ!"—thus at the second *vaṣaṭ*-call (26). At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the two Rauhiṇa oblations with the verse "By the banner of the day" (RV 10.88.6), one before the *vaṣaṭ*-call and the other before the second *vaṣaṭ*-call (27). He makes the sacrificer recite, "Of the Gharma consecrated with svāhā... (28). The Pratiprasthātṛ pours the milk from the milch-cow into the Mahāvīra vessel (29).
