With the formula, "For brilliance thee! For splendor thee! For power thee! For prosperity thee! Svāhā! (TS 1.4.34.c), he distributes it in all directions, pouring it out completely (30).

Having poured the remainder into the *upayāma* with the formula, "Thou art heat," he places the *mahāvīra* on the mound (*khara*) with the formula, "For so-and-so. If he should hate someone, he should utter that person's name; however, if he is not performing a malevolent rite, he does so silently. (31) In the *upayāma*, he offers fuel-sticks while anointing them with five verses beginning with "Of Pūṣan... (32). On the sixth day, after the two enclosures have been thrown out, he takes the anointed [stirring-stick] and the *mahāvīra*. With the formula, "To Rudra, the Hotṛ, svāhā! he hurls it toward the north-eastern direction. Having touched water, he takes the two unanointed [stirring-sticks] and offers a fuel-stick with the formula, "He has carried me across the day. (33)

With the mantra "The oblation has been offered," he performs the morning Agnihotra according to its ritual rules (34). Having invoked one another with the words "O divine Gharma, may we partake of thee," the officiating priests and the sacrificer consume it.

Those who have not been initiated consume [the remnant] by inhaling it. 35 Having washed the *upayāma* cup in the *adhinirṇejana* vessel, the rite is established from the pouring out until the consumption. 36 They purify themselves within the altar with the *rukmavatī* verses beginning with "O giver of life. 37 Having taken up the *mahāvīra* with the two enclosures, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse for it as it is being set down. 38 Either the later [verse] after the earlier, or the earlier before the later, or the later after the later; and on that [altar], the *parigharmya* vessels [are placed].

Having covered [the fire] with *darbha* grass and a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) with the formula, "Svāhā! To thee from the rays of the sun," and having carried it across by the path used for the consecrated (*dīkṣita*), he draws a stool to the south of the *āhavanīya* fire. With the formula, "Homage to speech! those holding plants purify themselves over the water used for washing. (39) With the formula, "Thou art the place of Iḍā," they throw clods of earth toward the west with their forefingers. (40) Having touched water and sprinkled [himself] with the formula, "The earth is peace," he gazes at the sun with the verse, "Upwards from the darkness... (41) [He gazes] with the formula, "Of Mitra... (42)

While looking on, [he performs] the *samīkṣaṇa* (inspection). Having cast away the cleansing-grass with the formula, "Thou art the under-layer for Brahman," having muttered the *Vāmadevya*, and having muttered the *pañcaindrī*, he recites from "May Indra of far-reaching fame [grant us] well-being" until the end of the *anuvāka* beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed... (43). By this rule, the afternoon rite is explained; it applies to the other two *kapāla* cakes, the *rauhiṇa*s. (44) The *rauhiṇa-stoma* is [designated] as "night. (45) He places a fuel-stick on the fire with the verse, "He has carried me across the night... (46). "The oblation has been offered... (47).

In the evening, he offers according to the ritual procedure of the Agnihotra with the formula, "Svāhā to you, for the constellations! Having covered [the fire], after sunset, the oblation is performed with the verse, "May the wind be auspicious to us. By this same procedure, the rite consisting of three *uvaruts* is explained; day by day, one *mahāvīra* [pot] is used. By this same procedure, the rite consisting of six *upasads* is explained; every two days, one *mahāvīra* is used. By this same procedure, the rite consisting of twelve *upasads* is explained; every four days, one *mahāvīra* is used. *Mahāvīra* is used. *Mahāvīra* is used. 47–51.

Now, therefore, follows the cleansing (utsādana). 1. He places the support-vessel for the curdled-milk offering (dadhigharma). 2. Having placed a mound (khara) in between, he pours out the unmixed [grain] for the purpose of external purification. 3. The call for action (saṃpraiṣa): he brings it once across the north side of the altar by way of the path used by the officiating priests. 4. Having placed a throne-seat (āsandi) in front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places the Mahāvīra vessels upon it—either one after another from west to east, or one after another from east to west—or the Parigharmya vessels upon that same seat. 5. Behind the Āhavanīya fire, they enter with the formula, "The Gāyatrī metre... and so forth.

The officiating priests and the sacrificer [pour] clarified butter into the *mahāvīra* vessel with the formula, "Thou art the light of animals" (VS 38.25); they pour honey and curds into it with the two following verses (VS 38.26–27). Having prepared the clarified butter, he kindles the bunches of *darbha* grass and, holding them at the height of his mouth, offers an oblation with the formula, "O Gharma, that heat of thine which is in heaven" (VS 38.28), and with the two following verses (VS 38.29–30) at the heights of the navel and the knees respectively. He sits down with the verse, "Anu adya naḥ" (VS 38.31). He offers five oblations with the formula, "Of Pūṣan" (VS 38.32), and with the two following verses (VS 38.33–34) he moves toward each of the directions. Rising up, he gives the command: "O Udgātṛ, sing the Sāman!"

"O Prastotṛ," he says; all of them perform the *nidhana* for him. "Today may we find one who follows us, one who is favorable to us"—thus they all mutter. With the words, "For the protection of the Brahman," he steps out after [the sacrificer]. With the words, "For the vital breath," he performs the second [step] at the midpoint.

Having reached the third [step] with "divas tvā" (TS 4.2.9.2.a), he establishes the washing-vessel upon the *catvāla* with "apa dveṣaḥ" (TS 4.2.9.2.b). Having touched water, he places two *khara* hearths to the north of the *uttaravedi* or of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; he fashions them in the shape of a man or in the shape of the sun. Having leveled them, sprinkled them, and spread *avakā* grass upon them, he places the *mahāvīra* vessels upon pieces of gold with the *vyāhṛti*s, either one after another from west to east, or one after another from east to west; and upon that [hearth], the *parigharmya* vessels of curd.

Having filled the vessels, he places them on both sides. (16) Having untied the Veda-grass-bundle, he spreads it out on both sides. (17) Having covered it with Darbha grass and a black antelope skin, he causes [the sacrificer] to step forward upon the seat with the words, "O four-cornered one. (18) The officiating priests and the sacrificer stand by [the Gharma] with the formula, "O Gharma, this has been prepared for thee."

If he should hate anyone, he should utter that person's name, saying "This one," provided he does not perform an incantation against them in silence. (19) With the formulas "The auspicious one" for the sprinkling around, and "Thee with the Avakā plant of the ocean; thee with the afterbirth of the snow," (20) having said, "Return again with vigor and with wealth," he turns back. (21) At this time, the sacrificer, standing to the north of the *uttaravedi* facing east and remaining upright, takes water in his joined palms with the formula "May they be friends to us," and throws it out toward the east outside the *vedī* with the formula "May they be unfriendly [to our enemies]. (22) This ritual procedure is performed three times.

While the water is being sprinkled around [the cauldron], he touches water and gives the command: "Sing the Vārṣāhara Sāman! (23). When the sprinkling is finished, [he recites] the *iṣṭāhotrīya* [verse]. (24). Once the sprinkling is complete, the officiating priests and the sacrificer worship from all sides with the names of the Gandharvas, beginning with: "Thou art Ranti by name. (25). The sacrificer [recites]: "O divine Gharma, this art thou... (26). Having said, "I turn back here," he turns around. (27). He pays homage, saying: "Homage to the gods! (28). He turns back again, saying: "Return with vigor and wealth! (29). [He takes up] the vessel of clarified butter... (30).

Taking up the *sruva* ladle, he gives the command: "Sing the Śyaita Sāman! (31) He sings while moving forward; the sacrificer approaches its *nidhana*. (32) "This [is] Viṣṇu... is for seizing the footprint. (33) With the two verses, "O Agni, you are the lord of the house," he worships the Gārhapatya fire. (34) "Viṣṇu has stepped forth... is for the oblation. "Him indeed, this one of ours... is the second.

With the *vyāhṛtis*, four [oblations are offered]. (35) He gives the command: "Sing the *Vāmadevya* Sāman! (36) Having filled the butter-vessel (*ājyasthālī*) and the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) with curds, and having drawn the stool (*āsandī*) near, they perform the purification at the *cātvāla* pit with the formula, "Homage to Speech," while holding herbs in their hands. (37) If the *mahāvīra* vessel should run dry, he should pour water over it with the verse, "May your dwelling be secure. While being replenished, (38) if the *mahāvīra* should break, he should offer oblations verse by verse with these two [verses], "O Gharma, do not harm us," and also with the *vyāhṛtis*. (39) The performance of the ritual act has been explained. (40)

"Dharma is the head"—with these words, he lays down the *gharma* brick at the proper time. (41) "To Pūṣan Āghṛṇi, svāhā!"—with this, he himself offers five oblations at the proper time. (42) "The fierce and the terrible"—with this, each group (*gaṇa*) of the *araṇyānukīrtana* hymns is recited at the proper time. (43)

Now, therefore, they proceed with the *dadhigharma* (curd-offering). At the midday pressing, having touched the cups (*graha*), and having washed the base-ring (*upayāma*) with *darbha* grass, the officiating priests and the sacrificer enter behind the *āgnīdhrīya* fire-shed, saying, "The *gāyatrī* metre. Having said, "O Hotṛ, speak," and having poured curds into the base-ring while reciting, "Thou art light," he issues the command: "The oblation is cooked; it is cooked for the gods! Upon hearing, "If it is cooked, offer it; if it is not cooked, let it simmer," he goes to his place and calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*. When the response is given, [he proceeds].

He issues the command, "Recite the offering prayer for the curd-heat (dadhigharma)! 5 Having recited the response, "O Indra, whom...," he does not offer the entire portion when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. 6 At the second *vaṣaṭ*, with the formula, "To those two, Svāhā! Vaṣaṭ! 7 He brings the portion for consumption at the *upayāma*. 8 Having gone to the *sadas* and said, "Invited, invite [us]! or "Invited, invite yourselves!", 9 they consume it with the formula, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; may that [be] in me. 10 Having washed the *upayāma* vessel for the *gharma* in the *mārjālīya* fire-pit with *darbha* grass, filled it with curds, and cast it away, [he approaches] the *āhavanīya* fire with the words, "From its impetuosity..."

He establishes [the fires] on the final day; the multi-day sacrificial sessions (ahargaṇas) [are performed]. With the words "Homage to speech," those holding herbs perform the ritual purification at the edge of the pit (cātvāla).

Then follows the ritual for the Asuri-cow: with the verses "O Vijra, scatter! Drive away! three times, and "O Vijra, come! eight times. If he should hate someone, he should call that person's cows together in the midst of his herd with the words "O Vijra, scatter! Drive away! and, having gone out before sunrise, to the south or west of the village, in a pure place on a natural salt-flat (iriṇa), he kindles a fire. Having cooked a mess of boiled rice (sthālīpāka) in the milk of a black cow from among black grains of rice, [he proceeds].

Having kindled that fire, swept around it, sprinkled water around it, and strewn it with reeds, he offers an oblation of cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) with the verse "With the tips of the reeds... Before the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having drawn out some matter from the right side of her thigh into the left part of her body by means of a reed-shaft, he climbs onto a mound, a tree, or a high place, and looks toward the village, the city, or the district which he hates while reciting the verse "Of the two firm ones..."; that person perishes immediately. He looks at the sun with the verse "Up from the darkness we have risen...". Having returned, he says "Homage to speech!
and, holding herbs in his hand, he purifies himself; he purifies himself.

One who is about to undergo the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*) should go forth before sunset during the northern course of the sun, under a bright lunar mansion on an auspicious day—excluding the ninth day—and having wrapped himself in an unwashed garment, he should remain standing for the entire night in a pure place to the north or east of the village, not speaking to women or Śūdras. On the following day, he should present [as offerings]: fire, the sun, a cow, gold, a Brāhmaṇa, water, a stone, and a maiden desiring a husband. There, in that very place, he should kindle the fire.

From the *aśvattha* tree that stands near the *caitya*, he should take four fuel-sticks (*samidh*) that have clusters of buds, are with their leaves, and are a span (*prādeśa*) long; having dipped them in clarified butter, he places them on the fire with the verses ending in the word *svāhā*, beginning with "The earth is the fuel" (*pṛthivī samid*). (3) Having handed over the vow (*vrata*) with the formula "O Agni, lord of vows" (*agne vratapate*), he should cause [the student] to recite the twenty-five sections (*anuvāka*) from the beginning. (4) He should give the binding-cloth, the cow, and the gold to the teacher (*guru*). (5) He should not eat at night; if he should eat, he should eat only by the light of a lamp. (6) During the day he should remain standing, and during the night he should remain seated.

And on the festival days (parvan) it should be done in this same way. Thus disciplined, he should practice for one year, or three, five, or seven [years]. He should also perform the Traividya-vrata. When it is completed, having discarded those [vows], he purifies himself with his hands full of herbs, saying, "Obeisance to speech. He purifies himself again.

In the forest, when about to study the *svādhyāya* during the northern course of the sun, under the light of the moon, in the forenoon, he should not study at night, nor after eating, nor while walking, nor having seen blood, nor a corpse, nor anything else impure, nor on the days of the lunar changes (*parvan*). (1) He may consume sacrificial food before sunset. (2) Having gone out before sunrise, to the north or east of the village, in a pure place, with seats in their hands, facing [the teacher], and keeping their eyes fixed on him, they should study the *svādhyāya* at the proper time, concluding with "Homage to Speech."

Thus, those whose hands are herbs perform the purification (mārjana). In every application of secret mantras, both the performance and the purification are required; both the performance and the purification are required.
Thus ends the Pravargya ritual in the Mānava Sūtra.

One should perform the *iṣṭi* sacrifices on the full moon day, the new moon day, during the bright fortnight, or under an auspicious lunar mansion, except for the ninth day. (1) An expiatory *iṣṭi* is performed when an occasion of misfortune arises; one should perform it immediately. (2) Having silently added fuel to the fires, one enters upon the vow, except in the case of those sacrifices with fixed times and the *samṛtayajña*. (3) The path between the *āhavanīya* fire and the *utkara* heap is the *tīrtha*; the path between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap is the *tīrtha* for those altars that include the *cātvāla*. (4) There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. (5) The two *dhāyyā* verses are "pṛthupājāḥ" and "tam sabādhaḥ."

The insertion (*dhāyyā*) occurs between the *samidh* verses and the *ājyabhāga* offerings; the insertion of the intermediate offerings (*ijyā*) occurs between the *ājyabhāga* and the *sviṣṭakṛt*. (7) The insertion of the *nigada* occurs at the invocation (*āvāhana*), at the final *prayāja*, at the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and at the *sūktavāka*. (8) Those [deities] that are not separated and share the same deity should be inserted once, facing the offering; those that are separated should be inserted separately. (9) One does not invoke the *vājina*s. (10) For the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and those [offerings] which follow it, the duration is three morae (*trimātra*).

The *ye yajāmahe* at the beginning, as well as *ehy āvaha*, *o śrāvaya*, and so forth; the first two [of these], *brūhi*, *preṣya*, *śrauṣaṭ*, and *vauṣaṭ*, have the penultimate syllable lengthened, as does the end of the *yājyā*. In that [context], the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) which are not *pragṛhya* glide separately. (11) In the *śastra* recitations and *anuvacana*s, the final syllable becomes *ukāra* when it begins with a vowel. (12) When there is a combination of *ṛc* verses, the first and last are recited three times. (13) One joins the *ṛc* with the *praṇava*. (14) In the *agnyādheya* sacrifices, there is the *ārambhaṇīyā* and the *anunirvāpyā*. (15) In the *anīkavat*, *sāṃtapana*, and *krīḍin* offerings, there are fifteen [verses].

There are sixteen *sāmidhenī* verses. For the Kṣatriyas Atri, Vadhryaśva, Vasiṣṭha, Vaiśya, and Śunaka, as well as for the Kaṇvas, Kaśyapas, and Saṃkṛtis, Narāśaṃsa is the second *prayāja*; for others, Tanūnapāt is the second, where both are traditionally recited. One should meditate mentally upon whichever deity one pronounces the *vaṣaṭ*-call for. One desiring heaven should sacrifice with an eight-potherd cake for Agni according to the procedure of the Full Moon sacrifice. "May Agni strike down the Vṛtras; you, O Soma, are the lord of the good"—these are the two *ājyabhāga* offerings that slay the Vṛtra. "Agni is the head... [etc.]

*bhuvo yajñasya* is for the oblation; *piprīhi devān agne yad adya* are the two *saṃyājyā* verses for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. (21–22) In the absence of a specific instruction, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*) applies. (23) If a potsherd (*kapāla*) is lost before the removal [of the cakes from the fire], one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara with the [cakes] already prepared. (24) The Hotṛ priest should be a descendant of Bhṛgu. (25) A one-year-old cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (26) This is the rule for the expiation (*prāyaścitti*). (27) *agne rakṣā ṇas tvam naḥ soma*—these are the two *ājyabhāga* portions containing the word "protect" (*rakṣitavat*). (28) *vaiśvānaro na ūtyā pṛṣṭo divi*. (29)

29. For the *havis* offerings, the two *saṃyājyā* verses beginning with "O Agni, do thou carry us across all [difficulties]" (*viśvāni no 'gne tvaṃ pāraya*) are those that contain the word "carry across" (*pārayat*). 30. In all *ārambhaṇīyā* rites, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is that of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*). 31. At the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the *ārambhaṇīyā* consists of either three *havis* offerings or four *havis* offerings. 32. For the rite of three *havis* offerings, there are six verses beginning with "O Agni-Viṣṇu, being of one accord" (*agnāviṣṇū sajoṣasā*). 33. For the rite of four *havis* offerings immediately following the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* offering, there are verses beginning with "Thou, O Agni, [grant] abundance in heroes" (*tvam agne vīravat*) and "Thou art Bhaga for us. 34. If the *bhagin* sacrifice is performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), it has a separate ritual procedure (*nānātantra*). 35. The ritual manual (*kalpa*) follows the *vairāja* pattern. 36. [The verses for] Agni are "Agni with the ancient hymn" (*agniḥ pratnena manmanā*), and for Soma... [text ends].

The two Ājyabhāga portions are recited as "gīrbhistvā vayam" and "vṛdhanvantau"; 37. for the oblation [the verses] are prescribed; 38. the two Virāj verses beginning with "preddho agne" are the *saṃyājyās*. 39.

In the *agnyādheya* sacrifices, for the Pavamāna offerings there are two verses beginning with *agna āyūm̐ṣi pavase*; for the subsequent two *havis* offerings, there are four verses beginning with *agne pāvaka rociṣā*, which follow after the *sviṣṭakṛt*. 1. The ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for the four *havis* offerings belongs to the Vairāja [Sāman]. 2. These are recited in the *āgniveśya* [text]. 3. For the subsequent [offerings], there are six verses beginning with *kimitte viṣṇo*. 4. In the *punarādheya*, one should place the case-endings (*vibhakti*) either before or after the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, as follows: *ye3yajāmahe samidhaḥ samidho'gnā ājyasya*.

"May Agni, Agni Tanūnapāt, partake of the clarified butter in Agni; may Agni, Agni, partake of the oblation in Agni. Thus [the formulas] are recited according to the traditional text. The last one is as it has been handed down. (6) "Awaken Agni with the hymn"—these six [formulas] are for the Ājyabhāgas, the Havis, and the Sviṣṭakṛt. (7) One who desires offspring or cattle should perform the two Āgneya Ājyabhāgas with the verse "Agni is the head" in the place of Soma. (8) [The formulas are: "May the divine Barhis partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the bestowing of wealth; may Agni, Agni, partake; may the divine Narāśamsa partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the bestowing of wealth; may Agni, Agni... and so on.

Just as the Self is supreme (9). One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat and a pap of barley to Varuṇa (10). "O Agni, you are far-extending; O Soma, you are a bull"—these two verses containing the word *vṛṣan* are for the two portions of clarified butter (11). "Agni, when born, shone forth"—these four verses are for the oblation (12). One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnimat, a pap to Mitra, a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya, [and cakes] to Agni Vratapati, Agni Pathikṛt, Agni Śuci, Agni Kṣāmavat, Agni Tapasvat, and Agni Janadvat.

Thirteen cakes on eight potsherds for Agni Pāvaka, for Agni Tantumat, and for Agni Vivik; 13. The ritual procedure for expiation (prāyaścitti); 14. "By Agni Agni is kindled"—this is the formula for sixteen oblations; 15. "Weaving yourself, you are the thread"—these two verses are addressed to Tantumatī; 16. "Your flames, O pure Agni, driven by the wind, spread in all directions, pure and fiercely consuming; the divine Navagvas, boldly breaking through, devour the forests."

"O Agni, the human clans praise you—the knower of the *hotrā*-offering, the discerning one, the best bestower of jewels, dwelling in secret yet visible to all, O blessed one, loud-sounding, easy to worship, and resplendent with ghee. Thus are the two *vaivicya* verses.

When it is said, "Recite for Agni while being churned," he begins with "Towards you, O God Savitṛ... He pauses at "...the greatest slayer of Dasyus. When it is said, "Recite for Agni when born," he begins with "The winner of wealth in every battle..."

He recites [the invitatory verse] with the words *bibhratīti viramati*. When it is said, "Recite for the fire being carried forward," he begins with *viśām agniṃ svadhvaro*. He concludes with *yajñena yajñam*. Standing right there, he recites the *sāmidhenī* verses. There are nine *prayāja* offerings beginning with *samidho agne*. The two *ājyabhāga* portions contain the word *viśvatavat*: *agne yaṃ tvaṃ naḥ soma*. There are sixteen [verses] for the oblations beginning with *agnir mūrdhā bhuvo yajñasya*. The two *saṃyājyā* verses are *gāyatrī*s: *sa havyavāḍ agniṃ stomena*.

"devaṃ barhiḥ"—these are the nine after-offerings (anuyājas). With "śaṃ no vāje-vāje," there is the non-interruption of the *vājina* offering; seated on the south side of the altar, the Hotṛ performs the sacrifice. He pronounces the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (*anuvaṣaṭkāra*) with "vājinasyāgne vīhi. During the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, at the time of leading forward the fire, he sits behind the Āhavanīya fire. When the command "Recite for the fire being led forward" is given, he begins with "pra devam."

Having recited the third [verse] by half-verses, he pauses (13). When the oblation has been offered, he rises with the words, "May he carry our offerings in succession," and he pauses at the words, "as if from an immortal birth" (14). He proceeds silently until the time for establishing the fires; then he begins with the words, "Stronger even than strength" (15). He concludes with the verse, "Thou art the messenger" (16). From the kindling of the fire onwards, it is explained according to the Vaiśvadeva ritual (17). The two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) contain the word "wealth" (*rayi*), as in: "Through Agni may one obtain wealth, the increaser of prosperity" (18). This applies to the five common verses that follow.

19. For the four [deities], there are eight verses beginning with *indrāgnī rocanā*. 20. *Piprīhi devān agne* and *yad adya* are the two *saṃyājyā* verses for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. 21. At the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice, he proceeds with the *dhvāna* formula. 22. He performs the sacrifice starting from the *prayāja* offerings. 23. He pushes forward the *barhis*-grass bundle. 24. In place of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, [he recites]: *svāhāgnīvaruṇau hotārāv*. 25. The two *ājyabhāga* offerings are accompanied by water, with the verses: *apsv agne sadhiṣṭava* and *apsu me soma ābhṛtaḥ*. 26. The oblation [is offered] with the verses: *ud uttamam* and *ava te heḍaḥ*. 27. Having recited *tvaṃ no agne*, [he continues with] *ye...*.

We worship Agni and Varuṇa, the two Sviṣṭakṛts. May Agni and Varuṇa have sacrificed; may they have sacrificed to the dear abodes of Agni; may they have sacrificed to the dear abodes of Soma; may they have sacrificed to the dear abodes of Varuṇa; may they sacrifice to the dear abodes of the gods who drink the clarified butter; may they sacrifice to the dear abodes of the two Hotṛs, Agni and Varuṇa; may they honor their own two greatnesses; may they offer the oblations; may they prepare the sacrificial foods; may those two Jātavedases enjoy the offerings. "Do thou [O Agni], for us..."—with these words he performs the sacrifice. 27

In the Sākamedha sacrifices, "May Agni strike down the Vṛtras"—this is the ritual procedure for the six [offerings] of the Anīkavant. This same procedure applies to the Sāṃtapana [offerings]. For the subsequent oblations, "Agni with the ancient hymn"—this is the procedure for the six Gṛhamedhīya [offerings]. He performs the sacrifice beginning with the Ājyabhāga portions. Having recited one verse, he recites another for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. It concludes with the Iḍā. "I praise Agni"—this is the procedure for the Ṣaḍḍina [offerings]. For those ending with the Vaiśvakarman [offering], the ritual procedure is that of the Vārtraghna. From the leading forward of the fire onwards, it is established as in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices.

After the five *saṃcara* verses, [he recites] "O Indra and Agni, ninety... and so forth; these six [verses] belong to three [deities]. (10) At the Pitṛyajña, he recites the one *sāmidhenī* verse, "Desiring you, we invoke you," three times. (11) He does not choose [the priests] with the formula, "O Agni, you are great, O Brāhmaṇa, descendant of Bharata, among men. (12) [He chooses them] with the formula as it is traditionally handed down: "Kindled by the gods, kindled by Manu... (13) At the announcement for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, instead of the standard announcement, he uses the announcement: "Bring Agni Kavyavāhana. (14) He performs the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings without the *barhis* grass. (15) [He offers] with the verses beginning, "O Agni, come to us... and "O Soma... and so forth.

The two Ājyabhāgas contain the word *jīvatu*. (16) The twelve subsequent [verses] belong to the Havis-sviṣṭakṛt offerings. (17) With the verses "idaṃ pitṛbhyaḥ" and "udīratām," the two portions are carried forward. (18) There are two Puronuvākyās for each [offering]. (19) Among these, he makes one verse the portion for the Ṛc and another the portion for the Dharma. (20) He performs the sacrifice with the third [verse]. (21) "Ye svadhāmaha" is the Āgū formula. (22) "Svadhā namaḥ" is the Vaṣaṭ call. (23) The full-moon ritual procedure applies to the offering to Aditi. (24) "Sutrāmāṇam" and "mahīm ū ṣu" are the Upāṃśu formulas for the oblation. (25) The Śunāsīrya sacrifice is explained by the Vaiśvadeva ritual. (26)

After the five *saṃcara* verses, [he recites] "pra vāyum" (RV 7.92.1), which consists of six verses for three [deities]. 27. He indicates the *upām̐śu* deities; he indicates the *upām̐śu* deities [with the formulas] "the two invitatory and offering verses," "he has accepted," "he has grown strong," and "it has been done," as well as the *upām̐śu* verses dedicated to Vāyu. 28.

The optional sacrifices (*kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ*) have minor deities (*upām̐śudevatāḥ*). Among these, one should give the *ekadhana* [cows] when no specific sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been prescribed. (1) For those sacrifices related to battle, the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is that of the *vārtraghnī* [offering]. (2) And for those sacrifices performed for malevolent purposes (*abhicaraṇīyāḥ*), the ritual procedure for atonement (*prāyaścitta*) applies to those beginning with the word "sa" [the *sāṃtapanīyā*]. (3) For those desiring a village, prosperity, or cattle, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word "wealth" (*rayimat*). (4) For those desiring a village and prosperity, the two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word "together" (*samvat*) and the word "thousand" (*sahasravat*); for one desiring cattle, they contain the word "thousand. (5) One should sacrifice with the *aindrāgna* [offering] according to the procedure for one desiring a village, among kinsmen who are divided or who have become separated. (6) Of that [offering]...

"O Indra and Agni, the luminous..."—these two are for the oblation (7). One who has rivals should perform [the sacrifice] according to the *vārtraghna* ritual procedure (8). The two *ājyabhāga* portions are *vārtraghna* (9). "O Indra and Agni, ninety..."—these two are for the oblation (10). The two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word *śardha* (troop): "He is welcome as the domestic lord, O Agni," and "O troop... (11). For one desiring progeny, the two *ājyabhāga* portions contain the word *vṛṣan* (bull) (12). "I sing forth to you two..."—these two are for the oblation. The two following [verses] are for the *sviṣṭakṛt* (13). When setting out for battle, the two *saṃyājyā* verses are those used for the battle-sacrifice.

Whether he has sacrificed with these two or not, having conquered, he should sacrifice with the subsequent [offering]. For that [sacrifice], there are two oblations for Indra and Agni beginning with "The luminous realms," which follow the previous two. When setting out toward a foreign territory, he should sacrifice with two oblations; if he goes with an army, the ritual procedure is that of the Vārtraghna [offering].

If one desires a village, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the two oblations is "yā vām santi... (16). There are four verses for the two offerings of two oblations (17). One who intends to settle on a field should sacrifice with the three-oblation rite (18). Its ritual procedure when desiring a village is [the same as before]. For the six oblations, [the verses] are "yā vām santi... (20). The two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word "sam" (together), namely "sam it sakhāyaḥ" (21). One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara for the sake of desire, that is, for all desires (22). The ritual procedure is according to one's specific desire (23). The verses for the oblation are "vaiśvānaro na ūtyā" and "pṛṣṭo divi" (24).

The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for those [offerings] dedicated to Vaiśvānara are as prescribed; 24. for those dedicated to Agni, they are "Agnirmūrdhā bhuvo yajñasya" (VS 27.1); 25. for those dedicated to Agni-Soma, they are "Agnīṣomā savedasā yuvametāni" (VS 7.11). 26. For other [deities], the verses are those possessing the characteristic marks (*liṅgavatyaḥ*). 27. One should sacrifice at the junction of time (*saṃdhi*) before the [fixed] time has passed. 28. This is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for the expiation (*prāyaścitti*). 29. One should sacrifice intending to rise up toward gain (*sanim*). 30. The two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word "wealth" (*rayi*). 31. The two verses for the oblation (*havis*) are "Ṛtāvānam" (VS 33.50) and [the following]. 32. The two *saṃyājyā* verses containing the word "gain" (*sanimatī*) are "iḍāmagne" (VS 33.51) and "tvaṃ no agne" (VS 33.52). 33.

When he has won [the prize], he should then sacrifice with the following verse (34). To him whom he hates, he should give as a sacrificial fee a cow that has won the prize, with her neck bound, and one year old (35). There are two oblations for Vaiśvānara (36). If he is about to eat food that is impure or unfit to be eaten, he should sacrifice (37). Lead or a black garment is the sacrificial fee (38). The two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) are protected (39). There are two oblations with the verse beginning "The All-encompassing" (viśvam vivyāca) (40).

After the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, [the following applies]: 40. Whether one has performed this sacrifice or not, having eaten [the sacrificial food], one should perform the subsequent sacrifice with the next [verse]. 41. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is the same. 42. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses have already been explained. 43. Likewise, there are sacrifices related to battle for one who desires: "May I alone be king as long as these barley or rice grains endure. 44. If another should run against him, the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is that of the *vārtraghna* [offering].

45. If he has survived death, [he performs] two oblations for one suffering from illness (*āmayāvin*). 46. The two *ājyabhāga* portions are those [verses] containing the word "survived" (*jīvitavat*). 47. The two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word "crossed over" (*pārayat*). 48. The ritual procedure is for one who has survived. 49. There are two oblations for one desiring prosperity (*bhūti*). 50. This is a *caru* offering of black rice.

The oblations are prescribed as being a span in measure (prādeśamātra). Having given away his entire property with the formula, "To Agni Jātavedas," he should sacrifice with three oblations. The ritual procedure for that [sacrifice] is intended for one desiring cattle. For the two sacrifices of two oblations, there are four verses beginning with "ny agniṃ jātavedasam. These two are prescribed for the Vaiśvānarīya sacrifice. [This applies] to one who is being falsely accused. Having fasted during the night and eaten at dawn, he remains silent in front of the village at the place where the sacrificial residues (saṃsrava) are collected. On the following day, having consigned the sacred fire (agnisamāropaṇa) and having churned out a new fire, he follows it with the sacrificial implements (yajñāyudha) for the sake of Agni.

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Surabhimat (59). The two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) are protected [as usual] (60). There are two oblations for the *havis* with the verses beginning "Agni is the Hotṛ" (61). After the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, there are three oblations for Agni Pavamāna and so forth (62). Having returned to his home, he should sacrifice with this three-oblation rite (63). This is the ritual procedure for expiation (64). The oblations are those prescribed [in the text] (65). The three-oblation rite begins with "To Agni, a cake on eight potsherds" (66). The specific desire is as prescribed (67): he who, having conquered by means of an army, seizes [booty] from another territory, should sacrifice with the subsequent [rite] after winning that human conflict (68). In that [rite], the verse "The great heaven... [is used].

"And may the earth, rich in ghee, [protect] us among the worlds"—this is for the offering to Heaven and Earth (68). A Brahmin should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma for the sake of desire, for the sake of all desires (69). The ritual procedure follows his specific wish (70). The subsequent verses are for one who desires prosperity (71). One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake of *śyāmāka* grain on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni in the spring (72). "The broad-chested one, him, the oppressor"—these are the six *dhāyyā* verses.

There are six additional [verses] for the *ājyabhāgas*, the oblation, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. (73) One desiring cattle should offer a *caru* of rice half-ground to Soma and Pūṣan. (74) "O Soma and Pūṣan..."—these two are the invitatory and offering verses (*puronuvākyā* and *yājyā*) for the oblation. (75) "And also for us, O Brahman... and "Grant us..."—these two are the *saṃyājyās* containing the word "thousand. (76) One desiring the office of a domestic priest (*purohita*) should offer a *caru* to Soma and Indra. (77) Its ritual procedure is the same as that for one desiring a village. (78) "Thee with me as thy companion... and "Thine is that, O Soma..."—these two are the invitatory and offering verses for the oblation. (79) Or, one who has committed an offense against a neighbor or one who is afflicted by disease should offer a *caru* to Agni and Varuṇa. (80)
The *tantra* is according to one's desire (81). "Thou art ours, O Agni; thou art ours, O Agni"—these are for the oblation (82).

One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation of white *vrīhi* rice in clarified butter to Soma and Rudra; it should be a vessel one span (*prādeśa*) in measure. (1) The clarified butter is from white cows. (2) He should sacrifice on the full moon day of the month of Taiṣya. (3) On that night, they should not throw water into his house. (4) They perform the functions of water with clarified butter during this sacrifice and at the *agnihotra*. (5) Having enclosed the sacrificial ground, he proceeds while the rays of light are rising. (6) The six verses of Manu beginning with "Agni, you, the ancient one, with song... and "Swiftly, like those who favor the gods... are the *dhāyyā* verses. (7) The two *ājyabhāga* portions are the *vārtraghnas*.

8. "O Soma and Rudra, you two..."—these two [verses] are for the oblation. 9. The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *gāyatrī* meter. 10. One should sacrifice with the *saumāpauṣṇa* [offering] immediately after the full moon. 11. One practicing sorcery should offer a *caru* of black rice to Soma and Rudra. 12. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is made of *śara* reeds, and the fuel (*idhma*) is from the *vaibhīdaka* tree. 13. "O Soma and Rudra, tear asunder..."—these two [verses] are for the oblation. 14. He who desires, "May a second rival be in my domain," should offer a *caru* of black-and-white rice to Soma and Rudra. 15. Half...

The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *mañjara* grass; the fuel (*idhma*) is half of *vaibhīdaka* wood. (16) He cooks [the offering] in milk that has been poured over. (17) One should offer a *māmikṣā* curd-mixture dedicated to Soma and Rudra. (18) One should cause a person afflicted by disease to perform this sacrifice. (19) This is the ritual procedure for one who has survived. (20) When the Hotṛ priest is about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, he wraps his face with his own garment.

When [the sacrifice] is completed, having led [the victim] to the forest, he should show it [to the sacrificer]. To him he should give an ox; one should kill that [ox] and eat its meat; this is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *anneṣṭi*. One who practices sorcery or against whom sorcery is practiced should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu (Āgnāvaiṣṇava). He should also sacrifice to Sarasvatī with clarified butter. This is the expiation for one against whom sorcery is practiced; the ritual procedure for one practicing sorcery involves the *vārtraghnī* verses. "O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one mind... O Agni and Viṣṇu, the great, dear domain of you two"—these are the verses for the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu.

“May Sarasvatī, the purifier, [protect] us; O Sarasvatī, lead us toward greater wealth”—this is for the offering to Sarasvatī (26). For one desiring sight, the two *ājyabhāga* portions are the *viśvavantau* verses (27); the two *saṃyājyās* are the *virāj* verses (28); the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a hundred measures (29). One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; these have been explained (30). Likewise, if he should think of a battle, [he should offer] three oblations with the verses beginning “O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one accord” and “Moving forward against the enemy” (31).

Of those [verses], one should make two the *puronuvākyās* and one the *yājyā*; likewise for the offering to Sarasvatī (31). At the proper times, there is the cake on eight potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu according to the ritual procedure of the Soma sacrifice (*adhvarakalpa*). At the time of the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice, when it has a separate ritual procedure (*pṛthaktantra*), there is a cake on one potsherd for Mitra and Varuṇa, or else curdled milk (*payasyā*) (32). For one whose rival is sacrificing with Soma, he should combine the ritual procedure of the pressing day (*sutyādhvarakalpa*) (33). The ritual procedure for the slayer of Vṛtra (*vārtraghna*) is recited for the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu (34).

Likewise, for the offering to Sarasvatī [there are] thirty-five; for the offering to Bṛhaspati, "O Bṛhaspati, enjoy our prayers" is the [verse]; for the offering to Mitra-Varuṇa, [there are] thirty-six; on the eighth [day], four [verses] are explained by their formulas (nigada); for one desiring rain, "Like Aurva and Bhṛgu, [bring] the pressing" are the two *dhāyyā* verses.

There are six additional [verses] for the *ājyabhāga*, the oblation, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* (38). Having placed the *māruta* [oblation] on the fire, before the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite, one should drip cow’s urine onto the *priyaṅgu* seeds (39). "O you whose names are dear" (*priyā vo nāma śriyasaḥ*)—these two [verses] are for the oblation (40). On a cake on thirteen potsherds; if it is a cow, that is the sacrificial fee. According to one's desire, [the fee is given] to the two sons (41). This is the rule for the expiation (42). "O Maruts, since from heaven... (*maruto yaddha vo divaḥ*) and "Forward to the race-courses" (*praipāmajmeṣu*)—these are for the oblation (43). On seven potsherds; there are eleven *sāmidhenī* verses of the *kayāśubhīya* hymn.
The first and last [verses] are recited three times (44). "Agni, warding off the Rakṣases" are the two Ājyabhāga portions (45). Four remain for the Havis-sviṣṭakṛt offerings (46).

One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and one on seven potsherds to the Maruts for a Kṣatriya who desires prosperity. (Verse 1) "O Indra, you are above all... and "Your strength..."—these are the two verses for the Indra offering, following the Marut offering. (Verse 2) One who desires that both the common people (*viś*) and the nobility (*kṣatra*) should come together and reach agreement should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and one on seven potsherds to the Maruts. (Verse 3) If he should desire that they become confused and lose their way, then having placed the two oblations, he should place one in the eastern part of the village...

He should cut off a portion from the rear half of the village [of rice]; let another [portion] also join it. 4. The ritual procedure for the Vārtraghna [offering]. 5. Having cut off a portion for Indra, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words, "O Hotṛ, recite for Indra. 6. He recites after [the Hotṛ]: "Come hither to us, O Indra. 7. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he gives the command: "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts. 8. He recites the offering prayer: "The spears are yours, O Maruts. 9. Having cut off a portion for the Maruts, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the words, "O Hotṛ, recite for the Maruts. 10. He recites after [the Hotṛ]: "O Maruts, whatever strength is yours. 11. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he gives the command: "Recite the offering prayer for Indra. 12. He recites the offering prayer: "Thou art great, O Indra."

13. "For you are the same in many places"—this is the *saṃyājyā* [concluding offering verse]. 14. As is observed in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *sūktavāka*, it corresponds to the specific deity being worshipped. 15. If he should desire, "May it be successful," having set out these two very oblations, he should sacrifice them according to their respective order; then indeed it becomes successful. 16. One practicing sorcery (*abhicaran*) should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts. 17. He should take the portion from the Indra-oblation first, without turning the ladle over, and then take the portion from below the Māruti-oblation. 18. One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) to the Maruts.

One should cause a member of the royal class who desires a village to perform sacrifice. Having poured out the curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) into a vessel and placed the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) in the middle of it, he takes portions from both and proceeds with the offering. He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) with the words, "O Indra, recite for the Maruts! Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he gives the direction (*preṣya*) with the words, "O Indra, offer to the Maruts! The two verses—the invitatory and the offering (*yājyā*)—are addressed to Indra and the Maruts. One practicing exorcism should offer a cake on twenty-one potsherds to the Maruts. Having proceeded with the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*), he places the cake upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and, using the wooden sword (*sphya*), [draws lines] saying, "I strike this one, the son of such-and-such."

25. With the wooden sword (*sphyá*) he cleaves [the earth] toward the east. 26. With the words "enā vyāghram" (with this [he strikes] the tiger), he praises the wooden sword. 27. In case of the lapse of the proper time, there is an offering to Pāthikṛt at the animal sacrifice, at the New and Full Moon sacrifices, at the seasonal festivals of the Cāturmāsya, or upon eating new grain, as well as for the Āgrayaṇa. 28. At the *vrātapatya* offerings when one desires a troop, there is an offering to Vratapati. 29. There is an expiation for four [offerings]; the ritual procedure for three is that of the Vārtraghna. 30. "O Agni, lead us..."—these sixteen are for the oblations. 31. One should also sacrifice to Viṣṇu with clarified butter. 32. He who desires [something], he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rudravat.

"Lest the Rudras shut up his cattle," [so it is said]. (32) If he should desire, "May it be pacified," he should offer an *aṣṭākapāla* cake to Agni Surabhimat. (33) The portions for the *ājyabhāga*, the *havis*, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* have been explained. (34) [He should offer] an *aṣṭākapāla* cake to Agni Annavat, Annāda, and Annapati, or [three] *aṣṭākapāla* cakes. (35) This is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for the Vairāja [sāman]. (36) For the oblation, [the verse is]: "O bull, for food, driven by the wind... (37) He who fears the *rakṣases* should offer an *aṣṭākapāla* cake to Agni Rakṣohan. (38) He should cause the sacrifice to be performed at night. (39) "Make thy strength... (*kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ*).

These are the eleven *sāmidhenī* verses; the first and last are recited thrice (making fifteen). "O Agni, warding off the demons" are the two *ājyabhāga* portions. Four remain for the oblation and the *sviṣṭakṛt*. One who competes for sovereignty, or one desiring food, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni. [The ritual] is established up to the placing of the oblations. With the formula "Thou art vigor," he should touch the oblations that have been placed. He offers with this same [formula] prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt*. "Yoke, indeed, those best summoning the gods"—these are the nine *dhāyyā* verses.

There are six additional [verses] for the *ājyabhāga*, the oblation, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offerings. (47) One who is a ruler but does not conquer should offer an oblation to Indra and Bṛhaspati. (48) Having offered [the portion] to Bṛhaspati and prepared [the portion] for Indra, he should proceed with the offering to both. (49) The ritual procedure is that of the *vāhnartra*. (50) "This is yours" and "Of this mouth"—these two are for the oblation. (51)

One should offer a *caru* oblation of clarified butter to Āditya for one who has been captured; he should perform the sacrifice for him. (1) The procedure is established up to the point of the pouring out [of the grains]. (2) Before the recitation of the *Sāvitra* formula, he should mutter: (3) "I shall make a portion for you, O Ādityas; cause such-and-such a person, the son of such-and-such a family, to be released"—here he should utter the name of the captive. (4) Having set down the sacrificial offerings, he places seven stakes made of *aśvattha* wood in front, within the altar, and wipes them clean. (5) When the ritual is concluded, he should drive them into the middle shaft-hole of the chariot-stand. (6)

"I bind these Ādityas for the discovery of so-and-so"—at this point, he should utter the name of the person who has been restrained. (7) If he does not discover him within seven days, having bound the splinters to the fuel-wood, he should sacrifice in this manner every seven days for a second period of seven days. (8) If he does not discover him in the first [period], having sacrificed with the next two [verses], he should sacrifice with the verse containing the word *dhārayat*. (9) If [he does not discover him] in the second [period], he should sacrifice with the following [verse].

If [the fire] is held at the end within the highest [layer], then, having bound the shoots onto the *idhma* used for the New and Full Moon sacrifices—or even if it has already been kindled—he should take a portion from the right foot of the obstructed [fire] with the mantra: "O you whose blessing is true, give consent; here is my mind. He should then take [a portion] from the dust of that right foot.

Now, if there should be one who has been a village-talkative person (grāmyavādī) [before], when he has been crushed in the assembly, they should lie down facing the wind, saying: "O Maruts, self-strong, drive away this man; go toward that king! From the house of the village-talkative person, having brought rice-grains, he should sort them into three parts. Those which are black, having bound them on a black antelope skin, he should set them aside. Those which are white, for them he should offer a pap of rice in ghee to Āditya. Having completed the offering to Āditya, he should go northward to those from whom he had sorted [the grains].

Having dug up an anthill mound, he offers with the verse, "That which was yours today, O terrible one... (VS 20.23). Having returned, he should sacrifice with an oblation to Varuṇa, concluding with a verse containing the word *dhārayat*. The two *ājyabhāga* portions are those [verses] containing the calls, "Come here, let me tell you this sacrifice... (VS 20.24) and "These Kṣatriyas indeed, whose mother... (VS 20.25). The two regular *saṃyājyā* verses are used. The ritual procedure for the *vārtraghnī* verses applies to the verse containing the word *dhārayat*. The two verses beginning with "The Ādityas, holding... (VS 20.26–27) are for the principal oblation (*havis*).

One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of white rice grains to Sūrya in clarified butter. (1) While removing [the oblation from the fire], he should place two gold plates weighing a *śatamāna* each: a silver one underneath and a greenish-yellow (*harita*) one on top. (2) At each *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* weight of three barley grains. (3) The ritual procedure (*tantra*) belongs to Soma and Rudra. (4) For the principal oblation, the verse is "Those auspicious horses of Sūrya. (5) In the *śatakṛṣṇalā* [offering], four *kṛṣṇalas* constitute one portion for the *avadāna*, one for the *prāśitra*, and one for the intermediate *iḍā*. (6) He hands over the pap to the Brahman priest. (7)

Having sucked [the milk], they offer the sacrificial foods (8). The *jīvitavān* rite is the ritual procedure (9). "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ yaḥ prāṇataḥ" is the formula for the oblation (10). One desiring the office of a domestic priest (*purodhā*) should offer a *caru* to Bṛhaspati (11). Its ritual framework is the same as that for one desiring a village (12). The two verses for the offering to Indra-Bṛhaspati are traditionally handed down (13). One desiring a village or desiring cattle should offer a *caru* in milk to Bṛhaspati (14). Having brought milk from the house of one who has many cattle and having mixed it with the water used for the formal pouring out (*praṇītā-udaka*), he cooks the *caru* (15).

One who desires to win a battle should offer a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati when the two armies are visible to one another. (16) The *prastara* bundle is without sacrificial grass; the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are arrows with feathers and roots. (17) While throwing the *prastara* into the fire, he should place it into the offering-ladle. (18) One should offer a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati at whatever time he should desire, "May there be the power of the *brahman*. (19) For the oblations, there are eight verses beginning with "Bṛhaspati, being first born... (20) He does not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call with a *bṛhatī* verse. (21)

He adds four syllables from the *anuvākyā* to the *yājyā*. He recites: "Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati; seeking the gods, we entreat thee. May the Maruts, the bounteous givers, come forward; O Indra, [grant] the *praśas*. He performs the sacrifice with the verse: "Be thou with us, O Agni, at the hymn. For the offering to Bṛhaspati, he uses: "O Bṛhaspati, enjoy our offerings; drink [the soma]."

The two offerings to Soma and Pūṣan are prescribed [in the standard texts]. Having placed the offering to Prajāpati on the fire before the carrying of fire around it, one should sprinkle it with cow's urine from a leather bag. The *vāstvamaya* and *kaṇika* [offerings] are the expiation ritual (*prāyaścitti-kalpa*). For the oblation, [the mantras] "namas te rudra manyave" and "imā rudrāya" are used. There is a sacrifice for the Niṣāda-sthapati; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed [in the texts]. A king desiring the status of a *parameṣṭhin* should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Parameṣṭhin. Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he should have a strung bow and three arrows [placed near him], [reciting]: "May Agni impart brilliance to thee."

He hands it to the sacrificer; that is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 32. One who has rivals should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to the Viśve Devās. 33. Having performed the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) and having placed the sacrificial cake upon the sacrificial grass (barhis), he should take the wooden sword (sphya) and, saying "I separate this one and me from that one," he should utter the name of him whom he hates. That [portion] which falls down upon the grass and clings to the wooden sword, he should cut off for Viṣṇu Urukrama. 34. He should then gather it back together, saying "I reunite this one and me with that one," for him who is dear to him.

One should not utter the name [of the deity] without having first invoked Viṣṇu, the wide-striding one; one should sacrifice first. (35) For one setting out on an army, one should offer a *caru* to Indrāṇī, having bound *balbaja* grass to the fuel-sticks. (36) For one desiring prosperity, the ritual procedure is for one desiring success. (37) "Who indeed knows?"—these are the ten oblations. (38)

The *saṃjñānī* sacrifice consists of four oblations with the formula "To Agni accompanied by the Vasus. (1) He who desires, "May they regard me as equal to the leaders," should sacrifice with this. (2) Its ritual procedure is that of one desiring a village. (3) Having taken portions together, he proceeds. (4) He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite: "Pronounce the invitatory prayer for Agni accompanied by the Vasus, for Soma accompanied by the Rudras, for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and for Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas. (5) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Agni accompanied by the Vasus, to Soma accompanied by the Rudras, to Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and to Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas."

6. He sends forth [the invitatory verses] with "Agni first" and "Together with Agni" for the oblation. 7. One should sacrifice with the *saṃjñāna* (reconciliation) formula dedicated to Indra. 8. With these verses beginning "May there be reconciliation for us from heaven," he offers for both [oblations] prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt*. 9. One should sacrifice with the four-oblation rite beginning "To Agni, an eight-potherd cake" when gold has been lost. 10. The two *ājyabhāga* portions contain the word "wealth" (*rayi*). 11. There are eight [verses] for the oblations beginning with "O Agni, give. 12. The two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word "gain" (*sani*). 13. One should indeed find [the lost item] and sacrifice again. 14. One seized by *rājayakṣman* (consumption) [performs the rite] on the new moon day, ending with the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*).

Having prepared other fuel-sticks and sacrificial grass and having girded himself, he should indeed sacrifice at night with the Vaiśvadeva; this is the rule for the expiation (15). There are two oblations, "the former" and "the latter" (16). He offers before the Sviṣṭakṛt with the verse beginning "As the Ādityas... (17). With the three oblations beginning "O Indra, King...", each subsequent cake-offering is larger than the preceding one (18). The ritual procedure for this [sacrifice] is for one who desires a village (19). There are three oblations with the verses beginning "In the eastern direction... (20). He recites the first [verse] after [the call] "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra, the King!", and he sacrifices to Indra, the Sovereign Lord (21).

He sacrifices with the middle [verse]. (22) "Recite for Indra Svarāj! He recites the middle [verse] for Indra Svarāj; "Sacrifice for Indra Svarāj! He sacrifices with the last [verse]. (23) "Recite for Indra Adhirāja! He recites this very same [verse] for Indra Adhirāja; "Sacrifice for Indra Adhirāja! He sacrifices with the first [verse]. (24) It is observed according to the sacrifice, both in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and in the *sūktavāka*. (25) For one desiring splendor, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is for one desiring prosperity. (26) The subsequent [verse] is for one desiring cattle. (27) "In whom..."—these four [verses] are for the two oblations. (28) The latter belongs to the *Ārkavata*. (29) Indra...

There are four [verses] beginning with *yārkavataḥ* (30). For one who is obstructed, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings have the *hūtavant* formulas (31). The two *saṃyājyā* verses are the regular ones (32). A barren cow is the sacrificial fee (33). For one who desires, "May I prosper in another's territory," the ritual procedure for that [sacrifice] is the same as that for one desiring a village (34). One who has attained prosperity should sacrifice [with this] so that his prosperity may not be surpassed (35). This is the rule for the expiation (36). For one who desires, "May I sacrifice with a sacrifice characterized by abundant sacrificial fees."

For her, the ritual procedure for one desiring cattle consists of thirty-seven [verses]. (37) The four-oblation sacrifice begins with "O Indra, who art accompanied by the Gharma... (38). The [verse] beginning with "To thee, the great one, as soon as born... belongs to the Manasvatī; for the others, it is handed down in the traditional recension. (39) There are seven [verses] beginning with "O Indra, those which release from distress... (40). One who is the eldest, of noble birth, and endowed with excellence should perform the sacrifice with the third [verse]. (41) The ritual rule is an expiation for two [cases]; the ritual procedure for one desiring a village is performed with a single [verse].

The *vārtraghna* verses for the subsequent [oblations] are fourteen, beginning with "viveṣa yat" (42). There are seven [verses] for the oblations beginning with "aindram ekakapālam" (43). For one whose rival performs a Soma sacrifice, there is the rite of the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, beginning with "indrā ya vajriṇe" (44); he should join this with the *sutyā-iṣṭi* (45). For the two preceding [oblations], the *vārtraghna* verses are those that have been invoked (46). The fourteen verses for the oblations begin with "arvāvato na āgahi" (47). Prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers over the cake on thirteen potsherds with the verse "indram naraḥ" (48). There are three [verses] beginning with "indrā ya manyumate" (49).

50. If they should seize him alive, they should cut him to pieces. 51. He who desires, "May I be wealthy and free from reproach," when about to sacrifice, should not say "O mind" for a full year. 52. For the oblations, he recites the four verses beginning with "To thee, the great one, as soon as born. 53. [He recites] the first two verses at the first and last [oblations]. 54. If the moon should rise while his *sāṃnāyya* has been set out, having offered the modified portions, he should divide the rice grains into three parts. 55. He silently pours the morning milk over the flour and prepares a flour-cake (*piṣṭacarum*). 56. Having divided the boiled milk, he proceeds with the ritual.

57. The ritual procedure for expiation (*prāyaścitti-kalpa*). 58. For the offering to Agni, [the verses] beginning with "O Agni, give, give to us" (*agne dā dā naḥ agne*) [are used]. 59. For the two following [offerings], the four [verses] beginning with "What of thee, O Viṣṇu? (*kiṃ te viṣṇo*) [are used]; [these are for] the northern and eastern [hearths]. 60. One who desires cattle, having performed the New Moon sacrifice, drives away all the calves silently. 61. For the six oblations, [the verses] beginning with "The *iḍā* of Agni" (*iḍām agne*) [are used]. 62. The three-oblation [sacrifice] consists of [the cake] on eight potsherds for Agni (*āgneyam aṣṭākapālam*). 63. On the final day, having pressed against a mountain, one should sacrifice, or else [press against] water. 64. The ritual procedure for expiation for one who has vomited Soma (*somavāmin*). 65. For the oblation, the two [verses] beginning with "With thee as my companion" (*tvā yujā*) and "That of thine, O Soma" (*tava tat soma*) [are used]. 66. The mixing-in of curds (*śrayaṇa*) is prescribed; the mixing-in is prescribed. 67. [End.]

Thus ends the first chapter in the *Iṣṭikalpa*. One should offer a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and a curd-mixture (*payasyā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa. For that [curd-mixture], there is a cake on eleven or twelve potsherds dedicated to the same deities. There are also cakes on single potsherds to be treated silently. [The procedure] is established up to the point of the performance (*pracaraṇa*). Having performed the rite with the cake for Agni, one covers the northern cake with the curd-mixture and divides it into four parts, moving eastward and first clockwise, with the verses beginning "O Mitra and Varuṇa, that which is yours in strength," for the Brāhmaṇa; and "O Indra and Varuṇa... [for the Kṣatriya].

For a Kṣatriya, [the formula is] "Agni and Varuṇa"; for a Vaiśya, [it is as follows]. Having taken equal portions, he proceeds with the spreading of the base (upastaraṇa) and the pouring over (abhighāraṇa). He offers the cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla) together with the remnants (saṃpāta), reciting at every step: "O King Varuṇa, that [portion] of yours which is among the gods, in bipeds, in quadruped animals, in plants, in trees, in the waters, on the earth, and in the quarters; O King Varuṇa, that [portion] of yours... Thus he recites the verse "yaste rājan varuṇa" everywhere. With the verses beginning "yā vām mitrāvaruṇā ojasi," he gathers [the portions] and takes portions for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering and for the Iḍā. The ritual procedure (tantra) may be performed according to his desire. Indra...

"O Varuṇa, O Sovereign!"—this is the formula for the offering to Indra and Varuṇa. (6) One who has rivals should offer a *caru* oblation to the Viśvedevas. (7) He cooks it with fresh butter. (8) "Every day, O Indra"—these two [verses] are for the sacrificial offering. (9) One desiring a village should sacrifice with this [rite]. (10) Having brought clarified butter from the houses of all the villagers, he cooks the *caru*. (11) The procedure is established up to the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). (12) He consecrates the enclosing sticks with the formulas: "Thou art firm" for the middle one; "Thou art fierce" for the southern one; "Thou art the overcomer" for the northern one.

He says, "Thou art honored," to the Āhavanīya fire; "Thou art a patron," to the Sun. 13. Up to the removal [of the oblation], it is established. 14. Having fashioned a vessel for the *āmana* offering out of clay or wood in the shape of a shell, he pours the remainder of the *caru* into it. 15. With the verses beginning, "O God, those who are born together with the *āmana*... and those who are of one mind," he offers four oblations from the *āmana* vessel prior to the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. 16. "In some place... is the *yājyā* verse. 17. A spotted cow or milch-cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). 18.

For as many horses as he may accept, for that many he should offer cakes on four potsherds to Varuṇa, and one caru-oblation to Aponapāt. With the verses beginning "O King Varuṇa, you who have the Gāyatrī metre," he offers four oblations prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. If he intends to accept [the horses] again, or if he should accept them again, he should offer half [of the cakes] to Varuṇa and half to both Sūrya and Varuṇa. The verse "Yukṣvā hi" is the additional one for the oblations to Sūrya and Varuṇa; the oblation to Aponapāt remains the same. The rest is identical.

There are twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses; 24. there are six *dhāyyā* verses beginning with *pṛthupājās tam sabādhaḥ*; 25. the rule for the expiation is as follows; 26. [the verses] for the *vāruṇa* offerings are those traditionally handed down; 27. [the verse] *yad adya sūrya* is for the *sauryavāruṇa* offerings; 28. [the verse] *upemasṛkṣi* is for the *āponaptrīya* offering; 29. he offers into the waters with the two following verses. 30.

One who is ill and desires long life should sacrifice with the Āyuṣkāmeṣṭi. It consists of three oblations on the previous day—namely, a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu—and five oblations on the following day. Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering in that rite, he takes five portions of clarified butter either in the Kāṃsya vessel or in a cup. Having tied a piece of gold with a blade of Darbha grass, he places it into the five portions of butter while reciting, "Thou art the life of Agni. He makes an offering in the eastern half with the formula, "Thou art the breath of Indra," and then, moving clockwise around the fire while reciting the subsequent formulas, he returns and offers the fifth portion in the center. As for the phrase, "that which [is offered] with the ninth... [the rest follows].

Having brought ghee for drinking, he draws out gold with the verse, "Of the purifying one... (RV IX.1.6), taking a third part; then, having drawn out two parts with the verse, "By the Bṛhat [meter] thee... (VS VIII.35), he places it on the bank. 6. Having carried it around in front of the Āhavanīya fire, he hands it to the sacrificer with the formula, "Thou art splendor" (VS VIII.36). 7. The sacrificer receives it with the formula, "This is luster" (VS VIII.37). 8. Having taken hold of the gold and blowing upon it, he drinks from it. 9. Having washed it, he ties it to the sacrificer with the verse, "This [splendor], O Agni... (VS VIII.38). 10. Having touched the hand of the Brahman priest with the formula, "Agni is life-span... (VS VIII.39), [he does so] for all.

The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) carry [the sacrificial fees] around; the *brahmán* priest receives them from the sacrificer. 11. At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives ten [cows]. 12. This is the ritual procedure for one who has lived [his full life]. 13. "O Agni, grant us life; O God, giver of life"—these are the ten verses for the oblations. 14. There is an offering of four oblations or five oblations beginning with "To Agni, a cake on eight potsherds" (*āgneyam aṣṭākapālam*), for one who desires, "May my offspring and cattle be numerous through procreation. 15. Now, if [an enemy] should attack him, he should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra before the [victim] has been released, and one to Prajāpati once it has been released. 16. At the time of taking down [the oblation], he should offer [to Kāma].

Having spread a base of ghee in the *camasa* vessel, he pours in curds, honey, clarified butter, parched grains, and water, with a strainer placed between; [he recites] "O Agni, come to us with good intention," "O Agni, bring wealth to us"—these are the ten oblations. For one desiring sight, there is an offering of three oblations beginning with "To Agni the Radiant. There are white rice grains, clarified butter from white cows, and a sacrificial pap cooked in milk. Together with the portions for the Brahman and the sacrificer, he presents the solar pap to the Brahman. When the *samiṣṭayajus* has been offered, [he presents] the solar pap.

Having formed four balls of food, he places them in his hand with verses addressed to Sūrya (23). Having consumed them, he consumes the sacrificer’s portion (24). With the verses "O Agni, thy pure [flames]" and "This Agni," he offers four oblations (25). Of these, the first and last are to be taken up from the front, while the others are from the back (25).

One who desires prosperity, or one who is being falsely accused, should sacrifice with the *sarvapṛṣṭhā* [offering]. He prepares twelve *kapālas*. [The ritual] is established up to the pouring out of the grains. For Indra associated with the *rathaṃtara*, for Indra associated with the *bṛhat*, for Indra associated with the *vairūpa*, for Indra associated with the *vairāja*, for Indra associated with the *raivata*, and for Indra associated with the *śākvara*—for each of these deities, he pours out four handfuls; or, having recited all the deities, he pours out exactly four handfuls. [The ritual] is established up to the placing of the potsherds. They are turned face upwards.

He places the potsherds. Then follows the *tri-caru* (the three-oblation rice-porridge), which is prepared until the point of offering. Having taken a portion from the eastern half of the middle [potsherd], he says: "Recite for Indra associated with the *Rathantara* [Sāman]! He recites: "We cry out to you, O Hero, like unmilked cows; to the lord of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, the lord of the earth. [Then the Adhvaryu says: "Offer to Indra associated with the *Bṛhat* [Sāman]! [The Hotṛ recites: "We, the poets, invoke you, Indra associated with the *Bṛhat*, while sacrificing; we invoke you, O Indra, as you stand firm, for the winning of booty."

"O Indra, lord of the virtuous, men [invoke] you in battles; you, with the steed, in the races. With these words he sacrifices. (9) Having drawn [the portions] around, drawing them all around clockwise, he cuts off the portions for the subsequent verses. (10) "O Indra, recite the invitatory verse for the Bṛhatī-meter! For we, the poets, invoke you alone for the winning of booty. O Indra, lord of the virtuous, men [invoke] you in battles; you, with the steed, in the races. Thus he recites. (11) "O Indra, sacrifice with the Rathantara-sāman!"

"Ye yajāmahe Indra. He sacrifices with the *mṛḍāntara* [verse]: "O Hero, we cry out to you for wealth in horses, like unmilked cows; to the Lord of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, to Indra, the Lord of that which stands still. (12) "O Indra, recite for the *vairūpa* [sāman]! He recites: "Thou hast filled... (13) "O Indra, sacrifice for the *vairāja* [sāman]!"

He offers with *bodhā su me*. 14. "O Indra, recite for the Vairāja!"—he recites this same [verse]. 15. "O Indra, sacrifice for the Vairūpa! You have filled [the worlds]!"—he offers. 16. "O Indra, recite for the Raivata!"—he recites *revatīr naḥ*. 17. "O Indra, sacrifice for the Śākvara!"—he offers with *pra u asmāi*. 18. "O Indra, recite for the Śākvara!"—he recites this same [verse]. 19. "O Indra, sacrifice for the Raivata!"

He sacrifices with the first [verse] (20), as is observed in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *sūktavāka* (21). Having drawn [the portions] around, drawing them all together, he cuts off portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* and for the *iḍā* (22). The ritual procedure (*tantra*) may be performed according to one's desire (23).

One who has vomited Soma should sacrifice with the Aiṣṭikī Sautrāmaṇī; one consecrated for the Rājasūya, one desiring prosperity, or one who has been long ill, should likewise sacrifice. 1. Having enclosed a space, he purchases the ingredients for the Surā from a eunuch using lead: *nagna*, rice, barley, wheat, and young grass. 2. Having said, "O seller of Surā and Soma, I purchase the Surā and Soma from you with this lead," he makes the purchase. 3. He mixes it with the formula, "Thee, the sweet, with the sweet. 4. He touches it with the formula, "Soma, be cooked for the Aśvins. 5. Thinking, "Tomorrow the Surā shall be produced," he observes the fast for the animal sacrifice.

6. [The ritual] is established up to the time of the altar (vedikāla). 7. At the time of the altar, the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares a mound (khara) in the form of an altar to the south, and the Adhvaryu prepares one to the north; it should be smaller than the mounds for the cups of milk (payograhāḥ). 8. The two [priests], the Agnīdh and the Adhvaryu, lead forward the fires. 9. To the south of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having made the supporting grass-bunches (upayamanī) from the mound and having sprinkled water, places them on the eastern half of the mound. 10. He sets out the vessels belonging to the animal sacrifice (pāśukāni pātrāṇi).

On the southern mound, the Pratiprasthātṛ places three earthen vessels for the *upayāma* cups, a wooden trough (*droṇa*), a hundred-holed filter (*śatātṛṇṇā*), and three *vāyavya* cups; on the northern mound, the Adhvaryu places two grass-strainers (*śaṣpapavitra*) and three *vāyavya* cups. (11) He brings forth both the clarified butter and the milk. (12) He deposits the clarified butter on the altar (*vedī*) and the milk on the mound. (13) Having placed the wine-jar (*surākalaśa*) on the head of the Āgnīdhra near the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), the Pratiprasthātṛ crosses to the south of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) and deposits it on his own mound. (14)

Success! From the vessels for the butter-portions (ājyagraha), he takes four spoonfuls of clarified butter each, containing speckled butter (pṛṣadājya). This is established up to the setting down of the butter-portions. Having spread out a tuft of wool over a wooden trough (droṇakalaśa), the Pratiprasthātṛ causes the *surā* to flow through it with the verse, "May [Soma] purify thy flowing liquor. The Adhvaryu takes the milk-portions (payograhas) with the verse, "O, surely, they who possess barley," holding them over strainers made of *śaṣpa* grass, specifically those for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutraman. The taking and the setting down are performed according to the respective deities.

"Thou art taken with a support; thee, the flawless, with the flawless [vessel]," thus the Pratiprasthātṛ, having mixed the Sura-cups with the Upayāmas, sets down the cup for the Aśvins with *kuvala*-flour, that for Sarasvatī with *karkandhu*-flour, and that for Indra with *badara*-flour. From the pit of the sacrificial post until the consecration (upākaraṇa), the procedure is established. He dedicates a goat to the Aśvins, a ewe to Sarasvatī, and a bull to Indra. The procedure is established up to the sprinkling (mārjana). Having poured the remnants from the Upayāma-vessels into the Vāyavya-vessels, they stand between the two fires, holding the cups.

With his right hands he takes the cups of liquor (*surā*), and with his left hands the cups of milk (*payas*). First is the *adhvaryu*, then the *pratiprasthātṛ*, and lastly the sacrificer. He causes [the *hotṛ*] to recite the invitatory verse (*anuvācayati*) with the words: "Recite for the Aśvins, for Sarasvatī, and for Indra Sutrāman, for the Soma-liquors mixed with *surā*. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he proceeds with the direction: "Prompt [the *hotṛ*] for the Aśvins, for Sarasvatī, and for Indra Sutrāman, for the Soma-liquors mixed with *surā* that have been set forth. Having offered at the *vaṣaṭ*-call and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*-call, he meditates upon the meditations: "Truly, this glory..."

"Let him come," says the Adhvaryu; "of the two tigers," says the Pratiprasthātṛ; "me from the two wolves," says the sacrificer (28). Having poured the residues from the principal [cups] into the *avanīya* fire and carried them around in front of the *āgnīdhra*, the sacrificer consumes [the portion] to the south, saying, "Whatever remains here... (29). He consumes the milk-cups with the formula, "For indeed, yours two are manifold," and the *surā*-cups with the nose [of the cup], if he is a drinker of *surā*. (30) With the verses beginning, "Two paths there are," he offers four oblations prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt*. The Pratiprasthātṛ, having placed the *śatātṛṇṇā* vessel upon the southern fire...

Having brought the remainder of the *surā*, he consecrates the flowing liquid with twelve verses beginning with "O Soma, you who have been observed" (*soma pracikitaḥ*), three verses at a time. One [priest] from the south is the *brahmán*, one from the west is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), one from the north is the *adhvaryu*, and one from the east is the *pratiprasthātṛ*. (31) He offers the animal-cake oblations (*paśupuroḍāśa*) on eleven potsherds for Indra the Good Protector (*sutrāman*), for Savitṛ, and for Varuṇa. (32) Having performed the ritual with the animals excluding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he proceeds with the animal-cake oblations, beginning first with that for Indra.

33. He cuts portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering from both the animals and the animal-cake offerings, as well as for the *iḍā*. 34. The ritual procedure (*tantra*) may be performed according to his desire. 35. Having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*), a mare is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). 36. The animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is thus completed. 37. The *hotṛ*-function for the animal sacrifice has been prescribed. 38. Vessels smeared with *surā* liquor he throws into the water. 39. "You two [have drunk] the *surā*" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the cups. 40. "The Hotṛ shall worship the Aśvins" is the direction (*praiṣa*). 41.
