"Like parents [protect] their son" is the offering verse (*yājyā*). 42. "O Agni, enjoy the Soma and the *surā*"—with these words he performs the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (*anuvaṣaṭkaroti*). 43. Indra...
"Ṣutrāmā," "tasya vayam," "tat savitur vareṇyam," "imaṃ me varuṇa," and "tattvā yāmi"—these are the verses for the animal-cake offerings (paśupuroḍāśa). 43.

Having performed austerity for twelve nights, he should sacrifice with the *traidhātavī* [offering], fasting for three nights, or practicing sorcery against an enemy. 1. He employs twelve potsherds. 2. [The ritual] is established up to the pouring out [of the grains]. 3. Having poured out rice for Indra and Viṣṇu, he pours out barley; then the rice. 4. [The ritual] is established up to the placing on the fire. 5. Having placed the rice-made [cake] on the fire and baked it until the carrying of fire around it (*aparyagnikṛta*), he places the larger [cake] made of barley upon it and bakes it until the carrying of fire around it; upon that, he places the largest [cake].

Having placed the rice-oblation on the fire, he performs the rite of carrying fire around it (paryagni). [This continues] until the removal from the fire is completed. Having sprinkled clarified butter over it, while holding the two upper portions above, he sprinkles the lower portion, removes it from the fire, and adorns it. Having placed the two upper portions, he cuts off portions from all of them—namely, from the sacrificial oblation, the *āhuti*, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the *iḍā*—so as to cross over them.

9. For one [sacrificer], there is a thousand at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); at the time of the sacrificial fee, there are three milch-cows, three pieces of gold, and three garments made of *tārpya* silk, other than the thousand. 10. For one who desires success or for one practicing sorcery, the sacrificial fee consists of [the aforementioned items] plus a thousand. 11. "O Agni, [grant] booty consisting of cattle"—these five are the *dhāyyā* verses; the sixth is in the *jagatī* meter. 12. He concludes with a *triṣṭubh* verse: "O Agni, three are thy strengths, three thy seats. 13. "Agni, the breaker of strength, thrice [of the day]"—these are the two *ājyabhāga* portions. 14. "Together with your work"—these two are for the oblation (*havis*). 15. "Three are the lifespans... [etc. (RV X.18.4).

15. "Agni am I"—these two are the *saṃyājyā* verses. 16. For one practicing exorcism, [the verses] beginning with "Vārtraghna" [are used]. 17. "O Indra and Viṣṇu, you have shattered the fortresses of Śambara"—these two are for the oblation. 18. A son should sacrifice with Soma. 19. One desiring rain should offer a pap (*caru*) dedicated to Parjanya. 20. "Sing forth to Parjanya"—these two are for the oblation. 21. "To Agni, an eight-potherd cake"—from the placing on the fire of these three oblations onwards, [one recites] "We know thee, O Agni," and for the two oblations, four [verses] beginning with "He who propped up. These are the sixth [sections].

A king or a domestic priest, desiring rain, should sacrifice with the Kārīrī offering. Having covered himself in black [garments], he undertakes the vow in the forenoon. He places fuel-sticks of reed (vaitasa), clarified butter, honey, and parched flour of karīra fruits upon a black antelope skin behind the Āhavanīya fire. While the sacrificer maintains contact with him, the officiant, making him recite the verses beginning with "anuvāta," offers the Vāta-oblations during the sacrifice. Having mixed honey with the parched flour of karīra fruits using the verses "māndā vaśā," he forms four balls and places them on the black antelope skin with the formula: "Thou art the tethering-rope of the stallion."

6. He consecrates the halter of the dark-colored horse with the formula: "For rain I bind thee. 7. He binds the dough-balls onto the black antelope skin with the formula: "For rain I bind thee. 8. Having fastened them to the Gadhakarṇa tree at its eastern end with the formula: "O gods who are givers of wealth," he should wait for the third part of the day. 9. If it rains, he should fasten them to the two western [trees] with the next two formulas and perform the sacrifice. 10. If it does not rain, having fastened them to the middle [tree] with the formula: "O gods who are givers of shelter," he should wait for the latter half of the day. 11. If it rains, he should fasten them to the western end with the final formula and perform the sacrifice.

11. If it does not rain, he should wait for the remainder of the day after having released [the victim] with the verse, "May the gods be with us for our prosperity. 12. If it rains, he should offer the oblation immediately. 13. If it still does not rain, they should remain right there. 14. When the next day has dawned, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dhāmachad, a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts, and a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya. 15. At the time of removing [the rice], having spread a base of ghee in a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, he adorns the balls of rice. 16. Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having taken a portion from the ball of rice and recited, "The thought by day," he says, "O gods who possess wealth..."

Having uttered "juhotyāyaraḥ," he pronounces the second [verse], "devāḥ śarmaṇyāḥ"; having uttered [the third], "devāḥ sapītayaḥ," he pronounces the third [verse]. With "sṛjā vṛṣṭiṃ divaḥ," he pronounces the fourth over the waters. With "ye devā divibhāgāḥ stha," he shakes the black antelope skin over the sacrificial grass (barhis). "O Maruts, cause him to rest; let the vigorous steed, swift as thought, the bull, the well-praised one, go forth. O Aśvins, clothe him with that by which this formidable [sacrifice] has been released, for his well-being."

Thus he consecrates the rainy-season wind from the north. (19) "The black path..."—with these [verses], there are six oblations of threefold [portions]. (20) The ritual procedure belongs to Agni and the Maruts. (21) With the final verse, he makes an additional offering to Sūrya. (22) This is the sacrifice named Kārīrī; one who performs this sacrifice shall not eat *karīra* fruits for a full year—this is the vow. (23)

The omission of the optional rites follows from the Rājasūya. 1. A pap of rice cooked in ghee for the Ādityas, those who are present and those who are becoming; 2. "Arvāñco adya" and [the next verse]—these two are for the oblation; 3. The Āgrayaṇa sacrifice; the ritual procedure belongs to the Vairāja Sāman. 4. "O Agni and Indra, of the donor... and "With which two you generated the light..."—these are for the offering to Agni and Indra; 5. "All the gods, increasers of Truth... and "All the gods, who are unfailing..."—these are for the Vaiśvadeva offering; 6. "May Heaven and Earth, the first-born..."—this is for the offering to Heaven and Earth; 7. "O Soma, those of yours that are bliss-bringing... and "Those which are your abodes... [are the verses].

In the *saumya* [offering], eight [verses]; in the *śunāsīrya*, four; for one desiring cattle or food, two for the sake of rain during the monsoon; in the *aindraturīya*, two; in the *devikā* offerings, four; "Anu naḥ adya anumatir anvid anumate" (May Anumati favor us today...), ten verses for the oblations; one desiring well-being should offer the two-potsherd cake to the Aśvins in the forenoon; this is the ritual procedure for expiation; "Prātaryajadhvam aśvinā" (Sacrifice early to the Aśvins)—these two [verses] are for the oblation; one desiring success in sacrifice should sacrifice with the *triṣamyukta* [verse], and one desiring cattle with the subsequent [verse]; "Indrā nu... [etc.]

With the verse "pūṣanā yan nirṇijā," there is an offering to Indra and Pūṣan (Aindrāpauṣṇa). (18) One who has been long ill should sacrifice with an offering to Vaiśvānara and Varuṇa. (19) One whose kingdom is as if unstable should cause him to sacrifice with this offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati (Maitrābārhaspatya). (20) One desiring all objects of desire should perform a sacrifice with the oblations of the Devasū. (21) Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, having offered the Vājaprasavya of clarified butter, he sprinkles [the sacrificer]. (22) With the sixteen verses beginning "tvam agne bṛhad vayaḥ," [he offers] the oblations. (23) One desiring food should sacrifice with the Aveṣṭis of the Quarters (Diśām aveṣṭis). (24) [This is] the Vairāja [sacrifice].

Kalpa 25: One who desires well-being should sacrifice with the oblations of the Truth-Messengers (Satyadūta). 26. The ritual for expiation (Prāyaścitti) follows. 27. [The rite] beginning with "He who [created] all these beings" consists of six oblations. 28.

Now, concerning the office of the Hotṛ: (1) as it is with the *sāmidhenī* verses, so it is with the verses for the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayanīyā*), those for the sacrificial post (*yūpyā*), and those for the churning of the fire (*agnimanthanīyā*); likewise [apply this] to the Maitrāvaruṇa’s circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), the *stokyā* verses, the *manotā*-hymn, and the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*). (2) He recites the direction (*praiṣa*) according to the agent [of the action]. (3) Directed by the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Hotṛ should perform the sacrifice (*yajet*). (4) Having been directed while the fire is being led forward, he recites "pra devam"; having stood up, he recites "ayamu ṣya"; while walking, he recites "ayam agniḥ"; standing behind the northern corner of the altar, he should wait at the half-verse "ūrṇāvantam."

5. When [the victim] has been slain, having spoken the remainder, he hands it over saying, "You are the messenger. 6. He should sit down. 7. Seated, when sent forth for the consecration of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with the verse *añjanti tvām*, he should wait at the half-verse of the third recitation. 8. Sent forth for the post being raised, with the formula *yad ūrdhvam ucchrayasva*, he should recite continuously and wait at *sam atriṇaṃ daha*. 9. Sent forth for the post being encircled, having recited *kṛdhī naḥ* and having concluded with *yuvā suvāsāḥ*, he should stand by. 10. Sent forth for the fire being churned, it is established as follows.

In the Vaiśvadeva [parvan], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. The procedure is established up to the invocation (*āvāhana*). There is no animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*). Prior to the offerings to the *ājyapa* deities, the Vanaspati offering is performed. The procedure from the *ājyapa* offerings onwards is established. Standing by way of the *tīrtha*, with the Maitrāvaruṇa in front, the Hotṛ behind him, the performer (the Āgnīdhra) behind the southern shoulder of the altar, and remaining straight and unbending, he grasps the staff with both arms, saying: "Thou art the seizer of fruit; may I be a seizer of fruit through thee; may I directly prosper. Having grasped the staff, he leans upon it over the altar.

Having placed [the fuel] on the right shoulder, standing with hands extended, he should await the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*). 16. "Commanded for the fuel-sticks, let the Hotṛ sacrifice to Agni with the words 'Agni with fuel-sticks' (*samidbhiḥ*)"—these are the ten commands (*praiṣāḥ*). 17. With the ten *hotrīyā* verses beginning, "Kindled today in the house of man" (*samiddho adya manuṣo duroṇe*), the Hotṛ should perform the sacrifice. 18. Both [the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ] should either not breathe between [the verses] or they may breathe between them. 19. At the commands, he should conclude with the verses: "The guardian of wealth, the unerring one; may they lean toward the gods; performing [their work], the two wise ones; spreading [the sacrifice], bestowing glory—O heroes, [be] the givers of oblations and hymns. 20.

When the *paryagni* (circumambulation with fire) is being performed, [the Hotṛ] is directed to recite three verses beginning with "Agni is the Hotṛ for us. (21) When [the Adhvaryu] says, "Command [the Maitrāvaruṇa]," the Maitrāvaruṇa recites, "Agni has conquered," and the Hotṛ recites, "The divine slaughterers... (22) [The Hotṛ continues: "...with his mouth, let him join the Rakṣas!"—this is the *upāṃśu* (whispered).

"Do not make his *vaniṣṭhu* cry out," [saying this] loudly, he should perform the *paridhāna* (concluding) with "O Adhrigu! He mutters softly, "The Adhrigu and the sinless. Being prompted for the drops (*stoka*), he recites the six verses beginning with "Be pleased with that which is most extensive. Being prompted for the *svāhākṛti* offerings, the *praiṣa* (direction) is: "Let the Hotṛ sacrifice to Agni with 'Svāhā! The Hotṛ should sacrifice with the verse beginning "Just born. The two *ājyabhāga* portions have their respective *praiṣas*. For the omentum, the animal-cake, and the animal itself, there are three [verses] each, starting with "O Agni, lead us."

The verses preceding [the *yājyā*] are the *puronuvākyās*, and those following are the *yājyās*; thus has the rule for the six-verse hymns been stated. (30) Now, for the offering to Indra and Agni: "A pure hymn indeed," "He pierced Vṛtra," "Both of you, O Indra and Agni," "To the people," "O slayers of Vṛtra, with songs, the sage"—thus has the rule for the six-verse hymns been stated. (31) Having recited the first verse when directed for the omentum (*vapā*), the Hotṛ issues the direction: "May he sacrifice to Indra and Agni with the omentum of the goat."

The second *yājyā* (verse for the offering). 32. Having been prompted (*preṣita*) regarding the *puroḍāśa*, the Hotṛ recites the third [verse] as the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), and the prompt is: "Let the Hotṛ worship Indra and Agni with the *puroḍāśa*"; the fourth is the *yājyā*. 33. "O Agni, [partake of] the *iḍā*"—this is the explicit prompt for the invitatory verse; "Agni, the well-shining" is the *yājyā*. 34. The invitation to the *iḍā* (*iḍopahava*) is established. 35. Prompted for the *manotā*, he recites thirteen verses beginning with "For you, O Agni, are the first *manotā*. 36. Prompted for the oblation (*havis*), having recited the fifth [verse], the Hotṛ recites the prompt: "Let the Hotṛ worship Indra and Agni with the oblation of the goat."

The sixth [verse] is the *yājyā*. At its half-verse (*ardharca*), one should expect the *vasā-homa* offering. (37) "O Vanaspati, sent forth for the gods" is the *anuvākyā-praiṣa*. "O Vanaspati, with the cord... is the *yājyā*. (38) Sent forth for the *Sviṣṭakṛt*, "Delight the gods" is the *anuvākyā-praiṣa*.

‘agne yadadya’ is the *yājyā* (39). The invitation for the *iḍā* is established (40). When summoned for the *anuyāja*s, there are eleven *anuyāja*s beginning with ‘devaṃ barhiḥ’ (41). The Hotṛ should perform the sacrifice with the first and last [formulas] of these (42). Both [the Maitrāvaruṇa and the Hotṛ] should recite the final one after [the other] (43). Summoned for the *sūktavāka*, the Maitrāvaruṇa says ‘agnimadya... sūktā brūhi’; having paused, he silently places his staff upon the *atipraṇīta* fire (44). The remainder belongs to the Hotṛ (45).

In the *paśubandha* sacrifice, for the words denoting the deity, the sacrificer, and the animal, there are three forms each: singular, dual, and plural. Among these, the masculine forms precede the feminine forms. When feminine and masculine [words] are combined, the masculine form prevails. Thus, "medhapataye" may denote the sacrificer, the animal, or the deity: [masculine] *medhapataye*, *medhapatibhyām*, *medhapatibhyaḥ*; [feminine] *medhapatnyai*, *medhapatnībhyām*, *medhapatnībhyaḥ*; [neuter] *medhīm*, *medhyau*, *medhīḥ*.

"Forward for him [is] Agni; forward for these two [is] Agni; forward for these [is] Agni; forward for her [is] Agni; forward for these two [is] Agni; forward for these [is] Agni"—in this manner, from here upwards, one should transpose the formula as appropriate. (3) For the limbs beginning with the pair of animals, there are plural forms: "The two forelegs are praised; the two shoulders; the two elbows; the two fore-shanks; the two hips are unbroken; the two thighs are jointed; the two knee-caps are like the leaves of the *sreka* tree. (4) Those items which are non-declinable (*avyaya*) and occur more than once are repeated twice.

We shall explain them as follows: "In one way, in one way; formerly, formerly; within, within; twenty-six, twenty-six; from the middle, from the middle; from the side, from the side; from the hip, from the hip; from the *śitāma*, from the *śitāma*; from the elevation, from the elevation; having praised, as it were, having praised, as it were; having extolled, as it were, having extolled, as it were; fat, fat"—thus [in the case of] the oblation, the *praiṣa*, and the *sūktavāka*. [The forms are: *adat*, *adatām*, *adan*; *ghasat*, *ghastām*, *ghasan*; *aghasat*, *aghastām*, *aghasan*; *karat*, *karatām*...

They seized, they seized most firmly, they seized; they ate. 6. Mother, father, brother, uterine sibling, friend, fellow-herd, the navel-form, the offspring, sound, eye, ear, speech, mind, skin, fat, oblation, sacrificial grass, eagle, breast—these are not to be modified [in the ritual recitation]. 7.

The rule for animals is prescribed by means of the offering to Indra and Agni (Aindrāgna). 1. One should give a cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in rites where no fee is specifically enjoined; it should be either three years old or four years old. 2. In the sacrifices (*ijyā*), the deities are Upāṃśu, Prajāpati, Vāyu, the Devas, Sūrya, Aditi, Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu and Varuṇa, Savitṛ, the Herbs, Heaven and Earth, Bhūmi, and Yama. 3. The animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*) beginning with the "tawny one for Soma" (*saumyaṃ babhru*) and ending with those for Yama are performed for specific desires (*kāmya*).

For these [sacrifices], there are six verses beginning with "Soma gave the cow" and ending with "Yama," [to be recited] four times. 4. We shall explain the addition of ritual acts. 5. He who is born as the last among these [brothers] should, if desiring cattle, sacrifice an animal dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan. 6. The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood. 7. One desiring cattle should sacrifice a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati. 8. The Āghāra-libations, the Āprī-verses, and the Sāmidhenī-verses are explained in the section on the piling of the fire-altar (Āgniciti). 9. At the time for the sacrificial fee, the fee consists of gold, a silk garment, and an upper cloth. 10. At the time of the distribution, there are twelve portions of the Prāśitra.

Having cooked the *brahmaudana* (sacrificial porridge for the Brahmins), he should give it to the *madhyataḥkārins*; to them he gives twelve boons each. 11. One desiring offspring or desiring cattle should sacrifice a ewe (*vaśā*) to the Devas, or one to the Ādityas, for the sake of whatever desire he may have. 12. It should be a cow that has calved once and has a hump (*malhā*). 13. Having made the uneven level, one who has rivals should sacrifice a dwarf bull to Viṣṇu. 14. He who thinks himself seized by evil or darkness should sacrifice this bull to Indra; however, he should first sacrifice a goat to Agni. 15. [This applies to one seized] by the evil of hunger.

One who has been struck by darkness should sacrifice a cow released again after being set free to Savitṛ (Sāvitra). (16) One desiring offspring should sacrifice a barren cow to the plants (Oṣadhībhyaḥ). (17) One desiring food should sacrifice two cows that have both calved to Heaven and Earth (Dyāvāpṛthivīyau). (18) On the following day, one should sacrifice a calf to Vāyu. (19) A Kṣatriya desiring prosperity should sacrifice a cow that has recently calved to Indra (Aindrīm sūtavaśām). (20) One desiring splendor should sacrifice to Indra the bull that is the son of that cow which has recently calved. (21) One should sacrifice a barren cow that has recently calved to Sarasvatī for the sake of non-abandonment (Anusṛṣṭim). (22) [One should sacrifice] a cow to Heaven and Earth.

One should sacrifice a female animal that has been pregnant for two years and is now miscarrying. 23. Or one should sacrifice a Gomṛga to Vāyu. 24. One whose father and grandfather have not drunk Soma should sacrifice an Anusṛṣṭa to Indra-Agni. 25. Wherever a clod of earth is produced from the ground, one should settle there.

One should sacrifice a hermaphrodite animal dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan for one who sacrifices a eunuch. (26) Before the offering of the oblation, having pushed the embers toward the south-west from the limbs that are not to be cut off, he offers with the formula: "To Nirṛti, Svāhā! (27) A black ram, variegated with one white foot, dedicated to Varuṇa—one who is afflicted by illness should sacrifice it on an island where waters flow on all sides. (28) One entirely black [is used] for one practicing sorcery. (29) [The ritual] is established up to the tying of the animal. (30) He ties it with the formula: "I bind the victim. (31) This is the seventh section concerning barren cows. (32) The bull.

33. [The victim] belongs to Bṛhaspati. 34. He should abandon it by the flaying of the skin of a black-spotted cow. 35. It is the eighth among bulls. 36. A Kṣatriya desiring prosperity should sacrifice a bull to Indra Vajrin. 37. While the oblation is being offered, he should mentally meditate upon him whom he hates. 38. If one is born on the first Ekāṣṭakā, intending to release it, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, then release it; thereafter, month after month for a year, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Now...

If one should be born on another Ekāṣṭakā, he too should be released in exactly the same manner. (39) When the previously released [victim] reaches the sacrificial ground, then one should sacrifice to Indra Ābhimātighna; a horse that has not yet been harnessed is the sacrificial fee. (40) When the second released [victim] reaches the sacrificial ground, then one should sacrifice to Indra Vṛtratura.

A hundred cows that have not yet calved constitute the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 41. Having sacrificed with these two and having struck down his evil rival, one who practices sorcery should offer to Brāhmaṇaspati a reddish, hornless bull, the son of Citrā. 42. He who thinks himself seized by evil and darkness should offer this spotted beast to the Aśvins. 43. One desiring splendor should offer three bulls marked with white spots on their foreheads in the spring; in the rainy season, those with white humps; and in the autumn, those that are white like the anūkāśa grass.

The tenth [offering] is for Prajāpati, performed in the twelfth month; 44. With the verses beginning with "namo mahimne," he offers five oblations before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering in all [the rites]; 45. The animals have black necks, either according to different ritual procedures (nānātantra) or according to a single ritual procedure (samānatantra). 46.

That ritual procedure which belongs to the *iṣṭi*-type Sautrāmaṇī is [the same] for the Kaukilī; those are the desires [of the sacrifice]; and they also apply to one who has vomited Soma. Up to the *saṃdhāna* (joining) [rite], it is established. With the verse, "Pour around the pressed juice," he sprinkles with the milk of a single cow at the first dawn, and with the milk of two cows at the second. Thinking, "In three days the *surā* will be produced," he observes the fast for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). The fast-day (*upavasatha*) is established. On the following day, there is an *ṛṣabha* (bull) dedicated to Indra; its first *anuvāka* is the *aprī* hymn. The regular *praisha* calls are used. [The verse begins: "O you who fill the people... (*ā carṣaṇiprā*).

The [section] consisting of six verses is established; the day before the Soma feast (upavasatha) is the tenth; on the following day, having moved northward, there is the sacrifice of three animals, in which Surā is used. Up to the *ātipāvana* rite, it is established. With the formula "Vāyu is pure," he should perform that for one who has vomited Soma; with "Of Vāyu, the pure," he should perform that for one who has passed through the filter too much (*somātipavita*). He recites the invitatory response, "Brahman, Kṣatra... With the verse, "O friends, do you who possess barley...", the Adhvaryu takes the milk-cups (*payograha*). Having mixed the cup for the Aśvins with flour of *kuvala* fruits, flour of wheat, and the hair of a wolf, he sets it down.

With *karkandhu* groats, with *upavāka* groats, and with a tiger’s hair, [he offers] to Sarasvatī; with *badara* groats, with *tokma* groats, and with a lion’s hair, to Indra. (16) From the hole for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭa*) until the introductory ritual (*upākaraṇa*), the procedure is established. (17) A ewe for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra; a she-goat for Sarasvatī, Indra, and the Aśvins; a ram for Indra, Sarasvatī, and the Aśvins. (18) The procedure is established up to the sprinkling (*mārjana*). (19) With the verse, "She who [struck] the tiger, Viṣūcikā," he purifies the sacrificer with a hawk’s wing-feather. (20) He has been purified.

He worships the cups with the section beginning, "Soma is King" (ŚB 4.1.5). Having recited the response, "The one rich in *surā*," they offer at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ* calls. Having meditated upon the meditations, he consumes the milk-cups with the formula, "O Aśvins, [with] Yama... He consumes the *surā*-cups with the verse, "For various indeed are your [ways]... Having offered the *vājaprasavya* oblation of the *pratiduh* cow, he sprinkles him—who is seated on the throne to the north of the northern altar—with the remnants of the offerings while reciting, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... He pours it over his head and lets it flow down from the face.

The Pratiprasthātṛ offers the remainder in the southern fire with the formula, "Earth! Svāhā! (24). He touches the limbs according to their respective characteristics with the formulas, "May glory be my head; may fame be my face," and so forth (25). With the call, "O Brahman, [come] back," he descends [from the cart] (26). Prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers sixteen oblations with the formulas beginning, "With the broth, with the horns and hooves, with lead, the thread... (27). He pours out the perforated pot (śatātṛṇṇā) (28). He causes the sacrificer to recite, "May the fathers purify me" (29). The Adhvaryu offers an oblation with the verse, "Those who are equal, of one mind... (30).

"Those who are equal, of one mind, living among the living, my own"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ [recites]. (30) "Two paths there are"—the Adhvaryu [recites]. "This oblation"—the Pratiprasthātṛ [recites]. (31) He offers eleven potsherds for the animal-cakes (*paśupuroḍāśa*) to Indra Sutrāman, to Savitṛ, to Varuṇa, to Savitṛ, to Varuṇa, to Indra Sutrāman, to Varuṇa, to Indra Sutrāman, and to Savitṛ. (32) [The rite proceeds] successfully until the time for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). (33) There are thirty-three sacrificial fees; among them, a cow and a mare that has not yet had a foal. (34) *Yad devā...* [and so on].

With the verses beginning with *devaheḍanam*, he offers three oblations prior to the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings. With the verse *dhāmno dhāmnaḥ*, he offers into the waters at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). With the verse *yad grāme yad araṇye*, he offers the second oblation. Having bathed, they wash each other's backs with the formula *pavitram asi*. With the verse *samāvavartat pṛthivī*, he makes an offering on the *gārhapatya* fire using the *sruva* ladle. The second and third *āprī*-invocations are used; for the fourth, the portions of the omentum (*vapā*) are taken. The invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākyā*) are those belonging to the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblations.

Those which are *yājyās* are the *puronuvākyās*, and those which are *puronuvākyās* are the *yājyās* for the omentum (*vapā*), the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) offerings. (40) The fifth *anuyāja* [is performed]. (41) The fast-day (*upavasatha*) is completed. (42) On the following day, the *ṛṣabha-tagnya* hymn is the penultimate [offering] for Indra Vayodhas. (43) The regular *praiṣas* [are recited]. (44) The last six verses are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* [verses]. (45) For the *sarvapṛṣṭhā* [sacrifice], the penultimate [verse is used]. (46) The ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *mṛgāreṣṭi* is the last [part] of the *Aśvamedha*. (47)

1. Before the time for the offering on the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*), eleven posts are [prepared]: ten for the *chaityas* and one for the *pātnīvata* which lies near. 2. They are measured separately, following the sequence beginning with the selection (*joṣaṇa*). 3. The first one that sprouts is the *svaru*; the post standing nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*) is surrounded by the others; they should not be too thick nor too thin, but equal in size and complete with their roots. 4. Having measured out the eleven posts and divided them into three parts, he measures the altar (*vedi*) with the third parts. 5. The procedure up to the *āgnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice is established. 6. Having bound two ropes around the *agniṣṭha* post, he silently releases the *viṃśati*.

He winds [the cord] around [the sacrificial post]. 7. The fast-day (upavasatha) is completed. 8. On the following day, having taken the draught for the Aśvins and having measured the axle of the chariot northward from the Agniṣṭha post, he traces the hole for the sacrificial post with the wooden sword (sphya); the others [he traces] in reverse order. 9. The procedure beginning with the anointing [of the posts] is established up until the winding of the cord around each one. 10. Having placed the resting-block (upaśaya) facing east between the two southern sacrificial posts, the sacrificial posts are to be anointed; the sounding-hole (svaru) and the noose (raśana) are done silently. 11. If he should practice sorcery, [he says]: "This me, so-and-so, the son of such-and-such a lineage and of such-and-such a woman, O Indra..."

With the words, "I fix [the post] with the thunderbolt," he should fix it. 12. On ground sloping toward the north, he erects the eleven posts; or three of them are equal in height at the center. 13. For one desiring rain, the post nearest the fire (agniṣṭha) is the shortest, and the others are successively longer. For one practicing sorcery, the post nearest the fire is the longest, and the others are successively shorter.

The [altar] is level for one desiring a firm foundation. 14 Or he may erect it on the previous day. 15 On the following day, having girt the ropes around the posts starting from the *agniṣṭha* post, he dedicates the animals. 16 He binds a black-headed goat dedicated to Agni to the *agniṣṭha* post; a ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī to the northern post; a brown animal dedicated to Soma to the southern post; and the others in reverse order: one dedicated to Varuṇa in the southern half. 17 He should designate the wild animal as the one lying near. 18 One practicing sorcery should designate his enemy, saying, "This animal is for you. 19 [The ritual proceeds] successfully until the stepping forward. 20

He takes hold of each one individually. 21. From the front of the sacrificial post-hole, they lead the other animals—the principal ones first—to the *śāmitra* fire. 22. They station them one after another, or from the front toward the back. 23. After all have been placed, they throw the fire-sticks (*upāsana*) together with the ropes, the *darbha* blades, the omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), and the *svaru* chips into the fire. 24. This procedure is established up to the removal of the omenta. 25. From behind the *śāmitra* fire, they carry the other animals—the principal ones first—past the animal by way of the enclosure, taking the preceding embers for the *āhavanīya* fire. 26.

One should offer before the omenta with the formula, "Svāhā to the gods," and after [the omenta] with "Svāhā to the Viśve Devas. (27) This applies except for the Savanīya offerings, the heart-spikes, and the animal-cake offerings. (28) When the deities are the same and not separated [by other rites], the *manotā* verse is recited once; when they are separated, it is recited for each individual animal. (29) The offerings of the fat are performed separately. (30) With the remaining portions, one should sacrifice toward the various directions; they carry the *adhyūghnī* (the upper part of the tail) to the *hotṛ*, and the *vaniṣṭhu* (the rectum) to the *agnīdh*. (31) Having taken portions from all the entrails together, he performs the *upayaj* sacrifices. (32) He causes the wives [of the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the tails (*jāghanī*).

They perform the sacrifices (33). Before the *anūbandhyā* [cow] and before the *vamiśa*, they proceed with the *pātnīvata* offering (34). The altar is that of the New Moon sacrifice; the clarified butter is for the animal sacrifice (35). To the east of the *gārhapatya* fire, he erects the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) so that it reaches below the navel and is provided with a top-ring (*caṣāla*) (36). The pit for the post is not strewn with grass (37). He encircles it in the middle (38). He dedicates the animal to Tvaṣṭṛ (39). Having carried fire around it together with the cord, he releases it and completes the rite with clarified butter (40). Having taken portions of clarified butter as many times as there are portions to be cut from the animal, [he offers them] to Tvaṣṭṛ.

"Recite for the clarified butter," [he says]; "Prompt for the offering of the clarified butter to Tvaṣṭṛ," [the Adhvaryu] proceeds. (41) In place of the omentum-offering, there is the animal-cake-offering; the Sviṣṭakṛt-oblation is with the fat of the animal, and the Upayaj-offerings are with clarified butter. (42) It concludes with the *śamyu* formula. (43) He takes up all the offering-spoons together. (44) Having concluded the Anūbandhyā sacrifice, he points out the sacrificial posts. (45) The set of eleven animals (*ekādaśinī*) may be substituted by the animals of the seasonal sacrifices (*kratupaśu*). That set of eleven is fixed in the fire-altar-building rites (*agnicityā*); it is on a single post, while the set of eleven posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*) occurs in all the *stoma* sacrifices. (46)

In a collective recitation, one should follow the formulas addressed to the sacrificer and the lord of the sacrifice: "Anu vām" (after you two), "anu vaḥ" (after you all); "anumantau" (you two who consent), "anumantaḥ" (you all who consent); "āvahatam" (bring hither, you two), "āvahata" (bring hither, you all); "devāyadbhyām" (to the two who go to the gods), "devāyadbhyaḥ" (to those who go to the gods); "ye badhyamānau" (the two being bound), "ye badhyamānān" (those being bound); "svarvidau sthaḥ" (you two are finders of heaven), "svarvidaḥ stha" (you all are finders of heaven); "svaritam" (found of heaven), "svarita" (found of heaven); "lokavidau sthaḥ" (you two are finders of the world), "lokavidaḥ stha" (you all are finders of the world); "lokamitam" (found of the world), "lokamita" (found of the world); "nāthavidau sthaḥ" (you two are finders of refuge), "nāthavidaḥ stha" (you all are finders of refuge); "nāthamitam" (found of refuge), "nāthamita" (found of refuge).

You two are finders of the way; you are finders of the way. Go to the way; go to the way. You two die; you all die. You two are harmed; you all are harmed. You two have perished; you all have perished. [Drive] the animals from the two nooses; [drive] the animals from the nooses. Go to the Marut deity; go to the Marut deity. O you two preparers! O you preparers! There for you two; there for you all. Abundant for you two; abundant for you all. Heaven for you two; heaven for you all. Moving from where they move—1 the remainder is to be supplied. "Mother, father"—this has been explained. 2

With the *daśahotṛ* formula, "The ladle is full with drops," he offers the oblation with: "O Indra, go to [the sacrifice], svāhā! (1). With the *caturhotṛ* formula, "The earth is the *hotṛ*," [he performs the rite]. The cup is drawn with: "O Lord of Speech, by the power of speech... The second [cup] is offered with: "May Soma drink of Soma. (2). With the *pañcahotṛ* formula, "Agni is the *hotṛ*," [he performs the rite]. The cup is drawn with: "O Lord of Speech, with the fivefold food... The second [cup] is offered with: "May Soma drink of Soma. (3). With the *saptahotṛ* formula, "The great oblation is the *hotṛ*," [he performs the rite].

With the formula, "By this food, O Agni," he takes hold [of the gift]. (4) Having touched water, he receives it facing east; or, if it is something to be given, facing toward it. (5) A verse addressed to Savitṛ precedes all [gifts]. (6) With the formula, "For Yama thee," he receives a horse and whatever has a single hoof. (7) With the formula, "For Rudra thee," [he receives] that which has two hoofs. (8) With the formula, "For Agni thee," [he receives] gold, tin, lead, and iron. (9) With the formula, "The divine women cut thee; the skillful ones stretched the thoughts; they wove for Bṛhaspati thee," [he receives] a garment. (10) With the formula, "For Prajāpati thee," [he receives] an elephant, a man, rice, barley, land, and living beings.

And another [rite]: 11. With the verse "For thee that art lying on thy back," he offers [an oblation] consisting of non-living things. 12. To every [verse], he appends the formula beginning with "Who has given this, to whom has he given? and ending with "O Desire, this is thine. 13. He who is not propagated with offspring or cattle, having put on a new, unwashed garment, shall subsist for twelve nights on heated milk, observing the vow, and sleep on the ground. 14. On the thirteenth day, at sunrise, having recited the *Daśahotṛ* formula, he performs an oblation with the words, "Go to Indra, svāhā! 15. Having breathed out, he performs an oblation with the words, "Go to Indra, svāhā! 16. He should recite the *Caturhotṛ* formula; it has been explained.

17. Likewise, one desiring glory should perform the Pañcahotṛ and the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ [offerings]. 18. At the beginnings of the seasons, he should sacrifice for a year. 19. One who, having sacrificed with Soma, considers himself worse off, recites the Saptahotṛ formula mentally and sacrifices with the Graha-oblation, saying, "By the law, food. 20. Their observances: together with three others, he should not eat for a year; he should not consume the leavings of these three.

One should not bestow [this knowledge] upon three types of persons. He who, having studied it, does not oppose it, should go to the forest, seat a learned Brāhmaṇa, tie up a bunch of Darbha grass, and explain the Caturhotṛ formulas according to his own ritual procedure. Soma-pressings separated by rivers, mountains, or boundaries, which are simultaneous and involve completed sacrifices, [are to be performed]. Before the morning litany (prātaranuvāka) of that [sacrifice], when the fire has been kindled, he offers the Saṃbhāra-yajus oblations as in the Dīkṣaṇīyā offering. With these [formulas], one performs them before the Prāyaṇīya day in the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha).

25. One should offer oblations with these [verses]. 26. With these very [verses] one should touch the guest-offering (*ātithya*). 27. One should recite these very [verses] for the *agnīdh* priest. 28. One who desires offspring should offer oblations with these [verses] between [the offerings to] Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives, throughout the year.

"O lord of the earth, lord of the world, lord of the great being, I choose you as my Brahman," with these words he chooses a Brahman who is learned in the *śruti* and descended from a lineage of seers (*ārṣeya*). At the time of the altar-construction, on the new moon day, or on the following day at the full moon, [he says]: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O divine Savitṛ, they choose you, Bṛhaspati, as the Brahman; him I announce to the mind. Mind to speech; speech to the Gāyatrī; Gāyatrī to the Triṣṭubh; Triṣṭubh to the Jagatī; Jagatī to the Anuṣṭubh; Anuṣṭubh to the Paṅkti; Paṅkti to Prajāpati."

"Prajāpati [chose] Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati, the Brahman of the gods, has chosen me, the Brahman of men. O Bṛhaspati, protect the sacrifice! I am the lord of the earth, I am the lord of the world, I am the lord of the great Being. You have spoken for my splendor, you have spoken for my luster, you have spoken for my hymn of praise, you have spoken for my glory, you have spoken for my food, you have spoken for my progeny, you have spoken for my firm foundation"—thus he murmurs when chosen. He follows along by the *tīrtha* (the path), passes behind the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) to the south, and, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), remains vigilant on the southern side.

He should address the seat with the mantra: "Sit down, O son of a remarried woman! Rise up, O son of a remarried woman! Sit on the seat of another—he who is more foolish than we. (Sūtra 4) Having cut off a blade of grass from both sides of the seat, he throws it away toward the south-west with his left hand, saying: "Expelled is Parāvasu along with evil! (Sūtra 5) Then he places his right foot upon the seat with the mantra: "Here I sit on the seat of Arvāgvasu," and his left foot within that space. (Sūtra 6) "Impelled by the divine Savitṛ, I announce this to Agni; I announce this to Vāyu. (Sūtra 7)

Saying "To the Sun," he sits down (7). He mutters: "May the Sun protect the sacrifice from heaven; may Vāyu protect the lord of the sacrifice from the intermediate space; may Agni protect me, the human" (8). While the Brahman priest is attending or while another is performing the ritual, whichever among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is nearest should sit there; or else, having placed a handful of *darbha* grass or a vessel of water on the Brahman’s seat, the seat shall not be empty—thus it should be (9). When [the Adhvaryu] says, "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters," [the Brahman replies]: "Lead forward the sacrifice; cause the gods to prosper upon the back of the firmament, in heaven."
May he be a sacrificer in the world. Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer. Impelled by Bṛhaspati...

"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, Oṃ, Praṇaya"—with these words he gives permission. (10) Thus permitted, he acts everywhere according to the traditional injunctions. (11) Even without being addressed, he gives permission to one who is about to sprinkle the oblation, to one who is about to perform the second tracing of the altar, and to one who is about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses. (12) And when addressed during the *pravara* invocation, he gives permission for the other applications of mantras. (13) He restrains his speech; if he releases his speech at an improper time, having uttered the formula to Viṣṇu (*vaiṣṇavī*), he should restrain it again. (14) "Go along the path of Truth; I gaze upon you with the eye of Mitra."

He gazes at the *prāśitra* as it is being brought forward (15). Having received it with the *sāvitra* formula, he places it on the sacrificial grass to the south, saying: "I set thee on the back of the earth" (16). He looks down upon it, saying: "With the eye of the fair-winged Garuḍa, I gaze upon thee" (17). Taking it with his thumb and ring finger, he eats it without letting his teeth touch it, saying: "O Agni, I eat thee with my mouth; with the belly of a Brāhmaṇa; they placed thee in the belly of Indra through the sacred word (*brahman*) of Bṛhaspati" (18). He rinses his mouth, saying: "I sprinkle thee with truth."

19. "Speech in my mouth, breath in my nostrils, sight in my eyes, hearing in my ears, strength in my arms, vigor in my thighs, and stability in my feet"—with these words, he touches his limbs according to their respective characteristics. 20. Having touched water, he begins at the region of the navel and mutters: "Thou art the belly of Viṣṇu," and [he continues with] "May all my limbs be unharmed; may my body be one with my body" over his various members. 21. He places the portion for the Brahman priest upon the Prāśitra-haraṇa vessel. 22. He eats it either before the *śamyu* formula or after the *samiṣṭayajus*. 23. By this same procedure, the portions for the Brahman are established for the *iṣṭi*, animal sacrifice, and Soma sacrifices.

The office of the Brahman priest has been explained. (24) Having been chosen at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), he dwells there after having consumed the *brāhmaudana* rice-mess. (25) On the following day, the procedure beginning with the gathering of materials (*saṃbhāra*) is performed for the Adhvaryu. (26) One who has rivals or enemies should turn a chariot wheel three times around the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*). (27) During the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings, while the altars are being prepared, one should scratch along the front of the Āhavanīya fire with the wooden sword (*sphya*) as far as the southern corner-post and the *pṛṣṭhyā*-line peg. (28) At the Soma sacrifice, [one should do so] with the *Apratiratha* hymn. (29) At the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), [one should do so] by way of the *tīrtha*.

Having emerged [from the water], he should go to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). 30. If someone should address him with the words "Offer the full ladle," he should grant permission. 31. At the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), having gone behind the sacrificial ground (vihāra) and passed to the south, and after the omentum (vapā) has been offered, he should perform the purification at the Cātvāla pit. 32. The choosing of officiating priests (varaṇa) according to the New and Full Moon sacrifices should be omitted in the Soma sacrifice. 33.

1. He attends to the rites beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering. 2. Once the Soma has been purchased, he approaches together [with the sacrificer] toward the east. 3. At the conclusion of the *gārhapatya* rite, he attends to the *gharma*. 4. Having risen, he stands in attendance. 5. While the vessels are being brought forward, he circumambulates. 6. Having performed the *prāṇabhakṣa* (inhaling the essence), he consumes it while not yet initiated. 7. He follows the *gharma* vessels along the *pṛṣṭhyā* line. 8. He follows Agni and Soma as they are being led forward. 9. If one should carry away the King (Soma), having handed him over to the Adhvaryu at the end of the *havirdhāna* shed, he proceeds north of the *āgnīdhrīya*, west of the *sadas*, and south of the *mārjālīya* and the *havirdhāna* shed.

Having gone to the south of the *ājya* vessels, he sits down facing north; this is the path of movement (9). On the following day, he attends to the *ājya* oblations as they are being taken up (10). As they are being lifted up, he walks around (11). He attends to the cups (*graha*) as they are being drawn (12). Having offered the two *vaipruṣa* oblations, they proceed for the *pavamāna* chant (13). When it is said, "O Brahman, we shall chant the *stotra*; O Praśāstṛ, give the command," [the Brahman says]: "O Stotṛ, increase the glory; do thou increase the deities; may the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament, in the heavenly world."

"Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer. "With the ray, for the sake of the dwelling, quicken the dwelling. "Bṛhaspati is impelled. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Om! Praise!"—with these words he gives permission. 14. These thirty-three *stomabhāgas* beginning with this one, and thirty-three *stotras*, are in the *aptoryāman*.

He authorizes each of them one by one. (15) When the omentum has been offered, having performed the purification at the *cātvāla* pit, having worshipped the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, and having entered the *sadas* by the western door, he sits down to the south of the *audumbarī* post facing north; this is the path of movement. (16) To the south of the *hotrīya* hearth is the path for the consumption of the portions from the *dhiṣṇyas*. (17) When the paths of movement have been separated at the ends of the pressings, they move out. (18) Having exited by the eastern door, he consumes the parched grains and the Soma. (19) The *avabhṛtha* and the *udavasānīyā* [concluding] offerings follow. (20)

In the piling of the fire-altar beginning with the Sāvitra [layer], one does not follow the *krama* formulas (21). While the fire-altar is being piled, he sits to the south of the right wing outside the sacrificial ground, facing the Nairṛta bricks (23). There, at the *prettati*, he restrains his speech (24). When the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, he releases his speech; he releases his speech (25). Thus ends the second chapter in the *Iṣṭikalpa*.
Thus the *Iṣṭikalpa* in the *Mānava-śrautasūtra* is completed.

One who is about to pile the fire-altar should collect the *ukhā* (fire-pan) on the full moon day, the new moon day, or on the *ekāṣṭakā*. 1. At the conclusion of the archetypal rites, excluding the *ṣoḍaśin*, one should pile the fire on the *uttaravedi*. 2. In the *sattras* and *ahīnas*, one should pile the *uttaravedi* either according to the *sāvitra* or the *nāciketa* rite, or without a fire-altar. 3. Having silently wiped the *juhū* ladle, he wipes the *sruva* spoon. 4. Having filled the *juhū* with eight scoops [of ghee], he offers an oblation while reciting the eight verses beginning with "yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ. 5. If he should desire the sacrifice...

Thinking, "May I dedicate [this] through the glory of the sacrifice," he should perform this *yajus* with the formula, "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice. With the verse, "Fulfill the hymn with the *ṛc*," he offers an oblation of four portions of clarified butter. To the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the spade (*abhri*)—made of bamboo, variegated, hollow, and sharp at both ends, or sharp at one end only. With the formula, "Run forward, O prize-winning steed," he consecrates the horse in front of the *āhavanīya* fire; and [he recites], "Yoke the donkey."

9. With the verse, "At every encounter, the most powerful," they lead the horse in front as they set out. 10. He mutters, "Bring the fire of the soil, like Aṅgiras. 11. Having arrived with the words, "We approach the fire of the soil, like Aṅgiras," he addresses a man whose vigor he intends to extract. 12. From where the sun rises, there he should say, while striking away the mound of an anthill, "We shall bring the fire of the soil, like Aṅgiras. 13. [He recites: "Agni has reached the forefront of the dawns."

14. They set out from the anthill. 15. Having arrived at the place called Vājyadhvāna, he mutters [the prescribed formula]. 16. With the two verses, "Stepping forward, O steed" and "Thine is the back, O steed," he causes the horse to step upon [the mound]. 17. While it is being stepped upon, the sacrificer should say of whomsoever he may hate, "Tread upon so-and-so! 18. He makes it step upward with the word, "Step up! 19. He consecrates the horse with the mantra, "It has stepped up. 20. With the two verses, "I sprinkle thee from all sides" and "Facing toward me," he offers oblations in the footprint of the horse. 21. "O Agni, lord of the prize, by the days... [he continues].

With the verse, "O Agni, we [take] thee around as a fortress," he traces the outline with each verse individually. (21) He takes up the spade with four verses ending in the names of the meters, addressed to Savitṛ. (22) With the remainder of the section beginning, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he digs. (23) With the formula, "Thou art the back of the waters," he wraps a lotus leaf [around the hole]. (24) With the formulas, "Ye two are a shelter" and "May ye dwell together," he spreads a black antelope skin and a lotus leaf to the north of the pit; the antelope skin is underneath, with its neck to the east and the hair side up, and the lotus leaf is on top, reaching to the navel.

The lotus leaf is at the eastern door (25). Upon it, he scatters the loose soil with the Yajus formula, "Thou art the soil-bringer, the supporter of all," and with three Ṛg-verses: "O Agni, from the lotus," "Dadhyañc the seer [knew] thee," and "Pāthya Vṛṣan [knew] thee. For a Brāhmaṇa, he uses Gāyatrīs; for a Rājanya, the subsequent Triṣṭubhs; for a Vaiśya, the final Jagatīs (26). If he should desire of someone, "May he be struck down," he should pile the fire-altar for him using both Gāyatrīs and Triṣṭubhs; having taken up [the earth] with a Gāyatrī, he should [pile it] with a Triṣṭubh.

27. He scatters [the earth] with the formula: "This is thy seasonal womb. 28. He touches what has been scattered with the formula: "O divine waters, may they unite with thee. 29. He pours water over the opening with the formula: "O divine waters, may they unite with thee. 30. He consecrates the loose soil (purīṣa) with the formula: "Well-born, with light... 31. He binds it with a cord made of muñja grass or of arka wood with the formula: "A garment of all forms for thee, O Agni. 32. Having taken it up with the formulas: "Arise, O performer of good sacrifice" and "Upright for us," he stands up. 33. He mutters: "Once born, thou art the embryo of heaven and earth. [He addresses] the donkey with the formula: "Be firm, O strong-limbed one."

He places [the earth]; with the words, "Be auspicious to the creatures," he consecrates the loose soil (purīṣa). The horses lead the way as they return. He consecrates the horse with the verse, "May the steed come forward"; the donkey with the verse, "Braying loudly, the lord of the assembly"; and the loose soil with the verse, "O Agni, come hither for the feast. With the formula, "The Truth, the Reality; the Truth, the Reality," he should consecrate the man with whom he might come into contact. Having prepared a mound (khara) to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he encloses it. Upon that, having spread darbha grass, [he places] the plants.
With the two verses beginning "pratigṛbhṇīta," he places [the vessels] on the mound; he gives the horse and the donkey to the Adhvaryu.

With the two verses beginning "vi pājaseti," he unties [the cord]. With the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he pours water from vessels made of *parṇa* bark and *valkala*. With the two verses beginning "mitraḥ saṃ sṛjya," he mixes it with five substances: goat’s hair, three types of powder from a black antelope skin, gravel, embers of bamboo, potsherds from a deserted site, and sand. Having consecrated the mixed substance with the three verses beginning "saṃsṛṣṭāṃ vasubhiḥ," he hands it to his wife with the formula, "makhasya śiro 'si."

He touches the lump of clay. (5) The wife prepares the fire-pan (*ukhā*), making it three-layered and square. (6) Having spread it out to the prescribed measurement, he raises its sides and places the layers in the middle. (7) While it is being made, the sacrificer consecrates it with the formulas: "May the Vasus fashion thee" for the first layer; "May the Rudras fashion thee" for the second; "May the Ādityas fashion thee" for the third; and while it is being smeared, "May the Viśve Devas, common to all men, fashion thee," using the *dhruvā* and other verses. (8) The wife [participates].

Two finger-breadths below the door, he makes a *rāsnā* (girdle) with the formula, "Aditi is thy girdle" (9). He makes the door above the *rāsnā* with the formula, "Aditi is thy opening" (10). In the cardinal directions, he makes two, four, or eight breasts (11). Having smeared it with a stalk of sugarcane and having fashioned it with the formula, "Having made this earth as a fire-pan" (12), he fixes it. For the remainder, he makes an *aṣāḍhā* brick marked with three lines (13). With the formulas beginning, "May the Vasus fumigate thee" (14), he fumigates the place of the hearth with horse-dung from the *gārhapatya* fire. In front... (15).

With the formula, "O Aditi, goddess, thee," he digs out the *āpākā* from the *gārhapatya* fire-place. (15) Having placed the *ukhā* with the formula, "Thee, the wives of the gods," he places the *aṣāḍhā* brick upon it. (16) Having enclosed it with *kupina* mats and having lifted it toward the cooking place, he cooks it from the *gārhapatya* fire with the formulas beginning with, "Thee, the goddess Dhiṣaṇā. (17) With the formula, "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people," he attends to it once it has been kindled. (18) With the formula, "May the god Savitṛ lift thee up," he lifts up the cooked vessel. (19) Having taken it up with the formula, "Arise, become great," he stands up. (20) Having carried it around in front of the *āhavanīya* fire, [he places it] on the mound (*khara*).

Having placed it down with the formula, "O Mitra, I entrust this cauldron to you," he hands it over to Mitra. 21 With the four formulas beginning with, "May the Vasus anoint you with the milk of a she-goat that has not yet calved," he anoints it. 22 Having cut off the head of a Vaiśya or a kinsman of a Rājanya who has been struck by lightning or killed by an arrow, he carries it away. 23 [With the formula: "This is the one belonging to him whose head this is; through this, may you be possessed of a head."

Even when cutting thus, he places a termite-mound split in seven ways and seven beans [therein]. (24) "May this be for our enjoyment and for our pleasure," with these words he places the head upon his hand. (25) "Sing of Yama, whose fame is widespread, who is the lord of this earthly world, the king who is not to be obstructed. Sing of Yama, whose fame is widespread, the king who is not to be obstructed; by whom the waters, the rivers, and the desert wastes were made firm, and by whom the sky and the earth were established.

"King Yama stands over the gift of horses that have golden manes, excellent endurance, golden eyes, and iron hooves—horses for one who has no horses. Day after day, leading away cattle, horses, men, and livestock, the son of Vivasvat (Vaivasvata) is not satiated, like a drunken man with liquor. Singing these verses of Yama while holding his head, he smears it with clay. 26

He sacrifices five castrated animals: a goat to Prajāpati, a horse to the Agnis, a stallion to the Kāmas, a bull, and a ram. 1. The ritual is established up to the *sāmidhenī* verses. 2. Without repeating himself, he recites twenty-four *sāmidhenī* verses. 3. "Forward for you, O strengths, reaching heaven"—these are eleven verses. 4. "May the years, O Agni, and the seasons increase thee"—these are ten verses, omitting the *jyotiṣmatī*. 5. The final verse belongs to the *āprī* hymns. 6. "Thou hast approached us"—these are three verses containing the word *apsu*. 7. He concludes with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse. 8. The ritual is established up to the *āghāra* libation. 9.

With the formula "Hiraṇyagarbha," he pours the *srauca* libation of clarified butter. (10) The procedure is established up to the carrying of fire around the victim (*paryagnikaraṇa*). (11) Having placed the animal dedicated to Prajāpati to the north, he carries fire around its head. (12) Having released the animals for which the fire has been carried around, they conclude the rite with the one dedicated to Prajāpati, [using] the *upāṃśu* deity-formula. (13) For that [animal], there is a sacrificial cake on twelve potsherds (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for Agni Vaiśvānara. (14) Having cut off the heads of the released animals, he should set them aside. (15) He should cast the bodies and the tongues into a lake.

Since he intends to make bricks, he should then immolate these five animals: a white goat with testicles and castrated, for Vāyu Niyutvat. Its *āprī* verses and *sāmidhenī* verses are those [of the standard sacrifice]. It has the same *āghāra* libation. For it, there is an animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for Prajāpati on twelve potsherds. Having placed the tongue among the portions to be cut off, one should set aside the head of the animal. The animal sacrifice is thus completed. He offers the initiation oblation (*dīkṣaṇīyā*): a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap of ghee for the Ādityas, and [a cake] for Agni Vaiśvānara.

The offering on twelve potsherds is established for those who have studied the Yajurveda. Having offered five oblations with the verses beginning "For intention, for application," he offers six oblations with the formula "To Kūta Agni, to Prayuj, svāhā. He performs the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti) with the verse "All [the works] of the god, the leader... The procedure is established up to the making of the fist. He places the fire-pan (ukhā) upon abundant embers in the Āhavanīya fire.

With the two verses, "Do not be afraid, do not be harmed," he lays down [the bricks]. (27) He places *muñja* grass upon the heated [fire-pan], or something else that ignites quickly. (28) He generates the fire by means of heating. (29) He should release the *āhavanīya* fire. (30) He does not engage it in worldly desires. (31) Having brought it, he should place it [on the pan]: either by churning for one who has lost his fortune (*gataśrī*), from the hearth for one desiring food, or from a lightning-strike for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). For one whom he should desire, "May his kingdom be subject to the wild dog (*prasena*)," he should bring it burning on a tree above, having taken it from a forest fire. (32)

Having kindled the fire in the *ukhā* pan, he places fuel-sticks upon it with the verses: "O swift one, whose libation is clarified butter," [he places] a piece of *krumuka* wood smeared with ghee; with "From the highest ridge," an *audumbara* stick; with "From the furthest distance," a *vaikaṅkata* stick; with "Whatever, O Agni, thou hast done," a stick of *śamī* wood that has not been cut with an axe; with the five verses beginning "That which the upajihvikā eats," an *audumbara* stick that has not been cut with an axe, or a *tailvaka* stick, for one practicing sorcery; and with "With thy two fangs, O Agni, the thieves," an *aśvattha* stick; and with "He who acts with hostility toward us."

One practicing sorcery should place a fuel-stick made of *śamī* wood that has been cut with an axe, or one of *tailvaka* wood; while doing so, he should meditate in his mind upon the person whom the sacrificer hates. With the two verses beginning "May I raise up their arms," he places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood and causes the sacrificer to recite them. He places a fuel-stick with the verse, "Brahman and Kṣatra are united."

He fastens on a golden ornament with a hundred spikes, [reciting] "The golden ornament, shining... (RV 1.35.2). 1. He wears it above the spikes. 2. He places a throne-seat. 3. Its legs are a span in length. 4. The rest is the same. 5. He places a sling made of muñja grass—either six-stranded or twelve-stranded—upon the throne-seat. 6. Having lifted the fire-pan with the verse "Night and Dawn... (RV 1.96.5), he deposits it in the sling. 7. With the verse "All forms... (RV 1.35.2), he fastens the loop of the sling; with "Night and Dawn... (RV 1.96.5), he fastens the black antelope skin. 8. "Thou art a well-winged bird... (RV 10.114.4).

9. Over the *strivṛt* [bundle] on the *garutman* [brick], he mutters the *śiras* formula: "Thou art the fair-winged Garutman; go to heaven, fly to the light! Having lifted up the *ukhya* fire and holding it over his navel, he strides four steps forward toward the east with the verses beginning, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu. 10. He mutters the *krandavatī* verse: "Agni has cried out. 11. With the four *punarvatī* verses beginning, "O Agni, thou who turnest back," he turns around clockwise. 12. Having turned back with the verse, "I have brought thee hither," he mutters it. 13. [He mutters: "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond... (RV VII.89.3).

He releases the sling-loop. (14) He consecrates the *ukhya* fire with the verse, "O Agni, great... (15). With the verse, "Ham! He is the dweller in purity... (RV 4.40.5), he places it on the *savatī* seat. (16) With the three verses containing the word "sit" (*sīda*), beginning with "Sit down in the lap of this mother... (RV 3.29.10–12), he worships the *ukhya* fire. (17) He worships it with the *Vātsapra* hymn, beginning with "From the sky... (RV 10.45). (18) The ritual procedure pertaining to the initiation (*daikṣa*) is established from the making of the fist onwards. (19) When he is about to take the vow, he kindles the *ukhya* fire with the verse, "By which the gods [attained] light... (RV 10.68.11).

He places a fuel-stick on the fire, the first one anointed with ghee, with the *gāyatrī* verse, "Worship Agni with the fuel-stick" (*samidhāgnim duvasyata*), for a Brāhmaṇa; with the *triṣṭubh* verse, "Forward, forward this Agni" (*pra prāyam agniḥ*), for a Rājanya; and with two *gāyatrī* verses for a Vaiśya. With the verse, "O Lord of Food, give us food" (*annapate 'nnasya no dehi*), he places one anointed with ghee. He places a fuel-stick with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I place you for Agni Vaiśvānara," saying "I place you at night" in the evening, and "I place you in the morning" in the morning. Thus [ends section 20–22].

When the sun has risen, during the day: (23) from the *pratimocana* onwards until the successful completion of the attendance (*upasthāna*), [he performs the rites] with the *sannavatī* verses; (24) at night, he attends [the fires] with the *vātsapra*. (25) Having been consecrated, he should seek his maintenance. (26) When about to set out, he takes up the *ukhya* fire with the verse, "O Viśve Devas, lift you up. (27) With the verse, "Ham! He is the dweller in purity," and with the *ham-savati* verses, he places [the fire] into the cart with the *sannavatī* verses.

Having poured [the ashes] together into two vessels, he places them aside. (28) "O Agni, come forth full of light," with these words he sets out. (29) If he should sneeze, he should consecrate it with the verse containing the word *krandat*. (30) If the fire-pan (*ukhā*) becomes full, he should place ashes for the sake of joining the bricks; for one desiring cattle, he should place soil (*purīṣa*). (31) One who travels as a wandering ascetic (*yāyāvara*) proceeds with the sacrificial fires (*sahavihāra*). (32) With the three verses beginning, "O divine waters, receive [this]," he scatters the ashes into the water. (33) With the two verses beginning, "Having settled in the ashes," he pours back handfuls of ashes. (34) With the two verses beginning with *punarvatī*.

Having returned and placed [the fires] in their respective places, he worships them with the two *bodhadvatī* verses. (35) One should not fashion bricks without having first performed the sacrifice to Prajāpati. (36) The duration of the consecration (*dīkṣā*) is prescribed as three nights, beginning from the formula "having carried [the fire] for three nights," and so forth. (37) While consecrated, he does not worship the *ukhya* fire with the *punarvatī* verses. (38) The earthen bricks are square, with straight lines, or marked with three lines; some are turned to the right and others to the left; they are free from broken parts or black spots; and three bricks for Nirṛti are black, baked with husks, and prepared by friction-fire (*nirmantha*).
Or, after the consecrations, he may combine the Kramas and Vātsapra following the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.

With the words, "Go away, depart," he chooses the site for the *śālāmukhīya* fire. Having measured a fathom (*vyāma*) there, he digs out either a circle or a square, sprinkles it with water, and encloses it twenty-one times clockwise with pebbles, saying, "You are piled; you are piled around. He pours sand over it, saying, "Thou art the ash of Agni; thou art the soil of Agni," and salt-earth, saying, "Thou art a means of recognition. When about to pile the fire, either the sacrificer or [the priest] mutters, "I take unto myself that Agni who is ours, O fathers. Having spread out the salt-earth and sand, he says, "This is that Agni."

In the middle of the fire-altar, he lays down four bricks facing east and joined together: two with the formula "O Agni, [bring] the *iḍā*," joined together in the front; and two with the formulas "Thou art the layer" and "Thou art the surrounding layer," joined together in the back. In all cases, he appends the phrase "with that deity" at the end of the mantras used for laying the bricks. With the verse "Fill the space, fill the gap," he completes the layer with thirteen bricks.

The phrase "tā asya sūdadohasaḥ" is to be supplied [to each verse]. (6) At each layer he throws down a piece of gold. (7) With the verse "pṛṣṭo divi," he covers the layer with loose earth from the location of the *cātvāla* pit. (8) In this manner, he piles five layers for the first Gārhapatya fire-altar: three for the second, and one for the third. (9) With the four verses beginning "saṃcite," "samitam," and "saṃkalpethām," he pours out the material for the *ukhya* fire. (10) With the verse "mātevaputram," he releases the *ukhā* pot. (11) He must not look at it while it is empty. (12) Having filled it with sand...

He should place [the vessel] with curds, ghee, or honey (13). With the verse, "That which is on the further shore of this space," he takes up the sling (14). They go toward the south-western intermediate direction (15). On a naturally formed saline mound, he lays down the bricks dedicated to Nirṛti with the three verses beginning, "Seeking him who presses not the Soma, who sacrifices not" (16). He does not perform the *tayādevata* rite (17). With the verse, "The noose which the goddess Nirṛti has bound for thee," he casts a net over the bricks (18). Having thrown the cord of the gold plate into the fire, he makes [the sacrificer] step upon the stool (19). "That which is on the further shore of this space... [etc. (20).

Thus, sprinkling water from the water-pot three times while moving counter-clockwise around the bricks, he goes around them. Having set the pot down, he goes back around three times without sprinkling. Saying, "Homage for prosperity," he turns back. "May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid; may they be for our drinking. May they flow toward us with peace and well-being. "Auspicious to us be the waters of the desert, auspicious to us be those of the marshlands. Auspicious to us be the waters of the ocean, and auspicious to us be those of the wells. "Auspicious to us be Mitra, auspicious Varuṇa, and may Aryaman be auspicious to us."

"May Indra and Agni be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us"—with these three verses, they cleanse themselves outside the cow-pen (22). They return without looking back (23). With the verse, "The dweller, the gatherer of riches," he worships the Āhavanīya fire of Indra (24). From the Prāyaṇīya offering onwards, the procedure is established up to the Upasad rites (25). There are six Upasad days, accompanied by the Pravargya ceremony (26). One should pile the fire-altar after each Upasad (27). Having performed the morning rite on the first Upasad day, he goes toward the sacrificial post (28) along the front, towards the east.

Having fixed the *pṛṣṭhyā*-peg at a distance of three steps or in an unlimited space, he prepares the altar (*vedi*) starting from the taking up of the measuring-line, just as in the Soma sacrifice (29). With the sacrificer standing with uplifted arms, having measured out a bamboo staff, he establishes the fire-altar (*agni*) at the site of the *uttaravedi* over a span of seven men (30). Its body (*ātman*) is four men; the wings and tail are each one man in measure (31). He adds an *aratni* to the two wings and a *prādeśa* to the tail (32). Having fashioned the head to be one-quarter of a man, in the middle of that which has been thus prepared—

Having placed gold upon a clump of *darbha* grass, he offers an oblation over it with the verse: "May the year be in harmony with the months" (RV 1.164.12). 33. With the formula, "May Prajāpati seat thee on the back of the earth; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm," he touches the earth in the middle of the prepared site. 34. To the south of the wing, with the formulas "The impelling [of the plough]" and "The Antaryāma [cup]," he fastens the yoke-pins to the yoke and the traces. 35. With the three verses beginning, "May Pūṣan yoke [the team]," and "May Savitṛ yoke [the team]," he consecrates the plough as it is being yoked. 36. He ploughs with the team of six oxen yoked together.

Or with twelve [verses] joined together (37). He recites the mantra over the raised [plow]: "The winner of cattle, the winner of horses" (RV 4.57.8). Over the two oxen, he recites: "Of the camel-like, of the *pīlu*-like" (RV 10.102.9) (38). With the verse "The plow, tipped with iron" (RV 4.57.8), he addresses the five [oxen]; with "O Indra, that which is moved by the hand" (RV 4.57.9), the sixth.

With each of these [oxen], he ploughs two furrows (sītā). Starting from the southern half of the wing, he makes a furrow through the middle; turning clockwise from the end of the northern wing, he ploughs southward first, then eastward, and finally northward. In this manner, he ploughs three furrows each time: starting from the southern hip, over the northern shoulder, and over the tail; then starting from the northern hip, over the southern shoulder. With the formula, "Be unyoked, O inviolable ones, you who go to the gods," he unyokes them facing south-east. He gives those oxen and the plough to the Adhvaryu priest.

Having mixed together wild and cultivated plants with clarified butter, he scatters the entire fire with fourteen verses beginning, "The plants that are first-born" (RV 10.97). 1. If he cannot find these, he should scatter barley grains moistened with honey in their place. 2. With the remainder of the mixture, he should worship the scattered fire. 3. From the various directions, he brings clods of earth from outside the sacrificial altar and piles them together in the middle of the fire with four verses beginning, "May it not harm us, O progenitor" (RV 10.97.20–23). 4. If he should desire of a certain people, "May they become hungry," he should bring clods of earth from that direction with the verse, "I take from here food and strength" (RV 10.97.24). 5.

"May you milk desire from desire," with these words he touches each furrow (sītā). (6) He constructs the *cātvāla* pit with a pair of oxen. (7) One should construct the *uttaravedi* altar measuring ten paces, ending with the sprinkling of water in the center of the fire-altar. (8) With the formulas, "You are piled; you are piled around," he encloses the fire-altar clockwise with pebbles. (9) With the six verses beginning, "O Agni, yours is glory and vigor," he pours down sand. (10) With the two verses addressed to Soma, "Swell up" and "May your milk [gather]," he arranges the head, wings, and tail; for the worlds are the expansions of the head, wings, and tail.

In the middle, [he places] the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick; 11. He steps forward toward the fire-altar from the north, following the tail-end; 12. In front of the *Śālāmukhīya* fire, upon a red bull’s hide with the neck pointing eastward and the hair side up, he arranges the first bricks of the layers; 13. He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verses for the fire-altars being led forward, saying "For the fire-altars" in a low voice, and "Recite for those being led forward" loudly; 14. When [the verse] has been recited once, they carry away the hide and lead the horse in front; 15. He places the hide behind the buttocks; 16. They mount the altar at the proper time.

With the words "All hostile armies... he causes the horse to step upon the place of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with its right foot; without turning it back, he makes it walk around. Having made the horse turn back, he fills twelve water-pots (*kumbha*) with water and places them upon the middle furrows with the twelve verses beginning with "Together they move..."—two pots at each of the [four] locations and four in the middle. With the verse "O Waters, you indeed... he mutters while looking at three water-pots. He prepares a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of wild rice in milk.
With the formula, "Boiled in heaven, take thy place," he places [the brick] to the south-east of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* within the range of sight. 20.

Upon the footprint, he places a lotus-leaf with its opening facing west and its navel below, with the formula, "Thou art the womb of heat. 1. Upon the lotus-leaf, he places a gold plate with its loop facing west and its rim above, with the formula, "The Brahman was born first. 2. Upon the gold plate, he places a golden man with his head toward the east and lying supine, with the two verses beginning, "Hiraṇyagarbha."

He touches it with the verse, "The swift one has leaped forth. He worships with the three names of the serpents beginning with, "Homage be to the serpents. He sprinkles [the ghee] with the five verses beginning with, "Display your power," reaching as far as the navel. He places a ladle made of *kārṣmarya* wood, full of clarified butter, to the south with the formula: "This Agni, with his thousandfold splendor, I set you down by the splendor of Agni. He places a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, full of curds, to the north with the formula: "Of the earth, of the sacrifice, of Indra—with his vigor I set you down."

Having caused a horse to smell a naturally perforated pebble (*svayamātṛṇṇā-śarkarā*), he consecrates it with the mantra: "Bhūḥ! (7). He makes it possessed of a sacrificial formula (*yajus*) with the words: "Thou art firm, a support" (8). He lays it down in turn with the formula: "May Prajāpati seat thee. In the [central] man [of the altar], he places the naturally perforated stone together with a Brāhmaṇa who is ignorant [of the ritual]. (9) The head [of the altar] should be perforated. (10) Having breathed over the layer (*citi*), he offers an oblation upon the naturally perforated stone with the words: "I offer upon the invincible one" (11). The sacrificer mutters: "I have stepped upon the earth" (12). He gives a boon to the ignorant [Brāhmaṇa]. (13) "Thou art splendor; may splendor be mine. (14)

He places the eastern *mahiṣī* brick with the verse, "Thou wast of old named Udapurā"; the western *maṇḍajā* with, "O Agni, those which are thy moist wombs"; the southern *kulāyinī* with, "O Agni, those which are thy moist wombs"; and the northern clod of earth mixed with *dūrvā* grass with two verses, beginning with, "From joint to joint it grows," so that the *dūrvā* blades may reach the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick. The eastern [brick] is the *mahiṣī*; the *vāmabhṛt* is on the west. There should be two *kāca* stones in the two shoulders.

With the two verses, "O Agni, that luster of yours which is in the sun," he lays down [two bricks]. With "The Virāj has sustained the light; you are the *bhūḥ*, the seed of the world," he lays down the *retaḥsic*. With "The Svarāj has sustained the light; you are the *svar*, the seed of the world," he lays down the second.

On the first layer, [one places bricks] for one who is sonless; on the second, for one who has sons; on the last, [for one desiring offspring]. 17. With the mantra, "The sovereign has established the light," he establishes the Jyotis-brick in front of the two Retahsic bricks. 18. With the mantra, "May Bṛhaspati settle thee," [he establishes] the Viśvajyotis brick. 19. Of that [brick], he places the Gharmestakā in front with the Anuvāka studied in the forest (Āraṇyaka). 20. With the mantra, "Thou art the invincible, the conquering," [he establishes] the Aṣāḍhā brick. 21.
