With curds mixed with honey, he besprinkles the spotted tortoise with the three verses beginning, "Honey the winds pour forth for the righteous," and with the formula, "I settle thee in the depth of the waters."

He places [the mortar and pestle] facing westward in front [of the fire]. The mortar and pestle, made of Udumbara wood and a span in measure: "For wherever you are employed, O little mortar, house by house, here speak most brilliantly, like the drum of the victors."

Having consecrated [the mortar] with this mantra, he threshes the rice grains within it (23). With the two verses, "Idam viṣṇur vicakrame" and "Pra tad viṣṇuḥ," he places the pestle to the south-east of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, pointing towards the north (24). With the remainder of the section beginning with "Naktoṣāsā syūtā devebhiḥ," he places the fire-pan (*ukhā*) to the north-east of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, as large as the mortar (25). Having yoked the fire with the two verses, "Agni yukṣvā hi ye tava" and "Samitsravanti," [he pours] curds mixed with honey upon the heads [of the bricks].

Having filled the apertures, he also throws pieces of gold into them: with "For the ear, thee! into the right [ear]; with "For brilliance, thee! into the left; with "For luster, thee! into the right eye; with "For light, thee! into the left; with "This has come into being" into the nose; with "May Agni [endow] thee with splendor" into the left [nostril]; with "The golden disk is for glory" into the mouth; and with "Thou art a giver of a thousand; for a thousand, thee! into the incision. 26. With "The Aditya embryo," he places the human head into the fire-pan (ukhā), facing westward and with its cut portion downward. 27. He places the other [heads] around it, touching the pan as they are carried around.

With the verses "The speed of the wind," "The horse's head" in front; with "The bull [beholds] the drop," the "bull's head" behind; with "Tvaṣṭṛ's wife," the "ram's head" from the south; with "The fire which belongs to Agni," the "goat's head" from the north. (28) With the "releases," beginning with "Do not harm this two-footed one," he should worship each one as it was placed. (29) Over the eyes of the human head, he makes an offering with the half-verse "The bright face of the gods"; over the left eye, with the verse "May Heaven and Earth... (30) If there is only one goat's head.

Having placed [the bricks] upon the fire-pan (ukhā) with the formulas for placing and the formulas for dismissal, he should worship the worlds; or rather, having performed the circumambulation among the worlds, he worships the fire-pan with those mantras for placing and the formulas for dismissal. 31 One should not pass between the animal heads and the naturally perforated stone (svayamātṛṇṇā); if one should pass between them, he should mutter, "Thou art the youngest. 32

On that northern [altar], he places the *puruṣaciti*. With the sections beginning with "Mā chandaḥ" and so forth, he places three [bricks] at a time simultaneously with each individual section, ending with the words "dhruvāḥ sīdata. From the northern half, he places the head of the serpent facing away [from the altar] using the names of serpents, or he may place it toward the quarters, or he may not place it at all. With the formulas beginning with "apām tvemantsādayāmi," he places five [Apasyā bricks] in each of the directions, starting from the eastern half and proceeding clockwise.

With the formulas beginning "By the Gāyatrī metre I settle thee," he places the *chandasī* bricks on the north side. 4. With the successive sections (*paryāyas*) beginning "This one in front is the earth," he places ten *prāṇabhṛt* bricks each with one section: five on the right shoulder, five on the left shoulder, five on the right hip, five on the left hip, and the fifth set in the middle. 5. With the sections beginning "The eastern quarter, the spring season," he places the *saṃyata* bricks just as he did the *prāṇabhṛts*. 6. The *ṛtavyā* bricks are placed upon *avakā* plants.

"Madhuśca Mādhavaśca," and so forth—these are their synonyms. With each single synonym, he simultaneously lays down two bricks on each layer (*cityā*), four in the middle layer. (He does so) with the formula "Thou art the internal union of Agni," adding [the subsequent part] appropriate to the season everywhere, ending with "Sit thou firm. With the formula "Thou art the path of Agni," he lays down ten bricks; of those, he lays down two on each layer. "O Agni, I have approached thee, the bull, the wise one, generating thee again as a youth."

"May our household fires not be single-stone; sharpen us with thy keen splendor. With this verse, he places bricks upon the altar-pile using a bull. He places straight lines on the tail, equal [in length], facing east at the back and west at the front. Turning to the right, he places them on the south side of the body [of the altar] with doors facing north; on the wing, turning to the left, with doors facing west. On the north side of the body, turning to the right, he places them with doors facing south; on the wing, with doors facing east. He completes the layer with a *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick. "O Agni, thy abodes... [with this verse].

In the place of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, he touches each layer (*citi*) as it is piled. (12) In the place of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, he offers oblations upon each layer with the verse, "O Agni, what [is] thy... (13). Everywhere he appends the verse, "That arrow of thine named Yuvā... (14). With the verses beginning, "The fire which is within the waters," he consecrates the layer-oblations one by one; with two verses, the last one. (15) Having sacrificed a dark-grey horse, he covers each layer with earth from the *catvāla* pit with the verse, "Thou art asked about in heaven. He covers, he covers. (16) Thus ends the first chapter in the *Cayanapraśna*.

Having performed the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites, they remain [there] for one night. After the two morning [Upasads], they begin the second layer with the Āśvinī bricks, starting with the verses beginning "A firm seat, a firm womb," five in each world. The Ṛtavyā bricks are laid down following the Āśvinīs, starting with the verses beginning "In harmony with the seasons," five in each case.

He joins [the formulas] everywhere with the words, "In harmony with the gods who possess wisdom. (3) The seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*) and the wind-bricks (*vāyavyā*) are laid down with the five formulas beginning with, "Protect my breath" (*prāṇam me pāhi*). (4) The water-bricks (*apasyā*) and the wind-bricks are laid down with the five formulas beginning with, "Make the waters swell" (*apaḥ pinva*). (5) The water-bricks and the bird-bricks (*vayasyā*) are laid down; four are placed in the eastern half with the formulas beginning, "The ruling power, the bird, the *mayantī* metre," and five each in the corners (*apyaya*). (6) The *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks common to all layers, as well as the loose earth (*purīṣa*), have been explained. (7) These two belong to the afternoon session.

Having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, they dwell [there]. 8. After the two morning Upasads, they begin the third layer. 9. Having caused a horse to smell a pebble that is a self-perforated stone (svayamātṛṇṇā), he consecrates it with the mantra, "Bhuvas. 10. He makes it possess the sacrificial formula (yajus) with the words, "O Indra and Agni, [place] this unshaking [brick]. 11. He lays it down in turn with the formula, "May Viśvakarman settle you. 12. In this case, there is no one who does not know [the rite], nor is there the giving of a boon. 13. Having breathed out and breathed in, he offers an oblation over the Adābhya and the Svayamātṛṇṇā with the words, "I offer the layer. 14. [He continues with the mantra: "I have stepped into the intermediate space."

The sacrificer mutters: "Thou art light; grant me light," over the first golden brick; "Thou art Aparājitā by name," over the second, the Maṇḍala brick (15). "May Viśvakarman settle thee," over the Viśvajyotis brick (16). With the formulas beginning "Thou art the queen, the eastern quarter," he places five Diśyā bricks in the worlds (17). With the formulas beginning "Protect my life," he places ten Āpyā bricks in the front half and twelve each in the others (18). With the formulas beginning "Thou art the head, the ruler," he places seven Ādityadhāmnī bricks in the east, [the eighth being] Yantrī.

The seven bricks of the Aṅgiras lineage, beginning with Rāḍ, are explained afterwards (20). The Lokampṛṇā bricks and the loose soil (purīṣa) belong to all the layers (21). Having performed the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites, they dwell [there] (22). After the two morning [rites], they begin the fourth layer with the Akṣṇayāstomīya bricks: "The swift one, the Trivṛt"—thus in front; "The sky, the Saptadaśa"—thus from the south; "The shining one, the Pañcadaśa"—thus from the north; "The supporter, the Ekaviṃśa"—thus from behind; "The embryos, the Pañcaviṃśa"—thus [from the west].

In the middle; he places fifteen bricks remaining, three in each of the worlds. He places them with the formulas: "Thou art the portion of Agni," in the east; "Thou art the portion of Indra," in the south; "Thou art the portion of the Nṛcakṣases," in the north; "Thou art the portion of Mitra," in the west; and "Thou art the portion of Aditi," in the middle.

The remaining [bricks] he places five after [the *lokaṃpṛṇās*]. (24) "With one they praised; creatures were produced"—with these seventeen *sṛṣṭi*-bricks he places them in the middle. (25) "The wife of the seasons"—with these fifteen *vyuṣṭi*-bricks he places three each in the worlds. (26) The *lokaṃpṛṇās* belonging to all layers and the *purīṣa* have been explained. (27) Having performed the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, they dwell [there]. (28) After the morning [rites].

They begin the highest layer with the verse, "Without rivals, O Agni... (VS 15.59). He places [the bricks] on the east with the words, "Drive away our born rivals" (VS 15.60); on the west with, "By force, drive away our born rivals" (VS 15.61); on the south he settles them with, "The forty-fourfold hymn-form, splendor, wealth" (VS 15.62); and on the north with, "The sixteenfold hymn-form, vigor, wealth" (VS 15.63). With the formula, "Thou art the soil of Agni," he places the *purīṣavatī* brick to the west of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*. [He places] one [brick] with the formula, "One is the metre"; forty *virāj* bricks at the corners, ten each. [He places them] with the formula, "With the ray for dwelling."

With the verses beginning "Kṣayaṃ jinva," one places thirty-three *stomabhāga* bricks in the quarters, starting from the eastern half and proceeding clockwise, seven in each quarter and five in the center. With the verses beginning "Thou art the queen, the eastern quarter," one places five *nākasad* bricks in the worlds. With the verse "This one before, the golden-haired," one places the five *pañcacūḍā* bricks above the *nākasads*, with the last one facing eastward toward the west. With the formula "I settle thee in the eastern quarter," he places the *kḷpti* bricks on the head, the wings, the tail, and the fifth in the middle. He distributes them right here.

He lays down the *retaḥsic* with the formula, "May Parameṣṭhin seat thee. He lays down the *viśvajyotis* with the formula, "May Parameṣṭhin seat thee. Having laid down the two seasonal bricks (*ṛtavye*), he lays down the five rain-winning bricks (*vṛṣṭisani*) in the worlds with the formulas beginning with "The wind from the front. Having laid down the *saṃyāni* bricks, he lays down the seven speech-bricks (*vāk*) in the eastern half with the formulas beginning with "Ambā and Ulā. With the formulas beginning with "For the ocean," he places two Āditya bricks in each of the corners and one in the middle. He places another Maṇḍala brick with the formula, "Thou art named Adhidyu. To the north-east of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, he places this [brick]...

He lays down eight bricks with various sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) beginning with "Agni," just as in the case of the *gārhapatya* fire-altar (13). With the verse, "By which the seers through austerity performed the sacrificial session," he lays down nine; of these, he uses eight [for the first layer] (14). With the verse, "May the years, O Agni, and the seasons increase thee," he lays down ten; two by two in each world (15). With the verse, "His fuel-sticks rise upwards," he lays down twelve *aprī*-verses, three in each of the *apriya* sections (16). With the verse, "From the out-breath he extends the in-breath," he lays down nine continuous bricks facing westward in front (17). With the verse, "Thee with the *ṛc*, with the metre... [he continues].

With the verses beginning with *sādayāmi*, he places two each at the corners (18). With *dūtaṃ vo viśvavedasam*, five in the worlds (19). With *indro dadhīco asthabhiḥ*, ten in the eastern half (20). He piles the meters: three each at the corners, and three between each [corner]. With the three *gāyatrīs* beginning with *ayam agniḥ sahasriṇaḥ*; with the three *triṣṭubhs* beginning with *abodhy agniḥ*; with the *jagatīs* beginning with *janasya gopāḥ*; with the *anuṣṭubhs* beginning with *saṃ samit*; with the *paṅktis* beginning with *ā te agne idhīmahi*; and with *enā vaḥ*.

With the *bṛhatī* verses beginning "Agni," and with the *uṣṇih* verses beginning "O Agni, of the booty consisting of cattle," he performs two and three [stotras]. "May Agni, when invoked, be auspicious for us; may his gift be auspicious, O fortunate one; may the sacrifice be auspicious, and may our praises be auspicious. And may our praises be auspicious; make your mind auspicious in the overcoming of Vṛtra, whereby you may prevail in battles. Whereby you may prevail in battles, stretch out your firm [bow] against those who are many and defiant; may we win through your protections."

Thus with the *kakubh* verses; "O Agni, kindled by us... (RV 8.44.1); "These men, O Agni, have generated Agni from the two fire-sticks by means of their insights and the movement of their hands—the praiseworthy one, visible from afar, the lord of the house, the active one" (RV 3.27.1)—thus with the *virāj* verses; "O Agni, him today... (RV 6.16.34); "I consider Agni the Hotṛ... (RV 1.127.1)—thus with the *padapaṅkti* verses; "O Agni, you are our closest relative... (RV 8.44.24); "To you, O most radiant, shining one... (RV 8.44.25); "For thus, O Agni... (RV 8.44.27)—thus with the *dvipadā* verses in the northern half [of the altar]. 21.

He lays down the Mahāvrata [bricks] with three Gāyatrī verses beginning "Come hither, for well we press for thee" upon the head; the Rathantara on the wing with two verses beginning "We praise thee, O hero," making three layers on the southern half, the middle, and the end; the Bṛhat on the northern wing with two verses beginning "Thee indeed we invoke," making three layers on the northern half, the middle, and the end; and the Vāmadevya on the body with the three verses beginning "In what way has the wonderful one appeared for us? at the middle.

The *yajñāyajñiya* [sāman] is at the tail; the two verses beginning with "yajñā yajñā vo agnaye" are on the rear half, at the middle, and at the end, with three elevations (or layers) each. The seven verses beginning with "yavā ayavā" are on the front half. With the verses beginning with "pṛthivyasi janmanā," there are two verses at each of the ends. With the verses beginning with "yā devyasīṣṭake kumāryupaśīvarī," there are three verses at each of the ends. To the nine verses beginning with "yā devyasīṣṭaka āyurdā," he adds the word "upaśīvarī" at the end; and the verse "yā devīḥ stheṣṭakāḥ suśevāḥ" is placed in the middle.

Simultaneously, three [bricks] with the formulas beginning "For self-power thee" (savayasaṃ tvā) and so forth; at each end, three [bricks] each. With the formulas beginning "Thou art the maker of much" (bhūyaskṛd asi) and so forth, he places five by five, moving clockwise. With the formulas beginning "Thee, the luminous one, I settle" (jyotiṣmatīṃ tvā sādayāmi) and so forth, at each end three [bricks] each, and two in the middle. With the formulas beginning "Kṛttikā is the lunar mansion, Agni is the deity" (kṛttikā nakṣatram agnir devatā) and so forth, he places the Nakṣatra-bricks in front, facing westward; in every case, he appends the formula "The splendors of Agni" (agne rucaḥ stha).

Full in front of the two Viśākhās, and full behind, full in front and in the middle—this full moon has triumphed. On which day the gods entered together into the highest firmament, rejoice here! [Recite] this over the full moon after the Bharaṇīs: "O Amāvāsyā, that portion which the gods assigned to you as you entered with your greatness—make our offspring complete with heroes; bestow upon us wealth, O blessed one, with excellent sons."

Thus, on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā), [he performs the rite]. With the verses beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ" (RV X.121.1) and others, he places two bricks at each of the corners. Having placed the first golden brick (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*) with the verse "Svarasi svarme yacha" (VS XV.56) and the bull-brick (*ṛṣabha*), he completes the layer (*citi*) with the space-filling brick (*lokaṃpṛṇā*). Having caused a pebble (*śarkarā*) to be smelled by a horse, he consecrates the naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇṇā*) with the mantra "Svaḥ. He makes it accompanied by the sacrificial formula (*sayajuṣ*) with the words "I settle thee in the seat of life" (*āyoṣṭvā sadane sādayāmi*). He lays them down in succession with the formula "May Parameṣṭhin settle thee. Here, there is no one who does not know [the ritual], nor is there the giving of a boon.

Having inhaled and exhaled, he makes an offering over the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with the formula, "I offer into consciousness" (abhiprāṇyāpānya citiṃ juhomīti). He offers upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the *adābhyā* verse. The sacrificer mutters, "I have ascended to heaven" (divamākramiṣam). The Pratiprasthātṛ places the northern *vikarṇī* brick, which has a pebble, upon the *vāyavyā* brick with the verse, "Like a neighing horse in the pasture" (prothadaśvo na yavasī). They both simultaneously place the *svayamātṛṇṇā* in the middle of the yoke. The procedure for all the layers (*sārvacitikam*) has been explained. He completes the layer with loose soil (*purīṣa*), except for that of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*. It has been explained that one building the first layer should build it knee-deep.

Having sprinkled the entire fire with a thousand fragments of gold and with [the formulas] beginning with "A thousand months," he sprinkles it with ghee: from the west, facing east, with the formula, "May the Vasus protect you along with the Rudras"; from the north, facing south, with the formula, "May Nitāna Māruta protect you along with the Maruts"; from the east, facing west, with the formula, "May the Ādityas protect you along with the Viśve Devas"; and from the south, with the formula, "May the Pitṛs, whose king is Yama, protect you along with the Pitṛs."

Facing north, [he says], "May the gods, with Indra as their chief and Varuṇa as their king, protect [us] from below and from above"; facing east in the middle, having circumambulated, the sacrificer mutters while milking [the altar]: "May the bricks be milch-cows for me," and he begins again at the northern end of the tail. On the last brick on the northern hip, he offers the Śatarudriya oblation with goat's milk or groats of *gavīdhuka* grass using an *arka* leaf, with the verses beginning "Homage to you, O Rudra, to your wrath," while standing knee-deep.

Holding [the vessel], facing south, he offers with "Homage to the great ones, to the small ones" at the height of the navel; facing north, with "Homage to Vāstavya" at the height of the mouth; facing east, he performs the descending oblations. With "Homage be to the Rudras who are in heaven," he offers at the height of the mouth; in the subsequent sequence, at the height of the navel; with the final [verse], at the height of the knee. He should place an *arka* leaf in a place where no path passes; he should place that which has fallen in a place frequented by cattle. "The Rudra who is in the waters, who is in the fire, who is in the plants..."

"To that Rudra who has entered all worlds, to that divine Rudra, let there be obeisance; Svāhā!"—saying this, he pours out an offering of *gāvīdhuka* groats upon that brick. (6) He should give a bow with three arrows to a Brahmin without asking for it. (7) With the verse, "O stone, the strength resting on the mountain," he goes around the fire three times from right to left, sprinkling water from a water-pot.

Having placed [the vessel], he sprinkles water three times and walks around it counter-clockwise. 8. The Udgātṛ sings the Gāyatra on the head with the Āgneya-Pāvamānī verses; the Rathantara on the right wing; the Bṛhat on the left; the Vāmadevya on the body; and the Yajñāyajñīya on the tail. He recites the Prajāpati-hṛdaya without a verse on the right armpit, while the Hotṛ chants the *anuśamsana* after it has been sung. 9. One must not step upon that which has been sung until the pouring over [of the earth] with the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone. 10. [He pours] with a frog, with an *avakā* plant, and with a reed-shoot, saying: "Thee with the *avakā* of the ocean; thee with the *avakā* of the frost."

With the seven [verses] beginning with "By the placenta," he draws all the fire across. Having restrained his breaths, he throws the frog used for the drawing across onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). With this [rite], he should strike down whomever he hates. He causes the sacrificer to recite the "milking of the meters" with the verse, "The sacrifice was offered by the Bhṛgus. He lets the Udumbara wood-sticks soak in clarified butter. Having performed the afternoon *Pravargya* and *Upasad* rites, they remain overnight. After the two morning [rites], having fastened a sandal of black antelope skin, [he recites] "Of the waters, this..."

With the two verses, "The path, obeisance to thee" and "For the taking away, for the flame," he steps upon the fire. (16) Having placed a piece of gold into each of five portions of clarified butter, he sprinkles the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with the formulas beginning with "To the wooden seat, vaṭ! up to the navel. (17) With the formula "To the finder of heaven, vaṭ!", he lifts the ladle upwards. (18) Into curds mixed with honey, he places a handful of *darbha* grass; with the three verses beginning with "O Lord of food, give us of food," he sprinkles the entire fire. (19) [He recites: "Givers of out-breath, givers of in-breath."

He descends [from the sacrificial post]. On the same day, having concluded the afternoon rites and having swept [the area], the vessels for the *gharma* and the *upasad* sacrificial grass for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma are prepared; this has already been explained.

With the verse, "Agni with his sharp flame," he offers an oblation of four ladlings. Having silently taken sixteen ladlings, he recites the eight verses beginning with "He who [supports] all these worlds" and offers half; then, having recited the subsequent section (*anuvāka*), he offers the remainder. He sprinkles three fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood with clarified butter. With the three verses ending in *svāhā*, beginning with "Lead him upward" (*udenam uttaraṃ naya*), he places them on the fire. The procedure for carrying forward the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) has been explained. With the verse, "Thee, O Agni, the All-gods... (*udu tvā viśve devāḥ*), he takes up the fire. May the five divine quarters protect the sacrifice.

With the verse beginning "The goddesses," he carries [the fire] from the northern part of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line to the end at the *āgnīdhra* shed using six verses. As the fire is being led forward, the sacrificer walks to the north and the Brahman priest to the south; the latter recites the ten-verse *Apratiratha* hymn beginning with "The swift one, sharpening his weapons. At the time of placing the stone on the *āgnīdhra* hearth, he places a stone there with the two verses beginning "This measurer stands in the midst of heaven. With the four verses beginning "The sacrifice, the summoner of favor, may come hither," they proceed to the end at the *āhavanīya* hearth. With the five verses beginning "Step forth with Agni," he steps upon the fire.

Having recited the verse, "O Agni, Night and Dawn, thousand-eyed," he makes an offering upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with milk from a black cow that has a white calf, using a vessel made of *udumbara* wood. Having placed the ritual materials and a piece of gold within it, and having settled the fire upon it with the two verses, "Thou art the fair-winged eagle; sit upon the back of the earth" and "Being invoked, O fair-faced one," he kindles it and lays on fuel-sticks: a stick of *śamī* wood with the verse, "Of the desirable Savitṛ," and a stick of *aśvattha* wood with the verse, "May we worship thee in the highest [place], O Agni, who art worthy of praise."

With the verse "Preddho agne" (VS 12.1), he offers a cake on eight potsherds made of *vikaṅkata* wood; with the *paṅkti* verse "agne tam adya" (VS 12.2), he makes an offering; with the verse "sapta te agne samidhaḥ" (VS 12.3), he offers the full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*); and with the remainder of the section beginning "citim juhomī" (VS 12.4–19), he makes the second offering. He should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Having cleansed both the *sruva* and the *juhū* ladles, he brings forward the oblation for Vaiśvānara. He cuts off the entire portion in a single cutting. Having poured clarified butter over the vessel and having sprinkled it twice, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse with the call: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Vaiśvānara."

Having caused the announcement, he gives the direction: "Sacrifice to Agni Vaiśvānara. (18) When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers in the middle with his hand. (19) He makes a straight, well-established offering over the remnant. (20) If it should turn back, it has been explained by the Brāhmaṇa. (21) He prepares seven cakes on seven potsherds that have been processed silently. (22) With the under-spreading and the sprinkling of ghee, he offers the remnants of the mixture with the Marut-gaṇas, beginning with the verses "Śukrajyotis" and "Citrajyotis," in the southern half and the eastern half, and with the verse "Ṛtajit. (22)

"Satyajic ca" [is recited] over the southern half; "Ṛtaś ca satyaś ca" over the southern and western halves; with the group [of verses] studied in the forest, "Īdṛṅ ca etādṛṅ ca" over the northern half; "Īdṛkṣāsa etādṛkṣāsa" over the northern half; "Sabharaso maruto yajñe" over the northern and eastern halves. (23) One should have a large ladle for the *vasordhārā* made of *udumbara* wood, with a handle as comfortable as possible; one should position it so that the stream will be established upon the *vaiśvānara* oblation. (24) [The rest is] silent.

Having taken twelve [ladles], while the sacrificer maintains contact, he offers the continuous *vasordhārā* (stream of wealth) with the five sections beginning with "May strength be mine, may impulse be mine," and so forth, ending with "To the Lord, to the Overlord," including the formulas: "One and three," up to "Thirty-three," "Four and eight," up to "Forty-eight," "The three-year-old male and the three-year-old female," according to the traditional recitation, and the verses beginning with "The milch-cows and the oxen," "Life is perfected by the sacrifice, breath is perfected by the sacrifice," and so on.

He should conclude with the *stoma* and the *yajus*, adding the exclamation *svāhā* at the end as prescribed. (26) Having thrown the splinters into the fire, he should cook a four-portioned mess of rice-grains that are still living in the remaining clarified butter and give it to the *madhyataḥkārin* priests; to them he should give four cows each. (27) Having mixed together wild and cultivated plants with clarified butter, he offers the *vājaprasavya* oblation with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, using the eight verses beginning with "O Agni, speak for us here" (*agne acchā vadeha naḥ*) and the six verses beginning with "All you Maruts today" (*viśve no adya marutaḥ*). (28) After each offering, he pours [the remainder] into a vessel.

He pours the residue down [the back] of the southern hip, behind the tail of the fire-altar. Having spread a black antelope skin upon the stool—[or] a goat skin for one who desires cattle—he sprinkles him while he is seated there with the residue, [reciting]: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... (VS 10.1). He lets it flow from the head down over the face: for a Brāhmaṇa, [he says] "Bṛhaspati for sovereignty!"; for a Rājanya, "Indra for sovereignty!"; for a Vaiśya, "Agni for sovereignty! (VS 10.2–4).

Or he should not consecrate a Vaiśya. With [the ladle] taken twelve times, he offers twelve *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, beginning with the sections starting "Ṛtāṣāṭ ṛtadhāmā. With each section, he offers two oblations: the first with "To him, svāhā! Vaṭ! and the second with "To them, svāhā! Vaṭ! To every one of these, he appends the formula, "May they protect this Brahman and Kṣatriya power for us," and also, "May they protect this Brahman and Kṣatriya power for us."

"Bṛhaspati Viśvakarman"—this is the twelfth [verse] for a Brāhmaṇa; "Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin" for a Rājanya; and "Amṛḍaya Dūreheti" for a Vaiśya. (32) Having offered it upon the *rathaśiras* fire with the *āhavanīya* while holding [the ladle] twice, he should give it to the *adhvaryu* at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (33) With the verses beginning "Thou art the ocean, full of mist, the giver of moisture," he offers oblations to the wind three times with his joined palms, or with a hollowed vessel made of a black antelope skin. (34)

The procedure from the enticing of the footprints until the pouring of the hearths is established. With the *vaihavī* bricks, he piles them upon the hearths, with a stone as the ninth; there are twenty-one in the Āgnīdhra hearth, eleven in the Hotṛ’s, eight each in the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s and the others, and six in the Mārjālīya and the animal-cooking hearth. The procedure up to the Agniṣomīya [offering] is established. He subsequently offers the ten-oblation *sarvapṛṣṭhā* sacrifice dedicated to Agni Gāyatra, Trivṛt, and Rathantara, following the sacrificial cake of the Agniṣomīya animal victim. It is performed in the same manner as the Devikā oblations.

5. The fast-day (upavasatha) is established. 6. On the following day, there is either an Agniṣṭoma, an Ukthya, or an Atirātra. 7. It is established [according to the ritual] up to the laying of the enclosing-sticks (paridhi). 8. Having placed the Āghāra-libation and the fuel-stick (samidh), he offers the Agni-yoga oblation with the verse: "I yoke the fire with power and with ghee. 9. He touches the two wings with the verse: "These two wings of thine, O Indu, are skillful. 10. He offers the five Anvāroha oblations with the verses beginning, "Making it himself. 11. It is established [according to the ritual] up to the formal dedication (upākaraṇa). 12. There is a single sacrificial post; he dedicates the animals of the Ekādaśinī set, or the seasonal animals (kratupaśu). 13. It is established [according to the ritual] up to...

At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), having brought forward a hundred gold mānas of a vessel full of honey along with the other fees, the sacrificer, after looking at it while reciting "The splendor of the gods... (*citram devānām*), hands it over to the Brahman priest. 15. This is established from the drawing of the Agniṣṭoma cups onwards. 16. Having drawn the Agniṣṭoma cups, he touches the fire-altar while reciting the two verses addressed to the waters, beginning with "Thou art the head of heaven" (*divo mūrdhāsi*). 17. This is established up to the *śamyor-vāk* formula. 18. He mutters the verse for the loosening of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), beginning with "I loosen thy cord, I loosen thy reins" (*vi te muñcāmi raśanām vi raśmīn*). 19. When the *śamyor-vāk* has been completed.
Suck this honeyed breast, O Agni, swelling in the midst of the waters;
enjoy the honeyed fountain, the wave, and enter the oceanic water.

Thus he mutters the *agnivimoka* (the release of the fire). 20. The *ānūbandhyā* sacrifice is established. 21. Before the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings, he offers the *ruces* with the verses: "O Agni, those splendors of yours which are in the sun," "O gods, those splendors of yours which are in the sun," and "Bestow splendor upon us. 22. With the verse addressed to Varuṇa, "I approach you" (*tattvā yāmi*), before the scattering of earth around the altar, having mixed curds and ghee, he makes offerings with the formulas beginning "Thou art Samīcī," proceeding in each direction with two verses and one in the middle. 23. Having concluded [the sacrifice], he performs the *udavasānīyā* offering with the formula: "By the initiation I have removed thee; by the austerity I have removed thee; by the Soma-pressing..."

"Thou hast been appeased by the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), thou hast been appeased by the cow, thou hast been appeased"—with these words of propitiation (*āpti*), as he is about to depart, he worships the fire-altar (*iṣṭakāgni*). The fire-piler (*agnicit*) shall not descend [into water] nor rise up for a year, nor as long as he lives; while it rains, he shall not run; he shall not eat the flesh of birds; he shall not approach a woman; having piled the second altar, he shall not approach the wife of another; having piled the third, he shall not approach any woman at all. If he should approach one, he should sacrifice with curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
"The fires that are full of soil and have entered upon the earth—you are the highest among them. Impel us toward life."

Having returned from his journey, he worships the brick-built fire (*iṣṭakāgni*) with the three verses beginning, "O Agni, day by day... for others. (26) Having piled the fire, he should sacrifice with the *iṣṭikī* Sautrāmaṇī. (27) The *punar-citi* consists of three layers. (28) Having laid down eight bricks with different formulas beginning, "By which the seers performed the sacrificial session through austerity," he covers the layer with loose earth (*purīṣa*). There are eight *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks on the first layer, eleven on the second, and twelve on the third. (29) A sacrificer desiring prosperity who has already piled [the fire] should pile the *punar-citi* before the [next] layer.

Having piled [the fire-altar], or while piling it, once the *uttaravedi* has been strewn with sand, he places eight bricks with separate formulas beginning with "In those places where the fire does not exist, let this be that fire," and thirteen *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; these amount to twenty-one. He deposits the fire with the verse, "This is your seasonal womb. He deposits it.
Thus ends the second chapter on the piling [of the altar].
Thus ends the *Cayanakalpa* in the *Mānavasūtra*.

In autumn, a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Vājapeya. There are seventeen initiation days (*dīkṣā*) and three Upasad days. He should have the *surā* prepared in an enclosed space. [The ritual] is established up to the preparation of the mound (*khara*). Behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares a second mound, dug out and without loose earth brought from elsewhere. [The ritual] is established up to the carving. The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of Khadira wood, four-cornered, and seventeen *aratni* in length; its top-ring (*caṣāla*) is made of wheat flour. It is not raised higher than that.

He extends [the sacrificial post] beyond the *caṣāla*. (8) It is established up to the time for the girdle of the *āsrava* vessel. (9) Having wound the girdle around it, he envelops the sacrificial post with seventeen cloths. (10) The *upavasatha* day is established. (11) On the following day, there is the *vājapeya* sacrifice consisting of seventeen [stomas], accompanied by the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, having the *rathantara* as its *pṛṣṭha* chant. (12) At the beginning of the pressings, he offers oblations with the mantra: "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for his fortune. (13) It is established up to the employment of the vessels. (14) Having employed the *āgrayaṇa* vessel, [he employs] the five *aindra* *atigrāhya* vessels.

He arranges seventeen vessels for Prajāpati made of *vāyavya* wood on the southern mound (15). Having arranged them together with the *dhruva* vessel, the Pratiprasthātṛ places seventeen earthen *upayāma* cups and a goat’s tail-hair strainer on the western mound (16). This procedure remains established up to the setting down of the *savanīya* jars (18). The Pratiprasthātṛ, having placed the *surā* jar on the head of the Āgnīdhra near the place of the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), and having brought it in through the western door, sets it down on his own mound (19) during the *nigrābhya* waters.

Having caused the sacrificer to recite the formula, he draws the *adābhya* cup from the *hotṛ*-cup into the *dadhigraha* vessel with the verse, "Agni [is the protector] of the morning pressing... He takes the third portion; with the words, "The Viśve Devas and the Maruts... this is the third pressing," he completes it as a double portion. With the formulas beginning, "I draw thee for Agni," he pulls out two shoots at a time, one by one in each turn. Having gathered them together into one, he shakes them with the two formulas beginning, "In the flight of the *reśīs*, I shake thee."

He shakes [the vessel] once, twice. 22. He touches it with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; thee, the bright one, I take for the bright one, O bright one. 23. It is offered while still remaining [in the hand]. 24. He goes to the north of the Hotṛ. 25. Having moved around to the south, having placed the cup opposite the southern joint of the enclosing sticks, he offers it with the verse: "The form of the bull shines forth like a peak. 26. Having circumambulated, he sets the vessel down in its proper place. 27. [He offers] with each of the verses beginning with "O divine Soma, thou art desirous... one by one.

Alternately, he pours out two by two the *aṃśu* and *adābhya* [juices]. 28 He gives sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*): a garment, an upper garment, gold, and four, eight, or twelve cows for the *aṃśu* and *adābhya*. 29 From the taking of the *upām̐śu* until the consecration of the two pressing-boards, the rite is established. 30 One who desires prosperity should take the *aṃśu* [juice]. 31 From the mixing [of the soma] until the oblation, he must not speak. 32 If he should speak, [he recites]: "May our breath come from afar, from the atmosphere, from heaven;
may it come from the earth. You are immortality; for breath, you!"

Thus he pours the gold [into the vessel]. Having mixed [the soma] once from the Hotṛ’s cup, he presses it once. Having mentally recited the verse, "With what splendor will the wonderful one appear to us?", he pours it once with his joined palms into the Dadhighraha vessel. He offers it with the formula: "When they have run forth after him... He offers with the formula: "May Indra and Agni grant me luster; may Soma and Bṛhaspati grant me luster;
may all the gods grant me luster; O Aśvins, bestow luster upon me."

Thus he touches water. 37. He takes the two *aṃśu* and *adābhya* cups at the *sahasradakṣiṇa*, the *sarvavedasadakṣiṇa*, the *sattra*, the *viśvajit*, the *sarvapṛṣṭha*, the *vājapeya*, the *rājasūya*, and the *aśvamedha*. 38. From the pressing of the *upāṃśu* onwards, the procedure is established until the drawing of the *manthin* cup. 39. Having drawn the *āgrayaṇa* cup within the *ukthya* sacrifice, he draws the five *natigrāhya* cups dedicated to Indra with the formulas beginning, "Thou art taken with a support; [I take] thee who sittest on wood," and so forth. 40. Having drawn them together with the *dhruva* cup, he should not cause the stream of the *śukra* cup to flow over.

41. Having spread out a tuft of grass over the *droṇakalaśa*, the Pratiprasthātṛ purifies the *parisrut* (fermented liquor) with the formula, "May he purify thy *parisrut*. 42. With the verse, "O, how much [wealth] indeed for those possessing barley," the Adhvaryu draws seventeen *prājāpatya* cups with a stream of pure (*śukra*) Soma; with the formula, "With this [Soma] as the end," the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the *surā* cups during the *upayāma* (supporting ladles). 43. The drawing and setting down of the *prājāpatya* cups are performed alternately. 44. [The same applies to] the drawing and setting down of the *prājāpatya* cups.

It is established up to the time of the girding. Having girt the sacrificial cord around [the post], he dedicates the animals: a goat for Agni, a goat for Indra-Agni, a ram for Indra, a ewe for Sarasvatī, a speckled cow for the Maruts, two ewes for Sarasvatī, and seventeen goats for Prajāpati—black, hornless, and of uniform color. They proceed with the omenta according to the traditional injunction. It is established up to the pouring out of the oblations for the midday pressing. Having poured out the oblations for the midday pressing, he pours out the wild rice (nīvāra) for Bṛhaspati, in an offering of seventeen śarāva-measures.

5. It is prepared from the time of placing it on the fire. 6. Having placed the Mādhyandina offerings on the fire, he cooks the *naivāra* (wild rice) in milk. 7. It is prepared up until the time of the ritual performance (*pracaraṇa*). 8. Having performed the Mādhyandina rites, he performs with the *naivāra*; [he gives the directions] "Recite for Bṛhaspati," "Sacrifice to Bṛhaspati," [with the formula] "Upāṃśu" for the deity. 9. The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is the same; having brought the *iḍā* portion in the same manner, he places the *naivāra* in the *cātvāla* pit. 10. It is prepared up until the time for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). 11. He ties golden garlands upon the sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). 12. Now, of the strength (*vāja*)...

With the words, "At the birth [of the world], the great mother," he brings down the chariot from the south, with its pole directed toward the east. 13. With the words, "In the waters is immortality, in the waters is healing," they bathe the horses. With the words, "Either Vāyu shall yoke thee, or Manu shall yoke thee," he yokes them. 14. With the words, "O Son of the Waters, swift-coursing," he wipes the forehead-straps. 15. Sixteen chariots are yoked silently. 16. Having offered the two *dākṣiṇā* oblations, he gives away seventeen sets of seventeen: seventeen gold coins (*niṣkas*), seventeen slave-girls, and seventeen elephants.

Seventeen hundred cows, seventeen hundred sheep, seventeen hundred goats, seventeen chariots, and seventeen riding-animals—having filled these seventeen sets of seventeen with abundant goods, he gives them to the Adhvaryu priest together with the *yajus*-yoked chariot. They lead the cows in front, the other items in the middle, and the chariots behind. Once the sacrificial fees have been led forth, the one yoked with the *yajus* stands at the edge of the *cātvāla* pit, while the others stand to the north of the *āgnīdhra* shed. At the time of the *māhendra* cup, they cause the artisans to display their skills in all directions.

The drums resound (22). To the north of the *caṭvala* pit, they strike a chariot axle (23). Upon it, he fastens a chariot wheel made of *udumbara* wood with seventeen spokes (24). He ties seventeen sheaths of grass to four branches of an *aśvattha* tree; he ties four to each branch, and five to one (25). Having mounted the chariot wheel, the Brahman priest, saying, "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, of true impulse, may I ascend to the highest heaven," turns it three times clockwise (26).

"Sing the Sāman of the Vājins," he commands. 27. He causes the sacrificer to recite the *ujjitī* formulas: "Agni won the one-syllabled [meter]," and so on through three rounds; he offers seventeen oblations with the formula, "To Agni, to the one-syllabled meter, svāhā! 28. With the words, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s stride, thou art Viṣṇu’s wide stride, thou art Viṣṇu’s step," he causes the sacrificer to take steps toward the yoke-yoked [chariot]. 29.

"The two hooks, the two descending hooks on both sides of the chariot, those dark ones that move toward the wind and fire, the far-darting, winged, vigorous ones—may those fires protect us, providing fullness."

With the verse, "O tree, firm of limb," he consecrates the wheel; with "The pedestal" (vanaspate vīḍvaṅga), he consecrates the base. With "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, in the true impulse of Bṛhaspati, may we, as possessors of strength, conquer strength, winners of strength," he mounts the chariot. Having recited the section beginning with "May the strong ones win strength," he descends. Once he has descended, the prince, acting as his deputy, mounts. With the verse, "O horse-whip, vigorous one, rich in vigor among the prizes," he takes up the horse-whip. With the verses, "Thou art a steed, thou art the sevenfold," he addresses the horses.

The others enter. 36. To the north of the *cātvāla* pit, they fix a post made of *udumbara* wood among seventeen sacrificial stakes (*sviṣṭup*). 37. They call that the "wood" (*kāṣṭhā*). 38. Having circumambulated it clockwise, they return. 39.

Having taken up the Māhendra cup, he introduces the Stotra. The wife puts on a garment made of Darbha grass; the sacrificer puts on a silk garment or a linen one, which has been soaked in clarified butter or used for anointing. When about to ascend the sacrificial post, the sacrificer addresses the wife, saying, "Ascend to heaven; come! She replies, "Let us both ascend to heaven. Having said, "I shall cause us both to ascend to heaven," and reciting, "May life be perfected by the sacrifice; may breath be perfected by the sacrifice," he mounts the post. Having ascended, the sacrificer mutters, "O gods, I have gone to heaven."

5. He offers thirteen oblations with the formulas: “Svāhā to strength! Svāhā to impulsion! and so forth. 6. While standing on the upper terraces, the commoners strike [the drums] with handfuls of salt-earth, saying: “For food thee! For strength thee! For the winning of strength thee! 7. He turns around toward each one of them as they do so. 8. When the chariots have returned, he offers an oblation with the verse: “May the impulse of strength come to me. 9. He consecrates the sounding drums with the formula: “O Indra, speak the speech! 10. He addresses the trees with the formulas: “The trees have made you sing; O Indra, release your speech!”

He offers the oblation for the unyoking of the chariot (rathavimocanīya). He gives one *kṛṣṇala* weight of gold to each of the race-horses. With the formula, "O two steeds, winners of the prize, having won the prize, smell the portion of Bṛhaspati," he causes the two draft-animals of the *yajuryukta* chariot to smell the *naivāra* grain. With the formula, "O two steeds, winners of the prize, having won the prize, may you wipe yourselves upon the portion of Bṛhaspati," he wipes the *jaiya* grass on the two front points of the *pṛṣṭhya* chariot. [He addresses the yoke-pole with: "Thou art the ruler, the controller; thou art the restrainer, the supporter; for cultivation thee, for security."

With "Thou art," he descends. With "Thou art splendor," he descends onto gold; with "Thou art nourishment," onto a goat-skin. Having spread a black antelope skin on the throne-seat with "Thou art the sovereign," and for one desiring cattle, a goat-skin, he causes the sacrificer to step toward the throne-seat with the formulas: "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, thou art the wide stride of Viṣṇu, thou art the step of Viṣṇu. He addresses him as he mounts the throne-seat: "Mount the heavenly couch; having mounted it, look forth upon men for the sake of agriculture, security, wealth, and prosperity, saying 'Thee! Thus he consecrates him as he ascends the throne-seat.

18. Having mixed together the wild and cultivated plants with clarified butter, he offers the *vājaprasavya* oblation with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, using the seven verses beginning with "O Agni, speak here for us. 19. The consecration (*abhiṣeka*) has been explained. 20. Then they present him with a parasol made of *udumbara* wood, having seventeen ribs. 21. The sacrificer accepts it with the formula, "Thou art a shelter. 22. When the recitation of the *śastra* is completed, the Adhvaryu takes up the principal cup from among the *atigrāhya* cups, namely the one dedicated to Mahendra. 23. They pay reverence to the *atigrāhya* cups. 24. O Indra... [the rest of the verse].

He offers with "Svāhā" when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, first among the *atigrāhya* cups (25). When the second *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he consumes the *atigrāhya* cups silently, just as he does for the *māhendra* cup (26). This is established up to the *ṣoḍaśin* goblets (27). When the *ṣoḍaśin* goblets have been turned away, he draws the cups for the Vājapeya, headed by the *hotṛ*'s goblet (28). The Adhvaryu takes the entire contents from the *pūtabhṛt* vessel into the *hotṛ*'s goblet and the principal goblet of the *prājāpatya* cups (29). With the formula, "You are united; unite me with prosperity," they go out toward the east with the Soma through the eastern door.

"You are separate; do not unite me with evil," [saying this], they go out westward through the western door with the *surā* libations. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the *prājāpatya* cups with the formula, "To Prajāpati, svāhā! (30). After the second *vaṣaṭ* call, he silently pushes back the embers toward the north and, having touched the *surā* cups, they all consume the Soma portions. (31) They carry away half of the cow and the *surā* libations for the race-winners (*ajisṛt*). They give the vessel of honey to the Brahman priest, and the golden or silver *kakubha* cup to the chief deputy. (32)

Having performed the *anuyāja* offerings with thirty-three cups of *surā*, the sacrifice is completed. (34) One who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice shall not descend before anyone, nor shall he rise up for anyone, even if that person is his superior in age, provided he is another performer of the Vājapeya. (35) They should address him as "Samrāj" (Sovereign).
(36) Thus ends the first chapter on the Vājapeya.

The twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is both a sessional sacrifice (*sattra*) and a non-sessional sacrifice (*ahīna*). (1) It may be performed by one person or by many. (2) Those who have not fasted may perform the non-sessional sacrifice; they may officiate for those who have not been consecrated (*adīkṣita*). (3) There is a fault in officiating for more than thirteen such persons. (4) During the *upasads*, one person should undergo consecration. (5) They should have the householder as the seventeenth member and follow the same ritual manual (*samānakalpa*). (6) Brāhmaṇas who are themselves the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should enter into the sessional sacrifice. (7) For them, the giving of fees (*dāna*) shall cease, as well as the initial injunction regarding Varuṇa. (8) Having said, "In whatever prosperity there is in this sacrifice, may that be ours together," [they should establish the fires] in the fires of the householder.

Those who perform the rites in the middle, such as the *madhyataḥkārins*, should combine the fires. He who combines the fires, or those on whose behalf they are combined, should mutter the verse: "Be you two of one mind for us. Having offered the *sāvitra* oblations and having separated the fires, they should offer the *agnihotra* sacrifices individually. The preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā*) is established [by the standard rule]. They should perform the fumigation and cooking over the fires of the householder. Having combined them, they should sacrifice with the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). The bricks should be prepared before the *upasads*. In the absence of a prohibition regarding their own specific duties, this applies to all.

One should modify the *yājamāna* formulas, which are prescribed in the singular, when there are many [sacrificers]. (16) It is established up to the *pravara*. (17) Having thus chosen the *hotṛ*, one chooses all [the officiants]: those of the same *gotra* who are not separated [by another *gotra*] only once, and those separated [by another *gotra*] for each individual person. (18) When [the rite] is completed, having set aside the fires, they should offer their respective *agnihotra*s separately. (19) It is established up to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering. (20) On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having piled the *vamiśa* altar, all who are about to press the Soma should undergo initiation (*dīkṣā*). (21) All partake of the sacrificer’s portion. (22)

From the *abhyundana* (overflowing) rite up to the *pāvana* (purification), the Adhvaryu initiates each of the *madhyataḥkārin* priests individually through the mouth of the Gṛhapati; the Pratiprasthātṛ initiates the wives through the mouth of the Adhvaryu; the Neṣṭṛ initiates the wives of the *ardhin* priests through the mouth of the Pratiprasthātṛ; the Unnetṛ initiates the wives of the *tṛtīyin* priests through the mouth of the Neṣṭṛ; and the Unnetṛ initiates the wives of the *pādin* priests through the mouth of the Neṣṭṛ. Another Brāhmaṇa initiates the Unnetṛ himself. This procedure is established up to the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-offering). The rites beginning with the initiation involving the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) up to the wearing of the garment (*prāvaraṇa*) are established for each one individually.

The placing of the fuel-sticks (samidādhāna) [is performed]; 25. for each [victim], the rites beginning with the releasing of the gold plate (rukmapratimocana) and ending with the Vātsapra hymn, as well as those beginning with the making of the fist (muṣṭikaraṇa) and ending with the announcement (āvedana), constitute the established procedure for the initiation (daikṣa) ritual. 26. One should consume the fast-food (vrata) mixed with clarified butter; they should provide maintenance for all the fasts without deficiency. 27. There are twelve initiations (dīkṣās). 28. The established procedure continues up until the purchase of the Soma (kraya). 29. The cow for the purchase of the King (Soma) has an additional ear when there are sixteen [stotras]. 30. There are twelve Upasad days. 31. Having performed the rites up to the spreading out (vyūhana) on the first day, they dwell [there]. 32. On the following day, the piling of the altar (citi) takes place on another day.

On another day, on the eleventh, having performed the rites up to the dragging away of the dung, they dwell there. On the following day, all are consecrated. When the [Soma] has been set in motion, they hand over the staffs of the consecrated to the Maitrāvaruṇa. The Upavasatha day is completed. On the following day, the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra sacrifice takes place. The procedure is established up to the bringing down of the King (Soma). He brings down the twelfth portion with a different garment. The procedure is established up to the making of the body-ornaments. Having removed the made-up body-ornaments in five parts, he distributes them.

He touches [the cups] with the *prāṇagraha* formulas, using the verses beginning "This one before" (*ayaṃ puro bhūḥ*) for each direction respectively, and with the fifth verse in the center. (41) On the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* days, and on the tenth day, the *aṃśu*, *adābhya*, and *prāṇagraha* cups are offered. (42) The procedure is established up to the *pravara*. (43) Having taken eight chips of fuel wood, he chooses the Hotṛ with the calls for the seasons (*ṛtupraiṣa*), etc., according to the traditional recitation; [he chooses] the sacrificers with the modification: "Agni is the leader of the divine clans, these pressing sacrificers are the leaders of men. (44) The procedure is established up to the consumption [of the Soma]. (45)

The householder consumes the *camasa* of the sacrificer. 46. This is established up to the time of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). 47. Having offered the two *dākṣiṇa* oblations, they should proceed day by day along the path of the sacrificial fees, shaking the black antelope skins while reciting: "This, I give as a sacrificial fee for my welfare, for my fame, for the heavenly world, and for immortality."

They should give a wandering gift (*prāsarpaka*) of gold, a garment, or a thousand cows; on the *Ahīna* sacrifice, they should give one hundred and eight. (48) They should distribute it equally and give it day by day. (49) On the final day, there is the throwing away of the horns and the dismissal of the companions (*sakhyavisarjana*). (50) At the ends of the pressings (*savana*), they move out. (51) Prior to the *Yajñāyajñiya* chant, he takes up the *Vasatīvarī* waters. (52) The ritual is established up to the *Hāriyojana* cup. (53) Being urged across, the *Āgnīdhra* stands behind his own hearth (*dhiṣṇya*) and announces the immediate pressing to Indra and Agni: "I announce [the sacrifice] to Indra and Agni. (54)

He announces: "To Mitra and Varuṇa, to the All-gods, to the Brāhmaṇas who are worthy of Soma and drinkers of Soma; O Brahman, restrain the speech! (54) The days conclude with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. (55) Following that, they restrain their speech. (56) Having offered the universal expiation with the verse, "Thou art the unswerving, O Agni," he places the fuel-sticks on the fire. (57) Having bound together the sacrificial grass and the fuel, and when the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, they release their speech. (58)

The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period is performed day by day. Its first day is a *sadyas-trivṛt-agniṣṭoma* with the *rathaṃtara-sāman*. [The ritual] is established up to the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant. They chant the *stotra* outside for the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* days, but inside the *sadas* for the others. With the sound of the chariot of Mahendra, he introduces the *stotra* with two blades of darbha grass. In all cases involving the *pṛṣṭhya* ritual forms, there are two blades of darbha. He causes the chariot to turn outside the sacrificial altar. Day by day, there are the unyoking of the yoke-horses, the commencement, the mounting, the verses containing the word *ap*, and the continuous offerings.

The *vasatīvarī* waters, the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*), and the milking of the cows for the milk-offerings [are prepared]. (8) Thereafter, he announces the Soma-pressing of the following day to the *Āgnīdhra*. (9) It is a fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*) *ukthya* sacrifice with the *Bṛhat* as its *Sāman*. (10) He introduces the *stotra* with the sound of a drum, provided that there is no thunder. (11) It is a seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) *ukthya* sacrifice with the *Vairūpa* as its *Sāman*. (12) He introduces the *stotra* by fanning [the fire]. (13) The rule for the *atigrāhya* cups is the same as in the *Vājapeya* sacrifice. (14) It is a twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*) *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice with the *Vairāja* as its *Sāman*. (15) "O Agni, purify our lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*)—this is the *atigrāhya* cup dedicated to Agni.

With the formula, "I take thee with the splendor of Agni and of the Brahman; I offer thee," he offers into the fire. He makes [the sacrificer] long-lived as he consumes [the draught]. 16. With the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) he introduces the *stotra*. 17. Having spread out *avakā* grass, he churns the fire into the lap of the *udgātṛ*. 18. After the Adhvaryu has offered into the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "Be ye two of one mind for us," he makes an additional offering over it with the *virāj* verse, "Enkindled, O Agni. 19. The *ukthya* sacrifice has twenty-seven verses and the *śākvara* as its *sāman*. 20. With the verse, "That power of his has shone forth," he draws the *atigrāhya* cup for Indra, [reciting] "And thee with the splendor of Indra..."

With the formula, "I offer with the vigor of the Kṣatra," he makes the offering; with the formula, "O Indra, bestow splendor," they two consume [the draught]. (21) He introduces the Stotra with water containing barley-grains. (22) They chant while the waters are resounding together. (23) When it is completed, they pour out [the water] at the Mārjālīya fire-altar. (24) It is an Ukthya sacrifice consisting of thirty-three [verses], having the Raivata as its Sāman. (25) With the verse, "His rays have become visible," he draws the Atigrāhya cup for Sūrya; with the formula, "I offer with the luster of Sūrya and of the plants," he makes the offering; with the formula, "O Sūrya, bestow splendor," they two consume [the draught]. (26)
The sixth day has its own *ṛtu-yajus* (27). He joins the *yājyā* with the *praiṣa*: "Ye3 yajāmahe! O Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus, drink the Soma with the *ṛtu* from the office of the Adhvaryu;
O Aśvins, drink the honey, you who possess shining fires and pure vows, you who are the bearers of the sacrifice through the *ṛtu*. (28)
Thus, when [the sacrifice] is completed:
"Harness today the chariot that comes hitherward, which carries heroes; here is your unyoking.
Mix the oblations with honey for our delight; come, O you who possess abundant wealth, and drink the Soma."

Thus, in the *vyūḍha* (expanded) arrangement [of the days], [the chant] begins with "Agni Gṛhapati from the *gārhapatya* fire" (30); in the *samūḍha* (contracted) arrangement, [it begins] with the same (31). In the *vyūḍha* arrangement, another *triṣṭubh* verse is prescribed (32). He introduces the hymn (*stotra*) with the lowing of cows (33). In the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) of the *ukthya* sacrifices, the response (*pratigara*) is the *śilpa* chant (34). The Maitrāvaruṇa priest recites the *Vālakhilyas* (35); the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites the *Vṛṣākapi* hymn (36); and the Acchāvāka recites the *Śaṃsatya* and *Evayāmarut* hymns (36). When the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) has concluded, they eat honey or clarified butter (37). The *chandomā* days are performed as *ukthya* sacrifices: the twenty-four-fold, the forty-four-fold, and the forty-eight-fold [stomas] (38).

The twenty-four-fold Agniṣṭoma is the tenth day, which is "speechless" (avivākya). On that day, they should avoid using words that have a corresponding form [to the name of the sacrificer]. If they are unable to do so, the Brahman, the Gṛhapati, or the observers may speak out. If two syllables remain when speaking out, they should inform the Hotṛ. He should then bring that Anuṣṭubh verse into indirect expression. At the end of the Patnīsaṃyājas, having stepped forward toward the east, [the Hotṛ recites]: "This one, with a thousandfold wisdom, is the vision of the sages; he is the thought, the light, the upholder of the law. Bradhna has brought together the converging dawns."
Spotless, of one mind, full of zeal at the time of the cow's milking.

Thus they stand by the Āhavanīya fire (6). Having crept forward to the Sadas, they sit down (7). Having entered the Havirdhāna, the Adhvaryu takes the mental draught (mānasa-graha) (8). Having made this [mental] vessel, [he thinks]: "O Vāyu, O Soma; you are taken with a base; for Prajāpati, thee!"—thus mentally he performs the taking and the setting down, as well as the commencement of the Stotra (9). Having chanted the Sārparājñī verses in their regular order, he looks at the Hotṛ (10). The Adhvaryu responds mentally to those [verses] (11). He addresses him, saying: "O Adhvaryu, speak the Brahman! (12). Om.

The Adhvaryu [recites] "m̐hotar. 13. The Hotṛ recites the Caturhotṛ formulas according to their sequence, together with the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, and finally the Saptahotṛ. 14. He responds with "oṃ hotar" and "tathā hotar. 15. Having responded and said "hotar" regarding the Caturhotṛs, he recites Prajāpati as the seventeenth. 16. Whether the Adhvaryu or the Hotṛ [recites], those who know that Prajāpati is the seventeenth and is inherent in the sacrifice, they—the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattra*)—prosper. 17. Their sacrifice does not falter, for it is grounded in Prajāpati.

By means of the sacrifice they find firm support. 18. "O, cause [the Hotṛ] to announce!"—thus it is traditionally taught. 19. Prajāpati, indeed, as the seventeenfold [stoma], is attached to the sacrifice. 20. Whether he follows from the *anuvākyā* or whether he proceeds from the *yājyā*, by that divine path he goes. 21. Their sacrifice does not falter; they find firm support in Prajāpati through the sacrifice. 22. "Om, Adhvaryu! So be it, Adhvaryu!"—with these words he responds. 23. Having responded, once the recitation (*śastra*) is completed, they perform mentally the rites beginning with the taking of the cup (*graha*) up until the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*). 24. Looking upon one another is the invitation (*upahava*). 25.

They consume [the food] with the *jagacchandas* verse. Having covered [the Audumbarī post], they restrain their speech while holding onto the Audumbarī post with the verses beginning, "May there be stability here, may there be self-stability here. Until the sun has set behind the trees or until the stars are visible, the two Adhvaryus, not passing beyond the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, hold onto a black antelope skin. Having held onto it together, they go out toward the east and recite:

"O Indra and Parvata, you who fight in the van, whoever shall attack us, strike him down, strike him down with the thunderbolt; strike him down, strike him down. May he find a deep abyss in the distance where he may perish."
O Hero, may you, the destroyer, crush our enemies on every side; may you destroy them from all quarters.

Thus they worship at the Āgnīdhrīya fire-altar (29). They place two fuel-sticks on the fire and choose their boons (30). The *udayanīya* Atirātra sacrifice is explained by [the rules for] the *prāyaṇīya* (31). It concludes as established (32). At the time of shaving, they have themselves shaved, including the top-knots (33). The *udavasānīyā* offering is performed separately (34).

In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), the cups begin with the *aindravāyava*: (1) in the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* rites and on the tenth day; (2) in the first three-day period of the *pṛṣṭhya*, they begin with the *aindravāyava*, then the *śukra*, and then the *āgrayaṇa*; (3) in the second three-day period of the *pṛṣṭhya* when it is combined (*samūḍha*) and in the *chandoma* days, one should repeat the threefold series; then, in the expanded (*vyūḍha*) form, they begin with the *āgrayaṇa*, then the *aindravāyava*, two times the *śukra*, the *āgrayaṇa*, and the *aindravāyava*. (4) The pressing for Upāṃśu is performed twelve times, eight times, and eleven times respectively.

In the *chandoga* [stotras], there are eleven, twelve, and eight [verses] respectively. By this, the applications of the potsherds (*kapāla*) and the *bhakṣa-mantras* are explained, as well as the invocations for the *pavamāna* [laud]. "Great is Indra by his might" is the *puroruc* for the *māhendra* [cup] in the *chandoga* [stotras]. "Thou art born, O Indra," [is used] in the *chandoga* [stotras] as well. This is the ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice (*paśukalpa*). He immolates the eleven animals distributed [among the deities]. On the day of the concluding oblation (*udayanīya*), there is a goat for Agni. Having emerged from the sacrificial session (*sattra*), they should perform the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* *agniṣṭoma*s with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The *sattra*s and *ahīna*s have the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) as their archetype.

For the Gavāmayana, they should undergo initiation on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha. 13. It is established up to the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra. 14. Following that, the Prāyaṇīya Ukthya is the Caturviṃśa. 15. Then follows the Abhiplava Ṣaḍaha: Jyotis Agniṣṭoma, Gaus Ukthya, Āyus Ukthya, Gaus Ukthya, Āyus Ukthya, Jyotis Agniṣṭoma. 16. One should repeat that [sequence] four times; they enter upon the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, which constitutes one month. 17. By means of that, they pass four months. 18. There are three Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas and one Pṛṣṭhya.

There is a six-day period, the Abhijit, and three Svarasāman days, which are either Agniṣṭomas or Ukthyas. In these, he offers the Atigrāhya cups day by day in continuous succession; at all [the Svarasāman days], he performs the placing with the *upayāma* formula. He draws [the cup] with: "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, for creatures, thee! He deposits it with: "This is thy womb; for Prajāpati, for creatures, thee! He offers it with: "For Prajāpati, for creatures! He draws [another cup] with: "For the intermediate space, for the trees, thee! He deposits it with: "This is thy womb; for the intermediate space, for the trees, thee!"

He sets it down with the formula, "For the atmosphere, for the trees"; he offers with, "To the waters, to the plants"; he draws [the Soma] with, "This is thy womb; to the waters, to the plants"; he sets it down with, "To the waters, to the plants"; and he offers with, "To the waters, to the plants. 21. That [period] from the beginning consists of two days; that is the month. 22. The first fortnight is to be carried together as one unit. 23. After that comes the Viṣuvat day, which is accompanied by the Sadivākīrtya.

The Agniṣṭoma consists of twenty-one [stotras]. (1) When the sun has risen, he begins the Prātaranuvāka recitation. (2) During that [recitation], he draws the Atigrāhya cups: the Saurya cup with the verses beginning *ud u tyam jātavedasam* (the *āvṛtta-saṃtanīs*); the Vaiśvakarmana cup with the verse *ayā viṣṭhā janayan* (the *prājāpatya*); and the cup for the herbs, waters, trees, atmosphere, progeny, and Prajāpati Vācaspati. (3) A white goat is to be sacrificed to Sūrya; it is dedicated to Upāṃśu. (4) If the white goat were not available at sunset, [one should sacrifice] a goat to Sūrya from the heaven.

"O Viśvahā, release all those who dwell in heaven; may he carry us across our enemies"—with these words he offers the oblation. (5) On the northern wing, the Svarasāmans and Abhiplavas are performed in reverse order. (6) After the Viṣuvat day, the Svarasāmans proceed in the forward direction. (7) Among them, the Saṃtanayas are performed in reverse order. (8) At their first [Saṃtanaya], he draws the Āditya Atigrāhya cup with the verse beginning "sutrāmāṇam. (9) On the following day, until the Mahāvrata, he draws the Vaiśvakarman cups in alternating fashion. (10) The Viśvajit is a Śilpa sacrifice; it contains all the Pṛṣṭhas at the midday pressing among the Pṛṣṭha-stotras.

The arts [are taught]. 11. The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period with the *trayastrim̐śa* as its commencement; 12. three *abhiplava* six-day periods; 13. the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period with the *trayastrim̐śa* as its commencement, followed by four *abhiplava* six-day periods—this constitutes a month. 14. By means of this, they complete four months. 15. Three *abhiplava* six-day periods, the *āyuḥ* and *go* days (two days), and the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). 16. After the *viṣuvat* day, the twenty-eight-day period, the *mahāvrata*, and the *atirātra* constitute a month. 17. Thus.

Then there is that which is to be performed by two [groups] and that which is to be performed by one. 18. The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, the *trayastrim̐śa* as the opening, and four *abhiplava* six-day periods constitute one month. 19. By means of this, they complete five months. 20. Two *abhiplava* six-day periods, the *āyus* day, the *go* day, two days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the ten days following the *viṣuvat*, the four-day period, the *mahāvrata*, and the *atirātra* constitute one month. 21.

The Mahāvrata is a Pañcaviṃśa Agniṣṭoma. (1) When the sun has risen, he begins the Prātaranuvāka recitation. (2) During that [recitation], he sets out the Atigrāhya vessels for the Arka cup: five to the east, one to the south, one to the north, one to the west, and one in the middle, facing himself. [He sets them out] for the Pṛṣṭhas, the Vṛttas, and the Saṃtanis; for the Saura, the Vṛttas, and the Saṃtanis; and for the Āditya, Vaiśvakarmana, and Prājāpatya cups. For the Vṛṣṭi cup, he prepares a clay vessel with four nipples.

A sixteen-fold oblation for Sarasvatī; a fifteen-fold for the Prāṇagrahas; a thirty-two-fold for Viṣṇu; a thirty-three-fold for Bṛhaspati. 3. At the appropriate time, he touches the two cups, the Āśvina and the Dābhya, with the Prāṇagraha formulas. 4. "Thou art Vāyu, named Breath; Svāhā! May the god Savitṛ grant me luster. "Thou art Life, named Sight; Svāhā! May the god Dhātṛ grant me hearing. "Thou art Form, named Color; Svāhā! May the god Indra grant me sovereign power."

You are Śruti, whose name is Satya; Svāhā! To you, for the god Bṛhaspati, grant me abundance of wealth. You are Bhūmi, whose name is Bhūti; Svāhā! To you, for the gods and the ancestors, grant me the embryo of the waters and the plants.

"I take you for the expanse of *ṛta*; I take you for the support of *ṛta*; I take you for the light of *ṛta*; I take you for the truth of *ṛta*; I take you for the measure of *ṛta*. With the verse, "This one has become the Puras," he takes the *pṛśni-prāṇagrahas* at their respective times. With the verse, "O Indra, come to us," he takes [the draught] from the eastern half with the formula, "Thou art taken with a base; for Indra, thee, who art accompanied by the *ṛk*. He deposits it with the formula, "This is thy womb; for Indra, thee, who art accompanied by the *ṛk*. With the verse, "We praise thee, O hero," he takes [the draught] from the southern half. With the verse, "For we invoke thee indeed," he takes [the draught] from the northern half.
Which of these worlds shall we now establish? Indra and all the gods together—may Indra, along with the Ādityas, establish for us the sacrifice, our bodies, and our progeny.
Thus, in the latter half [of the verse],
it came to be that he was the eldest among all beings, from whom the fierce one, of brilliant valor, was born;
as soon as he was born, he overthrew his enemies— he in whom all the protectors rejoice.
Thus, as applied for one's own benefit; now for the others in four stanzas:
O Lord of the Field, milk for us a honeyed wave, like a cow her milk—dropping honey, well-purified like clarified butter. May the Lords of Truth have mercy upon us.

"Thus, you are taken with a support; for Aditi, you who have four forms"—with these words he takes the third draught. "The great mother..."—with this [verse] he pours out the second portion. "This is the third pressing"—with these words he completes it. "This is your womb; for Aditi, you who have four forms"—with these words he deposits it. "The purifying Sarasvatī for us"—this is the draught for Sarasvatī. "You are Vāyu"—these are the *pṛśni-prāṇa* draughts. "This Viṣṇu..."—this is the draught for Viṣṇu. "Bṛhaspati, being born first..."—this is the draught for Bṛhaspati. 7

During the Māhendra [stotra], they exercise their crafts: (1) the *upariṣadya-uktha*; (2) the swing (*preṅkha*) for the *udgātṛ*; (3) the board (*phalaka*) for the *hotṛ*, and the grass-mat (*kūrca*) for the others. (4) The lute (*vāṇa*) has a hundred strings, a vessel made of *udumbara* wood, strings made of muñja grass, a handle of khadira wood, the shape of a lute, and is covered with the skin of a calf. (5) Having scraped it with a branch of reed (*vetasa*), he hands it to the *udgātṛ* and introduces the *stotra*. (6) He hands it to the sacrificer. (7) He causes it to be played until the conclusion (*nidhana*) of the *stotra*. All [the instruments].

The wives play various kinds of lutes, from among which are the *kāṇḍavīṇā*s. In all directions the drums resound; the earth-drum is the fifth, located behind the *āgnīdhrīya* shed, knee-high and half within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*), covered with the skin of a sacrificial animal, and provided with a tail as a handle. Eight female slaves, carrying water-jars and dressed in unwashed garments, attend upon the *mārjālīya* shed. There are two cows each, indeed fragrant cows, cows smelling of bdellium (*guggulu*);
cows who are the mothers of clarified butter—may they be present here in great abundance.
Singing thus, "This is the honey of the *madhūka* tree," she circumambulated him clockwise, treading upon his feet.
Indeed, the cows of Maṅgīra did not drink the water of the Gaṅgā;
they drank at the river Sarasvatī and then rose up toward the east.
Others say this [is honey]:
when one speaks harsh or vulgar words, Aṅgiras and Dāsaka prosper with welfare, while the village or the ox suffers from carrying its load.
"Others say this is honey:
'We swim here like rafts; let the pins move about here. Having swallowed the honey for you, we pull it out like a toothpick.'"

Having thus led [the water] around, they walk back along the front of the *mārjālīya* fire-altar. A *śūdra* and an Ārya stretch out a white, round skin, saying, "These [people] have driven away the prosperity; these have brought misfortune. Outside the *vedi*, the *śūdra* says, "These have succeeded; these have prepared the broth. Inside the *vedi*, the Ārya says, "These have won; these have prepared the broth. Having won, he places the *prasadasya* offering on the southern hip of the *vedi* in an enclosed space, where a *vṛṣala* couple stand, one as the *apagara* and the other as the *abhigara*.

The *pūrvah* says, "Much indeed have these performed unwholesome acts at this sacrifice—those who purify the *pīklojas*," and he goes outside the sacrificial ground (*bahirvedi*). The *abhigaraḥ* says, "Much indeed have these performed wholesome acts at this sacrifice—those who purify the *pīklojas*," and he goes inside the sacrificial ground (*antarvedi*). The *pūrvah* says, "A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), a loose woman (*pumścalī*), one of ignoble deeds, one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), and one of evil conduct have been excluded," and he goes outside the sacrificial ground. The *abhigaraḥ* says, "Shame on you, loose woman! You are the cleaner of another man's paramour; you are the washer of every man's penis," and he goes inside the sacrificial ground.

The *brahmacārī* [stands] to the north; having made a space for the exit from the *tīrtha*, they spread out a white skin with the neck upwards and the hairy side outwards. The son of the king, a Brāhmaṇa, or a Rājanya belonging to the king's faction, lies upon it. In front of the sacrificial post-hole, he fastens his armor. Having put on his armor, he goes around the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) clockwise, draws the bow thrice, and discharges the arrow thrice—[aiming] at the ashes, at the center, and at the necks [of the animals].

Having raised [the vessel] toward the east, he brings it back at the fourth [verse]. Having mounted the wooden board (*phalaka*), he responds (*pratigṛṇāti*) with the verse: "They all choose thy will" (*tve kratum api vṛñjanti viśve*) from the eastern half; with "When these three become helpers" (*yad ete trir bhavanti ūmāḥ*) from the southern half; with "Mix the sweet with the sweeter than the sweet" (*svādoḥ svādīyaḥ svādunā sṛja sam*) from the northern half; and with "Yonder honey, fight against with honey" (*adaḥ su madhu madhunā abhi yodhīḥ*) from the western half.
