He pours the *vṛṣṭigraha* into the *dadhigraha* vessel. When the *āditya* and *māhendra* cups have been offered, he pours the *dyugraha* into his own vessel.

They descend toward the portions of food being brought. 21. "I consume your greatness; I consume your splendor; I consume your praise; I consume your glory; I consume your food"—with these words, they consume it within themselves. 22. The oblation to be offered when the sun has set has been explained. 23.

The ritual procedure for the cups (*graha*) of the twelve-day rite has been stated. 1. In the *abhyāsa* (repetition) of the *abhiplava* [six-day period], one should perform the sequence beginning with the cup for Indra-Vāyu and ending with the cup for Śukra; when it is reversed, it begins with the cup for Śukra. For the *svarasāman* days, the sequence begins with the cup for Indra-Vāyu and ends with the cup for Śukra on the first and last days, and likewise in the *āyus* [stoma]; elsewhere, it is otherwise. 2. The arrangement of the animal sacrifices (*paśuklpti*). 3. There are eleven victims at the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* rites; they may be dedicated to Indra-Agni, or the sacrificial animals of the specific rite (*kratu-paśu*) may be used even in the interval, or all may be dedicated to Indra-Agni. 4. Six animals are to be immolated.

The white-backed animal dedicated to Bṛhaspati is for the thirty-third day; the cow dedicated to Heaven and Earth is at the Chandomas; its calf is for Vāyu on the second day; the speckled one is for Speech on the third day; the barren cow is for Aditi at the Avivākya; the three-colored bull dedicated to Viśvakarman is at both Mahāvrata rites. Or alternatively, one may practice the set of eleven animals distributed [throughout]. From that point, there are twenty-one additional animals.

At the twenty-first [day], a Vāmana [bull] sacred to Viṣṇu is to be immolated; at the twenty-third, a goat sacred to Agni for the Upāṃśu deity. (7) For those performing the Gavāmayana, there are twelve utsarjana days. (8) This is established up to the thirty-third day. (9) On the thirty-third day, he drives away the calves for the Sāṃnāyya offering to Indra. (10) He milks before the carrying around of the Vasatīvarī waters. (11) When the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, he calls for the next day's pressing two days in advance, and for the following day's pressing at sunrise. (12) Restraining their speech, they proceed with the rite dedicated to Prajāpati.

They establish [the fires] with thirteen *sāmidhenī* verses. He causes the *sāmidhenīs* to be recited silently along with the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*). Having performed the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) to Upāṃśu-devatā, he offers an eight-potsherd cake to Agni Vasumat in the morning. Having brought the evening milking into the unheated morning milk and having placed it together, he proceeds with the two loud calls (*praiṣa*). At the conclusion of the portion for the *Āgnīdhra*, they consume a third part of the curds from the Soma-drinking cups. [He offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Maruts.

Having reached midday, he proceeds with loud calls and accompanied by the *praiṣa* formulas (18). At the conclusion of the *āgnīdhra*-portion, they consume the other half of the curds from the Soma-drinking cups (19). Having offered a cake on twelve potsherds to the Viśvedevas in the afternoon, he proceeds with loud calls and accompanied by the *praiṣa* formulas (20). At the conclusion of the *āgnīdhra*-portion, they consume the remainder of the curds from the Soma-drinking cups (21). When the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings have been completed, he summons the *śvasutyā* (the pressing for the following day) (22). On the next day...

They commence with the Soma-sacrifices alone; this is their first release. Then there are four [sacrifices] month by month prior to the Abhijit; the sixth is after the Viśvajit; the seventh is then on the eightieth day; then four more month by month. If these should be in excess, they should undergo initiation on the new moon day; but if they complete the series, then on each twelfth day.
Thus ends the second chapter on the Vājapeya in the Mānava-Śrautasūtra; the Vājapeya-sūtra is completed.

Now we shall explain the supplementary rites (anugraha). 1. One should perform the evening oblation before sunrise, or the morning oblation before sunset. 2. One must not let the proper time lapse for the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Cāturmāsya offerings, the Animal Sacrifice, and the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice. 3. During the rainy season, if there is a mass of clouds, one should offer the oblation again after sunset if it was offered before sunset.

It is known from scripture that even if it has dawned and dawned again, one does not stumble nor does one suffer distress. There were indeed seers who were practitioners of ritual application; they offered the Agnihotra sacrifice every half-month. Therefore, one who is a wanderer, one who is ill, or one who is afflicted, offers the Agnihotra every half-month. He draws up fourteen portions taken four times each at once; there is a single fuel-stick and a single oblation.

He is fit for the half-month [rite]. (8) He should pour fourteen oblations into the *sruk* ladle, full with the *sruva* spoon; likewise, others for the *Gārhapatya* and *Dakṣiṇāgni* fires. (9) The mantras and the oblations for the *Sabhya* and *Āvasathya* fires are according to what has been heard [in the scriptures]. (10) By this very fourfold oblation, the morning oblation is explained. (11) When the *Agnihotra* has not been offered for six months, or when one has not performed the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *Āgrayaṇa*, or the animal sacrifice, one should offer two cakes on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat and Agni Pathikṛt, and then perform the *Āgrayaṇa*. (12) Together.

If one has maintained the *agnihotra* for a year but has not yet performed the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *āgrayaṇa*, or the animal sacrifice, he should offer two *aṣṭākapāla* cakes—one to Agni Tantumat and one to Agni Pathikṛt—and then offer cakes on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara; he should perform the intermediate oblations (*antaritāḥ homāḥ*). Alternatively, having offered a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he need not attend to those intermediate oblations. By this, he obtains everything: the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the animal sacrifice, and the *āgrayaṇa*. Having performed the *āgrayaṇa*, he should give a choice gift (*vara*) at the Āhavanīya fire—either a cow or a garment—in place of the horse; so it is known. [The section ends with] *indriya*.

"Or rather, he is deprived of that vigor by which his father and grandfather did not drink Soma. Therefore, one should give a full vessel of foodstuffs, roots, or fruits; but one must certainly not fail to sacrifice.

He pours out clarified butter (ājya). In its absence, oil is the substitute; in its absence, curds or milk. In their absence, barley flour or rice flour—having mixed these with water—one should prepare them for the purpose of clarified butter. Darbha grass is used for the strewn covering (paristaraṇa). In its absence, one should prepare materials for the covering using plants that have joints and stalks, excluding *kaṭasī*, *ira*, *śūṣa*, *śuṇṭhana*, *nalapa*, *rivāha*, *mūta*, *pava*, and *valvaja*. The fuel-wood pieces (*idhmakāṣṭha*) are twice the length of a span (*prādeśa*). The fire-drill wood (*araṇi*) is four finger-breadths in height.

Six *aṅgulas* in width and twenty-four *aṅgulas* in length, with eight *aṅgulas* left out from the base and another three *aṅgulas* [above that], it is known as the "womb of the deity" (*devayoni*); there one should churn the fire. (7) The enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are one cubit (*aratni*) in length; the sacrificial branch (*śākhā*) and the strainer (*pavitra*) are one span (*prādeśa*) long. The measure of the potsherds (*kapāla*) is one-fourth of a palm-span (*vipāṇitala*). (8) Having mixed those eight [potsherds] with clay, he spreads them out on the *gārhapatya* fire-altar. (9) By this same method, they become thirty-three each, becoming progressively smaller and smaller.

The reduction [of the size] of the *kapālas* should be according to the increasing age [of the horse], up to the measure of a skull. 10. He spreads out all the *kapālas* so that they are the size of a horse's hoof; as for what was said [previously], that is indistinct, for horses are of various sizes. 12. For a three-year-old horse, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) consists of four handfuls, even for the one dedicated to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivīya*). 13. In this very same way, they prepare the remaining flour-smear (*piṣṭalepa*). 14. Regarding the statement "the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are not sacrificed at the third establishment of the fires," Gautama says [they are not]; Vātsya says they are not [offered] at the animal sacrifice nor at the Soma sacrifice. 15. It is performed.
These two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice; for it is known: "If one were to omit the two butter-portions, one would omit the eyes of the sacrifice."

The teachers say: "If, after the calves have been driven away, thieves were to carry off the cows, or they were lost or died, how would one know of the *sāṃnāyya*? One should wait for the evening milking until midnight, and for the morning milking until midday. If they should arrive during that time, he should milk them three times with pauses: the second time with two pauses, and the third time with three pauses. If all have arrived, it is as prescribed in the tradition. If they do not arrive at all, he should mutter over the cow taken by the King (the bull): "O army... (the rest of the verse).

Thus, when cows have been seized by thieves, when they have vanished while speech was leading them forward, or when they have died, if [the cow] should arrive after this has been performed, one should milk her silently and give the milk to the Brahmins. (6) Whatever milk one obtains, one should milk it with three pauses. (7) If no milk is obtained, there shall be a five-śarāva-measure of rice-porridge for Indra, or a gruel of flour as the sacrificial substance. (8) It is indeed known: "Rice and barley are the milk of cattle; therefore, they offer these. (9)

When a son is born, he brings two fire-drills (*araṇī*) made from *aśvattha* wood that has grown from the heart of a *śamī* tree; they should be ten or twelve finger-breadths long. Having churned the fire with those two, he performs the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) for that boy. He may give him a name at that time, have his tonsure (*cūḍā*) performed at that time, initiate him (*upanayana*) at that very time, observe the vows (*vratacaryā*) at that time, and marry a wife at that time. That is the domestic fire (*śālāgni*), that is the fire for the domestic sacrifice (*aupāsanīya*); or rather, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) takes place in the father’s fire, because of the scriptural insight: "The self, indeed, is the name of the son. That [fire] is the one used for the *brāhmaudana* rite.
Having prepared this [fire], they consign it to the two kindling woods; having consigned it, they churn it again; having churned it, one should perform there sacrifices with unlimited rites.

We shall explain the *pañcāgnika* (the rite of the five fires). 1. The bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), the purification, the kindling, the strewing of grass, and the sprinkling of water are explained as being like the morning and evening establishment of the fires (*sāyaṃprātarādhāna*), as well as the oblation (*homa*). 2. He offers on the *sabhyāgni* with the formula: "O Agni Sabhya, who art seated in the assembly, enjoy [this], Svāhā! and on the *āvasathyāgni* with the formula: "O Agni Āvasathya, who art seated in the dwelling, enjoy [this], Svāhā! This concludes the oblation. 3. Having offered with the *vyāhṛti*s as prescribed, he offers at all times and during the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice on both the *sabhyāgni* and the *āvasathyāgni* with the verse: "And may the serpent Arbudi... 4. When the fire has been brought forward...

He establishes the *sabhyāvasathya* fires. It is not prescribed for optional rites (*kāmyā*). Indeed, it is known: "These five are the vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna; these five fires are established for their support and protection. The sacrifice is fivefold; thus, the entire sacrifice is grasped.

Now, if one who is about to die should establish the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he need not wait for a season, nor a lunar mansion, nor seek a suitable site, nor attend to the ritual materials (saṃbhāra). He does not recite the Sārparājñī verses, nor does he pronounce the Gharmaśiras formula. He should not cook the Brahmaudana rice-porridge. For who knows what tomorrow will bring? Having merely placed a mound from an anthill and Darbha grass as the ritual materials, he should repeat the formulas. It is known: "The earth is the sacrificial fuel (śamī); the Aśvattha tree is its embryo. Therefore, having brought two fire-drills (araṇī) made from it, he should produce fire by means of them.

Having churned [the fire], he should establish the *gārhapatya* with "Bhūḥ," the *dakṣiṇāgni* with "Bhuvaḥ," the *āhavanīya* with "Svaḥ," and both the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. (7) If he should die before the *pūrṇāhuti* offering, they should cremate him according to the rules for one who has maintained the sacred fires after having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*. If he dies after the *āgneyī* [offering] but before the *iṣṭi*, they should perform the *iṣṭi-saṃsthā*. And from that point onward, as long as he does not die, he should sacrifice with sacrifices of unlimited number. (8)

While he is away on a journey, having produced these fires for the sake of Soma, he should perform the sacrifice after taking up the materials for the *samījyā* (the sacrifice to be performed upon returning). Or, having sacrificed, there may be the abandonment of the fires, or rather not, because of the authority of the revealed scripture (*śruti*). For it is said: "He who abandons the fire is indeed a slayer of the hero among the gods. Therefore, one should not abandon them. Having cast the later fires into the former fires with the formula, "Be ye two of one mind for us, O you who belong to the common hearth," he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnimat.

One should perform the Agnihotra oblations with the Agnihotra itself, and not with Soma sacrifices nor with Havis sacrifices. For that [Agrayana rite], having cooked a mess of rice on the Gārhapatya fire and offered it to the deities of the Agrayana, one should consume it; or alternatively, having let a cow loose upon new grain, one should offer the Agnihotra with her milk. That [cow] is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or else the first-born calf.

In the spring, one should offer a *saumya* oblation of *veṇuyava* grains. (1) Some plants are domestic, while others are wild. (2) If the plants do not ripen, or if there is no new grain, one should release a cow to graze; with her milk, one should perform the *agnihotra*. (3) That cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or else a first-born calf. (4)

He offers with milk, or with barley-gruel, or with clarified butter, or with curds, or with sesame seeds, or with rice grains, or with flowers, or with water, or with *māmsa* (meat), or with *soma*. (1) There shall be no placing over the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) nor any sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) for curds, clarified butter, sesame seeds, rice grains, flowers, fruits, and *soma*. (2) One who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice should not offer *soma*; [for those living in the forest], one may offer fruits, excluding the jujube (*badara*), the *kuvala*, and the *karkandhu*. (3) If he cannot find any of these at all, having used whatever is available starting with fuel-wood (*śundhana*), he should say over the *Āhavanīya* fire: "In truth, I offer truth, svāhā!"—but he must certainly not fail to sacrifice. (4)

One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Pañcadaśa-Dākṣāyaṇayajña. In that [sacrifice], there are two times for the performance of the sacrifice: two full-moon days and two new-moon days. Among them, the earlier full moon is Anumati, and the later is Rākā; the earlier new moon is Sinīvālī, and the later is Kuhū. On those [days], there is a cake (puroḍāśa) dedicated to Agni.

The second [offering] is for Agni and Soma on the preceding full moon; for Indra and Agni on the new moon; for Indra, curdled milk (*dadhi*), on the subsequent full moon; and for Mitra and Varuṇa, clotted curds (*āmikṣā*), on the subsequent new moon. (4) For the curd, [the verses] are "O Indra, you from all sides" and "Your strength"; for the *āmikṣā*, [the verse] is "O Mitra and Varuṇa, stretch forth your arms"; and there is also the whey (*vājina*) for the Viśvedevas. (5) Gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (6)

Now we shall explain the rule for the sacrificial post-hole (yūpāvaṭa). 1. A tree that is thick, crooked, overgrown with creepers, broad, twisted, with a deformed trunk, with a crooked branch, with a withered top, encircled by a creeper, hollow, red, eaten by white-ants, eaten by woodworms, having little pith, or having its pith rotted by water—these are undesirable. One that is shaped like a bow, symmetrical from base to top, with many branches and many leaves—these are praised. 2. We shall now explain the sequence of their application. 3. Death, heart disease, abdominal ailments, and the end of the rains [result from using such trees].

His house is destroyed by fire; his offspring die young; he suffers from leprosy, scrofula, and chronic illness. Regarding the *Śrāddhakalpas*: for those in the former [sections], it is for one desiring stability; for those in the latter, it is for one desiring security (*yogakṣema*), Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the attainment of heaven; or indeed, for all [sections], it is for the attainment of heaven. Now we shall speak concerning the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). One should cause it to fall facing east. If it springs upward, one should know that the wife will set her heart on another man. If there is a hollow at the base, there will be abdominal disease; if at the bottom, a disease of the head; if it is twisted, a disease of the sides.

If the *agniṣṭhā* [post] should break, the sacrificer will die; if the *pṛṣṭhyā*, the wife; if the southern one, the eldest son; if the northern one, the younger son; if the south-eastern one, the *brahmán*; if the south-western one, the *udgātṛ*; if the north-western one, the *hotṛ*; if the north-eastern one, the *adhvaryu*. Or he should offer for the sacrificer with a verse not [otherwise] prescribed, namely "Trātāram" (RV 1.98.2); and for what is not prescribed, [he should use] "Kājava tvam naḥ agne" (VS 27.15) and "Sa tvam naḥ agne" (VS 27.16). If [the post breaks] in the sacrificial post-hole...

While it is being eaten, if bone, ash, husks, a skull, or hair should be found, he should throw them onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) or elsewhere, saying: "I cut away this ill-offering of the sacrifice. It should not be made too thick, lest people suffer from hunger; nor should it be too thin. One should proceed between these two extremes by means of the sacrifice. The sacrificer’s fingers are used for the measurement of the girth-rope (*raśanā*).

Having measured across with a cord, one does not measure the cord by the finger-joints. From the two ends, at the finger-joints, there is a reduction of one-tenth below; the reduction of the mark occurs within the space of one cubit (*aratni*) from the girth-rope.

In this very manner, there is a reduction of the characteristic mark at intervals of one cubit (aratni) upwards; it makes the rough part equal to a *kuṣṭha* measure. The ritual for the *cātvāla* pit has been explained. If, having set it down, it were to be lifted up again, the sacrificer would be liable to die. When about to set it down again in another way, he should mutter this: "Do not harm the sacrifice. The sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) are divided into five parts, or six, or up to twelve; of those on the north, they are divided into three parts, such as the three-cubit [post].

The *camasa* (cup) that has been set aside is traditionally held to belong to the Brahman; the one wiped on the side belongs to the Udgātṛs; the one with a single line belongs to the sacrificer; the one with two lines to the Maitrāvaruṇa; the one with three lines to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the one with a tuft to the Potṛ; the one without a foot to the Neṣṭṛ; and the spade to the Āgnīdhra.

Now we shall explain the distribution of the portions of the animal of the Soma-pressing after the omentum has been extracted. The two jaws together with the tongue belong to the Prastotṛ; the throat and the palate belong to the Āgnīdhra; the eagle-like breast belongs to the Udgātṛ; the right flank belongs to the Adhvaryu; the left to the Pratiprasthātṛ; the right thigh belongs to the Brahman; the left to the Sadasyas; both kidneys belong to the Neṣṭṛ and the Acchāvāka; the lips are common to these two; the feet belong to the Gṛhapati; and the lower parts of the shoulders, the three manikās, and half of the kīkasās [belong to the same].
One half of the shoulder-blade and three ribs belong to the Hotṛ; one half of the shoulder-blade and three ribs belong to the Unnetṛ;

and one half of the shoulder-blade belongs to the Śamitṛ (2). That [half] the Śamitṛ should give to a Brāhmaṇa who is not a Brāhmaṇa by birth (3). The tail belongs to the wife; she should give it to a Brāhmaṇa (4). The head belongs to the Subrahmaṇya.

That which he said regarding the animal for the next day’s pressing—these very thirty-six *ekapadā* verses carry the sacrifice; the *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables, cattle are connected with the *bṛhatī*, and man is connected with the *bṛhatī*. He who, knowing this, performs the distribution [of the portions] is like a *piśāca* or a butcher. Having cut off the two portions, Manu spoke first regarding the offering to Vāyu; from that, men have come to know this.

The Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, the Āgrahāyaṇī, the Ārambhaṇīyā, and the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) would be omitted when these are subsidiary parts [of another rite]. 2. One should bind the Pṛṣṭhyā-barhis; one binds the Ātithyā-barhis and the fuel (idhma) along with its enclosing sticks (paridhi) using formulas beginning with the *śulba*. 3. If the Anūbandhyā is a *payasyā*, there is the offering of the *svaru* at the Soma-pressing (*savana*). 4. Having emerged from the Avabhṛtha bath, there is the assignment of the sacrificial posts (*yūpa-anudeśa*). 5. Some say there are three *payasyās*. He who desires, "May my entire sacrifice be complete and full of essence," should immolate these three barren cows for the sake of the sacrifice.

For the sake of completeness and for the sake of sapidity, [he prepares] for Maitrāvaruṇī. (6) Having strewn [grass] to the north of the Gārhapatya fire for the vessels, he sets out the vessels. (7) Having placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the butter-pot, the milking vessels, and the *camasa* cups; having sprinkled the vessels with water; having caused the milking; having poured out the clarified butter (*ājya*); having carried fire around them (*paryagni-kṛtya*); having wiped the *sruk* and *sruva*; having purified [the butter]; having sprinkled the curd-mixture (*payasyā*) [with butter]; having taken it down from the fire; and having adorned it, he places it behind the *uttaravedi*. (8) Having performed the ritual with the two *ājyabhāga* portions, he sacrifices to the deities of the *anūbandhyā* cow with the *payasyā*, and to the *devikā* goddesses with the clarified butter. (9) The ritual ends with the *iḍā*. (10)

Now they prescribe the ritual procedure for one who desires both [results]: 1. Having sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva in the spring, he should sacrifice again with the Vaiśvadeva in the summer; 2. having sacrificed with the Varuṇapraghāsas in the rainy season, he should sacrifice again with the Varuṇapraghāsas in the autumn; 3. having sacrificed with the Sākamedhas in the winter, he should sacrifice again with the Sākamedhas in the cool season; 4. therein, there are two times for the sacrifice. 5. On the following day, or immediately, he should perform the Śunāsīrya sacrifice; 6. then he should sacrifice with the *pariplava* offerings.

He should sacrifice day after day with each one of those oblations (7). He should sacrifice with the Prasādyaska offerings (8). According to another method, having offered the morning oblation, he should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva in the forenoon, with the Varuṇapraghāsas at midday, and with the Sākamedhas in the afternoon.

On the following day, one should perform the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice on the same day, or [one may wait]. (9) Now, one may sacrifice with all [the Cāturmāsya offerings] together. (10) On the following day, the Vaiśvadeva; on the following day, the Varuṇapraghāsas; the Sākamedhas over two days; on the following day, the Śunāsīrīya on the same day, or [one may wait]. (11) Indeed, he who sacrifices with all the Cāturmāsyas together goes directly by the straight path to the heavenly world. (12) He should sacrifice with these [offerings] ending in an iṣṭi, or ending in an animal sacrifice, or ending in a Soma sacrifice. (13) Or alternatively, [he may sacrifice] at the conclusion of the Varuṇapraghāsas, and [perform] the Vaiśvānara-Pārjanya and subsequent rites. (14) Viṃ...

He performs the sacrifice of the Śitihavis offerings, excluding the Tryambaka and the Punarukta rites. (14) The Avabhṛtha bath and the Pitṛyajña are common [to these], as are the constituent parts of the Sākamedha ritual. (15) He should complete them on the same day. (16)

The Aśvamedha and the Puruṣamedha have been explained. We shall now explain the Sarvamedha. Its series of days consists of three days belonging to the Aśvamedha, five days belonging to the Puruṣamedha, a Vājapeya, and an Aptoryāma. On the day of the Aptoryāma, all [the rites] take place on that same day. Prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers the essence of all forest trees; this indeed is the "unrestrained" (nirargala) sacrifice. At the time of giving the sacrificial fee, he should give away his entire property. He should invite his kinsmen and then consign the sacred fires into himself. For it is known thus: "This indeed..."

The fire-hearth is the hand; therefore, one should consign [the fires] into the hand. (7) It is known from scripture: "In whichever direction those fires of that person may be, he should recite [the mantra] facing toward that direction. (8) It is known from the Śruti: "Wherever the blessing of the sacrifice might reach the sacrificer while he is present there," (9) in that case, those ritual vessels which are to be touched should not be used as *dharmapātra* vessels. (10) When there is a general conjunction of deities and substances, the distinction is made based on the similarity of syllables. (11)

Now we shall explain the rule for one who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni) when he has died. 1. An *abhivānyā* cow is that cow which is milked by means of the calf of another cow. 2. Having carried away the milk while holding a fuel-stick (*samidh*) at the bottom of the ladle-handle (*srugdaṇḍa*), he offers it as a libation. 3. If he should die at night, he should perform the morning oblation; if he should die during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), he should complete the remaining time until the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the Agnihotra and the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*). 4. If he should die during the southern course of the sun (*dakṣiṇāyana*), he should perform the Agnihotra and the Full and New Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

Having covered the body with a cloth that has not been burnt by the cremation fire, and having struck it with his foot, he should lead it away, saying, "Go forth! Go forth! toward the south-eastern direction. Or, he may cause it to be carried on a wheeled vehicle; he leads the head first. They follow its path; he should have the sacrificial vessels led in front of the dwelling-place, and the kinsmen follow behind. Four priests, wearing turbans and new garments, having turned their upper garments over the left shoulder (in the *apasavya* manner), carry the fire forward toward the south-eastern direction and perform the sacrifice for Soma accompanied by the Fathers (*somāya pitṛmate*).

The sacrificial cake is on six potsherds; the potsherds are placed face upwards. They should proceed with it silently and without looking at it, as in the rite for the ancestors (pitryā). The duties of the sacrificer are omitted, but he should appear together with his wife, thinking, "May I be superior. The rite concludes with the *iḍā*. Having dug a trench of the height of the sacrificer in front of the *gārhapatya* fire and behind the *āhavanīya*, one should pile up a layer (*citi*) therein. Having spread a black antelope skin over it and scattered sesame seeds, having brought the body through the ritual entrance (*atīrtha*) and placed it upon the layer, one should scatter sesame seeds over it.

With the formula, "Svāhā to our own heaven-world," he should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) mentally. 12. Into the openings he inserts pieces of gold: with "For the Ṛc, svāhā! into the right ear-opening; with "For the Ruci, svāhā! into the left; with "For the Bhāsa, svāhā! into the right eye-opening; with "For the Jyotis, svāhā! into the left; with "This has come into being, svāhā! into the right nostril; with "Of Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā! into the left; and with "O Agni, with thy splendor, svāhā! into the mouth. 13. With the verse "Hiraṇyagarbha" and with the Vyāhṛtis, he should offer [oblations] into the mouth. 14. The vessels are provided with pouring-spouts.

Having filled the *payaḥ* (milk) vessel, he places the *juhū* ladle together with the *prastara* grass-bundle on the right hip; the *upabhṛt* on the left hip; the *dhruvā* on the chest; the *agnihotrahavaṇī* on the mouth; the two *sruva* spoons on the nostrils; the *prāśitraharaṇa* on the forehead; the potsherds and the *ājyasthālī* on the head; the *vedāgra* and the gold fragment along with the *puroḍāśa* in the mouth; the two *sāṃnāyya* vessels on the belly; the two fire-sticks (*araṇī*) on the lap; the *śamyā* on the breast; the *sphya* and the *upaveṣa* on the sides; the *iḍāpātrī* on the stomach; the *ulūkhala* mortar and the *musala* pestle on the thighs; and [the *camasa*] on the feet.

The cart [is placed] between the thighs; the other sacrificial implements [are arranged] as prescribed. (15) If it is the piling of the fire-altar (*agniciti*), one should place twenty-one black bricks all around, or else red ones. (16) One should have a goat or a cow of a single color killed on the path leading to the removal of the corpse in the south-western direction. (17) Having extracted its omentum and covered its face, and having scattered sesame seeds over it, one places the limbs upon the limbs: the right limbs on the right [parts of the body], the left limbs on the left, and the head on the head; then one covers it with the hide. (18) If that...

One should not cause [the body] to be burned in the *gārhapatya* fire. Having cooked milk in it, having drawn out its essence, having covered the opening, and having scattered sesame seeds over it, one should set it ablaze with three bundles of *ulapa* grass. (19) If the body first reaches the *gārhapatya* fire, one should know that he will go to the world of the gods; if to the *dakṣiṇāgni*, to the world of the ancestors; if to the *āhavanīya*, to the world of Brahman; and if simultaneously to all the fires, one should know that he will go to all the worlds. (20) When the fires have been brought together, the *chandoga* priest should chant the first *sāman* three times.

He sings, "In the firmament he sings to the fair-winged bird"; "Thy smoke, O brilliant one, rises up"—this refers to the smoke; "When thou hast risen, O Agni, be gracious to me, for thou art great"—this refers to when it has blazed up. (21) With a piece of gold, he should scratch around [the fire]; the Adhvaryu should mentally pour water three times around that golden line, just as in the rite for the ancestors. (22) Having circumambulated silently and stood at his feet, he worships with the five verses beginning, "Obeisance to thy greatness. (23)

We shall explain the procedure for one who has died without having established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni). 1. The cremation is performed with the domestic fire (śālāgni) or by means of friction-fire (nirmantha). 2. If a child dies, one should mentally bury the body and the two kindling woods (araṇī) in the earth, reciting: "The earth is your body."

Before the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), after bathing, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*); [the same applies to] sacrifices and Vedic study. If one who has undertaken a vow should die, they should release the vow, complete the funeral pyre with wood, perform the cremation with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), and return without looking back. Having touched water from a steady source and sat down where herbs grow in abundance, they sing the *yamagāthā*. Having placed sprouts of *dūrvā* grass and shoots of *śamī*, *vaṭa*, and *apāmārga* on their heads, they enter the village behind the cows.

They should enter [the house]. (6) At the door of the cow-pen, having touched an unbroken stone and fire, they should enter. (7) Having dug a trench outside the door, placed a stone therein, and mixed milk with water, he should take up the deceased’s name and lineage and say, "Drink here; bathe here," and at the appropriate time, he should perform the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*). On the twelfth day, he should perform the *śrāddha* rite. (8) He should prepare many varieties of food, or one variety for each individual. (9) He should perform the rite dedicated to the deceased alone (*uddiṣṭa*); he should not perform it with the sacred fire. (10) The dismissal is performed with the words, "May you be pleased. Every month, until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is completed, he should regularly feed a Brāhmaṇa. (11)

If the deceased is staying in another country or has been killed in battle, one should bring back his body and cremate it according to the prescribed rule. (1) If one cannot find that body, one should bring back his bones, fashion a human figure with them, anoint it with honey and clarified butter, place it upon a funeral pyre, and cremate it according to the prescribed rule. (2) If one cannot find anything at all, having performed the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, one should set fire to a dry thicket and [burn] the sacrificial vessels. (3) All the kinsmen offer water; some say this also includes the daughter’s sons. (4) With the left hand, using the little finger and separated by *darbha* grass, [one offers water] for such-and-such...

Saying "I give," he should pour water with joined palms at the edge of the water—once on the first day, four times on the fourth, seven times on the seventh, and ten times on the tenth. (5) For those observing the ten-day period of impurity, there is restricted food and the collection of bones; this occurs on the fourth day. (6) He should feed an odd number of Brāhmaṇas. (7) Having cut off a piece from a Daśāha-plant, a Śamī-tree, and a cloth, and having sprinkled the bones with turmeric and milk-water, he places the bones into a leaf-cup using the little finger of his left hand and a Palāśa stalk. (8) [He does so] in the south-eastern direction.

Having dug a trench, he should pour [the earth] down with the formula, "Speech! (9). He gives ten milch-cows, ten oxen, ten garments, and ten bronze vessels as sacrificial fees (10). Those who perform [funeral rites] for the deceased increase their out-breath and in-breath (11). Therefore, for a year—or six months, according to some—one should be devoted to austerity and yoga (12). Having officiated at a sacrifice for a father, a brother, or a teacher, one is defiled (13). If [the deceased] should return after this has been done, one should rekindle the fires, perform the *āyuṣya* sacrifices, and from then on perform sacrifices of unlimited duration (14).
One should apply fifty on the head, ten on the neck,
one hundred on the two arms, and ten on the fingers;
one should apply thirty on the chest and thirty on the hips and abdomen.
One should give half of eight (four) to the testicles, half of twelve (six) to the generative organ;
one should give a hundred to the thighs, half of sixty (thirty) to the knees and shanks;
and exactly ten to the toes of the feet—this is remembered as the procedure for the deceased.

"Once her husband has died, a woman should not maintain the sacred fires; she is not to be initiated," says Śākalya. (1) "How should she perform the fivefold service? By means of service," says Māruka. (2) "If, having been examined, she is found to be of good conduct, the Adhvaryu priest should address the wife: 'She should maintain this domestic fire. (3) If, having been examined, she is found to be of good conduct," says Citrasena Vātsyāyana, the teacher, regarding the examination of the widow. (4) Devoted to her husband, observing his vows, sharing in his sorrows, and following his conduct, she should have a single braid of hair and wear clean garments. (5) She should not go to festivals, nor at improper times.

He should bathe, he should not rejoice, he should eat only once a day, and he should attend upon his mother-in-law, father-in-law, and teacher. He should attend to the household fire, avoiding fragrant substances and garlands, according to the ritual rules of the *pākayajña*. On the full moon and the new moon days, there is an offering of cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) to Agni, as well as the morning and evening oblations (*sāyaṃprātarhoma*).

And at the time of the festival-parvans, one should sacrifice to these deities: Soma, Tvaṣṭṛ, the wives of the gods, Rākā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, and Agni Gṛhapati (8). One should offer with clarified butter alone (9). These two, as a couple, come together; they establish the sacred fires together; they procreate offspring together (10). The former [world] belongs to the sacrificer, the latter to the wife (11). Because the wife of one who has gone abroad or is incapacitated observes the vow on his behalf from the southern half [of the fire], she therefore becomes a sharer of half [the merit] (12). [These are] the sacrificial verses (yājyās).

Women receive a half-share; the wife is a participant in the sacrifice of the sacrificer. (13) When he offers in the Āhavanīya fire, that is the sacrifice performed by the sacrificer; when offered in the Gārhapatya fire, it belongs to the wife. (14) And because their connection is seen in the passage, "May the wife go together with her husband to their good deeds," even in the case of a gathering [of offerings]. (15) The Śruti shows this very same thing in the Mantras, Brāhmaṇas, and Kalpas, because the female member of a couple is incomplete [without her husband]. (16) Regarding this, some burn the deceased wife with the domestic fire (śālāgni), others with the churning-fire (nirmanthya), and still others with all the fires; that is not correct. (17)
If one should ever cause his wife to perform the Agnihotra sacrifice with his own fire, he becomes a woman by that act, and his wife shall become a man. 18

Having kindled the *gārhapatya* fire, he should place the funeral urn (*ukhā*) upon it. (19) When it is heated, he should quickly cast into it cotton, powdered cow-dung, *muñja*-grass fibers, hemp, *śara*-reeds, *iṣikā*-grass, and *kramuka*-nut, along with clarified butter; or else, he should transfer the *aukhya* fire from the fire-generating wood. (20) Having offered the oblation with the formula, "O Agni, that dear body of yours which is associated with yoga, whether it be the *svaru*, the *ukhā*, or the *rādukhā*—by means of that, this vessel ascends; homage be to you, svāhā!", he should cremate it according to the procedure for the *aukhya* fire. (21) Now, if the sacrificer [dies] beforehand...

One should die following the sequence of the fire-installation (ādhāna) by distributing the fires into five parts; the *āvasathya* fire is to be given to the wife. (22) If there were no *āvasathya* fire, a fifth part from the *gārhapatya* fire is to be given. (23) There are no fire-drills (*araṇī*) for women, for their offspring are indeed born from [the husband]. (24) Having kindled that fire, they should warm their ornaments over it with the verse: "May Agni grant us wide space... (25) When the ornaments have been warmed, [they recite]: "We invoke Vaiśvānara, the all-maker, who is all-born and the source of all;
the fires of the assembly hall and the domestic hearth, though hidden in many ways, become women and the fires of the dawn. (26)

He offers with "Svāhā. (26) When he has departed on his own, everyone returns. (27) With the words, "Thou art vigor, thou art endurance, thou art strength, thou art splendor," they should reheat their respective ornaments over the domestic fire at the time of the fire-ritual. (28) Whosoever should depart from there, one should kindle that fire and attend to it. (29) If she has died, there is an oblation of cooked rice for Yama, or for Soma, or for Nirṛti. (30)

Now, therefore, on the thirteenth day, or after three fortnights, or a year later, or at a time of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), we shall explain the ritual procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the single water-vessel *śrāddha*. (1) To the west of the fire, upon level *darbha* grass, he places four water-vessels. (2) Among them, one vessel is for the deceased (*preta*), and three are for the ancestors (*pitṛ*). (3) He pours that vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors with the two verses beginning, "Those who are equal, of one mind... (4) In this very manner, the rule is explained as being identical to that of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. (5)

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). 1. The practice applies to the householder: having produced offspring, having seen [the growth of] his offspring, or having provided for their livelihood, and having entrusted the household to a virtuous son, he then performs the ritual disposal of his fires. 2. He should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Way) and an oblation on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara (the Universal Fire). 3. The procedure has been explained; the offering is established. 4. At the time of giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he should give away all his possessions. 5.

Having invited his agnates, he should internalize the fires within himself, for this is the meaning: "Agni is indeed my friend and witness of both good and evil deeds. (6) With the verse, "This is your seasonal womb," he should warm himself at the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, and Dakṣiṇā fires. (7) Having fashioned a human figure out of all the sacrificial vessels within the altar, he should kindle it with three blades of *ulapa* grass. (8) Today, one speaks here by means of the triple Vedic speech. (9) [He recites: "The Agni who is ours, I take into myself" from the Āhavanīya, the Gārhapatya, and the Dakṣiṇā fire.

He takes a handful of ashes. Just as this handful of ashes was brought from the quarters, so it goes back to the very quarters. Then, saying "So be it," he throws it away and departs without looking back. What he eats in the evening is his evening oblation; what he eats in the morning is his morning oblation; what he eats at the new moon is his new-moon sacrifice; what he eats at the full moon is his full-moon sacrifice. By eating of the new grain, he obtains for himself the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.

That he has his hair and beard shaved in the spring is his *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice; this is the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). He goes to the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits or subsisting entirely on alms. From that point onward, he enters the fire, undertakes the path of heroes (*vīrādhvan*), practices fasting (*anāśaka*), or enters the stage of the aged (*vṛddhāśrama*). He does not return again. If he returns, he becomes a slayer of a hero (*vīrahā*).

Now, therefore, we shall explain the movements through the *tīrtha*s (sacrificial passages). 1. The first *tīrtha* is between the *āhavanīya* fire and the *utkara* heap; the second is between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara*; the third is between the *cātvāla* and the *āhavanīya*; the fourth is between the *āhavanīya* and the *sruca*s (ladles); the fifth is at the southern junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). 2. The first belongs to Agni, the second to Varuṇa, the third to Vāyu, the fourth to the Aśvins, and the fifth to Viṣṇu. 3. We shall explain the performance of these in their proper sequence. 4.

The path between the *āhavanīya* fire and the *utkara* heap is the *tīrtha* for the ritual vessels, the wives, the maidens, the water, the clarified butter, the oblations, and the fuel-sticks; it is also the place for collecting the implements, milking, and gathering [the materials]. (5) The path between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap is the entrance for the officiating priests and the sacrificer, as well as the approach to the *sadas* hall. (6) The path between the *cātvāla* pit and the *āhavanīya* fire is for the circumambulation of the tail [of the victim], the circumambulation of the animal, and the bringing back of the omentum and the sacrificial post. (7) Between the *āhavanīya* fire and the offering-ladles (*sruk*) is the path by which the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer pass to the south.

The *pratikramaṇa* has been explained. 8. At the southern junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are the places for the call for the announcement (*āśrāvaṇa*), the command (*preṣaṇa*), the utterance of *svāhā*, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the salutation (*namaskāra*), the fuel-stick offering (*samid-āhuti*), and the world-sanctuary (*loka-tīrtha*). 9. These indeed are the five sanctuaries (*tīrtha*). 10. It is known that the five-year cycle is established in these sanctuaries as a "row" (*paṅkti*). 11. Sacrificial priests who enter [the sacrifice] at a non-sanctuary become short-lived and perish before their full span of life.

Those who have resorted to the *tīrtha* reach their full lifespan. He who, knowing this, conducts himself [in this manner], all his desires are fulfilled. Therefore, if he should conduct himself otherwise, half of his sacrifice is bound by the nooses of Varuṇa. His sacrifice does not go to the gods; his sacrifice does not go to the gods. Thus ends the supplementary chapter.

Now begins the Sūtra for the Rājasūya sacrifice. A king desiring sovereignty shall sacrifice with the Rājasūya. (1) A descendant of Bhṛgu is the Hotṛ priest. (2) On the full moon day of Āśvayuja, or on the new moon day, or on a day suitable for sacrifice, he undergoes initiation for the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma. (3) That [sacrifice] is completed according to its established procedure. (4) On the following day, he offers an eight-potherd cake to Anumati. (5) [The procedure] is established up to the pouring of the grains. (6) Prior to the pouring of the grains, one should make the top of the wooden pin level with the upper millstone. (7) That portion which extends beyond the wooden pin toward the west is for Nirṛti; it is a cake on a single potsherd. (8)

He cooks [the oblation] silently in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire; [he cooks] the Ānumata [oblation] in the Gārhapatya fire. They cook both together until they are cooked (s). From this point until the performance [of the main offerings], it is established (siddha). Having performed the two Ājyabhāga portions, he offers the oblation with the verse "Vīhi svāhā" in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, saying "juṣāṇa. Having gone to the south, having placed a single fire-brand on a natural saline hollow (iriṇa), he offers two stalks of *visraṃsikā* with the formula "juṣāṇā nirṛtir vetu svāhā. A black garment with frayed edges is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). "Svāhā! Homage! to Ya... [text breaks off].

Having offered this with the verse "He has done this" in the *gārhapatya* fire, they proceed with the ritual as permitted. At the time for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), a cow is the fee. The procedure is established up to the spreading of the *vedī*. Now, those pegs which extend beyond the *śamyā* to the north, having gone toward the water and having dug up a termite mound (*valmīkavapā*), he offers an oblation after saying, "I here expiate the field-disease (*kṣetriya*) of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so," and he covers it with a clod of earth while saying, "I here suppress the field-disease of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so. On the following day, [he offers] to the Ādityas, accompanied by the word *bhuvat*, in clarified butter.

From the *caru* onwards, it proceeds as prescribed [in the ritual manuals]. 18. On the following day, the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice is performed; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a first-born calf. 19. On the following day, beginning with the full moon, the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices are performed and should be concluded within a year. 20. On the following day, there is an offering to Indra consisting of a fourth part; a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a *caru* of barley for Varuṇa, a *caru* of *gavīdhuka* grain for Rudra, and curd for Indra. A milch-cow and a bull are the sacrificial fees. 21. From a place where waters converge, they bring back *apāmārga* plants.

Having prepared those groats, on the following day before sunrise, they proceed with the *apāmārga* plant. Having gone to the south toward a natural salt-flat (*iriṇa*), having placed a single firebrand there, he offers an oblation with a ladle made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... (VS 1.1). He follows [the offering] with the formula: "The Rakṣas is slain; we have struck down the Rakṣas. (VS 1.2).

The choice gift is [the fee]. 24. Having removed the five pieces of fuel at evening, he should spread them out in five parts and place the fuel on the fire. 25. With the verse, "O gods who sit in front," he offers in the eastern half; with the following [verses], he proceeds clockwise around [the fire] without turning back, and with the fifth verse, he offers in the middle. 26. Having swept together the Āhavanīya fire with the verses beginning, "Here I sweep away this Rakṣas," he offers in the eastern half with the formula, "To Agni sitting in front, svāhā!"; with the following [verses], he proceeds clockwise around [the fire] without turning back.

With the fifth [offering], in the middle, there is a chariot drawn by five oxen as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). On the night of the new moon, one who fears Rākṣasas or Piśācas should sacrifice with the Pañcedhmīya [rite]. On the following day, a Devikā-cow that has calved for the first time is the sacrificial fee. On the next day, there is an offering on three sets of potsherds: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap for Indra and Viṣṇu, and a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu; a dwarf is the sacrificial fee. On the next day, the northern [set of offerings]: a cake on eleven potsherds for Soma and Pūṣan, a pap for Indra and Pūṣan, and a pap for Pūṣan.

A dark-colored bull is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 32. On the following day, there is an offering to Vaiśvānara and Varuṇa: a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara, a barley-porridge (caru) for Varuṇa, and gold and a horse as the sacrificial fee. 33. On the following day, there is a porridge for Bṛhaspati at the house of the Brahman priest; these and others are the "jewel-holders" (ratnin). 34. They should provide a feast for the sacrifice in whose houses one should perform the daily offerings. 35. A porridge for Nirṛti, made from grains split by fingernails, is the size of a thumb-joint.

He cooks [the oblation] silently in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. Having gone to the south, having placed a single fire-brand on a self-made salt-flat or in a cleft, he offers [an oblation] with the formula, "To Nirṛti, svāhā! The cake for the Ratnins is prepared first; then, in the house of the King, there is a cake for Indra Ekādaśakapāla. A bull is the sacrificial fee. On the following day, he should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Yāman-muc and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman; a bull is the sacrificial fee. He should sacrifice every day. On the full-moon day, the Pārvaṇa sacrifice is performed. With the Traidhātavī offering, the sacrificial fee is whatever amounts to a thousand.

At the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering of the consecration (*abhiṣecanīya*) sacrifice, there is an oblation for Mitra and Bṛhaspati. (1) The vessel is made from a branch of the *aśvattha* tree that has broken off of its own accord. (2) They milk a white cow with a white calf in front of it. (3) That [milk] coagulates by itself, is churned by itself, and becomes clarified butter (*ājya*) that has melted by itself. (4) Then he offers the sacrificial food (*havis*) for Mitra and Bṛhaspati. (5) He cuts half of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) himself, while the other half is cut by itself; he prepares half of the fuel-wood (*idhma*) himself, while the other half is prepared by itself; and half of the altar-ground (*vedi*) is prepared by himself, while the other half is prepared by itself.

He prepares half [of the vessel] himself-made. 6. Those rice grains which are the smallest, they cook as a *caru* offering for Bṛhaspati. 7. Having placed clarified butter therein and poured in what has melted by itself, they throw in the largest grains. 8. Having pounded both together, they cook them together. 9. It is prepared up to the point of setting it down. 10. He sets down the offering for Mitra on ground that has not been dug, and the offering for Bṛhaspati on ground that has been dug. 11. It is prepared up to the point of the ritual performance. 12. They perform the ritual first with the offering for Mitra. 13. A horse is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the offering to Mitra; a white-backed [horse]...

For the Bārhaspatya sacrifice, there are either white cows with their calves for both [the sacrificer and the Brahman]; 14. There are twelve initiation days; 15. [The ritual] is established up to the purchase of the Soma; 16. They purchase the two Soma portions together at the place of the Abhiṣecanīya, using heifers with their testicles according to the specified locations; 17. He places the implements belonging to the Dāśapeya in the house of the Brahman; 18. [The ritual] is established up to the Agniṣomīya offering; 19. He subsequently offers eight oblations of the Devasū, beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati, of those who arrive," following the Paśupuroḍāśa of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice; 20. He proceeds in the same manner as with the Devikā oblations.

21. It is established up to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. 22. Before the *sviṣṭakṛt*, having touched the hand of the Brahman priest with the formula, "May Savitṛ impel you for all impulses," they cause the sacrificer to hear the call. 23. They take his name, saying "N.N."; [they take] his lineage, saying "the descendant of N.N."; [they take] his mother's name, saying "the son of N.N."; and [they take] his clan, saying "in the clan of N.N. He invokes sovereignty, saying, "For the people, for great kṣatra, for great lordship over the people. This is to be appended everywhere. 24. The fast-day (*upavasatha*) is established. 25. On the following day, the consecration sacrifice (*abhiṣecanīya*) is an *ukthya* sacrifice consisting of seventeen [stomas].

The *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant. 26. It is established up until the pouring out for the midday offerings. 27. Having poured out the midday offerings, he pours out [the oblation] for the Maruts on twenty-one potsherds. 28. It is established up until the placing of the fire-pan. 29. With the sets of verses beginning with "Śukrajyotis" and "Citrajyotis," he places twenty-one potsherds; he prepares the two milks for the Vaiśvadeva offering silently. 30. It is established up until the time for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). 31. Thus he gives the sacrificial gifts, either unmeasured or ten thousand. 32. [He proceeds] with the Marutvatīya offerings.

Having performed the offering with the *māruta* [graha], he proceeds with the *payasyā*. 33 With the formula, "O divine waters, O son of the waters," he makes the invocation and takes three portions of water. 34 With the formula, "O divine waters, O son of the waters," [he takes] those belonging to Sarasvatī.

"You are givers of kingdoms; give a kingdom to such-and-such," he adds to every [formula]. "You are the bull-wave," [he says] of those flowing upstream; "you are the bull-army," [he says] of those following downstream; "you are the lord of waters," [he says] of the rivers; "you are the unassailable," [he says] of the stagnant waters; "you are the carriers," [he says] of the flowing waters; "you are the vigorous," [he says] of those that run up the slope; "you are the mild," [he says] of those flowing slowly; "you are dwelling in the pen," [he says] of the well-waters; "you are sun-bright, you are sun-skinned," [he says] of those [waters] when it is hot and raining.

With the formulas: "Ye who appear as the vigor of the Maruts," for the hailstones; "Ye are the she-goats," for the drops; "Ye are the Śakvarī verses," for the froth from the cow's udder; "Ye are the sustainers of all, the sustainers of people," for the smooth curd; "Ye are unassailable," for the ghee; "Ye are the sap of plants," for the honey. (36) With the formula, "O divine waters, full of sweetness, mingle together," he mingles them in a wide vessel. Having gone around the north of the Hotrīya mound, he sets them down behind the Potṛ’s hearth with the formula, "Sit down, ye unassailable ones. (37)

Having tied it to two *darbha* blades, he takes up the gold plate (*rukmam*) with the formula, "Thou art the rubbed-off. (1) With the formula, "The bright ones I purify for you by means of the bright," he purifies [the ghee] with the gold plate. (2) With the formula, "Svāhā to the Rājasūya," he lets the gold plate fall after [the ghee]. (3) He causes [the ghee] to flow through [four ladles] made of *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, and *naiyagrodha* wood, respectively, with the formula, "Sharing the feast, brilliant, with vigor, one... (4) With the formula, "O Rudra, that name of thine which is beyond the mountains," he offers the remainder in the Āgnīdhrīya fire. (5) With the formula, "Soma, Indra, Varuṇa," he causes the sacrificer to recite. (6) [He places] curds, honey, and young grass-blades in a vessel of *udumbara* wood.

He causes the sacrificer to sit down. 7. With the formula, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra," he covers the sacrificial garment (*dīkṣitavāsas*) with a linen cloth (*tārpya*). 8. With the formula, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra," he ties on a white, pure [garment]. 9. With the formula, "Thou art the navel of the Kṣatra," he binds [the head] with a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*). Having applied fresh butter, he anoints the right eye with fifty [drops], and the left with fifty-one. 10. Having touched water, he announces the sacrificer at the end of the Gārhapatya fire-altar with the words, "Agni, the lord of the house, has been won over. He says to the sacrificer, "This is your people's king."

He mutters, "Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas. (11) He hands over the strung bow with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra. (12) Having given three arrows with the formula, "For the repelling of enemies," he mutters, "Protect him from the east; protect him from the west. (13) With the formula, "Thou art Mitra," he takes down the right [hand], and with "Thou art Varuṇa," the left, together with the arrows. (14) He should consecrate them with these verses beginning, "The golden-colored one at the dawning of the dawn. (15) [He gives the command: "Mount the fuel-stick! (16)

He strides through the quarters with his mind, not with his feet, beginning with [the formulas] "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu... (VS 5.20). Having wrapped the tiger skin with its neck pointing eastward and its hair facing upward, he spreads it out in front of the *sadas* with the formula, "Thou art the splendor of Soma" (VS 5.21). Having ascended it, the sacrificer mutters, "The head of Namuci has been cast down" (VS 5.22). With his foot, he throws a piece of lead toward the eunuch, saying, "The biting serpents have been driven away" (VS 5.23); and he throws a piece of red iron toward the one who shaves the hair. With the formula, "Protect me from death" (VS 5.24), he draws a silver disk under his feet; [he also draws] a golden disk. To Agni... [etc.]

He offers six oblations on the ground, saying: "Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā! (20). With the formula, "With the splendor of Soma," he sprinkles [the king] with gold from the middle; with a *pālāśa* branch from the south, the *brahmán*; with an *aśvattha* branch from the west, a *vaiśya*; with an *audumbara* branch from the north, a rival; and from the east, one who is a friend of the people, with a *naiyagrodha* branch. (21). Having poured the residues into the *pālāśa* vessel, he places it in the *āgnīdhra* fire-hall. (22). He offers six oblations on the ground, saying: "To Indra, svāhā! (23). With the formula, "Thou art the womb of Indra," he consecrates the horn.

"Those that have flowed downward and upward have come together"—with this [verse], he performs the sprinkling three times above the navel. (24) "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the winner of booty"—with this, he brings down the chariot at the edge of the *cātvāla* pit. "I yoke thee by the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the two directors," with this, he yokes it. (25) "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu"—with this, he places his foot upon the wheel; "the slayer of rivals," with this, he mounts it. (26) "Conquer in the impulse of the Maruts"—with this, he addresses him as he departs. (27) "This very [Soma] is the juice mixed with milk; for him, Indra has yearned from birth.
We awaken thee, O Lord of Bay Steeds, with sacrifices; be mindful of our hymn in the exhilaration of the juice. (28)

Thus, with this *ṛc* addressed to Indra, the Brahman priest follows [the king]; he overcomes the Rājanya. He shoots that arrow at him. Having taken the vow and said, "The mind has attained power through its own vigor," he proceeds. "This is the thunderbolt, the best winner of booty; by it may our son win booty"—with these words, he hands the bows to his wife. She receives them with her joined palms. Taking portions of both the *payasyā* of the Maruts and [the other offerings], having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with the *anirukta* formula, he consecrates the gold plates (*rukmān*) with a mantra.

1. "Thou art this much," [he says] over the silver [cord]; "Thou art a thread of gold," over the golden cord; "Thou art vigor," over the cord of *udumbara* wood, which is a green cord. 2. "Thou art Mitra," with these words he brings down the right [cord]; "Thou art Varuṇa," the left. 3. Having turned it back together with the weapon, he hands it to the deputy. 4. "In the assembly, may I be united with all the gods," with these words he dips his hands into the *āmikṣā*. 5. There he gives him gold, or ties on a piece of *udumbara* wood. 6. "Homage to Mother Earth," [with these words he takes] the skin of a boar.

He steps down from his sandals with the formula: "Thou art the wrath of cattle; may my wrath be like thine. He puts them on with the formula: "Thy name has been established as sovereignty. He mutters: "Thou art pleasant; thou art easy to sit upon. To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he places a throne-seat with the formula: "Thou art pleasant; sit upon this easy seat. As he is ascending the throne-seat, he addresses him with the formula: "Sit down, thou of firm vows. Once he has ascended, [he offers] with the formula: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! These are the *rathavimocanīya* offerings. He recites together: "Haṃ, he is the dweller in purity... etc.

The charioteer places the chariot upon the chariot-stand (11). Having given a hundred [cows] to the Adhvaryu, or intending to give them, he descends (12). Sitting on a cushion of gold and a golden seat, while being entertained, the Hotṛ recites the Śunaḥśepa legend (13). The Adhvaryu responds; when the Hotṛ addresses him with "O Adhvaryu, let us speak the sacred lore," he replies "O Hotṛ" during the Ṛg-verses, and likewise "O Hotṛ" during the Gāthās (14). When it is finished, he gives a hundred to the Hotṛ and a thousand to the one who responded (15). [He gives] to the officiants acting in the middle, and to the sacrificer...

The attendants sit around facing north; the Ratnin, the Senānī, and others, along with the Takṣan and Rathakāra, [sit] separately. (16) "You are my Brahman, you are the Brahman," thus the sacrificer addresses each one of those who perform the central duties. (17) "You are Savitṛ, of true impulse," the Brahman replies; "You are Mitra, very gracious," the Udgātṛ; "You are Indra, of true vigor," the Hotṛ; "You are Varuṇa, of universal vigor," the Adhvaryu. (18) "This is the thunderbolt; with it, may I prosper," saying this, he hands over the wooden sword (*sphya*) to the Brahman.

The sacrificer [acts] for the sacrificer; the deputy for the deputy; the commander of the army and those following him [act] for the commander of the army, until the scattering of the dice. Having performed the dedication to the deities with the wooden sword (sphyá), he scatters the prepared grains as if cooking them. Therein, he releases a four-year-old cow (paṣṭhauhī). Four men play with it: a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra. Whichever among them loses, he consigns that four-year-old cow to the cattle of the sacrificer. Then, having loaded four hundred dice onto a cart, he says: "The king has won! (udbhinnam rājñaḥ).

Saying, "This one has overcome the quarters," he gives five dice to the sacrificer. He gives a field to the Brahman priest. He chooses a boon. He calls out names that are auspicious: "The well-famed, the well-blessed, those whose kings are truthful. Having touched the mother of the man appointed to the wife's place and having taken hold of the appointed man, he offers an oblation on the Gārhapatya fire with the verse, "O Prajāpati, not from thee... while interchanging their names, pouring together the sap of Palāśa wood. [He announces] the two names: "This one is the son of so-and-so; so-and-so is the son of this one."

He intertwines [the verses]. He causes the one who has been appointed to recite the verse: "May we be masters of riches. Having taken portions from both the *payasyā* of the Maruts and [the other offering], they invoke the *iḍā* and consume it.

In the Māhendra [rite], one proceeds until the *avabhṛtha* bath; the vessels used for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the boar-skin mat should be carried to the vicinity of the *avabhṛtha*. One enters the *avabhṛtha* with *gāgula* grass. At the *avabhṛtha*, he offers an oblation into the waters with the formula, "To the grandson of the waters, svāhā!"; a second into a clump of *darbha* grass with, "To the grandson of vigor, svāhā!"; and into the *gārhapatya* fire with, "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā! The procedure up to the *anūbandhyā* cow is established. In the case of a *sūtavaśā* (barren cow) as the *anūbandhyā*, he makes her step forward four times with a four-footed animal.

He offers wild rice for the animal cake-offering (paśupuroḍāśa). He does not have his hair or beard shaved; he does not undergo consecration (dīkṣā); he hands over the staff. He concludes the rite with the Sāvitra formula: [he gives] to the sacrificer at the Gārhapatya fire, and to the wife at the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. When they have come together, they both consume that portion.

That is the continuity of the vows and the *agnihotra*. 11. "A cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ," and so forth—these are the ten *saṃsṛp* offerings. 12. Having established the *gārhapatya* fire in the place of the *āhavanīya*, they proceed eastward; he should sacrifice every day. 13. Just as one would prepare the *praüga-śastra* for the *vaiṣṇava* offering at the *daśapeya*. 14. He undergoes initiation for the *daśapeya*. The sacrificer puts on a garland of twelve lotuses; that is the initiation in the waters. 15. They perform everything on the same day.

He should take hold of a black antelope skin, a girdle, and a horn; he does not give away anything else until he has been initiated (dīkṣita). (16) Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation for the Prāyaṇīya sacrifice, he pours out the King Soma on the southern half of the altar. (17) Having completed the Prāyaṇīya, he immolates the young bulls to the east of the purchased Soma with the formulas beginning "Thou art of good birth" (svajā asi). (18) The procedure up to the Upasad rites is established. (19) There are three Upasad days. (20) The Upavasatha day is established. (21) On the following day, there is the Daśapeya Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, characterized by the Rathantara Pṛṣṭha-stotra. (22) The procedure up to this point is established.

23. Regarding the consumption [of the Soma]: one hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma; ten for each cup, having announced them according to their maternal and paternal lines up to the tenth generation. 24. A Brāhmaṇa who has a physical deformity should not consume it; nor should the son of a female slave, unless he announces himself [as such]; he may consume it at will. 25. Having passed over the thousandth [cow], he removes [the ritual implements] starting with the golden plate of the Hotṛ, as prescribed in the traditional text. 26. A goat is for the Subrahmaṇya priest; a heifer for the Unnetṛ; a castrated three-year-old bull for the Grāvastut; twelve pregnant four-year-old cows for the Brahman. 27.

28. He does not give to the *prasarpakas*. 29. Having drawn out the thousand [cows] for the *anūbandhyā* cow, he gives them to the Soma-drinking priests (*ṛtvij*). 30. He performs the *vaśātirātra* sacrifice. 31. He does not have his hair or beard shaved. 32. He concludes with the *diśām aveṣṭi* offerings. 33. He offers five oblations beginning with "A cake on eight potsherds for Agni. 34. On the evening of the full moon, prior to the morning *agnihotra*, he sacrifices with the *prayug* verses; [the offerings are] a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, and so forth—six [offerings] accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

The cart that carries the chariot is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). On the following day, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī), he undertakes the subsequent *prayuj* offerings, beginning with the *caru* for Sarasvatī and the *caru* for Pūṣan; the cart that carries the chariot is the sacrificial fee. On the following day, there is an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) for the Maruts, consisting of a spotted four-year-old cow that is pregnant. On the following day, there is the northern [offering] consisting of a ewe for Aditi that is pregnant and has a lamb. Having commenced with the Soma sacrifice in the evening, he performs the Agnihotra itself for one year, until the point of the animal sacrifice, every two days or every day. Whoever...

Intent on wisdom and devoted to truth, he sacrifices to Savitṛ the Impeller with oblations of clarified butter offered by Sātyadūta; these are the three introductory rites. (39) A red-eared horse is the sacrificial fee, as are a staff, sandals, and a dried leather bag. (40) Having given these to them, he sends word to the neighboring king, saying, "I have been consecrated; I have become a king. (41) On the full moon day, he undergoes initiation for the Keśavapanīya sacrifice. (42) On the new moon day, on the day of the sacrifice, there is an Atirātra rite without the Ṣoḍaśin cup, with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee. (43) At the time of the shaving, he sits upon a throne.

Those long-haired ones who first performed the sacrificial session, by whom this entire world is made to shine forth—to them let us offer praise and perform atonement; may there be well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.

Thus the sacrificer has his entire hair and beard shaved. The departure [from the sacrificial ground] is well known. 44. Immediately thereafter, he undergoes initiation for the Ahīna sacrifice with dice. 45. The Jyotis Agniṣṭoma is first; on the day of the new moon, there is an Atirātra. The departure is well known. 46. Immediately thereafter, he undergoes initiation for the Kṣatradhṛti. 47. It is a Triṣṭubh Agniṣṭoma with the Rathantara as the Pṛṣṭha-stotra.

The dwelling place has been prepared (48). Immediately thereafter, one should sacrifice with the *iṣṭis*: with the Devikā offerings, the oblations of the Devasū, the *iṣṭi* for Agni, the Sautrāmaṇī, the Vaiśvānara-Vāruṇī, and the Traidhātavī—yes, the Traidhātavī (49).
Thus ends the first chapter in the Rājasūya.

At a sacred place of divine sacrifice known by its auspicious name, the king should perform the Aśvamedha, desiring to obtain all his desires and wishing to conquer that world beyond. 2. They lead forth the priests on foot, mounted on equal vehicles. 3. On the full moon day of Phālguna, he should immolate a hornless bull dedicated to Prajāpati, possessing every form. 4. When the omentum has been offered and they have purified themselves at the Cātvāla pit, chariots rush toward all the quarters. 5. "The king should perform the Aśvamedha; let him permit it. 6. That sacrifice is thus completed as an established rite. He should immolate this very [bull].

One who desires all things should fast on the preceding full moon and fast on the following one. At sunset, they restrain their speech for the sake of the *brahmaudana* (the Brahmin’s rice-mess). Or, once the sun has risen, having added fuel to the fire with branches of cane, he worships the sun with the formulas beginning, "Homage to the beholder! Homage to the overseer! He offers twelve full oblations with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha. In four places—namely, in water, in the *dakṣiṇāgni*, and in the *gārhapatya*—he cooks the *brahmaudana*. On both sides [of the pot] he places gold plates, silver underneath and gold above.

Afterwards, the performers eat from the center of the *gārhapatya* fire-hearth; he gives them a *śatamāna* weight of gold. He takes a rope made of muñja grass or darbha grass, twelve or thirteen cubits long, for tying the horse, having dipped it in the *brahmaudana* rice-porridge, with the formula: "They have taken hold of this... He addresses the *brahmán* priest: "O *brahmán*, I shall tie the horse. The *brahmán* grants permission: "Bind him for the gods. With the formula, "Thou art the binder," he ties a three-year-old black horse.

They lead forward the son of the younger sister of the father—the Soma-drinker who is either tawny or reddish-tawny—and they lead the four-eyed dog in front. The Pāuṃścaleya follows with a pestle made of *saidhraka* wood. Having caused water to be poured down, he stations the horse in front, facing westward. Together with all those [attendants], there are four Adhvaryus. He sprinkles each one [of the victims] starting with the formula, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Prajāpati," and [he sprinkles] all [the victims] together with the formula, "To all the gods thee."

22. From all sides, Pauṃścaleya strikes the dog with a club made of *saidhraka* wood. 23. When the horse is being struck, the sacrificer mutters the formula: "He who desires to kill the courser... 24. Having first lifted his right foot, he causes the dog to float away toward the south into water below, while reciting: "The mortal is far away; the dog is far away... 25. As the horse steps forward, they drive it upward with a reed, a *vetasa* branch, or a wooden shovel. 26. He consecrates the flowing [horse] with the section beginning: "To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! 27. This...

He offers oblations at the three steps with the verses beginning "Viṣṇu," "That Viṣṇu," and "Viṣṇu of heaven" (RV 1.22.17–19), while [the horse] stands in the water. 28. With the mantra "Vibhūḥ mātrā, prabhūḥ pitre" (VS 23.14), he consecrates the horse. 29. With the mantra "ādityānām patvānv ihi" (VS 23.15), he releases it. 30. He entrusts the horse to the princes who are armored for a hundred [men], who are worthy of the couch, saying, "O gods, guardians of the quarters! 31. Four hundred [men] guard it without turning back. 32.

He proceeds with the Sāvitrī offerings. 1. In the forenoon, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Savitṛ. 2. He offers fifty oblations at one place, beginning with "To Hiṃkāra, svāhā! and so forth. 3. At midday, [he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ.

In the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ the Impeller. Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he performs four oblations with the verses beginning, "Here is stability, here is self-stability. He should sacrifice with these *iṣṭis* for a year and offer the oblations. Two lute-players should sing to him: during the day, with three verses addressed to a Brāhmaṇa—"You have sacrificed," "You have cooked," "You have given"—and with three verses addressed to a Rājanya at night—"You have fought," "You have performed a noble deed," "You have won such-and-such a battle."

In the case of a *saṃnipāta* (conjunction of calamities), because there is no destruction of what is eternally new (*apūrva*), one should offer oblations with verses addressed to the Aśvins in a horse-trough; if [the horse] does not come, one should offer it in a deer-trough. (8) An offering is also prescribed at the place where a mare dies. (9) After a year has passed, he performs the *Ṣaḍaha* sacrifice. (10) In that [sacrifice], they perform the rites up to the covering of the fire-pan (*ukhā*). (11) When it is completed, he gives two hundred [coins] to two lute-singers, as well as two chariots drawn by horses yoked to a wagon. (12) Having confined the horse in a pen, they break it in. (13) On the seventh day is the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), and on the eighth day the *Traidhātavī* is the initiation offering (*dīkṣaṇīyā*). (14)

Success! For those who have studied the Yajurveda: having offered daily the three Vaiśvadeva oblations beginning with "To Kāya svāhā, to Ka svāhā," and on the seventh day having offered the five Ādhvaraka oblations, he offers the six Āgnika oblations and the final Vaiśvadeva oblations. From the *pūrṇāhuti* until the *upasads*, the procedure is established. With the mantra "O Brahman, O Brāhmaṇa," the Brahman priest worships the chief officiant (*mukhya*) once the [fire] has been produced. The consecration (*dīkṣā*) lasts for one year, and there are twelve *upasads*. The altar is threefold in size, as is the fire-altar; there is no *uttaravedī*.

In the two Havirdhāna carts that carry the chariot, he erects twenty-one sacrificial posts (*yūpa*). The central post (*agniṣṭha*) is made of *nicudāru* wood and measures twenty-one cubits; the two side-posts (*upasthāvānau*) are made of *pūtudāru* wood; six are of *khadira* wood, six of *pālāśa* wood, six of *bilva* wood, three others, and three yet others.

On the middle day, he mixes the *vaṃśa* meat. Having taken the *vasatīvarī* waters from the quarters at the appropriate time and having brought them together, he deposits them; this is likewise for the subsequent *ukthya* and *atirātra* sacrifices.
