Day by day, he draws the *pṛṣṭhya* and *anatigrāhya* cups. On the middle day, he should perform the *pṛṣṭha-śilpa*. The *upavasatha* rite is completed as established. On the following day, there is a *catuṣṭoma agniṣṭoma* with the *rathaṃtara* as the *pṛṣṭha* chant. The sacrifice concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings as established. When the sun has set, the two [priests] sit upon the two mats.

With two *sruva* ladles they offer oblations: (29) having mixed together groats, parched grains, *masūrī* lentils, *karambha* porridge, fried rice, flattened rice, and *priyaṅgu* seeds with cooked food, he offers them with the formulas beginning "To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! up to one hundred and one [oblations]. (30) Repeating the formula "To one, Svāhā! To two, Svāhā! and so on, he offers throughout the night—ghee with even-numbered verses and food with odd-numbered verses. When dawn has broken, he offers with "To the Dawn, Svāhā! and when the sun has risen, with "To Heaven, Svāhā! (31)

The middle day consists of the Ekaviṃśa Ukthya sacrifice. 1. It is established [in its procedure] up to the employment of the vessels. 2. Having employed the Antaryāma vessel, he employs the two Mahiman vessels: one of gold for the southern [cup] and one of silver for the northern. 3. It is established [in its procedure] up to the drawing of the cups. 4. Having drawn the Antaryāma, he draws the two Mahiman cups with the verses "Hiraṇyagarbha" and "Yaḥ prāṇataḥ" for the drawing and the setting down. 5. It is established [in its procedure] up to the Bahiṣpavamāna chant. 6. "The light of the sacrifice purifies itself; the dear honey, the father of the gods, the progenitor, the radiant one."
He bestows a treasure hidden within the two self-sustaining worlds—the most gladdening, intoxicating, and Indra-like essence.

With the words, "Thou art a golden ornament on the neck of the horse," he fastens a gold necklace upon the necks of the horses. With the words, "Thou art a falcon, the Gāyatrī metre; thou art a well-winged bird, the Triṣṭubh metre; thou art a friend, the Gāyatrī metre," they seize the tail of the horse and creep toward the *pavamāna* [soma]. From the north, the Udgātṛ says to him, "I enclose thee with a hundred"; the officiating priests (ṛtvij) then withdraw from his enclosure. They give a hundred [cows] to the Udgātṛ. At the end of the *āstāva*, having led away the mare, they cause her to mount the horse. From the north, [he addresses her] with the words, "With a gold ornament, I [enclose] thee."

With the words, "We invoke this deity; O Udgātṛ, chant the Udgītha," he addresses the Udgātṛ. The invocation of that [deity] is performed by the officiating priests with the formula, "This deity is invoked. (12) He gives a hundred gold coins (*niṣka*) to the Udgātṛ. (13) They perform both: the Udgītha and the horse-shouting (*aśvasaṃkrandana*). (14) When it is completed, he bestows a hundred-measure weight (*śatamāna*) upon the Udgātṛs. (15) The ritual up to the introductory consecration (*upākaraṇa*) is established as already explained. (16) He consecrates two sets of eleven animals; the others [he consecrates] with a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, while covering those bound to the horse with the formula, "O Indra, for the sake of good work... (17) for the journey. (18)

"Vehat, vaiṣṇava, and vāmana" are for the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*). "Babhru, aruṇababhru," and so on, ending with "pṛṣata," are for the Viśvedevas. Regarding the word "many": one should understand three [animals] for the *gāyatrī*—three-year-olds; five-year-olds for the *triṣṭubh*; those at least five years old for the *jagatī*; two-year-old draft-oxen for the *anuṣṭubh*; three-year-old heifers for the *uṣṇih*; three-year-old draft-oxen for the *virāj*; four-year-old draft-oxen for the *paṣṭhauhī*; and four-year-old draft-oxen for the *paṣṭhavāh*. They yoke them.

He consecrates the yoking horse with the verse, "The sun-like [steed], ruddy and tawny," as it is being harnessed; with the two following verses, "They harness his willing [steed]" and "Raising up the banner for those without banners," he consecrates the standard; with the verse, "Like a cloud [thundering]," he consecrates the one clad in armor; with the verse, "Put on the quiver," he consecrates the quiver; with the verse, "Standing in the chariot, he drives," he consecrates the charioteer; with the verse, "Making loud noises," he consecrates the horses; with the three verses beginning, "O Tree, firm-limbed," he consecrates the chariot; with the three verses beginning, "Sweet-smelling seat," he consecrates the chariot-seat; with the verse, "The well-winged bird," he consecrates the arrow; and with the verse, "Like a serpent with its coils."

With the two verses, "O horse, strike the ground with your hooves" and "O horse, inspire the cattle," he strikes the drum. He mutters, "O you who rush toward us. Having gone forward to the east, he causes the horse to circumambulate [the fire] from left to right. When the [horse] has been set in motion, having caused it to lower its head toward the water that is reddish-brown like dawn, he brings it back with the verse, "As the wind has gone to the waters," to its original position as it was previously brought forward. They anoint it: the Mahiṣī anoints it on the face with *kāsāmbava* resin, saying, "May the Vasus anoint you"; the Vāvātā anoints it on the forelegs with *gulgulu* resin, saying, "May the Rudras anoint you."

With the formula, "May the Ādityas anoint you from the navel," [the priests] apply [ointment] with a piece of cloth from the tail of the horse. 23. They attach three-thousand-fold glass beads to the hairs; the chief queen (*mahiṣī*) attaches golden ones with the word *bhūḥ*, the favorite wife (*vāvātā*) silver ones with the word *bhuvaḥ*, and the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*) conch-shell ones with the word *svaḥ*. 24. With the verses beginning "The parched-grain eater, the active one," the wives scatter the remainder of the food-oblation over the horse. 25. Wherever it eats, there he should scatter a brick. 26. He sets aside the remainder of the clarified butter for the consecration. 27. The Hotṛ and the Brahman, standing on either side of the horse closest to the fire, ask each other: "Who?"
"Does the sun move alone? It moves alone," from this question and answer [it is known]. 28.

It is established up to the binding. With the verse, "He yokes the ruddy one," he binds the reddish-brown [animal] to the post standing near the fire; the hornless goat and the *gomṛga* on both sides of the horse, and ten *paryaṅgya* animals, covering them with the formula, "For the journey, for Indra, for good work, the ewe for Viṣṇu, the dwarf. The recipients of the sacrificial posts are those beginning with the brown and the reddish-brown. The wild animals begin with the formula, "For spring, the francolin partridges," and so forth; of these, there are groups of ten, fifteen, eleven, and ten. These thirteen each are placed alternately between the sacrificial posts.

He places locusts and mosquitoes on the limbs [of the horse], snakes in baskets, lions, tigers, and leopards in cages, crocodiles, fish, and frogs in jars, birds in nets, and elephants in enclosures; and he places water in boats, and other things as appropriate. (4) The rite is completed up to the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire). (5) They release those that have been circumambulated by fire—men and whatever other domestic animals are subject to the rule of release. (6) The rite is completed up to the *prakramaṇa* (stepping forward). (7) They lead a goat dedicated to Pūṣan in front of the horse. (8) While the horse stands still, he throws a blade of *darbha* grass toward it.

There are garments, upper garments, and golden cushions (9). With a neck-strap they immolate the Prājāpatya animals, and with a shoulder-hair-rope the horse (10). While it is being immolated, he offers three oblations, saying: "To breath, svāhā! To out-breath, svāhā! To diffused breath, svāhā! (11). He leads the chief queen forward with the words, "O mother, O motherly one," while the other ninety-nine wives follow silently along with her (12). Having disheveled their hair and tied it up, and striking their left and right thighs, [the priests] recite: "We invoke thee, the lord of hosts, of all hosts... (13).

Having tied up the horse’s right foreleg, they walk three times around it clockwise; then, having untied the right foreleg, they walk three times around it counter-clockwise, striking the left thighs with their feet while keeping their heads turned toward the north. 13. With the words, “O Vasu, mine,” they smell the feet [of the horse] within the enclosed space. 14. With the words, “I have conceived a male child,” the wife smells the horse from above while it lies on its back with its head pointing downward. 15. When [the horse] has been raised up, everyone mutters the verse, “I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan. 16. With their heads pointing westward, the wives prepare incisions with needles, [reciting] the Gāyatrī.

With two verses beginning with "triṣṭubh," the chief queen (*mahiṣī*) [cuts] with golden knives from the jaws and from the heart and chest; the favorite wife (*vāvātā*) [cuts] with silver knives from the tail. (17) There is no omentum (*vapā*) of the horse; they call the fat "candramas" and they extract it from there. (18) He roasts the *candramas* to the north of the horse.

(19) "There is but one dissector of Tvaṣṭṛ’s horse, and there are two restrainers; such is the season. Those limbs of yours which I prepare in due order, those I offer as balls of meat into the fire. (20)

Saying "svāhā," he places three cooked balls of meat into the Āhavanīya fire (20). Having cut portions from the horse on the north side onto a mat of vetasa reeds, he should pass over and cut portions from the other two (21). On both sides of the omentum, he offers the two Mahiman oblations: first with a golden vessel, saying "svāhā to the gods," and afterwards with a silver vessel, saying "svāhā to the Viśve Devas" (22). Saying "To Prajāpati," he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse for the omenta and the fat of the horse, the goat, and the ox, saying "O radiant one, recite the invitatory verse for the omenta and the fat" (23). Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, [he says] "To Prajāpati," [and then] "upām̐ śu."

"O Hotṛ, give the command for the fat and the marrow of the horse, the goat, and the ox," he says, and proceeds with the offering. Having taken portions from each animal as prescribed, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse for the subsequent animals: "Recite the invitatory verse for the fat and the marrow of the goats, rams, and oxen, for the Viśve Devas. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "O Hotṛ, give the command for the fat and the marrow of the goats, rams, and oxen, for the Viśve Devas," and proceeds with the offering. They dissect the boar dedicated to Prajāpati in the manner of a butcher. To the north of the horse...
He cooks the blood; they call it *tejanī* in the blood. Having cut off the portions, they cook the offerings for Prajāpati portion by portion. One should make the horse's meat on a spit.

Success! Up until the time for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā): 1. He gives the fee as he desires, if he should wish to obtain his desire. 2. Whatever wealth of non-Brāhmaṇas may be in the eastern direction, that he should give to the Adhvaryu, excluding land and two-footed property; whatever is in the southern direction, that to the Brahman; whatever is in the western direction, that to the Hotṛ; whatever is in the northern direction, that to the Udgātṛ. 3. Having drawn the cup for Mahendra, he introduces the Stotra. 4. "O Agni, you purify our lives"—these first seven [verses] are recited prior to the consecration.

He should perform [the rite] with the seven verses beginning, "Prajāpati moves within the womb. Of these, the first ones are the *prāṇabhṛt* (breath-sustaining) verses, and those following are the *apānabhṛt* (exhalation-sustaining) verses. (5) He is consecrated upon a hide of a lion. (6) A bull's hide is held above him. (7) Holding a golden disk above him while reciting, "The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas," he consecrates him with the remnants of the oblation, using the formula, "To Prajāpati, the supreme lord," according to his desire. (8) With the *Āprī* verses beginning, "Enkindled, anointing the hollow of thoughts," he takes hold of his hand. (9) "Drive away the Rakṣas, drive away the adversaries; break apart the jaws of Vṛtra!"
O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, strike down the wrath and the head of the enemy.

10. Having thus wiped his mouth, he strides the Viṣṇu-strides belonging to the Jagatī meter. 11. He offers oblations with the names of the months. 12. To the north of the horse, on a mat of Vetasa reeds, he cuts portions for the offering. 13. With the neck of a Gomṛga, he makes an offering at the *vaṣaṭ*-call of the Sviṣṭakṛt in the *tejanyā* vessel. 14. With the horse's hoof, made of iron, he causes the wives to sacrifice during the Varuṇapraghāsa and Avabhṛtha offerings. 15. On a mat of Vetasa reeds, he collects the animals dedicated to Prajāpati: two horses and a Tūpara goat facing east, and a Gomṛga facing west. 16. At the *vaṣaṭ*-call, four princes [participate].

They place [the fire] in the Āhavanīya. Having taken clarified butter for each oblation, he offers sixteen Aśvastomīya oblations with the verses beginning "To the grass with my teeth, svāhā! To that which has been studied in the forest by means of the Anuvāka, svāhā! and "May Mitra and Varuṇa not [abandon us]. The Upavasatha day is completed. On the following day, there is the Sarvastoma Atirātra sacrifice. The procedure is established up to the opening (Upākaraṇa). He dedicates eleven animals of the bovine class. The procedure is established up to the purificatory bath (Avabhṛtha). While the horse stands in water reaching its mouth, he offers three oblations on its head with the formula: "To Jumbaka, svāhā!"

He offers oblations with the formulas: "To Death, svāhā! and for the second [oblation], "To the murder of a Brāhmaṇa, svāhā! (25). He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice and he who knows this thus, cross over death, cross over evil, and cross over the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. (26) As many as smell the odor of the horse being offered, they all become possessors of the world of merit. (27) The rite for the Ānūbandhyā cow is established. (28) There are nine white cows dedicated to Sūrya as the Ānūbandhyās; while their omenta are being offered, they should stand facing the wind; thus they are released.

For those who have committed evil deeds (29), he offers the Mṛgāreṣṭi sacrifice consisting of ten oblations, following the animal-cake of those [deities], with the verse beginning "Homucaḥ" (30). One desiring prosperity, or one being falsely accused, should sacrifice with this [offering] which includes all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras.

One who is afraid or afflicted by disease should perform the Mṛgāreṣṭi sacrifice. Having moved northward, he should offer these at times when he does not know [the specific seasons], beginning in due order: he should tether the victim for Agni in the middle fork, that for Indra in the southern, and that for the Aśvins in the northern. The animal sacrifice is thus completed. Having cooked twelve *brahmaudana* (sacrificial porridges for Brahmins), he should give them to those who performed the central rites, and to them he should also give twelve cows. Alternatively, having sacrificed with the Devikā offerings, he should sacrifice with the Mṛgāreṣṭi; he should sacrifice. Thus ends the second chapter of the Rājasūya.

The rule for the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) has been handed down. All of them involve the maintenance of the sacred fires (*sāgnayaḥ*); the others [are characterized by] the *ṣoḍaśin*, the *tīvrasud*, and the *cāturmāsya*s, except for those whose initiation rites (*dīkṣā*) and *upasads* are performed without the fires. In those [sacrifices] where offspring, cattle, or procreation is the desired object (*kāma*), they include the *pravargya* rite; in those cases, the *uktha* is of the archetypal form (*prākṛta*). In the *rathantara* [sāman], or in that which has the characteristics of the *rathantara*, the draught begins with the *aindravāyava*; in the *bṛhat*, or in that which has the characteristics of the *bṛhat*, it begins with the *śukra*; in the *vāmadevya*, or in that which has the characteristics of the *vāmadevya*, it begins with the *āgrayaṇa*. In a sacrifice where the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a thousand, he draws the *pṛṣṭhya* and *anatigrāhya* cups. There is also the *anūbandhyā* [cow].

[There are] offerings to Mitra-Varuṇa, to the Viśvedevas, and to Bṛhaspati. Their enumeration is according to [the rules for] the Śunāsīrya and the Āśvadābhya in the Vājapeya sacrifice. (6) One who is about to sacrifice with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should first perform the *Traidhātavī* sacrifice and then sacrifice. (7) Cows and gold are not the sacrificial fees; rather, the fee consists of the objects [of the specific rites]. (8) In the absence of a specific instruction, however, the sacrifice concludes with the *Agniṣṭoma*. (9) The *Indrastrikadruka* sacrifices have the *Rathantara* as their *pṛṣṭha* chant. (10) One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and one wishing to conquer this world [should do so as well]. (11) [The Jyotiṣṭoma consists of] the *Agniṣṭoma* and the *Ukthya*.

One who desires all cattle should sacrifice, seeking to conquer the intermediate world; this is the Āyuṣṭoma Ukthya. One who desires everything should sacrifice, seeking to conquer yonder world; this is Indra’s Abhijit. One who seeks to conquer the victory of one who has not yet conquered should sacrifice with both Sāmans, having the Rathantara as the Pṛṣṭha-stotra. Indra’s Viśvajit has all the Pṛṣṭhas.

One who desires to conquer the universe should sacrifice. (15) He undergoes initiation with reference to [the Viśvajit]. (16) Before the Prātaranuvāka, the sacrificer puts on a golden garland weighing a hundred mānas and adorned with twelve lotuses. (17) He draws the Pṛṣṭhya and Atigrāhya cups. (18) He offers them following the order of the Pṛṣṭhas, and the artistic variations of the Pṛṣṭhas are performed. (19) At the time of the sacrificial fees, he gives away all his possessions and the garland. (20) The Vairāja is the Hotṛ-sāman, characterized by the color of the Bṛhat. (21) Having emerged from the Avabhṛtha bath, [he gives] a red cow with her ears, tail, and all her limbs intact.

He covers himself with the skin of a calf. Having completed the sacrifice, he performs the *udavasānīyā* offering. Wearing a turban, sleeping on the ground, and taking a vessel of unbaked clay, a sharp-pointed spade, and a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, he dwells for three nights at the *khanitra-jīvana* (the place where the spade is used for sustenance). They milk a hundred cows for the *āśira* mixture. These sacrifices have both *sāman*s and the *bṛhat* as their *pṛṣṭha*.

There are six *sādyaskra* sacrifices; among them, the first is the *ādityānāṃ trivṛt*. One who has enemies, one desiring heaven, or one desiring cattle should perform it. At the deep of night, having placed jars of milk on horse-chariots, the officiating priests bring them together.

They join the Udgātṛ behind at a distance of two *krośas*, the Hotṛ to the south at a distance of one *krośa*, and the Brahman with a broken-wheeled cart. 3. The clarified butter consists of fresh butter from a skin-bag. 4. The altar is a fertile field. 5. They initiate [the sacrificer] after sunrise. 6. They perform everything on the same day. 7. A three-year-old bull with testicles is the *soma*-purchase animal. 8. During the *upasad* rites, they proceed while closing their eyes in three places. 9. Having fixed the threshing-post in the place of the *cātvāla* pit, they plow barley with a plow-shaft.

For them, they pour out the *uttaravedi* and the *dhiṣṇya* hearths. Having turned around the *khalevālī*, they prepare the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) starting from the sprinkling. The *caṣāla* is made from a sheaf of barley. At the time of the *agnīṣomīya* rite, having performed the offering of the *paśupuroḍāśa* for Agni-Soma, he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters. At the time of the *savanīya* rites, having measured the sacrificial post, he dedicates the animals: the one for Agni-Soma, the *savanīya*, and the *anūbandhyā*. At the time of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he should give a white horse, harnessed to a golden ornament (*rukyapratimukta*), to the Udgātṛ of the Aṅgiras lineage.

At the time of the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice, there is a cake on one potsherd for Mitra and Varuṇa, or a *payasyā* curd-mixture. (15) For one year he shall not anoint himself with ointment, nor rub [his body] with oil, nor wash his feet after using them. (16) Having performed the *ekaviṃśa* as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* of this very sacrifice, one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice. (17) One who is younger than his elder brother or feels inferior should perform this sacrifice after having purchased the Soma according to the manner of the Aṅgirases. (18) A cow that has calved for the first time is the *somakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchasing Soma). (19) He gives a white horse to the Brahman priest; a reddish-brown mare to the Udgātṛ priest. (20) [The offering] for the Viśve Devas...

The Viśvajit sacrifice, characterized by all the *pṛṣṭha* chants, is for one who desires everything; he should perform it. Like the Viśvajit [is the Śyena]: 21. One practicing sorcery against Indra or Vasiṣṭha should perform the Śyena sacrifice. 22. He should settle upon a salt-flat or on unplowed ground. 23. The priests, wearing red turbans and red garments, with their sacred cords suspended around the neck, proceed as if acting harshly, carrying swords in their hands. 24. Having turned the two chariots about to serve as the *havirdhāna* sheds, they smear them; having approached a funeral bier, they use the skin of a cow that has been slaughtered for the funeral as the *adhiṣavaṇa* pressing-skin. 25.

The sacrificial post has its tip shaped like a wooden sword (sphyāgra), it is without a cross-beam (acaṣāla), and it is made of *tilva* or *badhaka* wood. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds, and the fuel (*idhma*) is made of *vibhītaka* wood. (26) He places the cups for the *manthin* draught in front of the *āgrayaṇa* vessel. (27) A red goat is the animal to be sacrificed at the Soma-pressing for Agni Rudravat. (28) He gives nine new items as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (29) [This is] the Ekatrika sacrifice for Prajāpati Udbhid; one should sacrifice with these "openings" (*udbhid*) for the piercing of these worlds. (30)

The first *vrātyastoma* sacrifice for the gods is the *catuḥṣoḍaśī*. (1) Four *vrātyas* who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) should perform this sacrifice for the sake of purification. (2) Their insignia are: a turban, a goad, a bowstring, a chariot with a crooked pole, a cart with a broken axle, a plank-covered vehicle, a garment with black fringes, two skins—one dark-blue and one white-spotted—and silver and gold ornaments; these belong to the householder. (3) For the others, there are garments fastened with cords, woolen cloths, and skins of red measure with double seams. (4) There are thirty-three [priests] on each side facing the householder.

They assemble. (5) He brings the thirty-four-horse chariot for the householder. (6) Having established the sacred fires and having placed [the fires] together within the householder’s fires, they should sacrifice. (7) This is established up to the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (8) To whomsoever he may hate, to him he should give the marks of a *vrātya* and the wealth of a *vrātya*. The sacrificial fee is thus. (9) A cruel woman is censured by means of the *ukthya*, the six-ṣoḍaśin, and the four-ṣoḍaśin; the youngest by the youngest rite, the two-ṣoḍaśin; and the eldest by the eldest rite.

One who desires preeminence should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut of Agni. (It is performed) with both *sāmans*, with the *rathaṃtara* as the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, with all *stomas*, with both *sāmans*, and with the *bṛhat* as the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*. For these [sacrifices], there are the *pravargya* rites; on the first day, the *śastras* are recited for Agni. It is a threefold (*trivṛt*) Agniṣṭoma Agniṣṭut. Having made the twenty-one-fold Agniṣṭoma *sāman* upon the verses addressed to Vāyu, one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with it. Having made the Vāravantīya Agniṣṭoma *sāman* upon the Revatī verses of this very same [rite], one who desires cattle should sacrifice with it.

One who has fallen away from a sacrifice should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma or the Agniṣṭut; whichever *stoma* he has fallen away from [he should employ]. (17) One who is ill, or one who desires food, or one who desires firm standing, should sacrifice with the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) *stoma*. (18) The first [sacrifice] belongs to Prajāpati, being a *trivṛt* [stoma] and unprecedented (*apūrva*). One who has rivals, or one who desires heaven, or one who desires cattle, should sacrifice [with it]. (19) Jamadagni’s arrow: one practicing sorcery should sacrifice with this, which is equal in ritual procedure to the Śyena. (20) The Bṛhaspatisava.

One who desires the office of domestic priest, the office of state minister, or spiritual preeminence (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice. (21) [The sacrificial animal] is ruddy, with reddish eyes, wearing a garland, and possessing three *śukriya* [mantras]. (22) When the *nārāśamsa* cups have been set down at the morning pressing, he assigns eleven sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). (23) At the midday pressing, having assigned twelve horses, he delays both types of sacrificial fees until the time for their distribution has passed. (24) At the time of the *māhendra* cup, after the *vājaprasavya* oblation of clarified butter has been offered while the altar mound has not yet been leveled, he consecrates [the sacrificer] according to his desire, addressing Bṛhaspati as "the domestic priest" while the latter is seated upon the throne on the northern altar. (25)

When the Nārāśamsa cups have been set down at the third pressing, he assigns eleven sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās). At the time for the dakṣiṇās of the Anūbandhyā cow, he causes them to be delayed. This is the Śunaskarṇastoma, the Sarvasvāra sacrifice. He who desires, "May I go to the heavenly world immediately after dying," should sacrifice with this. A hornless goat is the animal to be offered at the Soma-pressing; prepared food is the sacrificial gift; the Vāmadevya is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra. While the Ārbhava-pavamāna is being chanted, having said, "O Brāhmaṇas, establish my sacrifice," he sits down to the south of the Audumbarī post, covered and with his head toward the south.

It concludes in that very manner. 30. They pour out his portions [of food] at the Mārjālīya fire. 31. At the time of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), having carried him out by a way other than the sacred passage (atīrthena) and having caused him to bathe in the avabhṛtha, they cover him with another garment and lead him back according to the left-hand path (yathāsavyam). 32. At the time of cremation, they burn him from the Āhavanīya fire. 33. One who is living should go to the avabhṛtha. 34. The Upahavya sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati; it is undefined (anirukta) and is the first among the seventeen-day sacrifices. One who has rivals, or one desiring heaven, or one desiring cattle, should perform it. 1. A dark-grey horse is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); it is to be given to the Brahman priest. 2. It is the Soma sacrifice called Ṛtapeya, having the Bṛhat as its Pṛṣṭha-stotra.

Or one who desires a firm foundation should sacrifice. There are nine initiation days (*dīkṣā*) and three preparatory days (*upasad*), without the *pravargya* ceremony. The two performers of the vow remain with clarified butter; they are equal [in height] to the longest finger-joint at the four places, and to the shortest in the other cases. The procedure is established up to the *sarpaṇa*. Having uttered "Ṛta," they proceed. The procedure is established up to the time for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Having brought forward the Soma-cup filled with the shoots of the King Soma that has been prepared, together with the sacrificial fees, he gives it to the Brahman priest of the same lineage (*sagotra*). He should sacrifice with that. [The fee] for Agni is a *dūṇāśa* horse.

One desiring heaven should sacrifice. 10. In the forenoon, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; at midday, a pap to Sūrya; and in the afternoon, a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara; and at night, a pap to Cāndramasa. 11. For half a month, he performs the *pariyaṣṭi* at night. 12. At the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, there is one measure of twelve *mānas*; at the *prāyaṇīyā* and the *ātithyā*, two measures of twenty-four *mānas* each; at the *upasad*s, twice that amount; and at the *agnīṣomīya*, the *savanīya*, and at each pressing (*anusavana*), three times that amount. 13. At the third pressing, when the offerings have been set down...

At the Nārāśaṃsa cups of the Udayanīyā [offering], he gives a garland to the Udgātṛ. (14) A Vaiśya desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma. (15) However, his offspring becomes as if closed in. (16) They milk a hundred cows for the Āśira.

These are the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās). 17. On the day of preparation (upavasatha) for these, he causes thirty-four vessels of curds to be prepared. 18. Having placed the potsherds at the morning pressing, he milks sixty-six [cows] and cooks half of it. 19. When the King Soma has been purified, he pours out the draughts (grahas), sprinkling them with the cooked milk; at the midday pressing, [he does so] with the boiled milk. 20. The Kaṇvarathantara is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra. 21. For Indra is the Ukthya of intense flow, having the Rathantara as its Pṛṣṭha.

The King who has exceeded the Soma [limit], being engaged in battle, desiring a village, desiring prosperity, or desiring firm standing, should sacrifice. 22. It is established up to the point of the altar. 23. As far as the sacrificial posts, they dig out the altar. 24. He piles up the eleven [posts] facing east. 25. They milk a hundred pregnant cows for the *āśira* mixture, as in the *vaiśyastoma*.

And the mares are pregnant (26). Without consuming [the soma], they proceed by raising their own cups, pouring [soma] into them, and offering oblations (27). The Adhvaryu and the cup-assistants (camasādhvaryus), having responded to the Āchāvāka, consume the entire portions; the Adhvaryu and the cup-assistants do likewise for the two subsequent pressings (28). The Vājapeya and Rājasūya sacrifices have been explained (29).

The *rāḍ-virāj* [sacrifice] of Soma: one who desires royal power should sacrifice with the *samāna*. (1) The *virāj* of Agni: one who desires food should sacrifice. (2) The *upasad* and *punastoma*: the *upasad*s are for the Gandharvas and Apsarases; one who desires offspring should sacrifice. (3) The *punastoma* of Indra is an *ukthya*; he who, having received much [in gifts], feels as if swallowed by poison, or who feels as if torn asunder in the middle, should sacrifice with this. (4) The *catuṣṭoma* of Gautama.

One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *Aṃśu-ukthya*. First [the *Aṃśu*], then at the third pressing, having drawn the *ukthya*, he draws the *āgrayaṇa*. This is established up to the *agniṣṭoma-camasa*s. Having filled the *agniṣṭoma-camasa*s as before, he pours them into the *hotṛ-camasa* along with the vessels and the deposits. The *ṣoḍaśin* follows. [There are two sacrifices: "Bṛhaspati’s *udbhit* and *balabhid*"; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with these. Having sacrificed with the first, one should extend the month with the second. [There are two sacrifices: "Prajāpati’s *apaciti*."

One who desires honor should sacrifice. (13) Both have the *sāman*s; they have the *bṛhat* as the *pṛṣṭha*; these are the two *stoma*s of Agni. One who desires heaven should sacrifice. (15) He carries the fire-vessel (*ukhya*) for a full year. A thousand is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (16) The *ṛṣabha* and *gosava* belong to Indra. (17) The *ṛṣabha*: he who should desire, "May I be like a bull among my equals," he should sacrifice with this. (18) It has both *sāman*s; it has the *rathantara* as the *pṛṣṭha*. (19) The former is the Gaurāṅgirasa. (20) One who desires the highest office, or one who desires prosperity and sovereignty, should sacrifice with the *gosava*. (21) It is an *ukthya* sacrifice; it has both *sāman*s; it has the *bṛhat* as the *pṛṣṭha*. Ten thousand is the sacrificial fee. (22)
Cows are Bhaga; cows are Indra; to me the cows are the first draught of Soma.
O people, these cows are indeed Indra; I desire them with my heart and even with my mind, O Indra.

Having caused [the sacrificer] to recite "to Māhendra" at the time [of the offering], he sprinkles [the water] around [the fire] with "to Pārameṣṭhya," as desired, by milking back [the vessel]. 23. Prajāpati, Indra, the Stomakulāya, and the Marutstoma of the Maruts: one who desires prosperity should sacrifice with this. 24. He should cause three [sacrificers] to sacrifice with it. 25. The Kulāya belongs to Indra and Agni. He who should desire, "May I be like a nest (kulāya) for my offspring and cattle," should sacrifice with this; he should cause [another] to sacrifice with this. 26. For Indra, there is the Indrastoma Ukthya with the Bṛhat-pṛṣṭha.

One who desires sovereignty should sacrifice with the *samāna* [rite]. (27) The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of twelve hundred bulls. (28) This is the *stoma* of Agni. Two persons—the king and his domestic priest (*purohita*)—desiring union (*sāyujya*), or a Brāhmaṇa desiring the office of domestic priest, should sacrifice. (29) By means of the *vighana* [rite], one desiring cattle should sacrifice. (30) One practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the *saṃdaṃśa* [rite] dedicated to Indra. (31) [The ritual] is established up to the point of the altar (*vedi*). (32) As far as they dig up the altar for the sacrificial posts, (33) in a place sloping toward the east, he piles up the set of eleven [posts]. (34) The sacrificial fee consists of twelve thousand bulls and a thousand horses.

35. There are twelve *agniṣṭomas* and twelve *ukthyas*. All of these have a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of ten thousand; one desiring prosperity (*śrī*) should sacrifice with them. 36. There are the *ṛṣiṣṭomas*, the *ṣoḍaśins*, and the *aptoryāmas*. All of these have a sacrificial fee of ten thousand or a million; one desiring all things (*sarvakāma*) should sacrifice with them.

37. There are thirteen *atirātras*: 1. Of these, Prajāpati’s first is the *jyotis-atirātra*; one desiring success (*ṛddhi*) should sacrifice with it. 2. Indra’s is the *sarvastoma*; one desiring prosperity (*bhūti*) should sacrifice with it. 3. Prajāpati’s is the *aptoryāma* with all the *pṛṣṭhas*; one desiring all things should sacrifice with it. 4. Prajāpati’s is the ninefold *saptadaśa*.

One who desires offspring should sacrifice; these four [sacrifices] beginning with this one are characterized by the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. One who is the eldest son of the eldest wife and desires preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) should sacrifice with the Viṣuvat day, which is the hymn-form of the Ādityas. One who desires cattle should sacrifice with the Goṣṭoma. One who desires heaven should sacrifice with the Āyuṣṭoma. One who has rivals should sacrifice with the Abhijit. One who desires cattle should sacrifice with the Viśvajit. One who desires splendor should sacrifice with the Trivṛt of Agni. One who desires heroic power should sacrifice with the Pañcadaśa of Indra. One who desires offspring should sacrifice with the Saptadaśa of Prajāpati.

One desiring food should sacrifice with this; [the sacrifice] belongs to Āditya, has the twenty-one-fold stoma, and the Bṛhat as its Pṛṣṭha-stotra. One desiring firm standing should sacrifice; in all cases, the night-chant is fifteen-fold, and the junction is threefold.

One should sacrifice with the Paśumad Cāturmāsyas. Their ritual observances (*vrata*), time, and sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) are like those of the Haviryajñas; likewise for the fuel-sticks (*idhma*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the suspension of the Full Moon sacrifice. Before each respective festival, there is the introductory *Pāśukī Ārambhaṇīyā* offering. One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva [Paśubandha]. From the *cātvāla* pit up to the sprinkling of ghee (*vyāghāraṇa*), the procedure is omitted. On the following day, the Vaiśvadeva animal sacrifice takes place. The rite is established up to the tethering of the victim. He ties the victim to the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), and performs the *svaru*-rite with a chip of the enclosing-stick on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).

Or he performs the entire work of the *cātvāla* pit; having proceeded with the *vājina* offering, he stops at the time of shaving [the hair]. It has been explained that "for four months he does not eat meat. At the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, having fasted on the preceding full-moon day, he should immolate a ewe for the Maruts. He measures out the *uttaravedi* altar; he erects the sacrificial post and binds the animal to the post. Having pushed the embers toward the south within the enclosing sticks so that they do not touch them, he offers the *karambha* vessels. When the omentum has been offered, having performed the purification at the *cātvāla* pit, [he proceeds] for the offering to Varuṇa.

He drives away the calves; he does not offer the *svaru* splinter; he does not dedicate the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). He performs the *agnihotra* on the northern altar-ground. On the following day, a ram dedicated to Varuṇa is the animal victim. Having emerged from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) and having performed the rites belonging to the *Vāruṇapraghāsas*, he dedicates the sacrificial post. At the time of shaving the head, he causes [the hair] to be turned back. "For four months he does not eat meat"—this has been explained. In the *Sākamedha* sacrifices, on the preceding full moon day there is an animal victim for Agni, and on the subsequent one an offering to Indra-Agni; or, on the day of sacrifice, an offering to Prajāpati.

Or, with the Ekādaśinī animals (Sūtra 22), having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, they proceed with the Pitṛyajña; they go to the Tryambaka offerings with a single fire-brand (Sūtra 23); having returned, after performing the rite for Āditya within the sacrificial framework of the second fire, he points toward the sacrificial post (Sūtra 24); at the time of shaving the head, he turns back (Sūtra 25); "For four months he does not eat meat"—this has been explained (Sūtra 26); in the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice, there is an animal for Vāyu and one for Upāṃśu-Devatā.

That [sacrifice] has been explained by the Vaiśvadeva. 27. At each parvan, he brings forward the oblations following the animal-cake offerings, as in the case of the Devikā offerings. They proceed with them in the same manner as for the Upāṃśu sacrifice. 28. In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, there are seven [cakes] on the eastern altar, and one cake on a single potsherd for Varuṇa on the northern altar. 29. In the Sākamedha sacrifices, the Anīkavat and Sāṃtapana offerings are on the first day; at the appropriate time, the Gṛhamedhīya and the Pūrṇadarvya offerings are on the middle day; and the Krīḍin offering and the Mahāhavir offerings are on the last day. 30. In the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice, either an animal victim or a Soma sacrifice is prescribed. 31.

One should sacrifice with the Saumya Cāturmāsyas. In the place of the Vaiśvadeva, there is a Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma. There are ten initiation days (dīkṣā) and three Upasad days. He prepares the sacrificial post and the high altar (uttaravedi). He merely marks the Dhiṣṇya hearths. After the Maharyojana rite, they proceed with the Vājina offering. Having emerged from the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), he puts on a new garment; the Anūbandhyā cow is dedicated to Bṛhaspati. At the time of shaving, he stops [the ritual]. "He does not eat meat for four months"—this has been explained. In the place of the Varuṇapraghāsas, there is a two-day period.

There are sixteen initiation days and twelve *upasads*. 9. The *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma* comes first. 10. He pours out the *uttaravedi* at the *dhiṣṇya* hearths. 11. He erects the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and binds the victim to the post. 12. At the morning pressing, when the *dhiṣṇya* hearths have been distributed, he should maintain the fire on the *mārjālīya* for the sake of the *karambha* vessels. 13. On the following day, there is an *ukthya* sacrifice. 14. On the fourteenth day, he sacrifices to Varuṇa with the scrapings from the pot of Varuṇa’s cooked rice. 15. Having returned, the *anūbandhyā* cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa is offered. 16. At the time of shaving the head, he causes [the hair] to grow back. 17. Four...

"It does not eat me for a month"—this has been explained (18). For the Sākamedha sacrifices, there is a three-day period; there are fifteen initiation days (*dīkṣā*) and twelve preparatory days (*upasad*) (19). [The sequence consists of] an *agniṣṭoma*, an *ukthya*, and an *atirātra* (20). On the fourteenth day, during the third pressing of the third day, when the hearths (*dhiṣṇya*) have been spread out, having added fuel to the fire on the *mārjālīya* altar, they proceed with the Pitṛyajña after the *udayanīya* offering (21). From there, they go toward the Tryambaka offerings with a single fire-brand (22). Having returned, the *sūryānūbandhyā* is a barren cow (23).

He prepares the *paśupuroḍāśa* and the *caru* for Āditya in succession (Sūtra 24). He points toward the sacrificial post (Sūtra 25). At the time of shaving [the hair], he turns back from it (Sūtra 26). "For four months he does not eat meat"—this has been explained (Sūtra 27). In the section of the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice, there is a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma* and a *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma* (Sūtra 28). The *anūbandhyā* cow dedicated to the Aśvins is explained by the rules for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice (Sūtra 29). He prepares the oblations for the new and full moon festivals during the morning pressings, as in the case of sacrifices involving animal victims (Sūtra 30). Before the carrying around of the *vasatīvarī* waters, the *gṛhamedhīya* offering takes place.

Before the Prātaranuvāka, there is the *pūrṇadarvī* (full-spoon offering) as in the case of the animal sacrifices. 31. Those animals which belong to the animal sacrifices are for each day. 32. There are fifty sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). In the final [day], one hundred and twelve; in the final [day], one hundred and twelve. 33. Thus ends the third chapter of the Rājasūya. Following the Atirātra, the Ahīna sacrifices begin with the two-day rite and extend up to the twelve-day rite. 1. The initiation (*dīkṣā*) takes place on the full moon day. 2. The Upasad rites conclude after a month, according to the remainder of the Satyas.

The initiation (*dīkṣā*) [is performed] according to the statement elsewhere. Among those, in the cases of the one-day sacrifices (*aikāhika*), the one-day rites (*dharmas*) apply; in the others, the ten-night rites (*daśarātrika*) apply. For example, as with the *pṛṣṭhya* [stomas], the cups (*graha*), the leading [sacrifices], or the three-fold array (*tryanīkā*). One should divide the eleven [cattle] equally, or place them all in the final [day]. In the cases of the one-day sacrifices, the sacrificial animals belong to the one-day rites; in the others, they belong to the eleven. The Āṅgirasa [rite] is the first of the two-day sacrifices; he should not perform it who considers himself superior yet inferior, or who desires offspring or cattle. The *Jyotis* Agniṣṭoma is the first.

The *sarvastoma* *atirātra* with the *ṣoḍaśin* follows as the subsequent [sacrifice]. (9) A king desiring victory should sacrifice with the *caitraratha*. (10) The *jyotis* *ukthya* comes first; the *āyus* *atirātra* with the *ṣoḍaśin* follows as the subsequent [sacrifice]. (11) One who desires, "May I be free from harshness and rich in cattle," or one who, though rich in cattle, feels as if he were harsh, or one desiring progeny or desiring cattle, should sacrifice with the *kāpivana*. (12) The *agniṣṭoma* with the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* stomas comes first; the *sarvastoma* *atirātra* with the *ṣoḍaśin* follows as the subsequent [sacrifice]. (13) The *gargatrirātra* belongs to the Viśvedevas.

One who desires all things and wishes to conquer this world should sacrifice with this [rite]. The first three days of the ten-night period have their two middle days reversed; on that [day] is the night together with the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Every day they milk the seven cows for the *āśira* mixture. At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), a three-colored heifer, perfect in form, is prepared as the "thousandth" cow. He gives thirty-three hundred and three hundred [cows]. While those [cows] stand still, [the priest recites]:
"A thousand skins have I caused to come forth from the skin of Udbala. As such, bring us a thousand, O wealthy one, along with riches."
May wealth enter me again.

With these words, the sacrificer mutters [the mantra] into the right ear of the bull. 19. He offers a full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) on the Āgnīdhrīya fire with the verse, "Both have conquered. 20. He consecrates the released [bulls] with the following mantra: 21. "May he who is the means here come to us like a fortress; may he who is the guardian and lord of prosperity come to you.
O All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*), fulfill our desire as we approach."
Bestow cattle here; here may they thrive like the Śakā bird. Multiply right here, O men, and cause us to prosper.
Turn back, do not go away; follow us, O wealthy ones.
O Agni and Soma, you who possess the wealth of renewal, bestow riches upon us.
Bring them back again; let them abide with me, the lord of cattle. Bring them back again; let whatever wealth there is abide with me.
O Jātavedas, turn [the wealth] back; let there be a hundred returns for you, a thousandfold returns for you.
Then, by the nourishment of nourishment, restore to us what was lost, restore to us our riches.

"Return with vigor, together with wealth; I behold your vigor"—this is the *goyajña* (cow-sacrifice) for them. (22) He gives a hundred [cows] to one who knows their lineage (*ārṣeya*). (23) In the middle [of the cows], he gives the second [cow]. Among those [cows], he takes the *vehad* cow; its ear [he addresses with]: "Vigor you are; bestow vigor upon me; let wealth return to me. (24) He gives a hundred [cows] to one who knows [the lineage] but is not of a [recognized] lineage (*anārṣeya*). (25) Having led the *sahasratamī* cow by the southern path, he covers it with *darbha* grass to the north of the *uttaravedi* altar and establishes it facing east.
(26) "Smell the jar, O Great One! Let the drops enter you as rivers enter the ocean. (27)
May she, the one of wide streams and full of milk, yield a thousandfold for us; O Sūnṛtā, may wealth along with progeny enter into me again.

Thus he causes [the cow] to smell the Droṇakalaśa. (27) "Thou art desirable, thou art dear, thou art worthy of oblation; O Sarasvatī, thou art praised, beloved, great, and renowned—O inviolable one, may these names of thine announce us as doers of good deeds among the gods. With these names of cows, the sacrificer murmurs into her right ear. (28) He gives ten parts of her to the Brahman and five to the Āgnīdhra. (29) Saying, "One is mine," he releases the one that has been assigned into the sacrificer's cow-pen. (30) To these two he gives food and a garment of silk (*tārpya*); two shares of it go to the Brahman. (31) At the end, the third share goes to the others; among them is a dwarf (*vāmana*).
You are the support of a thousand; you are the dwarf belonging to Viṣṇu.
As such, bring us stability, being yourself possessed of wealth along with riches.
May wealth enter me again.

Thus [ends the section on] thirty-two [cows]. To one who is of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) but ignorant [of it], one gives a hundred [cows] (thirty-three). Just as in the Garga-trirātra, having given one thousand cows for each [day], he performs the ritual of the thousandth cow (sahasratamī-karman). The Aśva-trirātra of Prajāpati has been explained. The Vaida-trirātra belongs to Indra and Agni; a king desiring victory should sacrifice with it. There are three *atirātra* rites, each consisting of the *trivṛt* stoma and including the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. The *chandoma* days belong to the Ādityas. The Parāka [rite]: one desiring heaven should sacrifice with it. It is explained by the Garga-trirātra. One should desire this [result] from the gods.

The *Caturvīra* sacrifice of Atri is the first of the four-night rites (*caturātra*). He who desires, "May four heroic sons be born to me," should perform this sacrifice. It consists of an *agniṣṭoma*, an *ukthya*, and an *atirātra*. The second [four-night rite] belongs to Jamadagni.

One desiring limited prosperity should sacrifice. There are thirty initiation days (*dīkṣā*) and twelve *upasads*. He silently prepares the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) following the *upasads*, having processed them [with water]. Having adorned them, he places them down together with the clarified butter (*ājya*). Having performed the *upasad* rite, he offers the *upasad* oblation after having offered straight and firmly established oblations with the mantra: "O Agni, perform the office of the Hotṛ; perform the sacrifice! Bring hither Vaiśvānara the Father for our protection! O Indra and Agni, offer the oblation to the gods!"*

Likewise for the afternoon [offering]. 7. By this same rule, for the subsequent [offerings], there are cakes on two potsherds, three potsherds, and so on by the addition of potsherds, up to twelve potsherds. 8. O Aśvins, gods, sprinkle this sacrifice with honey for the sake of the sacrificer today; O Indra, offer the oblation to the gods. O divine Viṣṇu, stride out widely in this sacrifice for the sake of the sacrificer today; O Indra, offer the oblation to the gods. O divine Soma, bestower of seed, prosper for the sake of the sacrificer today in this sacrifice; O Indra, offer the oblation to the gods.

O divine Dhātṛ, as a good ordainer, ordain today at this sacrifice for the sacrificer; O Indra and the gods, offer the oblation! O divine pressing-stones, speak today at this sacrifice for the sacrificer sweet speech; O Indra and the gods, offer the oblation! O divine Anumati, approve today this sacrifice for the sacrificer; O Indra and the gods, offer the oblation! O divine Aditi, bestow today at this sacrifice upon the sacrificer the favor of the Ādityas; O Indra and the gods, offer the oblation! To every seat [of the gods]!

"Possessing offspring, active, enjoying, wise—O Indra, together with the gods, offer the oblation! O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, bestower of good seed, prosper today for the sacrificer at this sacrifice! O Indra, together with the gods, offer the oblation!"—with these [verses] ending in *svāhā*, he performs the kindling. (9) The Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, and Atirātra [sacrifices]. (10) Vasiṣṭha’s *saṃsarpa*: one desiring progeny should sacrifice. (11) The Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, and Atirātra [sacrifices]. (12) Viśvāmitra’s *saṃjaya*.

A king desiring victory should perform a sacrifice: a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*, a *pañcadaśa* *ukthya*, a *saptadaśa* *ukthya*, a *ekaviṃśa* *atirātra*, and a five-day period (*pañcāha*) characterized by the repeated performance of the *viśve devāḥ* [rite]. One who has rivals, or one desiring heaven or cattle, should perform this sacrifice. The first five days consist of the ten-night rite (*daśarātrika*). On the fifth day is the night of the Great Ones (*mahatām*). This is the *marutstoma* *pañcaśāradīya*.

One who desires abundance should sacrifice. On the new moon day of Vaiśākha, on a day suitable for sacrifice, he observes the fast for the animal sacrifice (paśubandha). The ritual is established as far as the introductory rite (aupākaraṇa). He dedicates seventeen spotted three-year-old cows that have not been milked. He dedicates seventeen spotted bulls, five-year-old oxen, as victims. For all animal sacrifices, there is the introductory rite, the sprinkling, the giving of water to drink, and the carrying of fire around the victims. They conclude the rite with the other [victims] after the release of the bulls. These are the expiations.

If they should seize [the victim] by force, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aprasahya; then, having offered it, one dedicates another animal of that same form, color, and age. If it is a cripple, one-eyed, or lame, [one offers] a pap to Bṛhaspati; if it is one-eyed, a pap to Sūrya on one potsherd; if it falls into a natural pit or a hole, a pap to Bhūmi on one potsherd; if it should fall down, a pap to Vāyu; if it should sink down, a pap to Nirṛti.

If one should be struck down by another, he should offer a *prājāpatya* cake on twelve potsherds; then he dedicates another animal of that same form, color, and age. (25) He offers heifers to the Maruts: speckled ones in the first year, dappled ones in the second, those with spots like fresh butter in the third, ruddy ones in the fourth, and tawny ones in the fifth. (26) On this day of sacrifice, he undergoes consecration (*dīkṣā*) under the *somā* constellation. (27) There are eighteen days of consecration and twelve days of *upasads*. (28) It consists of an *agniṣṭoma* with the *trivṛt* stoma, an *ukthya* with the *pañcadaśa* stoma, and an *atirātra* with the *pañcadaśa* stoma.
The seventeenth day is an Atirātra. 29. There are three bull-offerings dedicated to Indra and the Maruts as the Savanīya animals on one day, and five on the last day. 30.

One who is observant of vows and desires food should sacrifice to Prajāpati: a Jyotis Agniṣṭoma, a Gau Ukthya, a Mahāvrata, a Gau Ukthya, an Āyu Atirātra, and the six-day period of the seasons (Ṛtūnām ṣaḍahaḥ). One who desires stability should sacrifice: a Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha, a Trayastriṃśa [Stoma], and three [of these]. One who desires heroism should sacrifice to Indra: a Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, a Pañcadaśa Ukthya, a Saptadaśa Ukthya, a Jyotis, a Gau, an Āyu, and an Atirātra. This is the Pṛṣṭhya-avalamba of the gods.

A king desiring victory should sacrifice with [the Sattras]: 7. The Abhyāsanga, a five-day period, ending with the Viśvajit Atirātra. 8. The Saptarātra of the Ṛṣis; one desiring prosperity should sacrifice with it. 9. The Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, followed by the Mahāvrata and concluding with an Atirātra. 10. The second [Sattra] of Prajāpati; one desiring offspring should sacrifice with it. 11. The Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, followed by the seventeen-fold (saptadaśa) Mahāvrata and concluding with an Atirātra. 12. The third [Sattra] of the Ādityas.

One desiring cattle should sacrifice. 13. It consists of a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, with the *chandoma* as the *pavamāna*, the *mahāvrata*, and culminating in an *atirātra*. 14. This is the fourth [sacrifice] of Jamadagni. One desiring unlimited prosperity should sacrifice. 15. It is an *abhyāsaṅgya* five-day period, with the thirty-third day as the sixth, the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) *mahāvrata*, and culminating in an *atirātra*. 16. This is the fifth [sacrifice] of Indra.

One who desires vigor should sacrifice with the Trikadruka Tryaha, the Abhijit, the Viśvajit, the Sarvajit, the Sarvastoma Atirātra, and the Janaka Saptarātra of Prajāpati; one who desires progeny should sacrifice with this. [The Janaka Saptarātra consists of] four days of the Trivṛt stoma, preceded by the Agniṣṭoma, followed by the Viśvajit, the Mahāvrata, the Jyotis Atirātra, and the Devānām Pṛṣṭhya Stoma.

One who desires to obtain both types of desires should perform this sacrifice, which consists of a *sattrayajña* [comprising]: a *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* with the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* *sāmans*, and a *viśvajit-atirātra*. (21) The eight-night rite of the Vasus: one who desires divinity should perform it. It consists of a *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, a *mahāvrata*, and a *jyotis-atirātra*. (22–23) The nine-night rite of the Devas: one who desires long life should perform it. It consists of a *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, a *jyotis*, a *go*, and an *āyus-atirātra*. (24–25) This is the second [rite] of the Ādityas. (26)

One desiring cattle should sacrifice: the Trikadruka three-day rite, the Abhyāsaṅgya five-day rite, and the Viśvajit Atirātra. One desiring liberation from evil should sacrifice the Indra’s Trikakud ten-night rite. There are two Agniṣṭomas with the Trivṛt stoma; in the middle is an Ukthya with the Pañcadaśa stoma; then two Agniṣṭomas with the Saptadaśa stoma; and in the middle an Ukthya with the Ekaviṃśa stoma. He should sacrifice: three Agniṣṭomas with the Trivṛt stoma, three Ukthyas with the Pañcadaśa stoma, three Ukthyas with the Saptadaśa stoma, and an Ekaviṃśa Atirātra. [This is] of the Ādityas.

The Chandomadaśāha: one desiring cattle should sacrifice with it. 33. It consists of an Abhyāsaṅgya, five days, four Chandomas, and a Viśvajit Atirātra. 34. The Devānāṃ Pūḥ Daśarātra: one being subjected to malevolent magic should sacrifice with it. 35. A Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, a Jyotis Ukthya, a Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, a Gauḥ Ukthya, an Abhijit Agniṣṭoma, a Gauḥ Ukthya, a Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma, an Āyuḥ Ukthya, a Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma, and a Sarvastoma Atirātra. 36. The Pauṇḍarīka belongs to Kṣemadhanvan.

One who desires the supreme lordship or the sovereignty of heaven should sacrifice with the Ekādaśarātra. (37) It consists of six Abhyāsaṅgya days. (38) Having performed the ritual arrangements day by day, he gives thousands [of cows]; at the Catuṣṭoma, he gives a thousand horses. (39) The Dvādaśāha has been explained; such is the Dvādaśāha.
(40) Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Rājasūya.

One should apply the *abhiplava* six-day period to the *sattras*; the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) to the ten-day period within the *daśarātra*; and the other [elements] to the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* days. In the five-day rite, there is the *trikadruka* consisting of the *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus*. In the nine-day rite, there is the *abhijit*, the *svarasāman* days, the *viṣuvat*, the reversed *svarasāman* days, and the *viśvajit* with all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras. In the three-day rite, there is the three-day sequence of *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus*. In the commencement of the thirty-three-fold day, the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are in reverse order; the penultimate day is the *vrata* day, unless otherwise specified. The rites beginning with the twelve-day sacrifice follow this pattern.

The sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) have *atirātra* rites at both ends, with an addition of days up to forty-four; this is their arrangement of days. (1) For those desiring prosperity, they should undertake the thirteen-night session (*trayodaśarātra*), which consists of an *atirātra* with all the *stoma*s before the *chandoma*s in a twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). (2) The penultimate day is the vow for the subsequent [session]; for those desiring stability, they should undertake the thirteen-night session. (3) It consists of the ten days of the twelve-day rite, the *viṣuvat* day, and the *devasūkta*; for those desiring divinity, they should undertake the thirteen-night session. (4) There is a twenty-four-fold *ukthya*, a nine-night rite, and the *mahāvrata*.

Those desiring a firm foundation should undertake the thirteen-night sacrifice (7). The ten-night sacrifice consists of the Go and Āyus [stomas]. Those desiring a firm foundation should undertake the fourteen-night sacrifice (8). The Pṛṣṭhya is reversed; the Pṛṣṭhya [is repeated]. Those desiring divinity should undertake the fourteen-night sacrifice (9). The Pṛṣṭhya is flanked on both sides by three-night periods.

If they perform [the sacrifice] at a funeral pyre, in water, or at a wedding, they should indeed undertake it for fourteen nights. There is a *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha], the *mahāvrata*, and a *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] beginning with the *trayastrim̐śa* [stoma]. Just as there might be a *mahāvrata* on the *ekāṣṭakā* day, those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake the fifteen-night rite after the vow. It consists of a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭut* *agniṣṭoma*, flanked on both sides by three-night periods, and a *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha].

Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake the fifteen-night sacrifice (*pañcadaśarātra*). It consists of the *trivṛt* *agniṣṭut* *agniṣṭoma*, a three-night period, and another ten-night period, followed by an *atirātra* at the end. Those performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*) who desire prosperity should undertake this fifteen-night sacrifice. The ritual observances (*vrata*) for these are the same. Those desiring victory should undertake the sixteen-night sacrifice; it consists of a five-day period and a ten-night period. Those desiring glory (*śrī*) should undertake the seventeen-night sacrifice; it consists of a six-day period and a ten-night period.

Those desiring long life should undertake the eighteen-night rite; the vow for these is the same. Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake the thirty-night rite: the *pṛṣṭhya* [six-day period], the *svarasāman* periods, the *viṣuvat* day, the *svarasāman* periods in reverse order, the *pṛṣṭhya*, and the *trayastrim̐śa* as the concluding [day]. Those desiring food should undertake the twenty-one-night rite: three six-day periods, followed by the first *atirātra*. Those desiring food should undertake the twenty-one-night rite: a three-day period, a six-day period, a ten-night period, and the *mahāvrata*.

Those desiring cattle should undertake the twenty-two-night rite: a five-day period, a six-day period, and a ten-night period. Those desiring stability should undertake the twenty-three-night rite; this is the *sāṃsadāmayana*.

The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), the thirty-three-fold day with the *ahar* unexpressed, the *upahavya* arranged [sacrifice], the thirty-three-fold day with the *ahar* unexpressed, the twenty-seven-fold day, two twenty-one-fold days, the twenty-seven-fold day with the *ahar* unexpressed, the thirty-three-fold day with the *ahar* unexpressed, the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, the threefold day turned westward with the *ahar* unexpressed, the *jyotiṣṭoma* *agniṣṭoma*—those desiring food should undertake the twenty-four-night sacrifice: two six-day periods and a ten-night period.

Those desiring food should undertake the twenty-four-night rite; the vow is the same as in these [preceding rites]. Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake the twenty-five-night rite; the *go* and *āyus* [stomas] are placed before the six-day periods, but there is no vow. Those desiring victory should undertake the twenty-six-night rite; the three-day period is placed before the six-day periods, but there are no *go* and *āyus* [stomas].

Those desiring prosperity (*śrī*) should undertake the twenty-seven-night sacrifice (27). Those desiring long life (*āyus*) should undertake the twenty-eight-night sacrifice, following the same observances as these [preceding ones] (28). A five-day period, two six-day periods, and a ten-night period: those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake the twenty-nine-night sacrifice (29). Three six-day periods and a ten-night period: those desiring manly vigor (*puruṣa*) should undertake the thirty-night sacrifice (30). Following the same observances as these, those desiring energy (*ojas*) should undertake the thirty-one-night sacrifice (31). Following the same [observances] as these, but with the *Go* and *Āyus* sacrifices placed before the six-day periods and without the [usual] observance, those desiring cattle (*paśu*) should undertake the thirty-two-night sacrifice (32).

Three *pṛṣṭhya* six-day periods, a *viśvajit* *atirātra*, a five-day period, and a ten-night period; those desiring a firm foundation should undertake this thirty-three-night sacrifice. (1) Three six-day periods, with an *atirātra* at the beginning and one in the middle, a ten-night period, and the *mahāvrata*; those desiring a firm foundation should undertake this thirty-three-night sacrifice. (2) Three five-day periods consisting of *pṛṣṭhya* days, a *viśvajit* *atirātra*, and three five-day periods consisting of *pṛṣṭhya* days.

Those desiring firm establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*) should undertake the *triṇava* [stoma] for three days: three *tryahas*, three *ṣaḍahas*, the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), and the *mahāvrata*. Those desiring food (*annādya*) should undertake the *catustriṃśat* [stoma] for three days: three *tryahas*, three *ṣaḍahas*, the ten-night rite, and the *go-āyus* [sāmans]. Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake the *pañcatriṃśat* [stoma] for three days: four *ṣaḍahas*, the ten-night rite. Those desiring victory (*vijiti*) should undertake the *ṣaṭtriṃśat* [stoma] for three days; in these very [rites], the vow (*vrata*) is the same.

Those desiring prosperity (*śrī*) should perform the *triṣṭoma* sacrifice for thirty-seven nights; in these very [sacrifices], the *go* and *āyus* [stomas] are placed before the six-day periods (*ṣaḍaha*), and there is no vow (*vrata*) for those desiring long life (*āyus*). Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform the *triṣṭoma* sacrifice for thirty-nine nights; in these very [sacrifices], there is the vow, but the *go* and *āyus* [stomas] are not placed before the six-day periods.

Forty-four men desiring progeny should undertake this sacrifice: an Agniṣṭoma, two Ukthyas with the Trivṛt-stoma for three days, an Atirātra, nine Ukthyas with the Ṣoḍaśin as the tenth day having the Pañcadaśa-stoma, an Atirātra with the Saptadaśa-stoma, a Pṛṣṭhya Atirātra, and twelve Ukthyas with the Ekaviṃśa-stoma.

Desiring, "May we be separated from evil and live apart," they undertook this forty-nine-night rite. There are two Atirātras before each of the first four six-day periods (ṣaḍaha), and before the fifth, there is a twelve-night period followed by the Mahāvrata.

Those desiring firm establishment should undertake this forty-nine-night rite. There is an Atirātra with all the Stomas before the fifth of the six six-day periods (ṣaḍahas), and a ten-night period (daśarātra) after the sixth. On those days, they perform the Āñjīra and Abhyañjīra rites: with a decoction of Guggulu resin at the morning pressing, a decoction of Saugandhika at the midday pressing, and a decoction of Pūtudāru wood at the third pressing. When about to recite the Prātaranuvāka, they proceed in this manner during the morning pressing and likewise for the two subsequent ones.

Of the two *savana*s: those who do not know the Self should undertake this forty-nine-night rite. It consists of a twenty-four-fold *ukthya*, three six-day periods, the nine-night rite, a six-day period, the *go* and *āyus* sacrifices, the ten-night rite, and the *mahāvrata*; it is equal to a year.

Desiring to complete the work of a year, they should undertake this forty-nine-night rite: an Agniṣṭoma, five Ukthyas, an Agniṣṭoma on both sides, and an Ukthya in the middle with the Trivṛt stoma. By this same procedure, the three nine-night rites (navarātra) are explained, having the Pañcadaśa, Saptadaśa, and Ekaviṃśa stomas. The ten-night rite (daśarātra) consists of the Mahāvrata and the Sāvitra Kakubha.

Those desiring offspring should undertake this forty-nine-night rite. By the third [day], the penultimate [day] is explained; in the place of the *sarvastoma*, there is the *mahāvrata*. Those who desire, "May we not be smeared, may we not be anointed, may we not be entangled by evil," should undertake this forty-nine-night rite. There are six six-day periods, a ten-night period, and the *mahāvrata*. Those desiring stability should undertake this forty-nine-night rite. In that which is measured by a year, the *pṛṣṭhya* and *avadhi* [periods] are before the *abhijit*, and after the *viśvajit*.

Those desiring supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) should undertake the rite for sixty-one nights; those desiring long life should undertake it for three days, fourteen [days], six days, ten nights, the *mahāvrata*, or one hundred nights. 20–21. They press the Soma while moving forward, or they press it in the same place. 22. Or there is the conclusion at the end of the initiation (*dīkṣā*). 23. In the sacrificial sessions (*sattras*), there are six additional animal sacrifices: one for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, one for Viṣṇu, one for Pūṣan, one for Vāyu, and one for the Aśvins. 24.

Those desiring offspring should undertake the Gavāmayana; by this, the Ādityānām Ayana and the Aṅgirasām Ayana are explained. 1. The Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa Stomas are for the six-day periods (ṣaḍahas) before the Viṣuvat day, and the Pṛṣṭhya is at the beginning of the months; after the Viṣuvat, the Pañcadaśa and Trivṛt are used, with the Pṛṣṭhya in the middle of the months. 2. The Bṛhaspatisava takes the place of the Abhijit, and the Indra-stoma that of the Viśvajit; following that is the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha and the Daśarātra in its expanded form (vyūḍha), consisting of Agniṣṭomas with Trivṛt stomas, as well as the Udbhid and Balabhid sacrifices.

That [sacrificial session] consists of twenty-eight days: a six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) with the *pṛṣṭhya* chant in the middle, the *go* and *āyus* days, and a ten-day period (*daśāha*) with the *chandomas* having their stomas reduced. The remainder is explained by the *Gavāmayana*. Those desiring heaven should undertake this; it is the *Aṅgirasām Ayana*. There is a threefold hymn-form (*trivṛt-stoma*) for the six-day periods: a *pṛṣṭhya* chant precedes the months prior to the *Viṣuvat*, and a *pṛṣṭhya* chant follows them after the *Viṣuvat*. Between the two six-day periods, there is the *go*, the *āyus*, and the ten-day period with the *chandomas* in direct order (*anuloma*). The remainder is explained by the *Ādityānām Ayana*.

Those desiring heaven should undertake the Dṛtivātavator-ayanam. They pass the months prior to the Viṣuvat day by means of each successive day of the Pṛṣṭhya [ṣaḍaha]. In place of the Viṣuvat, there is the Mahāvrata. With those same days repeated in reverse order, the first and last days thereafter are accompanied by Atirātras. Those desiring prosperity should undertake the Kuṇḍapāyinām-ayanam. For one month they remain consecrated (dīkṣita).

In that month, they purchase the King (Soma). There are twelve *upasads*. Having concluded the final *upasad* in the afternoon, having set aside the Soma and the *mahāvīra* vessels, they pass the months by means of the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and each of the four *cāturmāsya* seasonal sacrifices. Having concluded the full moon sacrifice for half a month and the new moon sacrifice for half a month, they perform the *śunāsīrya* sacrifice; then, having removed the [old] fires and performed the rites beginning with the carrying forward of the fire up to the milking of the cows, they dwell [there]. On the following day...

Starting from the *prātaranuvāka*, they pass five months with five *pṛṣṭhya* days, one by one. [There are] eighteen *trayastrim̐śa* days, the *daśarātra*, the *mahāvrata*, and the *udayanīya-atirātra*; that constitutes a month. They consume the *soma* from cups without handles (*atsaruka*). He who is the *hotṛ* is the *adhvaryu*; he who is the *udgātṛ* is the *achāvāka*, the *neṣṭṛ*, and the *brahmā*; he who is the *maitrāvaruṇa* is the *pratihartṛ*; he who is the *prastotṛ* is the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* and the *grāvastut*.

The Pratiprasthātṛ is the Agnīdh, and he is the Unnetṛ. He studies for one month; the Gṛhapati is the Gṛhapati, and the Subrahmaṇya is the Subrahmaṇya. (16) They do not go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices. Those desiring prosperity should undertake them. (17) [This is] the Kṣullakatāpaścita. They remain consecrated for four months; they perform the Upasad rites for four days. (18) They pass the months by means of four Pṛṣṭhya days, one by one. Those desiring heaven should undertake them. (19) [This is] the Madhyamatāpaścita.

They remain consecrated for a year; they perform the *upasad* rites for a year. The *Gavāmayana* is the *soma*-pressing. Those desiring progeny should undertake the *Mahātāpaścita*. They remain consecrated for three years; they perform the *upasad* rites for three years. The *Gavāmayana*, the *Ādityānām ayana*, and the *Aṅgirasām ayana* have the *soma*-pressing for three years. The first and last days are *atirātra* sacrifices.

Those desiring supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) should undertake the twelve-year sacrificial session of the Naimiṣīyas; by each of those days, they pass three years at a time. Those desiring heaven (*svarga*) should undertake the thirty-six-year sacrificial session of the Śāktyas; by each of those days, they pass nine years at a time. The sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) at the Soma-pressings are made of meat.

For those desiring prosperity, they should perform the *pṛṣṭhya-puroḍāśas* using the flesh of excellent wild animals, parrots, peacocks, and *māmya* birds, as is appropriate. (26) The *Sādhyānām Ayana* lasts for a hundred years. By means of those very days, they pass twenty-five years with each single day. Those desiring heaven should undertake it. (27) Between two *Atirātras*, there are a thousand days, consisting of one hundred repetitions of the *Daśarātra*. This is the *Sahasrasādhya*. Those desiring, "May we be separated from evil," should undertake it. (28)

He undergoes initiation at the confluence of the Sarasvatī. For one who has been initiated, the shed, the Āgnīdhra fire-hall, the Sadas, and the Havirdhāna sheds are provided with wheels. They measure [the site] only as far as the altar; he does not construct an altar, nor an Uttaravedi. The sacrificial post, fixed in a mortar, is to be dragged [to its place]. They press the Soma, but they do not dig the Uparava pits. At the Atirātra, having offered the omentum of the Savanīya animal, he drives away the calves for the sake of the *sāṃnāyya* offering to Indra. Having concluded the Agniṣṭoma, he binds the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*). Having concluded the Ṣoḍaśin, [he prepares] the evening [libation].

8. Having concluded the Atirātra sacrifice, they perform the Sāṃnāyya offering. 9. Having concluded the Sāṃnāyya, the Adhvaryu stands in front of the Āhavanīya fire and throws a wooden pin (śamyā) towards the east. Wherever it falls, that is the location of the Gārhapatya fire. From there, at a distance of thirty-six steps, the Āhavanīya fire is established. 10. Having carried [the materials] around there and having established the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds at a height equal to the Agnīdhra altar, they perform the Sāṃnāyya offering.

By means of that, they proceed through the first half of the month (the waxing fortnight). On the full moon day, there is the *gaurukthya* sacrifice; when the full moon sacrifice is completed, they perform it. By means of that, they proceed through the second half of the month (the waning fortnight). On the new moon day, there is the *āyurukthya* sacrifice. They pass the first halves of the months by means of the *sāṃnāyya* offering, and the second halves by means of the full moon sacrifice. Those intending to undergo initiation release a bull among a hundred cows. When those [cows] reach the number of one thousand, that is the time for rising [from the vow]. If all [the cows] have perished, that is the time for rising. If the householder has died, that is the time for rising. [Or] at the Plākṣa spring.

Having reached the rising point, when the thousand [cows] have been completed, there is the Gaur-udayanīya Atirātra sacrifice. When all [the cows] have been struck down, and the householder has died, there is the Viśvajit and the Āyus sacrifice. If they should rise before reaching the Plākṣa spring, they should perform the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in a lake to the north of the central mound. While proceeding toward the Plākṣa spring, one should offer a pap (caru) to Aponapāt at the confluence of the Dṛṣadvatī river. Having reached the Plākṣa spring, the Udayanīya Atirātra is to be performed at the place of sitting (niṣad).

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kāma; having given a mare and a woman as two milch-cows for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), they should go down to the Yamunā for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at Kārapacava. Those desiring heaven should undertake the *Sārasvata* session, which is the session of Mitra and Varuṇa. The session of Indra and Agni, as well as that of Aryaman, is explained by the session of Mitra and Varuṇa. In the session of Indra and Agni, they strengthen [the sacrifice] with the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* stomas in alternating succession.

They should repeat [the sacrifice] every three days during the course of the sun’s northern journey (*udagayana*). On the full moon day, they perform the *Abhijit* sacrifice; on the new moon day, the *Viśvajit*, as previously described. Those who desire, "May we become the most excellent among all creatures," should undertake this rite.

"May we attain the path that leads to the gods"—with these words, on the following new moon, the sacrificer, having had his hair and beard shaved, bathed, and put on two unwashed linen garments, fastens a black antelope skin behind the Āhavanīya fire while he is not yet initiated. In the forenoon, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; at midday, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Agni; and in the afternoon, a pap to the Viśve Devas. He should consume that [offering]. He should perform this very sacrifice of three oblations. He should sacrifice with it for a year.

One who has been initiated shall perform no other act than that of wearing the black antelope skin during his vows. (30) When the year is completed, having emerged from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), the sacrificer shaves off all his hair and beard. (31) Those desiring prosperity should undertake the *turāyaṇa* rite. (32) For a Brāhmaṇa, it lasts for one year; he is a cowherd.

One who kindles the fire for the Naitandhava sacrifice remains engaged for a year. When the year is completed, having bound the fires and established them, he should offer an oblation on the bank of the Dṛṣadvatī—a cake on eight potsherds for Agni. To the south of the Dṛṣadvatī, he should cast a yoke-pin's distance; having reached the Triple-Fig tree, he should descend into the Yamunā for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). It is there that he becomes invisible to men. One desiring heaven should undertake the Dārṣadvata sacrifice. Between two Atirātra rites, there are Agniṣṭomas.

Every ten-day period constitutes a year; the twelfth is the *viṣuvat* day, during which the *sarpasāman*s are performed. 37. In the *Āyur-vijaya*, they study [the hymns] of such serpents as Jarvara the householder, Dhṛtarāṣṭra Airāvata, and Brahman. 38. Those desiring prosperity, those desiring immortality, and those desiring heaven should undertake the *Sarpa-sattra*. 39. Between two *atirātra*s, there are a thousand *trivṛt* years, or a ten-night period; having entered each year continuously, it is thus a thousand-fold for Prajāpati.
