Those desiring offspring should undertake [the sacrifice] for a year. By means of four *pṛṣṭhya* days, they reach fifty-five years each; thus, through five [such cycles], they complete five hundred and fifty years. Those desiring, "May all our offspring be born after us, and may we go to the world of Brahman," should undertake the *Viśvasṛjām Ayana*, the thousand-year sacrifice. Regarding this, a verse has also been spoken:
"The Viśvasṛjs performed the first sacrificial session (*sattra*), proceeding with the thousand-fold generation.
From that was born the protector of the world, the golden bird named Brahman."

Thus [ends section] 43. May Sarasvatī ordain, may she ordain [the rites] 44. Even for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there is the *Cāturhotṛka-gonāmika* sacrifice for twelve nights, three nights, or one night. 1. He attends to the fire according to the ritual procedure of the *pākayajña*. 2. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for victory in battle consists of the spoils of war; in the case of the seven *sthavīrya* [sacrifices], either a garment or gold should be given. 3. One desiring cattle should perform the rite under the asterism Revatī or Citrā. 4. With a broken or leaking vessel, he should neither wash his hands nor drink; some say it must not be done with a metal vessel, while others say this is a prohibition against using that particular material. 5. Of whomsoever he might wish ill, [he should do so] with respect to his cattle...

In the middle of the forest, one should call [the cattle] by reciting the names of cows. Having placed a horned cow facing west in front [of the fire], and having spread *darbha* grass underneath, one who desires cattle should offer three oblations on its head with the formula, "To the beloved, svāhā! (Kāmyāyai svāhā). At the latter part of the day, having brought a burning [firebrand] from the house of an enemy, he should keep watch through the night while kindling it. The subsequent [portion] is explained in the *Nigama*. On ground sloping toward the east and containing roots, one desiring cattle should wash his hands at sunrise and [approach] a clump of *darbha* grass.

He should pour out a vessel of water, saying, "O Desire, turn me toward my desire. Having gone with the cows, he should say, "You are praised; you are auspicious. On the Ekāṣṭakā day, he should have a cow carved limb by limb at a crossroads and give it to whoever comes along. On the following day, one who desires cattle should have another [image] made and feed the Brāhmaṇas. The subsequent [formula] is explained in the Nigama. "Come as one more prosperous, come as one more excellent"—these are the seven [verses]; "You are indeed a divine cow, you are mindful, you are wise"—these are the seven subsequent ones.

Of these [verses], the first end with *anuprāṇa* (breath after), while the others end with *ehi* (come). 15 He recites the invitatory formula (*anunigada*) beginning with "O goddesses, together with the increase of wealth. 16 One who desires to conquer in battle, when two armies are visible to each other, should offer oblations with the former [verses] and recite the latter [invitatory formula]. 17 Wherever he may come upon plants with their roots or cattle, there he should mutter these seven verses ending with *ehi*. 18 At the *saptasthavīrya* sacrifice, there is clarified butter for seven cows, and a cooked mess (*sthālīpāka*) in the milk of seven [cows]. 19 This applies to one whose seven elders are the very last [of his kin].

Having offered with the former [verses], he should recite the latter. 20. If there be a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who is very prosperous, one should drive away from him a bull-calf among his cows with [the formula]: "Ye are the Ilāndās; Pūṣan’s asterism is nourishing. 21. Having released it in its own cow-pen with [the formula] "Give me life," he should call out to another [cow] with "Come, thou more wealthy one! Come, thou better one! 22. Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* of milk for Sarasvatī, he should offer oblations with two verses addressed to Sarasvatī; with this [rite] one desiring a village should sacrifice, as well as one desiring cattle. 23.

One desiring cattle should cook four śarāva-measures of boiled rice in the milk of all [the cows] and give it to Brahmins. (24) It has been explained that what is cut off should not be given. (25) One should say of that cow, "Bhadram, bhadram" (blessing, blessing); one should say "bhadram" means auspiciousness; one should say it is meritorious and praiseworthy. (26) Having given a cow to one who is not initiated for sacrifice, one should mutter: "May that not harm me; may it not overpower me. (27)

"May they become possessed of heroes"—this has been explained regarding those from whom the offering is taken (1). "May we become [prosperous]"—thus [he addresses] the members of the assembly (2). He should either wash their feet or stand near them (3). "The auspicious ones have brought forth the auspicious"—this has been explained, or simply "the auspicious ones have brought forth the auspicious" (4). On the Ekāṣṭakā day, having silently mixed all [the grains], [he says]: "The auspicious ones have brought forth the auspicious; the bright ones have brought forth the bright. O venerable ones, you have brought forth for me a ram; O venerable ones, you have brought forth for me strength through the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; find for me what I have found."

"Those who were born as meritorious ones have been born as meritorious; those who were born as variegated ones have been born as variegated. O venerable ones, you have been born as worthy for me; O venerable ones, you have been born together with me for the increase of wealth. May you find for me the knowledge of kinship. With these words, he should address both [the male and female children] born together. (5) He should say "a cow," he should say "she is to be a cow," he should not say "she is slain," he should say "she is made," he should not say "she is pregnant," he should say "she is one who gives birth. (6) Having soaked a stalk of sugarcane in water...

With red iron [he should mark] it, [reciting]: "Thou art the world, thousandfold; Indra gave thee to Sṛma. As great as this [world] is, so do I make this mark of the cows; may I perform it for even more, for the highest year. He should thus make the mark on six or four cows.

8. "He is male, she is female"—thus [he recites] with the exchange of genders. 9. "That which is split on the right"—this has been explained. 10. "May offspring of all forms rejoice here"—with these words, he should consecrate the cows as they return in the evening. 11. "May Aryaman unite you together"—with this, he should unite the cows that were his previously and those he may obtain from elsewhere. 12. "The wealthy thread"—with this, he should stretch out the cord either towards the east or towards the north. 13. Having mixed curds with clarified butter, he strokes [the cow] with the formula: "I stroke you along with wealth and prosperity. 14. Of that [cow]...

The vows of one whose calf has been released shall not be deficient. (14) They should not walk over one another, nor should it rain upon them, nor should the sun scorch them. (15) When intending to release the bull, thinking "the father of the calves," he should mutter into the right ear of the bull as he releases it: "I release you, the bestower of heat, the bestower of glory, for the increase of wealth. (16) If there be a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who possesses many cattle, one desiring offspring should bring twenty-one young bulls from his cow-pen and offer twenty-one oblations. (17)

One who desires cattle should offer three oblations on the ashes with the formula "To the desirable one, svāhā! after having stationed a cow that goes in front and stands facing west behind [the fire], having spread darbha grass underneath, and using the names of cows, the divine cows, and the *ākṛti*-oblations. There are four *ākṛti*-oblations with the verse beginning, "Those whom Indra drove forth. (18)

With these [verses], one should offer oblations in the cow-pens among the cows in the forenoon; with these at midday when the cows have not yet returned; with these in the afternoon when they have gone to the cow-pens. With these, he consecrates the horses in battle: "Those who support friends, those who support the ruling power. With "I choose for you the ruddy ones," one desiring cattle should offer seven oblations of clarified butter. One should not drive away a cow from the *aśvattha* tree on the full moon day, the *aṣṭakā*, the new moon day, or under the *citrā* constellation. [He offers] with "The splendor of the cow" and "Of the protected one"; with "Thee, for both gods and men."

The [formula] "I do what is pleasing" has been explained; [it is used] for a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*), "I do what is pleasing to her" for a maiden desiring a husband, and "to such-and-such" at the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*). The subsequent *nigada* has been explained. One desiring food should perform the Śabalī-rite. On the thirteenth day after sunrise, having gone to a forest where one does not hear the sound of a village or of cattle, and having seated a learned Brāhmaṇa, he should take hold of a bunch of *darbha* grass and call out three times, "O Śabalī, O Śabalī, come! [He should also call] whatever else there is, except for dogs or donkeys.
If he should promise, that is success. (27) If he should not promise, he may call him again after a year, but he should not call him a third time.
(28) Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Rājasūya;
thus ends the Rājasūya-kalpa in the Mānava-sūtra.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the *Śulba* (the cord for measurement). 1. One should prepare a cord provided with loops, equal in length, stretched out straight as the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, according to the requirements. 2. Between Citrā and Svātī, Śravaṇa and Pratiśravaṇa, Kṛttikā and Pratikṛttikā, and Tiṣya and Punarvasu—this is the eastern region; and there are two loops at the ends of the cord, each measuring a *yuga*. 3. Six, ten, seven, seventeen, one, two, and five: having measured with these equal parts, one should draw the outline.

Having fixed the end of the cord at the southern shoulder, one should scratch a line toward the east; having fixed it at the southern hip, one should scratch a line toward the west. Having fixed the end of the cord at the northern shoulder, one should scratch a line across from the shoulder. In this same manner, [one proceeds] to the north, to the front, and to the rear.
The *khara* for the eastern fire-altar should be a square of one cubit (*aratni*);
that to the rear should be shaped like a chariot wheel, and that to the south should be the shape of a half-moon.
One should draw the mandala from the center with a measurement of one koṭi;
the entire mandala together with its [surrounding] area is increased by one-third.
In the square, one should cause the diagonal cord to meet at the center.
Having drawn that [line], one should likewise draw a half-maṇḍala with half of its measure.

Having measured a cord between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires, one should mark a point on the third part from the end. Leaving a fourth part from the middle, and having brought together the two ends of the cord at the mark, one should mark a point to the south for the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. By reversing this very procedure, one should mark a point to the north for the *utkara* (the rubbish-heap).
Whatever the length of the cord may be, the addition (of earth) should be exactly that much.
The gnomon (śaṅku) shall be half of the [total] length; the marking-line (nirāñchana) shall be half of the gnomon.
This is proclaimed as the rule for making it square on all four sides.
The pole (īṣā) is one hundred and eighty-eight [units], and the horizontal axle (tiryagakṣa) is four hundred.
Eighty-six [units] constitute its yoke, and the chariot is said to be made of *cāraka* wood. Having measured the characteristic mark on the pole at six and nine [units],
there is a loop of forty-three finger-breadths by rule at the mark.
This altar is fully described as being equal in size to a chariot for the animal sacrifice to Indra and Agni; for other animals, it is six cubits long.
The eastern half should be six *aratnis*, and the marking out is done with half an *aratni*.
Half [the length] for the two hips, then half for the two shoulders, and one and a half for the neck—this is the measurement for the animal sacrifice (pāśukī).

Half a śaya from the shoulder-joint are the two hips; two [śayas] for the spine, two for the posterior part, then one and a half for the front part, then one and a half for the marking out (nirāñchana).
One shoulder-measure (aṃsa) is one and a half [aratnis], and the other shoulder-measure is likewise one and a half;
the cord (pāśa) is then at the cubit (aratni). The altar for the Maruts (mārutī vedi) is a flowing stream;
all ten-fold cords have a marking in their middle.
One should mark the eastern half at the fifth [intersection]; the diagonal line toward the northeast is known as the ancestral (paitṛkī).
All seven cords lie [therein], and its center is the point of intersection.
One should mark the eastern half at the fifth; the diagonal line toward the northeast is known as the ancestral.

To the east of the *pra-vaṃśa*, one should construct the *patnīśālā* (the hall for the wives) measuring four *śaya*s; at a distance of three *prakramas* from the *pra-vaṃśa* is the end of the *vedi* (altar), and from the end of the *vedi*, the *sadas* (the assembly hall) is at one *prakrama*.
One should know that the *sadas* is nine [units] long, and the space between the *sadas* and the *āgnīdhra* is four [units].
There are four [measures] of three [units each]: the Havirdhāna [shed], the Aruṣī [pit], and the space between them;
having measured one *pada* for the sacrificial post-hole, the remainder is for the Uttaravedi.
The Āgnīdhra [shed] is exactly six *aratnis*; the cord consists of thirty-six *prakramas*. 3.

The twelve-triplet consists of the *lakṣikā*. One measures out the altar (*vedi*), the *sadas*, and the *havirdhāna* in successive order: a fifteen-fold [rope], a twenty-one-fold [rope], and another triplet. Beyond that is another triplet, and among the twelve, it is called the "noose" (*pāśada*). This is the supreme measurement of the ropes for the Soma sacrifice. (4) The side-measuring rope (*pārśvamānī*) should consist of three steps; the cross-measuring rope (*tiryaṅmānī*) should be one step.
But the rope which runs diagonally across it (*akṣṇayā*)—with that one should make a ten-step [square]. (5)

Half of a quarter [of the cord] is for the fourteenth [section], and then again, from the ninth [section], there is a noose of three and a half [quarters]; this is the excellent cutting of the *sadas*.

Having measured the cord with ten axle-lengths of a chariot and eleven [axle-lengths] plus one *uparava*-depth, they say that its twenty-fourth part constitutes the *ekādaśinī* (the group of eleven) for each altar.
If a *śikhaṇḭinī* altar is to be constructed, one should remove two and a half [units] from the edge of the altar;

that should be eight *aṅgulas*, and half of that for the goddess’s altar to be properly established. One should observe that [space] facing east, and one should know those [features] as the *śikhaṇḍinī*. 8.
Five and seven, and then one more each;
this is declared to be the altar for the Kaukili and also for the Cāraka sacrifice.
Furthermore, if the sacrificer should be free from disease by birth, [he may perform it].
How should the measuring instruments be applied there by the practitioners?
The tip of the lotus stalk is sixfold in circumference and is considered equal to the hair of a three-year-old heifer.
Three three-year-old barley grains are prescribed as half a mustard seed;
they say a mustard seed is double that, and a barley grain is three mustard seeds.
Six barley grains placed side by side constitute the measure of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
A *prādeśa* consists of ten finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), a *vitasti* is twelve *aṅgulas*,
an *aratni* is two *vitastis*, and a *vyāyāma* is four [aratnis]. A *puruṣa* consists of one hundred and twenty *aṅgulas* measured by the joints of its own fingers.
Now, if there should be twenty-five hundred [grains] arising from the forefoot, one should know that three *yavas* make a *kṛṣṇala*; three *kṛṣṇalas* make a *māṣa*.
By this measure of the *kṛṣṇala*, they say a *niṣka* is fourfold.
The third and fifth parts of the person are the means for that;

furthermore, half of that [fifth part] and another [half] constitute the three-layered altar (tricitika), provided it is a fire-altar (agniciti). The middle layer is measured as eight by eight, and the [uppermost] layer is eleven-fold.
One should lay down eight bricks in each alternating manner; the last layer consists of twelve.
"The last layer consists of eight, [and] twelve"—thus ends the Śulbasūtra.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the subsequent bricks. 1. With his arms raised, the sacrificer measures out a bamboo pole. 2. One [pole] is equal to that; the second has a cubit (*aratni*) added. On it, there is a mark at one *puruṣa*, and marks at both the *aratni* and the span (*vitasti*) at half a *puruṣa*. 3. Having enclosed the top of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), leaving a remainder, he joins two *puruṣas* along the cord and drives in a peg (*śaṅku*) with a five-fingered measure; [he does so] at the junction of those two and at their two ends. 4. Having placed the two bamboos on either side of the middle peg, [he proceeds] to the south.

It causes a prick at the intersection of the man's length. (5) Having placed a bamboo pole upon the middle peg and having moved it upward, he drives a peg to the south at the intersection of the man's length. (6) Having placed a bamboo pole upon the eastern peg, he drives a second peg to the south at the intersection of the man's length in front; and likewise in the rear at half [the distance]. (7) By this, the northern half is explained. (8) Having placed bamboo poles upon those two pegs which lie on both sides of the middle peg of the southern section, [he proceeds] to the intersection of the man's length to the south.

He makes a mark. Having placed a bamboo pole upon the middle peg and having moved it up over the mark, he drives in a peg to the south with a span (aratni) [of the bamboo] remaining. Having placed that peg which has a span remaining to the east of the middle one, and having joined the second [peg] to the south-east at a distance of half a man's height (ardhapuruṣa), he drives in a peg; in the same way [he does] to the west. By this very method, the northern wing is explained. [The measurement of] the tail is as follows: at the place where there is a span for Savitṛ. To the east of the front [peg], he measures out the head by means of a five-fingered cord at a distance of half a man's height.

The eighth part of the *vyāyāma* on one side, the fourth part on one side, and the fourth part on both sides are for the construction of the *gārhapatya-citi*. One should have the first square made with a tenth part of a man’s height on one side and half of a tenth on the other; that is the second. With a tenth part on one side and one and a half parts on the other, that is the third; with a fourth part on both sides, that is the fourth. Their height is three-fifths of a man’s height, except for the *nākasad*, the *cūḍā*, and the *ṛtavyā* bricks; now, regarding the middle one...

And from the fifth and sixth Vaiśvadevī bricks, those [two] should be half as high; having placed loose soil (purīṣa) in between, he should lay down the northern one for the sake of the joining of the groups and for the sake of non-interruption. He should place whatever else there is other than the bricks into the pits. Regarding this, there is a verse:
"One should dig pits for the fire-pan (ukhā), the animal heads, the tortoise, the mortar, the two offering-spoons (srucau), the pot-bricks, and the sacrificial porridge (caru)."

One should place them facing each direction: those oriented toward the east in the middle of oneself, on the head, on the two wings, and also on the body, having divided them equally. One should place each subsequent one further north, joined together, extending east-west, south-north, and diagonally, according to the specific instructions; four others in front, five behind for the seasonal offerings, and in the north-eastern half of the *gārhapatya* fire-altar. The remainder [is covered] with four *śarāva*-measures. These same [bricks], oriented north-south, are placed on the second layer.

The remainder [is measured] by four squares (8). As the first [line], so the third and the fifth; as the second, so the fourth; by that rule one should pile [the altar] in alternating fashion (9). Then he makes the other [lines] for the Āgnīdhrīya: nine steps, with a stone in the middle; four quarters in each direction on the Āgnīdhrīya; four half-steps on the Hotrīya; two and a half in the corners; and two and a half in the middle. On the Mārjālīya, there are six [steps] directed eastward.

One should place twenty-five bricks with their faces turned eastward upon the two shoulders, the tail, and the enclosing wall; twelve each on the front of the two wings, five each toward the rear, and five each facing north around the head. The remainder is filled by four-cornered bricks. One should place twenty bricks facing north on the two hips along with the wings, likewise on the south and north sides of the second layer; eleven each on both sides of the tail, and five each facing east around the head.

The remainder [is filled] with four layers (catusrā). Just as the first [layer], so are the third and fifth; just as the second, so is the fourth. By this rule, one should pile [the fire-altar] in alternating fashion. 13. In the *upasads*, he places two [bricks] in the first layer, three in the middle, and six in the subsequent ones in regular order; in the twelfth [layer], he places them in alternating fashion along with the *purīṣa* (filling earth). 14. By this same rule, having divided [the altar] evenly over the year, when it has reached knee-height, he piles it double [in size]; for those that follow, triple; and having raised the northernmost [line] by one [unit], he proceeds with the ascent (*abhyāyana*).
One should place the *atirikta* bricks for the sake of increase. (Sūtra 15) That which begins with the mantra and ends with the touching [of the fire] is the characteristic of that person.

(Sūtra 16) A bunch of *darbha* grass, a lotus leaf, two golden men, golden bricks, pebbles, the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone, *dūrvā* bricks, and *naivāra* grain—these are placed in the center, up to the fifth layer; the *svayamātṛṇṇā* is in the middle, on both sides of it. In that [layer], the *kumbheṣṭakā*s are in the middle, the two *sruca*s are in the south and north, and the remaining bricks are in the intermediate directions.

Afterwards, one places the *kulāyinī* and the two *dviyajus* bricks upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; the two *retaḥsic* bricks are placed on the two flanks, the *dviyajus* being on the northern flank; the second *ṛtavyā* and the *retaḥsic* are in front on that northern flank; the *viśvajyotis*, the *maṇḍala*, the *ṛtavyā*, the *gharmeṣṭakā*, the *aṣāḍhā*, the tortoise, and the bull are placed facing east on the southern side of the northern flank, and the mortar and pestle facing east in the northeast corner in front of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*.

He places the heads joined together with their heads in the middle of the *cokhā*. Behind that, he places the man’s head and the man’s layer (*puruṣaciti*), consisting of thirty-six bricks facing westward in groups of three on the two hips. Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Three for the necks, six for the two shoulders, two each for the two arms, nine for the trunk, five for the two shanks, and one each for the hands and feet."

Thus, having divided the eight apasyās equally among the furrows (*vaṃśa*), one places the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks in each of the ninth furrows: first in the northern furrow in front, then in the southern furrow behind; then in the southern furrow to the right, then in the eastern furrow to the left; then in the northern furrow behind, and then in the southern furrow to the right. The second [set] is on the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; the fifth is on the marshy ground (*anūpa*). In the ninth [furrow], they are excessive in measure, just as [the first set was placed]: first in the southern furrow in front, then in the northern furrow behind; then in the southern furrow to the right, then in the northern furrow to the left; then in the eastern furrow to the right, and then in the northern furrow to the left.

On the second [layer] of the naturally perforated stone (*svayamātṛṇṇā*), the fifth [brick] is placed to the west, south, and north; on the second [layer] of the naturally perforated stone, the fifth [is likewise]. The Vaiśvadeva bricks are placed in the marshy regions (*anūpa*) in each direction, beginning with the northeast.

And having divided equally those two [spaces] between the southern and northern [lines] at their meeting point, one should place the *Atharvaśiras* before the first of those two spaces. Having divided it equally among the spaces, one should recognize the head, wings, and tail in the first spaces. On the first space, one should place the head; on the others, each subsequent [space] for the wings and tail. In the fourth [space], one should lay down the *lokeṣṭakās*: facing eastward on the two wings and facing northward on the tail. The remaining [bricks] are placed behind the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, one by one, starting from the front.

On the south, those beginning with the Vaiśvadevī; on the north, those beginning with the Purīṣī. 6. On the middle [part] of the head, the Gāyatra; on the head itself, the Rathantara, Bṛhat, and Yajñāyajñiya, according to the traditional recitation. 7.

On the second layer, to the east of the Svayamātṛṇṇā, there are three each in the first, second, and third rows: the Ṛtavyās, Vāyavyās, and Apasyās, respectively. There are three each in the southern *vaṃśas*; two each in the northern and southern [of the remaining]; and in the ninth, the remaining ones are on both sides like the Apasyās. 1. On the third layer, there are ten and twelve [bricks] on both sides of the ninth.

In the eighth layer, there are seven bricks on the east and seven on the west, aligned with the *svayamātṛṇṇā* and half as high; eight bricks with different mantras [are placed] on the last course, or on the fourth. In the ninth layer, one by one, on both sides of the northern *vaṃśa* (ridge-pole) in the middle, the first brick is placed, and the others in alternating order. In exactly the same way, the *spṛt* bricks are placed on the east, in the middle of the southern *vaṃśa*, the first being placed first, and the others in alternating order.

In the sixth, seventh, and eighth layers, one should place pairs on the south and odd bricks on the north; there should be seventeen on the south and fifteen on the north. On the fifth layer, one should place one brick each upon the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks; the remainder belongs to the *chandas* and the *virāj*s, according to their respective measures. In the sixth, seventh, and eighth layers, one should place them on both sides according to the number. Having filled [the gaps] with half-bricks, one should place the *stomabhāga* bricks on the south facing east, and on the west, the even ones; on the north, one should place the triple sets, making a total of thirty-one.

Then, one facing west with the *trivarga* [formula], and then the *nākasad* with the *purīṣavatī* verse; with barley and so forth, the *upaśīvarī* bricks, soaked in ghee, according to their respective order. The fourth [set] is in the middle, as with the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks; the *atimātrā* bricks are placed in the middle; the *svayamātṛṇṇā* is placed together [with them]; and the *vikarṇī* is to the north—thus for the *suparṇa*.
To whatever extent a brick, once made, shrinks through drying and baking, to that same extent the preparation should be made larger; one who desires evenness should act accordingly.

And always, the bricks decrease by a thirtieth part; as much as they are diminished, the construction should be made so that it remains equal, for one who desires symmetry. Each one [is increased] by one hundred and fifty, and that is further augmented by six finger-breadths.
The measurement of the bricks is modified; whatever is other than this [is the modification].
One should specify the measurement of the *vyāyāma* as nine thousand two hundred and sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
But for all the other hearths (dhiṣṇya),
the settled rule is that there shall be one thousand and nine hundred and sixty-six finger-breadths (aṅgula) for each one; [that is,] eleven thousand and six hundred.
A field of one hundred thousand [fire-altars] is prescribed for Agni;
whether it be the original (prākṛta) or the modified (vaikṛta), having made the head at a distance of seven and a half [units], one should then pour it out upon the field.
Eight hundred minus four steps are proclaimed here; those who know the field recognize this as the field of the [Veda] together with its limbs and its head (the Upaniṣads).
The self (ātman) is to be made four hundred [steps], and the two wings are recorded as three hundred each.
There are ten in the tail and exactly one hundred in the head; the [central] part consists of twenty-five.
When the groups of thirty-one, thirty-three, and even fifty are not possible, the brick should be divided in two.
"By means of the decrease or increase of bricks, the wise man should cause the mantras to be destroyed within firm structures of one hundred [bricks] by means of the brick-portions. Also,
there are bricks for the four backs, or for the wings, tail, and head.
The underlaying is from the quarters and from the worlds; likewise, the world itself is lost.
By the knower, the underlaying should be understood within the self through the Rathantara, Bṛhat, and Lokas, as well as the other Gāyatra and sacrificial verses. 12–13.
The number of *yajuṣmatī* bricks for all the layers is fixed;
hear from me as I declare it for each individual layer:
the first has one hundred and eighty-six, and the second has seventy.
The third layer consists of thirteen; the wise say there are one hundred [bricks];
the fourth is said to consist of one hundred and three bricks; and the final layer consists of three hundred and fifty-six. 15.
All these are *yajusmatī* bricks by which Agni is brought forth;
one should fill up the remainder of the layers with *lokapṛṇā* bricks.
All these have been handed down in their entirety as far as the *Yajurveda* extends.
This indeed constitutes a thousand when spoken of together with the pebbles.
These, when properly placed, become milch-cows; they yield all desires for the sacrificer in that world beyond.
"He who knows Prajāpati as the sixty [years] remembered as the year goes to the world of Brahman, to the vault of heaven, to the summit of the sun. (19)

Thus ends the section on the northern bricks for the Vaiṣṇava altar; let us offer salutations to those who know the cord-measurements (*śulba*) in every respect, to the enumerators, and to the teachers who have proclaimed this to us.
We honor this earth, which, like one who bestows honor upon us, is our most excellent, increasing, and sacrificial honor within our own home;
the earth is distinct, straight, a stake, a cord of muñja grass, and level.
No image should be fashioned on a painting and the like; the lunar day and asterism are auspicious for Varuṇa.
All altars (vedis) should extend toward the east; the ritual procedure is that pertaining to the body of Yaska.
Everything is equal by half; the cutting [of the lines] consists of five knee-lengths.
In the middle [of the hall], for the sake of the *ṛtavyās*, the *nākasad*s, and the two *pañcacūḍā*s,
the area intended for the construction and other purposes is eight and a half *aratnis*.
The *havirdhāna* is established by means of a cart, and the *kharas* are established by means of vessels.
The *cātvāla* pit is prepared with animal victims; the mounds for the fires are provided with sacrificial oblations.
The mounds for the *ratnins* are half a *maṇḍala* in extent and four-cornered.
These are one *aratni* in thickness; when their size increases, the thickness increases accordingly.

The eastern [line] should be marked with twenty-four parts; the western [line], having been marked with twenty-four, should be on the south. It should be marked with twice eight [parts] on the south, and having extended it with thirty [parts], one should remove the excess.
(7) Having stepped out toward the north to the *cātvāla* pit, then to the *śāmitra* fire;
if there is an abundance of animals, there should be an increase further toward the north. (8)

Having set aside the length and the arm-span, one should multiply the width separately by one and a half; that [product] multiplied by all [the other factors] is the volume (ghana). One multiplies the length by the length, and the width by the width.
Those who know the science [of mathematics] understand that the square root of the sum is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).

(10) Between the constellations Śravaṇa and Abhijit, or Bahula and Āṣāḍhā, or Citrā and Svātī, or between the waters and fire, they say the sun rises in the east at night. (11) On a circle marked with a gnomon, it is both in the east and in the west.
(12) Or, if the sacrificer should be free from disease by virtue of his birth...
How should the measuring instruments be employed there by the performers?

If a woolen thread or a hair is spread out, and a mustard seed and a barley grain are each increased sixfold, that becomes one *aṅgula* in the measurement of a man; twelve of those they call a *prādeśa*. Two of those are known as an *aratni*; a *prakrama* is equal to an *aratni*, and it should consist of two *prādeśas* in the case of the *citis*. Four *prakramas*, each reduced by one and a half *aṅgulas*, shall be fixed. Therein, there are eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpas*), increasing by four in each successive *sattra*. On a single altar (*vedi*), there are two fires, excluding the *iṣṭakās*.

It occurs as follows: If the altar is separate, then a separate fire is prepared. [The measure] is twenty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) wide; a hundred [finger-breadths] is fixed as the standard. A man is five cubits (aratnis) tall, or ten paces [in length]. According to the principle of deficiency or excess, the measurement for each body is as follows: eighty-six [finger-breadths] is said to be a yuga; eighteen [finger-breadths] is called an akṣa. The entire assembly of the chariot is equal to the tantra; they shall fix the two-yoked chariot and the pole. Now, regarding the circle: he who would construct a circle of four men, listen to this method of construction proclaimed by those who know it.

The perpendicular from the equilateral triangle equal to the diameter of the circle forms a four-sided figure; from the diagonal, which is one-third of the eastward extension, that becomes a circle. One should make a man [equal] to a man; its diagonal would be two men, and from its diagonal, by means of two, it would be four men. The diagonal-measure (karaṇī) is two men, while the hip and the arm would be double; like the *tri-kuṣṭha*, there is a triple perpendicular, and from that, the eight parts of a man in the square.
And the diameter is five parts, and that which is three times the diameter.
That circumference of the mandala does not exceed the radius (vāla).
Having divided the diameter into ten parts, one should then remove three parts; that which remains square will be the width of the mandala. 13–14.
One should divide the square into nine parts; the tips of the bows [the corners] are divided three by three.
One should remove the fifth part from the height with soil until it is sixfold here. 15.

A man [measuring] four *ratnis* is prescribed for the construction of the *sikatā* (sand-altar), while half a *bhuja* is assigned for the other. Then, one should have its constituent parts (*karaṇas*) fashioned by turning it three, four, five, or three times; whatever is auspicious regarding the methods of piling (*cayana*), that which was constantly declared by the ancient seers (*ṛṣis*) should be followed. The altar is to be known through its drawing, measurement, accumulation, reversals, and the perfection of its dimensions. One should measure all [altars] according to their proportions, both in length and in width. Those altars which were shown by the ancient seers of old are remembered as being either square, equal in length and breadth, or consisting of five parts (*pañcāṅgī*).

And this rule which has been established for mortals: therein this cord of five parts, derived from the pair, is of such length that by it we measure everything, except for the Kaṅkāla, the Ja, and the Śyena; of these, I shall state the defining characteristics. 20.

This [line] is the *mitā* (measured), characterized by half of the *samayā* (equal line); from that, on the fourth [mark], there should be a *nirāñchana* (non-marking); then, half of what remains is equal to the width of the *caya* (the mound). One should proceed here with this [measurement] by four *kuṣṭhas*. Then one should lay down the eastern [line] equal in length; then one should fix two pegs (*pāśa*) and also the middle one. Having released [the cord] behind, then having stretched it eastward from the middle [peg] toward the south, one should fix a peg at half the width by means of the *nirāñchana*. Likewise, one should do so at the western and northern middle [points].

23. That [measurement] is for the *vāsuvedi*s. 24. Now, this measurement [is applied] to the hips (*śroṇi*); however, the removal of the cord (*pāśoddharaṇa*) should be performed. 25. One should draw lines on both hips in the cardinal directions, drive stakes (*śaṅku*) into them at equal intervals, and from those [stakes], one should draw lines all around. 26. If it is made of bricks (*aiṣṭika*), one should not draw both; rather, one should draw the remaining two. 27. In the eastern third part and in the western [third part], the *siddha-upasthita* [spaces] are located, as are the *utkara* and the *dakṣiṇāgni*. 28. Now, another drawing for this [altar] should be in the middle, with nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in each direction. 29. Half of the measurement is the *mṛd-śamana*; this is designated as the "distinction" (*viśeṣa*).
The special measurement and the standard measurement shall be according to the command of the authority.

Another half-measurement shall be used; at the sixth knot, together with the twenty-fourth, one makes the characteristic mark. That is the marking by means of a diagonal line across the transverse measurement; the remainder is from the knot to the middle of the shoulder-blade. The two hips are [measured] therefrom; here the Āgnīdhra fire-altar is taught.
One should know that the diagonal measurement of the fire-altar is indeed the same as its diagonal measurement in the twenty-one-fold [altar],
or else it is the human [measurement] when measured across in ten directions.
One should know that his field [of measurement] is the eleventh;
both arms, however, for a man with smooth limbs, are measured transversely and diagonally. From one hundred and one [units], one should increase the two arms by two [units] each.
Thus, regarding the *avalambaka-kuṣṭha* which is sixteen finger-breadths [in length],
this is the procedure for the measurement of the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice.
The Saumikī [altar] is three parts of a *prakrama*,
and the Uttaravedi is established with three others plus a third;
or the *prakrama* may be fourteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and by that [measure], the Saumikī [is determined].
One should measure it with twelve hundred [units] for one who desires cattle;
the fourth [section] is the forest-space, measured with six, nine, or seven [units].
Or, the other wheel should be measured with nine [units]; one should not draw a line at half the *karaṇa*.
The rule regarding these [fires], beginning with the Sāvitra, is that one should deposit them in four [places].
One should bury [the fire-pan] in earth reaching up to the knees when it is reddish-brown and fill it with water.

(5) Furthermore, the characteristic of the Gārhapatya [fire-place] is twofold: either square or circular. One should mark out a square measuring a *vyāyāma* (the distance between the tips of the outstretched arms) with four sides each measuring half a *puruṣa* (man’s length), or a circle. (6) A square extending to three-quarters of a *vyāyāma* and having a width of one-seventh [of its side] is piled first toward the east and then toward the north; in the case of the twenty-one-fold [fire-altar], however, it is done in reverse order. (7) A square extending to one-third of a *puruṣa* and having a width of one-sixth [of its side]...

The *prathika* should be extended at that [end], and by that it should be equal in the middle; the remaining two corners, measured as equal to the *prathika*, are made by its width—this is the *viśākha*. (8) Its length should be divided into six parts, and two and a half of those should be situated as an equilateral triangle—this is the *caturasravipāṇaka*. (9) The *prathika* is half of that which is measured as the *prathika*; these are the four measuring instruments for the mandala, determined by their respective parts. (10–11) In the center of this, there are four bricks.

Two [measures] each for the two preceding and following [parts]; two *pratīka*s; two *ardhaviṣāṇika*s; again, indeed, again he returns to the circle; it is equal and complete in the two *ardhaprathika*s. Then, the twenty-first [verse], 12. Or one should transpose it with the north-facing [verse] by transposition, thus successively. 13. "A verse and a half, and a quarter-verse, having the measure of a quarter-verse and a foot, and the height of a half-verse"—so they say are the *karaṇa*s in the *gāyatra*. 14.
Having made a cord four times as long as two men (*dvipuruṣa*) and well-measured, those who know it recognize it as having five parts, with its divisions known and its ends restrained. 15.
The piercing from the middle of the two loops is said to be the Gāyatra measurement;
it is half a puruṣa including the jewels. Measured by that, it is square. By the expansion at the ends of the wings and tail, [the others] are measured by the Gāyatra and the other [metres]. 16

The bricks [are prepared] by drying and baking; however, they decrease by thirty from the measure. (17) Thereafter, one should cause the field to be excavated to the extent of three or four parts and have Śiva installed. (18) On that northern shoulder there are twenty-five [bricks] facing east; ten on the tail; two sets of twelve on both sides of the wings; five should be placed on the tail; fifteen facing east should be given on the head.

There are eighty-four in the two wings, fifty in the self, and thirty in the tail; there are ninety-nine in the tail, twenty in each of the shoulders and hips, and they say there are ten in each of the two wings. Ten and one-half bricks are placed on the head, facing east and north. All those joined by their feet are first laid down in the east.

The second [set] consists of the *vāgyuj* bricks and Aśvinī bricks; one should pile them in this manner alternately upon the paths of his knees. The *dhiṣṇya* hearths consist of three-footed bricks with small areas, each having a single layer (*ekacitikā*) and provided with four functional parts; they include both the mantras for piling the fire-altar (*agnicityā*) and the supplementary bricks (*atiriktā*). There are four bricks measuring one and a half [units], two in the middle, and the *nakula* brick is a fourth part. The stone is the ninth in the *āgnīdhra* hearth. From here, we shall describe the *hotrīya* hearth.

In the two shoulders and the two hips, there are *nakulakas* based on the *padyās*; externally, in the three directions, and internally, there are fourteen *padakacaturthas*. That which consists of eight *padyās* in each direction, in the cardinal and intermediate directions [makes twenty-six]. In the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* [section], there would be ten and one in the middle; two by two *caturthas* and a *nakulaka*. On both sides, there are three *padyās*, two in the middle, and two and a half in the remaining parts; in the rest, there are eight. There are six and a half [units] in the *mārjālīya*.

The *saṃmārjālīya* fire-altar should be to the south of the *śāmitra* fire and behind the *cātvāla* pit; this same arrangement applies even in the ritual procedure for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).

There are thirty-seven and a half bricks on the right wing, four on the head, and likewise thirty-six on the body. In the *śyena* altar, the tail consists of fifteen bricks; in the *alaja* altar, the tail consists of seventeen bricks, while two bricks each are arranged on the head and on the body and wings.

In the *pratimā* [altar] for the *nara-caturtha* sacrifice, there are eight parts (*bhāga*) for the tail (*puccha*), four for the feet, and seven for the head; the body (*ātman*) and the two wings are to be known as being like those of a hawk (*śyena*). (2) For the *śyena*, *alaja*, and *kaṅka* [altars], the width of the tail is eight and a half parts, the body is four, the head is two, and for all of them, the wings are five parts each. (3) For the *śyena*, *alaja*, and *kaṅka*, the tail is said to be two, three, and four *kuṣṭha*s [respectively].

The five eyes have wings as their vessels and are surrounded by eyes; one should bring two parts to the tail, and like the *trikuṣṭha* bird, three parts from the tail-base. From the tail of the *śyena*, one should remove [the space] for the head in the *kaṅka*; however, one should remove the two feet. There should be twelve and a half lines toward the east, and it should be measured with one hundred and twenty lines toward the north. In the *kaṅka-citāvalaja*, there are fifteen parts, and thirteen and a half toward the north.
The cord should measure three-fourths and be thirteen and a half; there is a mark in the middle, and the drawing-out is done by means of fourth-parts.
Four *bhāgikas* are [the first four]; another is recorded as being at the fifth and a half;
and half-measures are at the eighth, while another is at the ninth and tenth;
or another is twelve and a half. 8.

Then, having stretched lines toward the east, one should drive a peg into the eighth [mark] between the two loops, or having struck the loop at the fourth; having fastened it to the middle, there is no further marking. 9.
Having drawn out, pushed forward, and released from the middle, one should draw out on both sides at the tenth [mark]; the portions are two, four, and also six and a half;
having struck [the cord] from the front, one should perform it in this manner.
Having fixed an equal gnomon at the fourth [mark], then having stretched cords eastward from there with loops at the fifth-and-a-half and the sixth-and-a-quarter [marks],
and having grasped the western gnomons at the seventh-and-a-half and the eighth [marks].
Then, having released the two pairs [of pegs],
one should pull out the fourth and ninth pegs, both of which are at the end;
having cast the loop in the eighth, the restraint is achieved by that very eighth.
Then, at every eighth part of those two [measures], having fixed a loop and secured it to the first peg,
one should drive a peg into the tenth part for the middle of the tail of the *alaja* [bird-shaped figure]. (14)
The peg for the *kaṅka* bird is prescribed at seven and a half [units] when it is visible.
Having fastened the noose on the triple-jointed [pole] and having secured it with a tenfold [rope], the two subsequent pegs should be placed using these very same two goads. 15–16.
At the twelve-and-a-half [mark], there should be a three-pointed noose for the purpose of restraint.
At the first noose and at the second, two pegs (śaṅku) should be placed, as well as the subsequent ones.
Having fixed the second [peg] on the north, one should remove the southern one when they are level.
On the fourth day, one should strike the peg; one should perform the opposite on the [next] fourth day, having restrained it for half that duration.
Thus, the cord of the Śyena has twelve characteristics.
One should construct four [units] for these using three and four parts;
there are nine divisions for the eye, the half-eye, and the five corners, respectively.
One should place two five-cornered [units] in the eastern part, and then two half-eyes.
In the two wings, one [line] each; likewise for the two flanks and the counter-flanks (22).
The center is filled with nine parts and sprinkled with eyes;
on the tip of the wing there are five petals, and thus it is ordained by the eye (23).
One should fill the two [triangles] at the tip with alternating eyes, the pentagon situated facing west, the half-eye at the throat-joint, and this immeasurable head.
Two [half-eyes] are at the joints of the two wings, and likewise another half-eye at each of the joints of the tail.

Ten and five [are added] at the tip of the tail and the tip of the wing, making twenty-five; in the case of the Aupamāna fire-altar, in the transposition of these, and in the construction of the layers, the measurement by cord, the reduction, and the perfection of the Śyena— this is the established rule.
The wings, including the curved and the fringed parts, are prepared in the same manner as the fore-part;
the tail is well-known from the middle [of the model], and in the Śyena sacrifice it is accomplished by means of a cord.
Nine pegs are driven into the front portion prior to the ninth [measurement] for the purpose of making the fourth part.
One should leave half a *pakṣa* (wing) uncurved, for it would otherwise be so;
the third and fifth parts of a man are its construction, and furthermore, that of the altar (*citi*).
Then the other half should consist of three layers (*tricitika*), if it is an altar of fire (*agniciti*). 1–28.
The first layer consists of eight by eight bricks; the middle layer is eleven by eight and is arranged with alternation;
one should place eight more, and the highest layer is twelve.
The field for the Prauga altar is fifteen manas in length, and half of that for the other.
From the middle of the ten-fold section, there is this *trikuṣṭha* as well as the *karaṇa*;
likewise, on both arms there is the twenty-first, and for the other [arm] there is half;
the cutting of the shoulders and hips should be on both sides, and that becomes the *prauga*.
From the four *cātvāla* pits, the fire is to be gathered together; it is without bricks.
From the quarters, it is to be gathered with soil; the rite is performed by dividing [the soil] according to the proper method.
Today, the funeral pyre (*śmaśānacit*) is to be surrounded, being circular or square in shape.
The shaft of these [sacrificial ladles] should be one-tenth of their droṇa-capacity;
one should make the mandala square like that of the Gārhapatya fire,
and the Vāruṇa ladle should be exactly one-and-a-half times the width of the two arms.
One should duly divide the established [measurement] tenfold, both externally and internally;
there should be three *kuṣṭhas* and a *viṣāṇa* at the joint, and that same arrangement is applied in reverse.
The construction of the square is thirty-two parts for the two arms.
Then, by means of those two, the rule for the *gāyatra* [altar] is as follows:
the square of fifteen parts is the measure of the two arms; from that, there should be one and a half [parts], and it is recorded that there are two hundred layers (*citayaḥ*).
There should be fifty-five, fifty-two and a half, and three hundred and fifty square bricks; the wings should consist of one thousand, with the *uṣā* being the thousandth.
Thirty-one parts of the two arms constitute the construction, and the same applies to the two subsequent [sections].
They shall lay out a thousand squares for the sacrificial sessions. 12.

The wealth [of the ground] should be ten and a half *puruṣas* square; it should be circular like a chariot wheel. The nave, the spokes, the holes, and the rim—whatever exceeds the spokes [is the rim]. 13. The spokes are half a *puruṣa* in length and one-eighth of a *puruṣa* in width; there are twenty-four of them, three *nādis* long. 14. Hereafter, I shall explain the making of the holes.

The rim (nemi) should be made with twice the seventh part [of the diameter], and the spokes (ara) with an eighth part; the modification (vaikṛta) is by the twenty-fourth part. The space within the nave (nābhi) should be like a prauga (triangle), and the inner space by an eighth part.

One should pile two bricks for the nave, four for the nave itself, three for the spokes, and [one] for the rim according to their respective portions. The alternating pattern is prescribed as being like a well (kūpa). 15–16.
One should draw the opening for the nave with a width equal to one-fourth of the *viṣkambha*;

the rim (*nemi*) should be forty-three finger-breadths [in circumference] and four and a half finger-breadths [in thickness]. The rest is accomplished according to the rules, as well as whatever perfections are required for the sacrificial piling (*cayana*). 17–18.

He who, having studied this very method of recollection as it truly is, measures out the Raurava fire-altar, indeed becomes honored by all and attains the same world as the makers of the Śulba-sūtras.
Now, regarding the chariot-wheel-shaped altar described in brief by Viṣṇu,
which is established according to its constituent parts, there are three lines each further and further outward.
Into whose mandala seven and a half men dissolve, according to the wise; others,
three more than the [standard] fields, are liberated in the apertures— of that [deity],
the arrangement of the wheel is such that its expansion exceeds the spokes and the rim.

The diameter of the mandalas and their constituent parts shall be one-third [of the whole]. One should draw the navel with half a human unit; thereafter, within the scope of the expansion, the rim (nemi) shall exceed the spokes by a sixty-third part, and the abode of the syllables [is formed].
One should construct the middle [section] with three hundred and fifty-one and a half finger-breadths, and the surrounding outline with two hundred;
on the first layer, one places the bricks of the chariot-wheel's rim.
You know [the total] as three hundred and four more than four;
in the second [layer], let twenty-four bricks be added—
the five-cornered and the three-cornered ones— at the joints of the spokes and the rim.
With one thousand and seven hundred and sixty-eight bricks, the five layers of the wheel are completed.
Thus ends the section concerning Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the Śulbasūtra. 8.16 Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for receiving gifts (pratigraha-kalpa). 1. One should accept a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) provided one is not unlearned in the Vedas, not impure, not lacking the sacred thread (upavīta), not with disheveled hair, and not afflicted by distress; nor should one do so without water present, nor at an improper time. 2. [The mantra] "Belonging to Savitṛ" is recited first, and "Who this... is recited afterwards. 3. With the words "To Prajāpati thee," one should accept a female human, an elephant, a man, land, and all other living beings except barren soil; with "To Candra thee," the head; with "To Yama thee," the single-hoofed animal; with "To Rudra thee," the cow; and with "To Agni thee," [the horse].

Gold, tin, lead, iron, and bronze; the *gnās* cut [the cloth], the *apases* stretched [the warp], and the *dhiyas* wove it, saying "For Bṛhaspati, thee!"—thus [he gives] a garment; saying "For Uttāna, thee! he causes [it] to resound; saying "For the Viśvedevas, thee! a parasol; saying "For Śrīkāma, thee! a house, a village, and a bed; saying "For Indra and Agni, thee! a goat, a ram, and a buffalo; saying "For Varuṇa, thee! a water-jar, a well, and a pond; saying "For Samudra, thee! a water-pot, a conch, a pearl-oyster shell, coral, and whatever else is from the sea.

"To Tvaṣṭṛ," [he says] for camels; "To Soma," for juices; "To Draviṇodas," for fragrant garlands; "And to the Vanaspatis," [he says]; "To Vaiśvānara," for chariots. 4. If various sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) have not been collected, he should accept that gift [with this formula]:
"On earth, who perceives both merit and evil?
Āditya perceives both the performed merit and the evil."
When the giver has died while the recipient still lives,
to whom does the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) belong as it remains suspended between the two?
Having accepted the sacrificial gifts, Varuṇa bestows them upon Viṣṇu;
he is the giver of all truths, again and again at the time of birth.

Thus, having taken a woman by her hand, having mounted a hero with his two arms upon an elephant that acts as an arm, having taken a man upon the back, a horse upon the tail, gold, and having put on a garment; having stepped forward, having placed an umbrella without a breath [upon it] on the staff, a chariot on the pole, a village in the middle, and having entered a house, having ascended a bed, having placed a goat at the ear, a ram in the wool, a buffalo on the horn, having taken a water-pot, having looked at a well, having descended into a pond, and having taken a water-jar, a conch, a pearl-oyster shell, and coral— [The above is the continuation of the ritual sequence.]

And whatever else is of the sea—having lifted up camels with a stake, donkeys and mules with a goad, having licked up juices, having taken up perfumes and garlands, having climbed trees, and having taken food—one should, having gone out from the house of a Śūdra and performed external purification, mentally repeat the mantra. For a Brāhmaṇa, the mantra is *śrāvya*; for a Rājanya, it is *japa*; for a Vaiśya, it is *upāṃśu*; and for a Śūdra, [it is silent]. He who, knowing thus, accepts [the gift], purifies the giver, purifies himself, and purifies the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), thinking:
"May I know [the fee] among the gods. Thus ends the ritual for acceptance.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for one born under the *Mūla* asterism. 1. If the birth occurs in the first quarter of *Mūla*, it is desired by the father; in the second, by the mother; in the third, it brings wealth; in the fourth, it brings grief to the family, or the person becomes a sharer in merit for himself. 2. In that case, one should prepare a water-pot; having recited over it the *Rudra-hymns*, the *Apratiratha*, and the *Rakṣoghna-sūkta*; 3. A second water-pot should be provided with four outlets, and into it one should place roots shaped like a boat; 4. Of these, the primary ones are the roots.

I shall speak [of them]. The first [group consists of]: *kāśmarya*, *sahadevī*, *aparājitā*, *adhaḥpuṣpī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *balā*, *pāṭalā*, *mayūraśikhā*, *madhupuṣpikā*, *cakrāṅkitā*, *kākajaṅghā*, and *kumārī*. The second [group consists of]: *vaijayantī*, *apāmārga*, *bhṛṅgaraja*, *lakṣmaṇā*, *jātī*, *vyāghra*, *pattraka*, *cakramarda*, *kapileśvarā*, *aśvattha*, *saha*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *śamī*, *arka*, *rohitaka*, and *bilva*. Having filled [the vessels] with these and similar [plants] by their roots, one places the root in the center.

And one should make [an image] of gold, provided with the seven grains. I shall state the roots of those [trees] that are prohibited: *tilvaka*, *dhava*, *nimba*, *śālmalī*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *śleṣmantaka*, and all thorny trees excepted. Therein he should perform the consecration for the father, the child, and the mother; for the husband of the sister-in-law, they sprinkle him while he is seated on a stool made of *akṛti* wood, with the combined flow [of water] from the head down to the mouth. "May glory and fame be mine," [he says]; thus he touches his limbs according to their respective characteristics. After they have bathed, [he offers] an oblation to Nirṛti over milk.

Having cooked the *sthālīpāka* (rice-oblation), having prepared a fence-stick (*paridhi*) and fuel (*idhma*) made of *kāśmarya* wood, and having cleansed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; having offered the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions, and having offered four oblations from the *sthālīpāka* with the verses beginning "To him who presses [the Soma] but does not sacrifice" (*asunvantam ayajamānam*), he should offer fifteen *ājya* oblations with the hymn "With what splendor? (*kayā śubhā savayasaḥ*). He should offer five oblations with the verse "Do not harm our offspring" (*mā naḥ tokāya*) and five with the verse "That body of yours, O Rudra, which is auspicious" (*yā te rudra śivā tanūḥ*). Having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the two verses "O Agni, protect [us] with lead" (*agne rakṣā sīsena tantram*), when the rite is completed, there is a black cow, and black and blue [objects], and something made of gold.

One should give seven kinds of grain to the preceptor (*ācārya*) and a black ox to the *brahmān*. According to one’s capacity, one should give gold to the *brahmans*. (10) One should feed the *brahmans* with *kṛsara*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and food mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*). (11) All shall be auspicious, secure, healthy, and endowed with all blessings and the perfection of all auspiciousness. (12) Thus has the rule been ordained by Manu regarding the deity Nairṛta and the *gara-yoga*. In the *makarī* [yoga], which brings peace, it is auspicious, bestowing wealth, grain, and prosperity, protecting the entire family, removing fear and grief, and bringing good fortune and luck. (13)

Thus ends the procedure for the pacification of those born under the *mūla* asterism and others, according to the *Mānava-sūtra*. Now follows the pacification of twins (*yamala-śānti*). 1. If twin sons, two oxen, or two mares should be born [together], 2. when a year has passed, or twelve years, or twelve nights, one should bring seven types of wood—fig (*aśvattha*), udumbara, vikaṅkata, banyan (*nyagrodha*), plakṣa, śamī, śamaka, priyaṅgu, and white mustard—and [the seeds] of white mustard. 3. If one cannot find these, there shall be a golden bath (*hiraṇya-snāna*).

Having seated [the bridegroom] facing east upon a four-legged auspicious seat with the four verses beginning "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ," they should cause four widows or four celibate students (brahmacārins) to bathe him using a clay vessel with a hundred holes placed between, while a thousand-holed [vessel] made of birch-bark is held [over it], reciting the two sections beginning with "Yā oṣadhayaḥ samanvatīḥ. 4. Once bathed and adorned, the husband and wife should circumambulate the fire from left to right. 5. Having sat down on darbha grass behind the fire, [he should offer oblations] of the cooked mess of rice (sthālīpāka) dedicated to the Maruts with the two *priyavatī* verses.

He offers seven oblations of clarified butter. A bull and one cow are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Having dug seven furrows to the east of the fire and filled them with scented water, he should step across each verse by verse with the eight verses beginning with *hiraṇyagarbhaḥ*, starting from the *jaya* formulas and ending before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; he should mutter the eighth verse. We shall explain this according to the procedure for the consecrated fire (*āhitāgni*). He should offer a cake on thirteen potsherds to the Maruts. A cow that has recently calved is its sacrificial fee. If he cannot find such a cow, [he should give] a field of good soil.
One should give a well-prosperous field of barley or a field of sesame. If these are not available, one who is covered in hair-cloth or skin should enter the *vāḍava* fire; this is his act of grace.
Thus ends the rite for pacifying the birth of twins.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for Āśleṣā. (1) In the first quarter [of the asterism] there is the destruction of the mother; in the fourth, the destruction of the father. (2) In that regard, having taken the hundred medicinal herbs prescribed in the Mūla-vidhāna, having poured them into a copper vessel and placed them in a *pariṣava* vessel, having scattered rice grains around it, one should place upon them a piece of gold weighing one *niṣka* as a serpent facing downwards. Then, having performed a ceremonial bath with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should wrap it with a pair of garments and a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and with fragrant substances.

With flowers of five colors, incense, lamps, various offerings of food and edibles, betel-leaf and other items, and various kinds of fruits—saying "Homage be to the serpents"—one should worship a golden serpent. Then, having established four jars and first filling them with water from a mountain stream, one should fill the others as well; therein, one should place seven types of earth in the first, and *devadāru*, *mustā*, white mustard, blue lotus, turmeric, *guḍūcī*, and sandalwood in the second; all medicinal herbs in the third, and having placed all these things in the fourth;

Having consecrated [the vessel] with the four mantras beginning with "Go to the ocean," and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, the sacrificer—having purified himself on an auspicious day, under an auspicious lunar mansion, at an auspicious moment, and during an auspicious hour, having put on two unwashed garments, and having paid homage to the preceptor (ācārya) who is adorned with perfumes and other ornaments—together with the officiating priests (ṛtvij), performs the recitation for the declaration of a holy day (puṇyāhavācana). Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila) in the midst of the water-jars (kalaśa), having established the fire, and having cooked the sacrificial porridge (sthālīpāka), he offers the two pouring oblations (āghāra) and the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga). After that...

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations separately for each deity: with the verse *sāvitryā savitre vayam* for Savitṛ; with *someti somāya* for Soma; with *sunvantamayajamānam* for Nirṛti; and with *sahasraśīrṣā* for Viṣṇu. (5) One should offer oblations of fuel-sticks, parched grain, sesame, and clarified butter with the mantra *namo astu sarpebhyaḥ*. (6) Having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and the expiatory offerings (*prāyaścittāhuti*), and having offered the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the teacher, together with four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), should draw water mixed with all medicinal herbs, sesame, and mustard from a jar and consecrate the child, the mother, and the father by sprinkling them with four jars of water. (7) The remaining details regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) are explained as before. (8)
Thus, in the Mānava-sūtra, Śaṅkara spoke regarding the rite of Āśleṣā:
"Listen now to the characteristics of children at the time of the eruption of their teeth."
O best of the Bhārgavas, if a child’s teeth first appear on the upper jaw, or if its birth occurs together with the eruption of teeth,
it will devour its mother, its father, or even itself.
In this regard, I shall declare the rite of pacification; listen as I speak it.
A twice-born man who knows the Dharma should place the boy upon the back of an elephant or on a boat; in the absence of these, he should place him on an excellent golden seat.

O Bhārgava, one should then worship Dhātṛ with all medicinal herbs, all fragrances, seeds, flowers, and fruits, as well as with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), jewels, banners, and the sacrificial porridge (sthālīpāka). 3.
In this case, the rite should be performed for seven days, as well as the feeding of Brahmins; on the eighth day, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should likewise be given to the Brahmins,
consisting of gold, silver, land, and even one's own self.
Since the emergence of the teeth is a common event, hear now the ritual bath that follows:
having seated him upon an auspicious seat, one should bathe him with earth, roots, and fruits,
as well as with all medicinal herbs, seeds, and fragrant substances.
One should bathe and worship Fire, Moon, and Wind here;
first, one should install Keśava, the God of gods, there. One should then offer clarified butter into the fire for those very deities according to the prescribed rite.
Then, worship and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, one should bathe the shining image with its parasol over its head using seeds;
and with those very seeds, which are very smooth, the children should perform the worship.
Widowed women, Brāhmaṇas, and likewise friends are to be honored.
Thus ends the rite for the pacification of the defect of teeth as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Women who give birth out of season, as well as those whose offspring are born prematurely;
Non-human beings, those without private parts, and likewise those without sexual characteristics;
those with deficient limbs or with extra limbs— whether they be born as women,
or even as beasts, birds, and reptiles.
One should predict the destruction of that region and of the family;

the king should banish them from his own kingdom. Then, O best of the twice-born, women and those worthy of honor [should be protected], and by the satiation of Brahmins with fruits and other offerings, peace is attained in the world for one who has encountered [calamity].

Thus ends the peace-rite performed at the time of procreation. Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the recitation of the Rudra-hymn. 1. To the north of the village or in front of it, having performed the removal of impurities in a pure place—whether by a river, a natural pool dug by the gods, or a pond—one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). 2. One should perform the Rudra-bath. 3. Having bathed with the mantra "Salutation to Śambhu" (*namaḥ śambhave*), one should perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) ten times with the mantra "Incalculable thousands" (*asaṃkhyātā sahasrāṇi*). Then, having emerged from the water and put on a garment, one should sip water (*ācamana*) and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Rudra: with the mantra "That which is yours, O Rudra" (*yā te rudra*) upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*); and with "Those who are in this great ocean" (*ye asmin mahaty arṇave*)... [upon the heart].

"Those who are numbered on the head"—thus [on the forehead]; "Salutation to Nīlakapardin"—thus on the two eyes; "Salutation to Śruta and Śrutasena"—thus on the two ears; "Having drawn back the bow"—thus on the mouth; "Salutation to Nīlagrīva"—thus on the throat; "Salutation to that weapon which is unstrung"—thus on the two arms; "Salutation to the Girikas"—thus on the heart; "Hiraṇyagarbha"—thus on the navel; "Salutation to the Gaṇas"—thus on the buttocks; "Salutation to Mīḍhuṣṭara"—thus on the hips; "O Rudras, these [are yours] who are powerful"—thus on the private parts; "Do not harm our great one"—thus on the two thighs.

With the mantra "pathāṃ pathirakṣaye," he assigned [the protection] to the feet; with "kavacam," the armor; with "namo bilmine ca," the sub-armor (*upakavaca*); and with "pramuñca dhanvanaḥ," the weapon (*astra*). (4) With "ya etāvantaḥ," the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) is performed. (5) One should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) with the mantra "oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya. Having placed the syllable *oṃ* on the head, the syllable *na* on the nose, the syllable *mo* on the forehead, the syllable *bha* in the middle of the mouth, the syllable *ga* in the region of the throat, and one should place the syllable *va* on the heart.
One should place the syllable *te* on the right hand and the syllable *ru* on the left;
likewise, one should place the syllable *drā* in the center of the navel and the syllable *ya* on the feet.

To Indra, the protector, the lord of the eastern direction; salutation to Indra. To Agni, the lord of the southeastern direction; salutation to Agni. May the path be easy for me; to Yama, the lord of the southern direction; salutation to Yama. To Nirṛti, the lord of the southwestern direction, who [punishes] the one who does not press the Soma and does not sacrifice; salutation to Nirṛti. For that purpose I approach you; to Varuṇa, the lord of the western direction; salutation to Varuṇa. With your teams of horses come to us; to Vāyu, the lord of the northwestern direction; salutation to Vāyu.

O Soma, you with your powers, salutation to Kubera, the lord of the northern direction! Salutation to Īśāna, the lord of the northeastern direction!
