"O Earth, be pleasant! Salutation to Ananta, the lord of the downward direction"—this is the "sealed direction" (diksaṃpuṭa). 7. Having performed the rite of Raudrī in this very manner within oneself, one is liberated from the sins residing in the skin and bones. 8. By this procedure, there are no afflictions caused by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, messengers of Yama, Śākinīs, thieves, and the like, neither in a village, nor at the birth of a child, nor at a Śrāddha, nor when invited, nor in the presence of cattle. 9. They all see him as blazing. 10. One should meditate upon oneself in the form of Rudra. 11. Three-eyed.

Five-faced and ten-armed, gentle, adorned with all ornaments, blue-necked, marked by the crescent moon, resembling pure crystal, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), with a tiger skin as an upper garment, holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) in his hands, bestowing fearlessness, holding a trident (*triśūla*) in one hand and a bow (*pināka*) in another, mounted upon the shoulders of a bull, bearing half of Umā’s body, blazing, with tawny matted hair, endowed with a crown of matted locks, making his topknot radiant, drenched in nectar, and joyful.

Having thus meditated upon Rudra—the one who is saluted by gods and demons, accompanied by the deities of the quarters, eternal, perpetual, auspicious, fixed, undecaying, immutable, all-pervading, stainless, the Lord, and the universal-formed—the twice-born should then properly begin his recitation (japa). (12) In a well-concealed place, the size of a cow-hide, smeared with cow-dung or otherwise prepared, having fashioned a lotus-shaped pedestal for the Linga, he should sprinkle it while reciting "mā no mahāntam" and install it; then he should worship it with "namaḥ śambhave ca. (13)

*Sadya*, *Vāma*, *Aghora*, *Tatpuruṣa*, and *Īśāna*—this is the invocation of Rudra. Regarding the mantra *sadyo jāta*: Sadyojāta is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Brahmā is the deity (*devatā*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*). *Haṃ* is the vehicle; he is the western face, the principle of earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*), and his form is Brahman. *Hrāṃ*; the application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of the western face. *Sadyo jātaḥ*, obeisance to the western face; I invoke you.

Regarding the mantra "vāmamadya savitaḥ," Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Viṣṇu is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the meter, Garuḍa is the vehicle, and the northern face is the element of water. For the invocation of the form of Viṣṇu as the northern face, this is the application (viniyoga). [Recitation: "O Savitṛ, grant me what is desirable today"; salutation to the northern face; I invoke you.

Regarding the mantra *aghorebhyaḥ*: Aghora is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Rudra is the deity (*devatā*), Bṛhatī is the meter (*chanda*), and the one whose vehicle is a bull is the southern face; its essence is the element of fire (*tejas-tattva*). For the form of Rudra, *hrūṃ*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of the southern face: *aghorebhyaḥ*, salutation to the southern face, I invoke you.

For the mantra *tatpuruṣāya*, the Seer is Tatpuruṣa, the Deity is Sūrya, the Metre is Gāyatrī, the Vehicle is the horse, the Face is the eastern one, and the Essential Principle is Vāyu. *Hraiṃ* is for the form of Sūrya; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of the eastern face. *Tatpuruṣāya pūrvavaktrāya namaḥ*, I invoke.

For the mantra "tam īśānam," Īśāna is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Word (*śabda*) is the deity, the *bṛhatī* is the meter; the one whose vehicle is the tortoise, whose face is upward, and whose element is space—homage to the one of white form (*śvetarūpa*); this is the application (*viniyoga*) for the invocation of the upward-facing face with the syllable *hrauṃ*: "I invoke Tam-Īśāna, the upward-facing face, homage."

One should employ the *gāyatrī* verse beginning with "ā tvā vahantu" eight times, O Rudra (14). One should meditate upon Rudra (15). Having meditated upon the blue-throated Mahādeva, residing on Kailāsa together with Umā, the three-eyed Lord, one shall attain perfection (16). Then one should begin the recitation (*japa*) with the eight sections (*anuvākas*) beginning with "namaste rudra manyave" (17). In the first section, the meter is *gāyatrī*; there are three *triṣṭubhs*, three *paṅktis*, and seven *anuṣṭubhs*. In the final section, the first [verse] is...

There are two *bṛhatīs*, two *triṣṭubhs*, twelve *anuṣṭubhs*, and two *jagatīs*. (18) For the remaining verses of various meters among the Rudras, the deity is Rudra and the seer is Aghora. (19) In the *Śatarudriya* when it is recited for the purpose of destroying all sins, this is the application (*viniyoga*) for the *japa*. (20) The eight sections beginning with "Salutation to you, O Rudra, to your wrath" (1.114.1). (21) Having meditated on the installation according to the characteristics [of the verses] starting from "Incalculable thousands... (2.33.1), one should meditate on those who are as high as the mouth [of a vessel] with "Salutation to the Rudras who are in heaven" (2.33.1), and on those who are as high as the navel with "Salutation to the Rudras... (2.33.2).

One should meditate with the mantra "To those who are in the intermediate space" at the height of the navel; with "Obeisance to the Rudras who are on the earth" at the height of the knees. (22) Having recited "To the non-terrible ones," one should dismiss [the deity] with "He who [guards] the paths. (23) Reciting the *Apratiratha* hymn, one should return home. (24) One should sprinkle oneself with that water. (25) This is the rule for the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) for both bipeds and quadrupeds. (26) Thus ends the rule for the daily recitation in the *Mānava-gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*.

Furthermore, I shall explain the procedure for the occasional rite (*naimittika*): having bathed according to the previously stated rule and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should take water in a conch shell or, as available, in a vessel, and cast *dūrvā* grass, flowers, water, and unbroken rice grains toward the northeast. 2. For whomsoever one recites [the mantra], for that person it is likewise: once, twice, thrice, or seven times; if for the sake of health, eight times; if all are present, three times; in the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional rites, it is unlimited. 3. If Rudra [is recited] for offspring...

One should perform the *abhiśamana* (appeasement) in the north-eastern direction while muttering the *Śatarudriya*; one should continue muttering it while walking about. (4) If muttered for one day, one is liberated from diseases and sins. (5) By muttering it for three days, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and from leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and other ailments. (6) According to this rule, one should not [mutter] in a village, nor at the birth of a child, nor when invited to a *śrāddha*, nor in the presence of cattle, nor during the first or last watch of the night; one should remain celibate (*brahmacārī*), nor upon seeing an outcaste (*antyaja*), nor upon seeing a woman in her menses, nor should one engage in physical exertion. (7) When [the recitations] are completed...

Having prayed for his desires as he wishes, and having recited the mantra "aghorebhyaḥ," he should dismiss [the deity] with the verse "yaḥ pathaḥ. (8) He should sprinkle the patron (*yajamāna*) with that water. (9) Reciting the *Apratiratha* hymn, he should return to his home. (10) The Brāhmaṇa who performs this recitation shall obtain all his desires. (11) If performed contrary to the rules, it results in the opposite for both the Brāhmaṇa and the patron. (12) 2.

Having bathed with purity, having conquered the senses, and having received the blessing, one should recite the Rudra-mantra after performing the assignment (*viniyoga*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), deities (*devatā*), and applications (*nyāsa*). 1. For the *Aghora* [mantra]: the seer is Aghora, the deity is Rudra, the meter is Bṛhatī; its application is for all rites and for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). From the end of the section beginning with "I make the rat your animal, O Rudra" (*ākhuṃ te rudra paśuṃ karomi*) up to the end of that Anuvāka is the Heart. From the end of the section beginning with "This Viṣṇu strode out" (*idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame*) up to the end of that Anuvāka is the Head. The six verses beginning with "O Brahmanaspati" (*brahmaṇas pate*) and "The Brahman was born first" (*brahma jajñānam*) and "Brahmā among the gods" (*brahmā devānām*) is the Tuft (*śikhā*). The *Apratiratha* [mantra] is...

The two six-verse hymns beginning with *kavacamādityānāmavasā nūtanena* are the eyes; the *Śatarudriya* is the weapon (2). Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) ending with the invocation and dismissal (3). Having prostrated, one should announce the recitation (*japa*) (4). One should offer oblations of *palāśa* wood-fuel soaked in clarified butter, along with sesame oblations, using the three verses beginning with *namaḥ śambhave*—six or twelve times (5). He who is devoted to bathing, libations, recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, and performs the recitation for a full year, obtains tenfold the fruit; even a slayer of a Brahmin is thoroughly purified. So too a drinker of spirituous liquor, a stealer of gold, a killer of a cow, or the husband of a low-caste woman.
He is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra (6).
O Rudra, that which is given by one who mutters the *rudra* is fit for infinity (7).
Thus ends the procedure for the recitation of the *rudra* in the *Mānava-gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the *pravara* (ancestral invocation). 1. Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "He chooses the *ārṣeya* (the ancestral seers); he thus goes to his own kin, and also for the sake of continuity. 2. He chooses one, he chooses two, he chooses three; he does not choose four, nor does he choose more than five. 3. Here, some prescribe a single *ārṣeya* common to all classes, saying "after Manu"; for what reason? Because "creatures are descended from Manu. 4. One should not choose an *ārṣeya* [belonging] to gods or to men.

One chooses the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*) by means of the sages (*ṛṣi*) themselves. Regarding this, there is a scriptural injunction (*śruti*): "He who chooses a lineage beyond [his own] ancestors would miss the blessing of the sacrifice. Furthermore, he who chooses the lineages of others is cut off from the plants, the cattle, and the ancestors. This rule applies to all other classes of people except for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. From here upwards, the Adhvaryu priest chooses [the ancestors]; as before, from there downwards, the Hotṛ priest chooses them, using forms that are both beneficial (*taddhita*) and vocative (*āmantrita*). We shall explain the Bhṛgus first.

Jāmadagnya, Vātsya, Ānuśātaki, Vaihati, Paila, Śaunakāyani, Jīvanti, Kāmbalodari, Vaihīnari, Vairohitya, Lekhyāyani, Vaiśāki, Vaiśvānara, Vairūpākṣi, Paukāśeralānām, Pārṇili, Vṛkāśvakānām, Uccairmanyu, Sāvarṇi, Vālmīki, Śeralānām, Vaiṣṭapureya, Pālākṣi, Taulakeśinām, Samṛtabhāga, Ārtabhāga, Mārkaṇḍeya, Maṇḍu, Māṇḍavya, Vibhāṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkeyārvanānām, and Sphenamadbhūtī.

[The descendants] of Sthaulapiṇḍi, Śaiṣāpatya, Śārkarākṣa, and Devamatī; Āyaṇa, Arcāyana, Āhvāyana, Gāṅgāyana, Vaiśampāyana, Vāyavyāyana, Auduntyāyana, Saurayī, Dārbhi, Mālāyana, Śārṅgarava, Gālava, Cāṇūkeya, Vaikarṇi, Śaunakarṇi, Śauṇḍakarṇi, and those of the Sāṃkṛtyaitiśāyana lineage: Yājñeya, Bhrāṣṭreya, Kṣmālā, Aṇḍa, Pārimaṇḍalāyana, Āluṇdhi, Krauṣṭi, Saudhakī, Paiṅgalāyana, Sātyakāyana, Kaucahasti, and Kovahnaṇḍi.

Sāṃkhyamitra, Cāndramitra, Cāndramas, Ānulomi, Kauṭilya, Śaunakāyani, Kāṃsyāyani, Śāradvata, Maudgalya, Vādyāleheya, Nimithi, Śākalyoṣṭrākṣi, Vākāyani, Anumati, Jaihmyāśama, Śokajihvātma-damani, Vāṭāra, Kirāṇi, Mājānāti, Kāśakṛtsna, Auṣusruca, Traiṇa, Vaihīkāri, Śaukrāyaṇa, Śākṛṇi, Śākaṭāyana, Goṣṭhāyana, Golāyana, and Ḍākavyāyana—among these, there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of five *ṛṣis*.

[The lineage is] Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Aurva, Jāmadagna—thus the Hotṛ; "as Jamadagni, as Urva, as Āpnavāna, as Cyāvāna, as Bhṛgu"—thus the Adhvaryu. (12) The Vaidas are those descended from Nimiṭha; for them, there is a pravara of five ṛṣis: Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Vaida, Naimiṭha—thus the Hotṛ; "as Nimiṭha, as Vida, as Āpnavāna, as Cyāvāna, as Bhṛgu"—thus the Adhvaryu. (13) The Āvadhyāyanas and Mauñjāyanas have a pravara of three ṛṣis.
The Hotṛ priest says, "O Bhārgava, O Cyāvāna, you are invincible," and the Adhvaryu priest says, "Like Cyavana, like Bhṛgu, [you are] invincible.

14. 1. Now, regarding the Jamadagnis: the Vidas, Prācīnayogis, Pulastyas, Vaidabhṛtas, Krauñcāyanas, Abhayajātās, Taugāyanas, Āvaṭas, Śākarṇins, Bhālvaśayas, and Bhārgavas—among these there is no intermarriage. 2. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.

"Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnavāna"—thus [the Hotṛ]; "Āpnavāna-like, Cyavana-like, Bhṛgu-like"—thus the Adhvaryu. 3. The Baudheyas, Mārgapathas, Grāmyāyaṇis, Athanaikasīs, Āpastambis, Vibhīllikārṇis, Kārdamis, and Ārṣṭiṣeṇas—among these, there is no intermarriage. 4. For them, the *pravara* (ancestral invocation) consists of five ṛṣis.

"Bhārgava, Cyāvāpnavāna, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Anūpa"—thus says the Hotṛ; "Anūpavat, Ṛṣiṣeṇavat, Apnavānavat, Cyavanavat, Bhṛguvat"—thus says the Adhvaryu. (5) The Āpiśāyanas, the Kāpiśāyanas, the Drauṇāyanas, the Khālāyanas, the Avicakṣas, the Maitreyas, and then the Āmodāyanas and the Āpiśalas—among these there is no intermarriage. (6) Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.

The Hotṛ priest invokes them as Bhārgava, Vādhryaśva, Daivodāsa; the Adhvaryu priest invokes them as Bhṛguvat, Vadhryaśvavat, Divodāsavat. (7) Among these—Vaitahavya, Yāska, Mādhūna, Mauka, Jīvantyāyana, then Bhāgaleya, Bhāgavijñeya, Kauśāmbeya, Vṛkāśvaki, Mādāhi, Gaurikṣita, Dairghyacita, Vāleya, Pāñcadhanā, and Pauṣṇāvata—there is no intermarriage. (8) Their pravara consists of three ṛṣis.

For the Bhārgavas Vaitahavyas and Sāvedas, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ says, "Bhārgava, Vaitahavya, Sāveda," and the Adhvaryu says, "Like Saveda, like Vitahavya, like Bhṛgu. (9) For those whose ancestors are Vatsas and Purodhasas, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ says, "Bhārgava, Vātsa, Paurodhasa," and the Adhvaryu says, "Like Purodhasa, like Vatsa, like Bhṛgu. (10) For those who have the Vedas and Viśvajyotis as their ancestors, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ says, "Bhārgava, Veda, Viśvajyotis," and the Adhvaryu says, "Like Viśvajyotis, like Veda, like Bhṛgu. (11) For the Pārthas and Ainyas, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.

The Hotṛ priest says, "Bhārgava, Vainya, Pārtha," and the Adhvaryu says, "like Pṛthu, like Vena, like Bhṛgu. (12) The Gārtsamadas and Śunakas (13)—namely the Yajñavacas, Saukaris, Kārdamāyanas, Rājabādhavyas, Caikṣas, Coras, Śrotriyas, and Pratyaras—among these Śunakas, there is no intermarriage. (14) Their *pravara* consists of a single ṛṣi: the Hotṛ says "Gārtsamada" and the Adhvaryu says "like Gṛtsamada. Alternatively, if it is a *dvyārṣeya* (two-ṛṣi lineage), the Hotṛ says "Bhārgava-Gārtsamada" and the Adhvaryu says "like Gṛtsamada, like Bhṛgu. (15) 2

We shall explain the Aṅgirasas: the Aucathyas, the Gautamas, the Tauḍeyas, the Abhijitas, the Voghāyas, the Naikākṣas, the Rāhūgaṇyas, the Kṣairakaṭas, the Ekastamaras, the Karotis, the Sāralopas, the Kāśapārīs, the Pauṣpiṇḍas, the Bhāgalas, the Vaḍauḍavas, the Upabindus, the Māntharas, the Īṣās, the Rauhiṇāyanas, the Amalakas, the Krolayimas, the Krauñcas, the Kroṣṭṛs, the Āruṇayas, the Pārthivas, the Saudāminis, the Kācākṣas, the Kauralyas, the Akṣas, the Apādapakṣas, the Vāsamūlis, the Vaṃśas, the Mulmis, and the Śapitṛs.

Vāsapuṣpi, Sauṣya, Saukṣmāyaṇa, and Kauḍalya—among these there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of five *ṛṣis*: Āṅgirasa, Aucathya, Gautama, Auśija, and Kākṣīvata. The Hotṛ priest invokes: "Like Kakṣīvat, like Vaduśija, like Gotama, like Ucathya, like Aṅgiras. The Adhvaryu priest responds: "Like Aṅgiras. For the Āyāsyas, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: Āṅgirasa, Āyāsya, and Gautama. The Hotṛ priest invokes: "Like Gotama, like Āyāsya, like Aṅgiras. The Adhvaryu priest responds: "Like Aṅgiras. Now, for the Ātreyāyaṇis, Mādhūkarṇis, and Vālkalis...

[The lineage] of Saupiṣṭya-Agniveśyas: Śālāthala, Vārāha, Śauṅga, Kṛpaṇaparṇa, Prāvāhaṇeya; Māślāya, Vyāyogic-chandāta, Khārigrīvīṇa; Aiṣumati, Śādya, Kāvakika, Āvikāyana; Naitundila, Vaidhaṃkī; Vaidhakīka, Yācarātaki, Manahāla; Sauvastambi, Taulvali, Pauṣuyāvaddiśī; Śālavālauha, Devamata, Harikarṇa, Drāṅgava, Caucaya, Kaumudagandhi, Khāriṇādi, Rājastambi, Sāmastambi.

The Somastambis, Audameghis, Gāṇḍakis, Lohitakis, Kāṇḍakas, Dhānakas, Kulakas, Sātyamugris, Śaivayathas, and Bhāradvājas—among these there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja. The Hotṛ priest invokes them as "like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, like Aṅgiras," and the Adhvaryu priest likewise. Furthermore, there are the Kāṇāyaṇas, Kaivalyas, Vatsatarāyaṇas, Krauṇḍāyanas, Vārddhanayas, and the Vāmśāyanas.

Bhrāṣṭrakṛt, Bhrāṣṭrabindu, Aindrāli, Sāyakāyana, Kolī, Krīkā, Nīsāṃtvakṛt, Snāpurāvaṭa, Lāvaki, Bhālūvi, Rūpamarkaṭi, Protsaṅgi, Śyāmāyana, Paiṅgalāyana, and Sāṃbharabhāma—among these, there is no intermarriage. For them, the *pravara* consists of five ṛṣis: Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja, Śainya, and Gārgya. The Hotṛ priest says: "Like Garga, like Chinin, like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, like Aṅgiras. The Adhvaryu priest says: "Like Tittiri, like Ari, like Kavi, like Bhūma."
There is no intermarriage among these Gargas. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Āṅgirasa Śainya Gārgya," [thus] the Hotṛ; "Garga-vat Śini-vat Āṅgiras-vat," [thus] the Adhvaryu. 11.3.11.3.

The Kapistaras, Svastitars, Bindus, Daṇḍins, Śaktis, Patañjalis, Bhojavas, Jjarudhus, Viśālīs, Śītakis, Ardhās, Rājakeśas, Uccuṭīs, Śāṃśāpis, Kalaśīkaṇṭhas, Kārīrayas, Vānyāyanas, Vāmadhyāyanas, Kāpyas, and Kavayas—among these, there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: for the Hotṛ it is Āṅgirasa-Mahīyava-Urukṣaya; for the Adhvaryu it is Urukṣayavat-Mahīyavavat-Aṅgirovat. [Also included are] the Saṃkṛtis, Pautimāṣis, Taṇḍis, and Śambhus.

Among the Śevapāyanas—namely the Jānakis, Tailvakas, Vyālātavyas, Ārṣabhis, Lāṅgandhis, and Cārāyaṇīs—there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: Āṅgirasa, Sāṃkṛtya, and Gaurivīta. The Hotṛ priest invokes them as "Gaurivītavat, Saṃkṛtivat, and Aṅgirovat," and the Adhvaryu priest likewise. Among the Haritas—namely the Kautsas, Śaṅkhas, Darbhas, Paiṅgas, Bhaimagavas, Mādrakāris, Gāṇakāris, Hāstidāsins, Lāveraṇis, and Kālaśītas—there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.

The *hotṛ* priest says, "Of the Aṅgirases, Ambarīṣa, and Yuvanāśva"; the *adhvaryu* priest says, "Like Yuvanāśva, like Ambarīṣa, and like Aṅgiras. 6. Ruru, Gākyāyana, Daśa as the third, Śākaṭāyana as the fourth, Gardabha, Nārī, then Prākāra, Sauvāra, Markaṭa, Ramaṇa, Śaṇa, Kaṇva, Mārkaṭaya, Rāmaṇeya, and Śāṇāyana—among these, there is no intermarriage. 7. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the *hotṛ* priest says, "Of the Aṅgirases, Ajamīḍha, and Kaṇva."

"Like Kaṇva, like Ajamīḍha, like Aṅgiras"—thus says the Adhvaryu. (8) Now, there is no intermarriage among these: the Vaiṣṇuvṛddhis, Śaṭhamarṣaṇas, Chatṛṇas, Potṛṇas, Gotṛṇas, and Bādarāyaṇas. (9) Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Āṅgirasa, Paurukutsa, Trāsadasyava"—thus says the Hotṛ; "like Trasadasyu, like Purukutsa, like Aṅgiras"—thus says the Adhvaryu. (10) For the Rathītaras, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Āṅgirasa, Vairūpa, Pārṣadaśva"—thus says the Hotṛ.

"Pṛṣadaśvavat, Virūpavat, Aṅgirasvat"—thus says the Adhvaryu. (11) For those of the Ṛṣabhaga lineage, there is a *pravara* consisting of three *ṛṣis*: "Āṅgirasa, Vāmadevya, Gautama"—thus says the Hotṛ; "Gotamavat, Vāmadevavat, Aṅgirasvat"—thus says the Adhvaryu. (12) There is no intermarriage among these: Hiraṇyagarbha, Chatraka, and Mudgala. (13) Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Āṅgirasa, Bhārmyaśva, Maudgalya"—thus says the Hotṛ; "Mudgalavat, Bhṛmyaśvavat, Aṅgirasvat"—thus says the Adhvaryu. (14)

The *pravara* for the Ṛkṣas and Bharadvājas consists of five ancestors: Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja, Vāndana, and Mātavacasa. The Hotṛ priest says, "Like Matavacas, like Vandana, like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, and like Aṅgiras"; the Adhvaryu priest says the same. (15) Now, as for those families who belong to two lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), such as the Śauṅgas and Śaiśiras—the Bharadvājas being the Śauṅgas and the Katas being the Śaiśiras—there is no marriage between them. (16) Their *pravara* consists of five ancestors: Āṅgirasa... [and so forth].
"Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja, Śauṅga, Śaiśira"—thus says the Hotṛ; "like Śiśira, like Śuṅga, like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, like Aṅgiras"—thus says the Adhvaryu. 17.4.

We shall now explain the Viśvāmitras. The Vaiśvāmitras, Devarātas, Aikitakas, Gālavas, Vāratantavas, Kuśikas, Vātaṇḍas, Śalaṅkas, Āśvāvatāyanas, Śyāmāyanas, Yājñavalkyas, Jābālas, Saindhavāyanas, Bābhravyas, and whoever is a Vārṣīya or Sāsitya; furthermore, the Sauśrutās, Audheprās, Saurathāyas, Kājāliyajayas, Ārjunākṣis, Pāryodarīs, Sumantus, Jaiminis, and Kharavākhalis—among these, there is no intermarriage. For them, the *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis.

The Hotṛ priest recites: "Vaiśvāmitra, Daivarāta, Audala"; the Adhvaryu priest recites: "As Daivalada, as Devarāta, as Viśvāmitra. There is no marriage between these [groups]: Devaśravas, Devatara, Śraumata, and Kāmakāyana. Their *pravara* (ancestral invocation) consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Vaiśvāmitra, Daivaśravasa, Daivatara. The Hotṛ priest recites: "As Devatara, as Devaśravas, as Viśvāmitra"; the Adhvaryu priest recites accordingly. These are the three *Raiṇava* families: the Kātyakas, the Śvodūraṇas, and the Śvodūhayas; there is no marriage among them. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.

For the Vaiśvāmitras, the *hotṛ* recites: "Kāthaka, Kāthya, Kāthaki"; the *adhvaryu* recites: "like Kāthya, like Kātha, like Viśvāmitra. (7) Now, among those of the Kamaṇḍakas, Dhanañjayas, Pilakaṭas, Pārthivas, Bandhalas, and Pāṇinas, there is no intermarriage. (8) Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the *hotṛ* recites, "Vaiśvāmitra, Mādhucchandasa, Āghamarṣaṇa"; the *adhvaryu* recites, "like Āghamarṣaṇa, like Madhucchandas, like Viśvāmitra. (9) Among the Ajās, Mādhucchandasas, and Mārgamitras, there is no intermarriage. (10) Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.

The Hotṛ priest [recites] "Vaiśvāmitra Mādhucchandasa-ājya," and the Adhvaryu [responds] "like Madhucchandas, like Viśvāmitra. 11. According to the Āśmarathyas, for those belonging to the Kāmalāyati lineage, the Hotṛ [recites] "Bandhula Kauśika," and there is no intermarriage among these. 12. For them, the *pravara* (ancestral invocation) consists of two Ṛṣis: the Hotṛ [recites] "Vaiśvāmitrāṣṭaka," and the Adhvaryu [responds] "like Aṣṭaka, like Viśvāmitra. 13. For the Pūraṇas and the Vāridhāpayantas, there is no intermarriage. 14. For them, the *pravara* consists of two Ṛṣis.

For the Vaiśvāmitra-Pauraṇas, the Hotṛ says, "Vaiśvāmitra-Pauraṇa," and the Adhvaryu says, "Like Pūraṇa, like Viśvāmitra. (15) For the Gāthin-Raiṇavas, their *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis; the Hotṛ says, "Vaiśvāmitra-Gāthina-Raiṇava," and the Adhvaryu says, "Like Reṇu, like Gāthin, like Viśvāmitra. (16) For the Hiraṇyaretasas, the *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis.

For those of the Vaiśvāmitra-Hiraṇyaretasa lineage, the *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis: the Hotṛ says, "Vaiśvāmitra, Hiraṇyaretasa," and the Adhvaryu says, "Possessing seed, possessing gold, like Viśvāmitra. (17) For those of the Suvarṇaretasa lineage, the *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis: the Hotṛ says, "Vaiśvāmitra, Sauvarṇaretasa," and the Adhvaryu says, "Possessing seed, possessing gold, like Viśvāmitra. (18) For those of the Kapotaretasa lineage, the *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis.

For the Vaiśvāmitra-Kāpota lineage, the *pravara* is: "O Retasvat, Kapotavat, Vaiśvāmitravat," says the Hotṛ; "O Adhvaryu, [invoke] like Viśvāmitra, like Kapota, like Retasvat. (19) For the Ghṛtakauśikas, the *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis: "O Vaiśvāmitra-Ghārta-Kauśika," says the Hotṛ; "O Adhvaryu, [invoke] like Viśvāmitra, like Ghṛta, like Kuśika. (20) For the Śāṭharamāṭharas, the *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis.

The *hotṛ* says, "Vaiśvāmitra, Śāṭhara, Māṭhara," and the *adhvaryu* says, "like Maṭhara, like Śāṭhara, like Viśvāmitra. (21) Now, among these—Sāhula, Māhula, Uhala, Kohala, Jaṃbila, Śāvila, Śātila, Phāhula, Yāmila, Yādadhi, and Śādadhi—there is no intermarriage. (22) Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.

For the Vaiśvāmitras, the *sāhula* [branch]: the Hotṛ priest says "Vaiśvāmitra, Sāhula, Māhula," and the Adhvaryu priest says "Vaiśvāmitra, Sāhulavat, Māhulavat. 23. Now, for the Udumbarāyaṇis, Śaiśiras, Taikāyantis, Tārukṣyāyaṇis, Velāyanas, Vedāyanas, Maudāyanas, Caudāyanas, Gaṅgāyanas, Kātyāyanas, Kātyāt-kīlas, and Kārīlācakīs—among these, there is no intermarriage. 24. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ priest says "Vaiśvāmitra, Kātyāt-kīla," and the Adhvaryu priest says "Kīlavat, Katavat, Vaiśvāmitravat. 25. 5.

We shall explain the Vasiṣṭhas. 1. For those Vasiṣṭhas who are other than the Upamanyus, the Parāśaras, the Kuṇḍinas, and the [others], there is a single *ṛṣi* lineage (*ekārṣeya*) *pravara*. 2. They are: the Vaidyāghrapadyas, the Aupagavas, the Vaigrayas, the Sāsāmalāyanas, the Kapiṣṭhalas, the Auḍulomas, the Āśvalāyanas, the Vaiṭārakas, the Gopāyanas, the Baudhāyanas, the Cūḍākavyāyanas; then the Vāhyākīs, the Jātūkarṇyas, the Haritayas, and also the Vākurayas; and those who are the Āyaḥsthūṇas, the Śucivṛkṣas, the Laumāyanyas, the Brahmavādins, the Brahmakṛdas, and the Brahmavidas.

The Bahmavileyas, the Svastikaras, the Kāṇṭheviddhis, Maṇḍi, Cauli, Caulika, Kālohalī, Saumanasāyaṇi, Āvaṇi, Cauli, Gauriśravasa, and Arjunākṣa—among these there is no intermarriage. For them, there is a single *ṛṣi* lineage (*ekārṣeya*) as their *pravara*.

The Hotṛ [says] "Vāsiṣṭha," and the Adhvaryu [says] "Vasiṣṭhavat. 4. We shall now explain the Upamanyus: the Śailālayas, the Mahākarṇas, the Kauravyas, and then the Traivarṇas; the Kapiñjalas, the Dāvalas, the Śikhīs, the Bhāgavittāyanas, those who are the Ḍokavyāyanas, the Oṃpālakhīs, the Vāvālkalayas, the Śāntātapas, the Kārḍuris, the Ākatmāveyas, and also the Lavayas; the Yorthas, then the Sachāgyāyanas, the Ālavyāyanas, the Kaumārāyaṇas, the Kaulodakis, the Audgāhamānas, the Evākaries, the Lākṣmaṇeyas, and the Gāṇḍūlavoddhakis.

The Sāṃkhyāyanas, Aupamanyavas, Kauṇḍodarīs, Kaidarbhīs, Nāhakīs, Bāhavīs, Dhaumāvatas, Mauñjāyanas, and Śaśakāyanas—among these there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: Vāsiṣṭha, Ābharadvasa, and Aindrāpramada. The Hotṛ priest recites: "Aindrāpramadavat, Ābharadvasuvat, Vasiṣṭhavad"; the Adhvaryu priest recites: "Vasiṣṭhavad, Ābharadvasuvad, Aindrāpramadavat. The Prārohayas, Vaikalayas, Plākṣayas, and Kaumudādhyas [belong to this same lineage].
The fifth among these is Hāryaśvi; these are the red Parāśaras.
The Kāṇḍūśayas, the Vāhatas, the Jāṃjayas, and the Maimanāyanas—Gopāli is their fifth; these are the Nīla Parāśaras.
The Kārṣṇājinās, the Kapiśroḍhas, the Kārkayas, the Śāntātapas,
and Puṣkarasādi as the fifth— these are the Kṛṣṇa Parāśaras.
The Āviṣṭāyanas, Vārṣṇāyanas, Śmāmeyas, and Lokāyas;
Vaikṣire is their fifth—these are the Gaura Parāśaras.
Khāllāyana, Vārṣāyaṇi, Pūrṇa, Bilva, and Yūpa—the fifth among them is Nārṇi; these are the Śukla-Parāśaras.

These are the thirty Parāśaras; there is no intermarriage among them. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: Vāsiṣṭha, Śāktya, and Pārāśarya. The Hotṛ priest invokes them as "like Parāśara, like Śakti, like Vasiṣṭha," and the Adhvaryu likewise. There is no intermarriage among the Aupasvastis, the Svastayas, the Ālohāyanas, the Mādhyaṃdinas, the Ākṣitis, the Paippalādins, the Divaṃkarṣīs, the Kuṇḍinas, and the Mitrāvaruṇas. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.
"Vāsiṣṭha, Kauṇḍinya, Maitrāvaruṇa"—thus says the Hotṛ; "Mitrāvaruṇavat, Kauṇḍinavat, Vasiṣṭhavat"—thus says the Adhvaryu. 11.6.

We shall now explain the Kaśyapas: the Āgrāyaṇas, the Agrāyaṇas, the Graivāyaṇas, the Vṛṣagaṇas, the Somabhūtas, the Śonavyas, the Mauṣakiris, the Itikāyanas, the Audavrajis, the Māṭharas, and the Kaijālis; then the Lākṣmaṇayas, the Vaidhakayas, the Ślokatyas, and the Bhaumanis; the Devatayas, the Gomeyadas, the Utthās, the Svayaṃsvāpas, the Dhūmrāyaṇas, the Subabhrus, the Aurṣyāyaṇas, the Kārṣyāyaṇas, the Svāroyaṇas, the Ḍākavāyaṇas, the Śatrubhayas, the Bhiryogādins, the Śarakas, the Kāṣṭāyaṇas, and the Śākādas.

The Śālihotras, Ājānanāthas, Kuvamimas, Cakridas, Dākṣapāṇis, Mārīcayas, Māṣaśarāvis, Agniśarmāyaṇas, Hāstidāsīs, Yailas, Mailitas, Anyakṛtis, Kauṣītakīs, Saumiśrīs, Kāṇḍās, Vāyanis, Vāruṇis, Vaivaris, Śaivarayas, Jighānas, Hastikāśyapas, Paiṭhīnasas, Kaikasiyas, Pratiṣeyas, Sauśyavasas, Moyas, Saryāgnivasas, Mopas, Dārbhas, Pālaśāyinas, Kadukas, and Bhaikṣis—among these, there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.

[The lineage] exists as follows: Kāśyapa, Āvatsāra, and Naidhruva; the Hotṛ priest [recites] "nidhruvavat, avatsāravat, kāśyapavat," and the Adhvaryu [recites] the same. 3. The Ānaṣṭayas, Bhāgurayas, Śyenapas, then the Ajāpālayas, Śairīṣis, Audavāhis, Śairaṅghris, Aupaśavīyas, Saumyakṛkas, Auṣīs, Kālāśis, Laukākṣas, and Idandhas—among these, there is no intermarriage. 4. For them, the *pravara* (ancestral invocation) consists of three *ṛṣis*.

The *hotṛ* [is called] Kāvyapāvatsāra Vāsiṣṭha; the *adhvaryu* [is called] Vasiṣṭhavat, Avatsāravat, and Kaśyapavat. Śambhuja, Alibhra, both Bhūpapurodha and Jalandharamuja, Mayūra, Paryagoṣṭha, Gardabhīmukha, Hiraṇyabāhu, Ādityavarṇa, Saudāmilubha, Śauśila, Gobhila, Kuhalo, and Vṛkakhaṇḍa—these are the Gukurantas. Uttara and Śāntiketu—these are the Devajātis. Vedāyana, Jāṅgharāyaṇa, and Śatrūhāyana...

The Audameghas, Tṛṇavastas, Śāṇḍilas, Mahākās, Bhallakas, Vāyukis, Tārkalis, Tetrucodvudis, and Sauṣmiṇeyas—among these there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: for the Hotṛ, it is "Kāśyapa-Asita-Devala," or "Śāṇḍila-Asita-Devala"; for the Adhvaryu, it is "Devala-vat Asita-vat Kaśyapa-vat," or "Devala-vat Asita-vat Śāṇḍila-vat."

We shall now explain the Atris. The Kārmaryāyaṇis, the Śaṅkilayas, the Ādyas, the Śākhārathas, the Āghrāyaṇas, the Vāmarathyas, the Gopavanas, the Tārṇabindavas, the Auḍālakīs, the Śaunakarṇyas, the Vālūtapayas, the Gauragrīvins, the Kairandis, the Caitrāyaṇas, the Nākarṣyayantis, the Paurindas, the Vatsas, the Athapas, the Galis, the Chāgalis, the Bhāgalis, the Vāhudantyas, the Indreyas, the Dauchāyātreyas, the Saiddhūtakīs, the Varṣāṇakis, and the Kṛṣṇachandogas—among these, there is no intermarriage.

Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Ātreya, Arcanānasa, Śyāvāśva"—thus [recites] the Hotṛ; "like Śyāvāśva, like Arcanānasa, like Atri"—thus [recites] the Adhvaryu. Plākṣi, Dākṣi, Vyāli, Paurṇavi, Aurṇavābi, Śilambin, Mauñjakeśin, Bhalandana, Vaijavāpin, Śirīṣa, Maiyaṇya, Dūti, Saupuṣpi, Sāmapuṣpi, Somapuṣpi, Hiraṇyapuṣpi, Candrin, Kardrin, Kākaśīrṣin, and Kākālaśin—among these there is no intermarriage. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.

We shall explain the Agastis. 1. Kukūla, Upaka, Balakā, Lāṃvakāyana, Śālaṃkāyana, Dhāriṇi, Dhauraṇī, Saudhanva, Saukṛtya, Kalmāṣadaṇḍi, Rapautu, Autu, Āyaṇa, Śaurbhya, Gavyādhila, Śilādya, Śaivapatha, Arbuda, Aida, Ilama, and Evayāyadu—among these there is no intermarriage. 2. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Āgastya, Dārḍhacyuta, Idhmavāha"—the Adhvaryu priest recites, "Hāta, like Idhmavāha; like Dṛḍhacyuta; like Agasti. 3. Akra...

Among these—Śakra, Śukra, Jātya, Haimaudaki, and so forth—there is no intermarriage (4). Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Āgastya, Māhendra, Māyobhuva"—thus the *hotṛ*; "Māyobhuva-vat, Mahendra-vat, Agastya-vat"—thus the *adhvaryu* (5). The Kāyeyas have a slope toward the east; among these—Akra, Śukra, Śuddha, Haṃsa, Cāṣa, Bhāṣa, Haimavarcas, and Himodaka—there is no intermarriage (6). Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Āgastya, Haimavarcas, Haimodaka"—thus the *hotṛ*.

The *Adhvaryu* [recites]: "Himodaka, Himavarcas, Agasti"—thus for these. (7) There is no intermarriage among those belonging to the groups beginning with Akri, Cakri, Arci, Carci, Himodaki, and Pāriṇaka. (8) Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ says "Āgastya, Pināyaka, Pāriṇaka," and the *Adhvaryu* says "Pāriṇakavat, Pināyakavat, Agastivat. (9) There is no intermarriage among those belonging to the groups beginning with Nandi, Vimali, Dhimali, Mimītaki, Pināyaki, and Sāyaki. (10) Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ says "Āgastya, Pināyaka, Sāyaka."

"Sāyakavat, Pināyakavat, Agastyavat"—thus says the Adhvaryu. For those whose middle [ancestor] is Pūraṇa, their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Āgastyamādhyamapauraṇa"—thus says the Hotṛ. "Pūraṇavat, Madhyamavat, Agastyavat"—thus says the Adhvaryu. 12. 9.

The *pravara*s have been explained. We shall now explain the modifications (*vaikṛta*). 1. Now, there are two origins for Brāhmaṇas; we shall explain their origin and their formal adoption (*pratipatti*). 2. Those whose lineage of progeny has continued unbroken through the male line are those of a well-endowed family (*saṃhitakulīna*). 3. Those who, for seven, or even five generations back, are endowed with noble birth, Vedic learning, conduct, and character, and who possess truthfulness and immortality, are "possessed of fathers" (*pitṛmant*); they are "possessed of grandfathers" (*paitṛmatya*) and "possessed of ancestral seers" (*ārṣeya*), and are thus eligible for officiating as priests (*ārtvijīna*). 4. Now...

The son given in adoption (*dattaka*), the son bought (*krītaka*), the son made (*kṛtrima*), and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*)—those who are born through the acceptance by another and thus belong to different ancestral lineages (*nānārṣeya*) become *dvaimātura* (belonging to two lineages). As is the case with the Śauṅga-Śaiśirīs, the Bharadvāja-Udameghas, and the Laukākṣīs, as well as whatever other families are produced in this same manner, their *pravara* lineages shall be exactly so. When there is a conjunction of two *pravara* lineages, the first belongs to the progenitor and the latter to the adopter. Or rather, three [belong] to one and three to the other.

One should not do it in that manner; therefore, one chooses either three or five [representatives]. (7) Now, if there are those born of a paternal uncle or a relative who share a single *ṛṣi* ancestry and belong to a family of common interest (*saṃhitakulīna*), they belong to the adoptive father alone. (8) Now, if these [adopted sons] have no offspring by their own wives, they shall take the inheritance and offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to them for three generations; if such offspring exist, they shall offer to both [the biological and adoptive fathers], according to the teaching of the Teacher. (9) One may perform two [funeral rites] at a single *śrāddha*, or one may perform them separately, designating each individually with a single *piṇḍa*.

One should recite two [ancestors]: the adoptive father and the biological father, up to the third generation. If the *ārṣeya* (the lineage of ṛṣis) is not known, one should choose the first of these very *pravara*s. Or, by means of inquiry, one should assign whichever [lineage] one considers appropriate for him. Or, in the case of a Kṣatriya, there may be the *pravara* of his domestic priest (*purohita*) or the *pravara* of his teacher (*ācārya*).

By this very [rule], the *pravara* of the Vaiśyas is explained. (12) If he chooses the *sārṣṭi* [formula], the Hotṛ says, "Mānava-aiḍa-paurūravasa," and the Adhvaryu says, "purūravovat-iḍāvat-manuvat. (13) They should choose the *sārṣṭi*. (14) A Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya should have the same *pravara* as their domestic priest (*purohita*). (15) The recitation of the names of the Ṛṣis is auspicious; it brings wealth, fame, and long life. (16) He who studies the chapter on *pravaras* has performed hospitality for each individual Ṛṣi for a thousand divine years. (17)

The non-attainment of the lineage of sexual union is not contradictory for the intermediate sages (ṛṣyantara). 18. This great Śakuni is completed; it is the root of the Vedas and the summit of Dharma, increased and augmented by the Rudras and the elders. 19. One should not give this to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has not resided [as a student] for a full year. 20. He who studies the Pravarādhyāya stands above all those who purify the assembly (paṅktipāvana); he who studies the Pravarādhyāya [stands above all]. 21. Thus ends the Pravarādhyāya in the Maitrāyaṇī Śākhā.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the *śrāddha*. Having kindled the fire by friction, and having invited on the previous day an uneven number of Brahmins who do not belong to his own *gotra*—men who have maintained their lineage for ten generations on both the maternal and paternal sides, who are distinguished by learning and austerity, who perform auspicious deeds, and who are pure and dressed in white garments—he should, in the afternoon, feed them. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he should provide purification within a consecrated circle (*maṇḍala*) and, after they have sipped water (*ācānta*), he should seat the ancestors facing east and the Viśvedevas facing north. He should prepare two vessels for the *arghya* offering.

Three [balls] for the gods and one each for the ancestors, or one for both groups; having poured water with the verse "The paths come together," having purified the *sumanas* flowers and thrown in barley grains, and having said, "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas," he should, being permitted by the Brahmins, scatter the barley grains clockwise with the verses, "O Viśvedevas, increasers of Truth" and "O Viśvedevas, who are unfailing. Having placed the two strainers in his hand and recited, "Golden-hued, pure ones," he says, "O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya* offering."

Having said, "I shall invoke the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers," and being permitted by the Brahmins, he should scatter sesame seeds clockwise while reciting, "We invoke you who desire [us]; come hither, O Soma-loving fathers. Having placed two purifiers (pavitra) in his hand and having pronounced the names and lineages, he should say, "O my father, this is your *arghya*; O grandfather, O great-grandfather."
May there be born in our own family one who would give us milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day, during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism,
from vessels made of gold, silver, and udumbara wood.

A gift given with a sword crafted by an Ārya attains imperishability. One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) with the verse, "The water on the earth" (*payaḥ pṛthivyām*); honey with the verse, "The winds [bring] honey for the one who follows the Law" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*); and ghee with the verse, "Life comes from ghee" (*āyur ghṛtam*). Having sprinkled [the food] with the formula, "I sprinkle thee with truth through the Law" (*satyam tvartena pariṣiñcāmi*), or silently, he performs the consecration of the vessel with the formula, "The earth is thy vessel" (*pṛthivī te pātram*). Taking the thumb of the Brāhmaṇa [guest], he says, "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering for the gods" (*viṣṇo havyam rakṣasva*) for the Viśvedevas; "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering for the ancestors" (*viṣṇo kavyam rakṣasva*) for the Pitṛs. Having placed water in his hand and having recited "Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ" three times, he recites the three-verse hymn beginning with "The winds [bring] honey for the one who follows the Law" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*).

"May the fathers be pleased; may the grandfathers be pleased; may the great-grandfathers be pleased"—saying this, with speech restrained, he should offer the most desired foods with the words, "May they be satisfied. (5) He recites the Sāvitrī three times and the first three sections (anuvākas) of the Veda three times. (6) Having said, "O fathers, rejoice here! Having created offspring, O you who are worthy of sacrifice, we invoke you, the peaceful ones; O fathers, rejoice here," they depart. (7) While the ancestors are eating, [the priest recites] the five verses beginning with "Prepare your power," and "He knows that for you," and "O Agni, purify us again. (8) "May the fathers purify me. (9)

One should recite [the mantra] eight times; then one should ask, "Are you satisfied? and they reply, "We are satisfied. When they have sipped water once, one should pour out the scattering of food (vikira) on the ground with the words:

"Those living beings in my family who have been consumed by fire and those who have not been consumed by fire—may they, through the water given upon the ground, attain satisfaction and reach the supreme goal."

Having thus poured out water, he should place the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) as in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Then, having sprinkled the ground with water and said, "May it be well-sprinkled," and having caused [the ancestors] to rise with the words, "Arise, [may there be] inexhaustibility," and having stepped forward with the mantra, "In strength, in strength," he should circumambulate [the site] clockwise with the mantra, "May [we] not be deprived of strength. He should give silver or a full vessel. The performer of the *Śrāddha* liberates ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin, even from great transgression.
And he who never offers the *śrāddha* to the ancestors is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
Whatever [libation] one offers with water to the ancestors during the *śrāddha*, being composed in mind—
By that alone, one obtains the entire fruit of performing the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
"The fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña)" (15.2).
Thus ends the Mānava-Śrāddhakalpa. Now we shall explain the Vṛddhi-Śrāddhakalpa. 1.
Moreover, when prosperity has arrived, the installation of deities is prescribed;
it is the cause of the increase of people, being handed down through the traditions of their castes, duties, and families.
And in all rites and ceremonies, the Mothers, together with the lords of their hosts, [should be worshipped].

These seven, beginning with Brahmāṇī, as well as Durgā and the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrādhipa), are to be worshipped with effort; when worshipped, they in turn bestow worship. They are traditionally remembered as the seven [Mothers].
At every increase of prosperity, they should always be worshipped first, followed by the Nāndīmukha ancestors.
Three [mothers] are to be honored on the father’s side, and likewise three on the maternal grandfather’s side;
these are declared to be the mothers, with the father’s sister as the eighth.
Having drawn their images upon white idols, or having written them on cloth and the like, [one should worship them].
Or even upon heaps of unhusked rice, one should separately offer various food offerings; moreover,
one should cause a stream of wealth (vasordhārā) made of ghee alone to be poured against the wall,
making it seven or five [streams], neither too low nor too high.
One should, with a concentrated mind, recite there mantras that bestow long life for the sake of peace.
The worship of the Mothers is prescribed with auspicious songs and instrumental music. Those rites which are to be performed repeatedly by ritual practitioners should be performed thus.
In each individual ritual performance, these [deities] do not become mothers, nor does the *śrāddha* rite itself.
When performed in groups, the worship of the Mothers is done once;
the *śrāddha* likewise occurs only once, though the *homamantras* are recited separately for each.
Hereafter, I shall explain the specific detail that occurs here:
having seated the invited Brahmins in the morning, an even number on both sides, one should offer them *kuśa* grass with the hand alone, held straight. 10–11.
Green Darbha grass is for the *yajña*; yellow is for the *pākayajña*;
with their roots intact it is for the ancestors (*pitṛdaivata*); and variegated is for the Viśvedevas.
It is consecrated by the *pitṛtīrtha* at a length of twelve finger-breadths. 12.
One should always serve the ancestors here with devotion, just as one would the gods.

Having seated them upon *kuśa* grass after they have been invited with the words "to the ancestors," one should cause the *arghya* offering to be presented to the ancestors while omitting their lineage names and personal names. (13–14)
In this rite, the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) is not required, nor is the ancestral (pitrya) part of the hand prescribed;
one should perform the filling of the vessels and other such acts using the divine (daiva) part of the hand.
[The Brahmins should sit] with the eldest on the left, in pairs, with the tips of their hands and the tips of their pavitras facing each other.
Having prepared the *arghya*, it should be presented; here, it is not given to each individual separately.
(16) The threefold silent recitation (*japa*) of "madhu, madhu" intended for those wishing to eat, which follows the *gāyatrī* mantra, is here devoid of the *madhumatī* verses. (17)
One should never recite here for the benefit of the ancestors while they are eating;
rather, a different recitation, one that destroys Rākṣasas, should be performed, as in the case of the gods.
"It is prepared" and "Are you satisfied?"—these are prescribed as the questions at the appropriate places.

When it has been said, "It is well-prepared," one should offer the remaining food. (19) One should say, "It is well-prepared," when they are satisfied. [One asks: "Are you satisfied? at the *pārvaṇa* rite.
Likewise, one should scatter the *vikiro* offering and perform the oblation without the *ṛc* verses. (20)
Food should be offered for those gods who do not drink Soma and are excluded from the sacrificial portions; this is the Vaiśvadeva scattered offering (vikira).

(21) In rites of prosperity (vṛddhi), one should feed an even number of guests, no fewer than nine, proceeding in a clockwise direction; they use barley in place of sesame seeds. (22) One should deposit rice-balls mixed with curd, unbroken grains, and jujube fruits. (23) This gratifies the Nāndīmukha ancestors. (24)
One should perform the invocation and other rites, saying, "The ancestors are Nāndīmukhas.
They should say, "May they be pleased," and one should cast down the rice-balls (piṇḍas) with the words, "Svāhā!
Having worshipped the paternal ancestors beginning with the mother, one should likewise worship the maternal ancestors.
Likewise, some should feed the maternal grandmothers and even an even number of Brahmins. At a rite for prosperity (abhyudaya), there are two rice-balls (piṇḍas) for each paternal ancestor;
at a Pārvaṇa rite, there is one rice-ball for each of the three ancestors separately.
Water should be offered to three [ancestors], and the offering of rice balls proceeds for three;
beyond that, it is declared to be the *nāndīmukha* rite, which removes [the need to state] the name and lineage.
In the sacramental rites of a son, the father should offer [the oblation] to his own ancestors.
At marriages and other such occasions, a son should always indeed offer [oblations] to his own ancestors.
One should not commence a Vedic rite without first performing a Śrāddha for the ancestors;
even before that, on the preceding day, one should first [offer to] the Nāndīmukha ancestors.
The wise declare that this applies to the establishment of the sacred fires, to the two oblations, as well as to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice,
the bali-offering, the new-moon sacrifice, the full-moon sacrifice,
and the Āgrayaṇa cooked sacrifice.
There should be only one person representing the *śrāddha* among these, not separate individuals for each.

Then, having sprinkled the ground with water, he should offer it while saying, "May it be well-sprinkled"; he should present the even-numbered guests with water, saying, "May the waters be auspicious"; and he should present flowers, saying, "May there be mental well-being"; and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), saying, "May there be no misfortune.
The offering of the inexhaustible water (*akṣayyodaka*) is prescribed to be performed in the same manner as the offering of the *arghya*.
One should always perform that with the dative case-ending (ṣaṣṭhī), and never with the dative (caturthī).
When all requests have been granted by the best of the twice-born,
one should always pronounce the benediction (*svasti*) while grasping the tips of the [guests'] thumbs in pairs.
Having performed [the rites] for the preeminent Brahmin and having bowed to him, one should then follow after him.

(34) Thus ends the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* in the *Mānava-sūtra*. Now follows the supplement (pariśiṣṭa). The year is Prajāpati. Of that [year], the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), and the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) belong to the gods; midday (*madhyandina*) belongs to human beings; and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) belongs to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Furthermore, it is worshipped in both ways. (1–2)
One should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony day after day with food,
water, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.
[The occasions for *śrāddha* are] the *aṣṭakā*, the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), and the two solstices (*ayanadvaya*).
The excellence of the recipient Brahmin and the times for the Śrāddha ceremony have been proclaimed.
At a wedding, upon the birth of a son, at a sacrifice for the ancestors, at a Soma sacrifice, at a sacred ford,
and when a Brahmin arrives— all these are occasions for one whose father is still living.
A son should perform the Anvaṣṭakya rite upon reaching Gayā,
as well as the Śrāddha for his mother on her anniversary day, even while his father is still living;
and those sixteen days during which the sun is in Virgo.

These [rites] are equal to sacrifices; what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible. From the fifth day onwards of the dark fortnight: one desiring a son should [perform it] on the fifth; one desiring wealth on the sixth; one desiring cattle on the seventh; one desiring health on the eighth; one desiring splendor on the ninth; one desiring food on the tenth; one desiring prosperity on the eleventh; one desiring increase on the twelfth; one desiring fame on the thirteenth; one desiring health for a person killed by a weapon on the fourteenth; and on the new moon day, one desiring all things. One desiring nourishment should perform the *śrāddha* with sesame seeds; one desiring prosperity with cakes; one desiring splendor with ghee, molasses, and sesame seeds.
One who desires well-being, good fortune, or health, or one who desires all things, [should offer] excellent rice, *kṛsara* rice, mung beans, curd, and barley-gruel.
On the day before, the ancestors indeed enter into the Brahmins who have been invited;
therefore, the sacrificer and his attendants should remain that night as celibates.
If one sets out on a journey after having both given and eaten at a *śrāddha*,
his ancestors partake of that [offering] for that entire month.
If, after having both given and eaten at a *śrāddha*, one engages in sexual intercourse...

During that month, his ancestors, subsisting on semen, consume it. A horse becomes the recipient of a *śrāddha* offering, while a crow eats it again. One who performs [forbidden] acts is born as a slave, and one who approaches women [inappropriately] is born as a village pig.
One should feed two at the rite for the gods and three at the rite for the ancestors, or one at each; even if very wealthy, one should not indulge in excessive expansion.
One should attend to the hospitable treatment, the place and time, the materials, and the excellence of the Brahmins.
These five [faults] destroy the merit of a funeral feast; therefore, one should avoid their expansion.

With great effort, one should feed at the *śrāddha* a reciter of the *Bahvṛca* who has mastered the Veda, or an *adhvaryu* who has reached the end of his branch, or a *chandoga* who has completed his study. (15–16)

One who maintains the five fires, one who knows the *trisuparṇa* hymns, one who knows the *triṇāciketa*, one learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born of a lineage where the daughter was given in marriage according to the *brahma* rite, and likewise one who chants the *jyeṣṭhasāman*;
as well as a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a sister’s son, a father-in-law, and a teacher.
One should feed at the Śrāddha the daughter’s son, the master of a Vaiśya household, a kinsman, the officiating priest, and the person for whom one performs sacrifices.
(18) If those Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas do not eat at someone's Śrāddha, that Śrāddha remains unperformed; it does not reach the ancestors. (19)
If Brāhmaṇas who belong to the same Vedic branch do not eat at one's Śrāddha, that Śrāddha becomes Āsura; it does not reach the ancestors.
One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a teacher, and a perpetual celibate student—
Brahmins who have lived a hundred years should be known as purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvana).
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at someone's śrāddha,
the satisfaction of that person's ancestors shall be eternal, extending through seven generations.
"May sesame seeds protect against the Daityas, and may Darbha grass protect against the Rākṣasas;
therefore, they should be given in offerings by one who desires his own prosperity.
Thus ends the Śrāddhapariśiṣṭa.
